Part A. Principles

Part A

The tourniquet

A tourniquet is a controlled crush injury over a controlled ischaemic limb, and both halves of that sentence produce complications. Nerve injury tracks cuff pressure and the pressure gradient at the cuff edge, so the pressure should be set from the measured limb occlusion pressure plus a margin rather than from habit. Tissue injury tracks time, with no proven safe limit and a steep rise in neurological complications beyond two hours. Deflation delivers a bolus of cold, acidotic, potassium-rich, embolus-laden blood to the right heart over about ten minutes, and the frail patient feels it. For knee replacement, the randomised evidence shows a tourniquet saves about four minutes of operating time at the cost of more pain on day one and roughly double the rate of serious adverse events.

What the cuff does to the limb

A pneumatic tourniquet does two separate things, and the complications sort themselves by which one caused them. Under the cuff it compresses tissue: skin, fat, muscle and, most importantly, nerve. Distal to the cuff it stops blood flow: muscle, nerve and endothelium go without oxygen for as long as the surgeon needs, and then get it all back at once. The separation is worth keeping, because pressure drives the first and time drives the second.

Compression injury is a pressure-gradient injury. Nerve fibres under the middle of the cuff are squeezed evenly; fibres at the proximal and distal edges are sheared, because tissue a centimetre away is at a different pressure. The classic histology is displacement of myelin at the nodes of Ranvier under the cuff edge, and the clinical picture is a conduction block that usually recovers over weeks to months. The two levers that shrink the gradient are a lower cuff pressure and a wider cuff, which is the whole argument for setting the pressure from the limb occlusion pressure rather than from a number printed on the machine. The radial nerve is the most vulnerable in the arm, where it lies against the humerus under the cuff; in the leg the sciatic nerve, and particularly its peroneal division, carries the risk. Skin is the second compression casualty: friction blisters from an unpadded cuff and chemical burns from skin preparation that has pooled beneath it and is pressed into the dermis for two hours.

Ischaemia distal to the cuff follows a timetable. Nerve conduction fails first, within about half an hour. Muscle depletes its high-energy phosphate, switches to anaerobic metabolism, acidifies, and leaks potassium and lactate into the trapped venous blood; the limb cools. By two hours there are ultrastructural changes in muscle, and the longer the cuff stays up beyond that, the more of the change is irreversible. Endothelium is the quiet victim: ischaemic endothelium becomes leaky and adhesive, which is the substrate for the reperfusion phase.

Reperfusion is the third injury and the one the patient notices for weeks. Oxygen returning to ischaemic tissue generates free radicals, primed neutrophils adhere to the activated endothelium, capillaries leak, and the limb swells. The result is post-tourniquet syndrome: a swollen, stiff, weak, dysaesthetic limb for days to weeks, worse after longer inflations. The pain mechanism tagged “tourniquet” in the Part B model is partly this reperfusion oedema and partly the cuff-site injury; both scale with time, and the cuff-site component scales with pressure too.

Pressure: limb occlusion pressure and the margin

The pressure that occludes arterial flow in a given limb depends on the patient’s systolic pressure, the circumference of the limb, the width and shape of the cuff, and the thickness of the soft tissue under it. A fixed pressure of 250 mmHg for the thigh and 200 mmHg for the arm, or systolic plus 100 mmHg and systolic plus 50 mmHg, overshoots in most patients and undershoots in a few. The limb occlusion pressure (LOP) is the minimum cuff pressure at which the distal arterial signal disappears, measured with a Doppler or a plethysmographic probe at the time of application; most modern tourniquet systems measure it automatically in under a minute. A safety margin is then added to cover the rise in blood pressure with surgical stimulation and the change in limb position during the case. The tiered margins that have become standard, originally published by AORN, are 40 mmHg for an LOP below 130 mmHg, 60 mmHg for 131-190 mmHg and 80 mmHg above 190 mmHg.

The randomised trials consistently show that the LOP method gives a lower pressure with an equally dry field and, in most of them, less pain. In 164 knee replacements the LOP group ran at a significantly lower pressure with no loss of field quality; pain was not different, but 40 of the 47 wound complications at discharge had occurred with cuff pressures above 225 mmHg, and there were no infections at or below that pressure. In 311 knee replacements the LOP method gave pressures of about 224-240 mmHg against 262-265 mmHg for systolic plus 150, with less thigh pain and better early range of motion. In 60 ACL reconstructions the LOP group ran at a mean of 180 mmHg against 275 mmHg and had less tourniquet-site pain for the first five days and lower opioid use.

Two practical points follow. A wider, contoured cuff placed at the greatest circumference of the limb occludes at a lower pressure, so cuff choice is part of pressure choice. And when the surgeon asks for more pressure because the field is wet, the usual reasons are venous (incomplete exsanguination, a cuff that has slipped, a limb that has been lowered), not arterial; a brief deflation and re-exsanguination is often the better answer. Where the LOP cannot be measured, the old defaults are the fallback: about 200 mmHg for a normotensive arm and 250 mmHg for a normotensive thigh, higher in obesity, and never more than is needed.

Time: the two-hour convention and what sits behind it

There is no proven safe duration. The convention of two hours for a continuous inflation comes from the ischaemic timetable of muscle and nerve and from the complication series, not from a trial. In the Norwegian national survey of 63,484 operations under a tourniquet there were 26 possible tourniquet complications, 1 in 2,442 operations, of which 15 were neurological; two were permanent, which is 1 in 31,742. The lower limb rate was 1 in 3,752 and the upper limb 1 in 6,155, and two of the complications followed inflations of three hours.

Beyond two hours the risk climbs steeply. In 1,166 knee replacements with tourniquet times above 120 min, neurological complications (peroneal, tibial or both) occurred in 7.7% of patients, with an odds ratio of 2.8 for every additional 30 min; younger patients and those with a flexion contracture over 20 degrees were at higher risk, and in the subset with tourniquet times of 180 min or more, a longer deflation interval reduced the risk only modestly. In a register series of 641 knee arthroplasties, tourniquet time over 100 min carried an adjusted odds ratio of 2.4 for complications of any kind.

The rules in practice are a mixture of that evidence and consensus:

  1. Plan the case so that the cuff comes down at or before 120 min. Tell the surgeon the inflation time at 60 and 90 min without being asked.
  2. If the surgeon needs longer, deflate for 10-15 min with the limb level, then re-inflate. The reperfusion interval restores some high-energy phosphate and washes out metabolites, but it is a partial measure; the total time still counts, and a second inflation of 60 min is about the most that is defensible.
  3. Treat three hours of total inflation as a hard ceiling, and expect a post-tourniquet syndrome of weeks after anything near it.
  4. Record inflation and deflation times; the tourniquet clock is one of the few numbers in orthopaedic anaesthesia that will be read in a courtroom.

Inflation and the drugs that are already in the limb

Exsanguination by elevation or by an elastic bandage returns a few hundred millilitres of blood to the circulation, enough to matter in a patient with a poor ventricle, especially for bilateral lower limb cases. Avoid the elastic bandage where it could dislodge something: infection, tumour, a known deep vein thrombosis, a fracture haematoma. Elevation alone exsanguinates adequately for most knee and ankle surgery.

Anything you want in the limb has to be there before the cuff goes up. The antibiotic is the important one: the infusion should be complete, with a few minutes for tissue distribution, before inflation, and for a cefazolin dose given on the way into theatre that usually means waiting rather than inflating. The reverse also applies: drug sequestered in the limb at inflation returns at deflation. In a pilot pharmacokinetic study, plasma sufentanil rose 30-60 min after the cuff came down in most patients, an argument against a large opioid dose in the minutes before inflation and for watching the patient in recovery after a long case.

Tourniquet hypertension is the other inflation phenomenon. Thirty to sixty minutes into an inflation under general anaesthesia the blood pressure and heart rate climb, usually by 20-30% and sometimes much more, and do not respond well to deepening the anaesthetic. It is the autonomic expression of tourniquet pain (see below) and it resolves with deflation. In a randomised trial of knee arthroscopy under general anaesthesia it occurred in 68.8% of patients given saline and 37.5% of those given lidocaine 1.5 mg/kg IV ten minutes before inflation. A working block prevents it, small doses of a short-acting vasodilator or beta blocker contain it, and chasing it with volatile agent produces a hypotensive patient at deflation.

Deflation: what arrives at the right heart

Deflation is the most predictable physiological event in orthopaedic anaesthesia, and the frail patient and the patient with a poor right ventricle get into trouble in a window you can see coming.

 t = 0        cuff down
 0-30 s       embolic shower to the right heart (marrow fat, debris)
              pulmonary artery pressure rises 25-40%
 1 min        end-tidal CO2 peaks (CO2 production up ~80%)
 2-4 min      acidosis worst; lactate and potassium peak;
              cerebral blood flow velocity up ~50%
 0-15 min     MAP and CVP fall as the limb refills
 10 min       end-tidal CO2 back to baseline
 10-30 min    metabolic washout complete; core temperature dips
 to 30 min    transient hypocoagulable state (fibrinolysis)
 30-60 min    sequestered drug returns to plasma

The embolic load is real and visible. In 40 knee replacements monitored with transoesophageal echocardiography, the embolic signal peaked 30 s after release, pulmonary artery pressure rose by 25-40%, the emboli were marrow in origin, and the load was greater in older, heavier patients with fattier marrow. For most patients it passes unnoticed. For the patient with pulmonary hypertension, a dilated right ventricle or a patent foramen ovale, it is the moment of risk, and bilateral simultaneous deflation doubles it.

The metabolic washout follows. Oxygen consumption rises by about 55% and carbon dioxide production by about 80% at 2 min, end-tidal CO2 peaks at 1 min and is back to baseline by about 10 min, potassium rises by a mean of 0.28 mmol/L after an inflation of 60-120 min, lactate peaks about 2 mmol/L above baseline and the acidosis is worst at around 4 min and gone by 30 min. The CO2 raises middle cerebral artery flow velocity by about 50% at 2-4 min, which matters in the patient with a tight intracranial compartment. The numbers scale with the muscle mass that was ischaemic and the time it was ischaemic: a thigh for two hours produces several times the load of a forearm for forty minutes.

The haemodynamic fall is the one you treat. Blood pressure and central venous pressure fall for about 15 min as the limb’s vascular bed, dilated by ischaemic metabolites, refills with a few hundred millilitres of blood. Under a spinal with an already reduced venous capacitance, or in a hypovolaemic patient, the fall can be steep.

The rule set for deflation:

  • Know the time; be at the patient, not at the chart.
  • Have the patient normovolaemic before the cuff comes down, with a vasopressor drawn up and, in the frail or cardiac patient, running.
  • Increase minute ventilation by about half for five minutes around deflation in the ventilated patient, which blunts the CO2 peak and the cerebral hyperaemia; in the spontaneously breathing patient expect a brief rise in respiratory rate.
  • Deflate one limb at a time for bilateral cases, with 10-15 min between them.
  • Treat a potassium problem only in the patient who arrived with one: 0.3 mmol/L on top of 5.5 mmol/L in the renal patient is a different proposition from the same rise in a fit patient.
  • Expect cooling and keep the forced-air warmer on through deflation.
  • Watch the field: the transient hypocoagulable state and the reactive hyperaemia mean the wound bleeds more in the first half hour than it did during the operation. Tranexamic acid given before incision (see blood management) is the counter.

Tourniquet pain under regional anaesthesia and why it happens

Tourniquet pain is a dull, deep, poorly localised ache that starts 30-45 min into an inflation, builds steadily, is relieved only by deflation, and appears in patients whose surgical block is working perfectly. It is the characteristic failure mode of a spinal or an epidural for a long lower limb case, and the mechanism explains both why the block does not cover it and why the usual rescues do not either.

Three things combine. First, the pain is generated under the cuff and in the ischaemic muscle, by compression and by the metabolites of ischaemia, at a dermatomal level (L1-L3 for a thigh cuff, T2 and C5-T1 for an arm cuff) that a block aimed at the operation may only just reach. Second, the fibres that carry it are predominantly unmyelinated C fibres. A-delta conduction under the cuff is stopped by the compression itself at about 30 min, which removes the sharp, localised component and leaves the slow, burning, C-fibre component unopposed; the intrathecal morphine study that showed partial protection against a standardised thigh tourniquet was built on this C-fibre hypothesis. Third, as a spinal or epidural regresses, C-fibre transmission from the cuff site returns before pinprick sensation at the same level has returned, so a block that still tests as adequate can be transmitting tourniquet pain. Under general anaesthesia the same input shows as tourniquet hypertension and tachycardia; central sensitisation through NMDA receptor activation by the ischaemic barrage is the proposed reason it is so hard to suppress once established.

The comparative evidence favours a dense block over a thin one. In 60 patients with lower limb tourniquets of 60 min or more, tourniquet pain was less frequent under spinal than under epidural anaesthesia to the same sensory level, and an alkalinised epidural solution removed the difference, which fits a density explanation. Intrathecal morphine 0.3 mg gave partial prophylaxis at the cost of urinary retention and vomiting.

What to do, in order of usefulness:

  1. Plan the block for the tourniquet, not the incision. For a thigh tourniquet of an hour or more under a spinal, use a full dose of hyperbaric bupivacaine with an intrathecal opioid rather than a low-dose, short-acting technique, and accept the longer recovery.
  2. Add sedation that acts on the central component: small doses of ketamine or an alpha-2 agonist work better than more propofol.
  3. Under general anaesthesia, treat the hypertension as sympathetic output rather than as light anaesthesia.
  4. Ask the surgeon how long the cuff really needs to be up. Deflation is the only complete treatment, and many surgeons will deflate once the bony work is done and close in a bloody field.
  5. In the awake patient with a peripheral block and a thigh tourniquet, the plan was wrong from the start; the block covers the operation and the cuff site is outside it. A forearm or calf tourniquet is tolerated for 20-30 min by most patients; a thigh tourniquet beyond that needs a neuraxial block or a general anaesthetic.

The total knee arthroplasty tourniquet debate

A tourniquet is used in most knee replacements because it gives the surgeon a dry field for the bone cuts and dry cancellous bone for cement interdigitation. The question is whether that convenience costs the patient anything, and the randomised evidence now says it does.

The Cochrane review pooled 41 trials and 2,819 patients. With a tourniquet, serious adverse events (thromboembolism, infection, reoperation and the like) were more frequent: a risk ratio of 1.73 (95% CI 1.10-2.73), from 29 to 59 per 1,000, with moderate certainty. Pain on day one was 1.25 points higher on a 10-point scale (0.32-2.19). Intra-operative blood loss was 147 mL lower but post-operative loss 58 mL higher, and total blood loss and transfusion (RR 1.20, 0.86-1.67) were not different. Surgery was 3.7 min shorter. Hospital stay was 0.34 days longer. Function at 12 months was probably not different. The feasibility trial that followed, randomising 53 patients to an inflated or a non-inflated cuff, saw the same trend to more thigh pain and more adverse events with the inflated cuff and one new ischaemic brain lesion on post-operative MRI.

The honest reading is that the tourniquet’s benefit is to the surgeon’s view and the operating time, that the cement-interdigitation argument has not been shown to translate into implant survival in the trials that exist, and that the costs land on the patient as pain, reperfusion injury to the thigh and a higher complication rate. Surgeons vary: some have abandoned the tourniquet with tranexamic acid doing the work, some inflate only for cementation (which keeps the time under 30 min and most of the benefit), and some use it throughout. The anaesthetic position is to make the no-tourniquet or short-tourniquet knee easy for the surgeon: tranexamic acid before incision, a normotensive but not hypertensive patient, and a working block so that the field is not fogged by a sympathetic surge. The primary TKA and unicompartmental cards carry the per-operation detail.

Contraindications and the patients who need a different plan

There are no absolute contraindications in the sense that a tourniquet can be justified in almost anyone for a short time, but there is a list of patients in whom the default should be no cuff, or a short one, with the surgeon told in advance.

  • Severe peripheral vascular disease, calcified vessels on the radiograph, or absent distal pulses: the cuff can crack plaque and thrombose a vessel, and reperfusion of an already marginal limb is poorly tolerated. Previous vascular surgery or a bypass graft in the limb is a contraindication to a cuff over it.
  • An arteriovenous fistula in the limb.
  • Known deep vein thrombosis in the limb, or a high clinical suspicion of one: exsanguination and inflation can dislodge it.
  • Sickle cell disease: the stagnant, acidotic, hypoxic limb is a sickling chamber. If a tourniquet is unavoidable, exsanguinate completely, keep the inflation short, keep the patient warm, oxygenated and hydrated, and expect to treat a crisis.
  • Severe crush injury, heavily contaminated open fracture, local infection or tumour: a cuff can be used, but exsanguinate by elevation rather than by bandage.
  • Fragile skin (long-term steroids, rheumatoid disease, the very elderly) and the paediatric limb: skin and compression injury risk is higher, and padding and pressure matter more.
  • Poor cardiac reserve for bilateral cases: the exsanguination volume at inflation and the embolic and metabolic load at deflation are both doubled; stage the deflations and consider whether the second side should be done at all.
  • Raised intracranial pressure: the CO2 and cerebral hyperaemia at deflation are an avoidable insult.
  • Severe uncontrolled hypertension: the LOP will be high and the margin pushes the set pressure into the range where wound and nerve complications rise.

The rule set

  1. Decide before the case whether a tourniquet is needed at all, and for how long; the knee replacement evidence is against routine use.
  2. Widest contoured cuff, smooth padding beyond both edges, sealed distal edge, placed at the greatest circumference.
  3. Antibiotic complete before inflation.
  4. Measure the LOP after positioning and set the pressure to LOP plus the tiered margin (40, 60 or 80 mmHg); record both.
  5. Exsanguinate by elevation where there is any question of clot, infection or tumour.
  6. Call the time at 60 and 90 min; plan for deflation at 120 min; a reperfusion interval of 10-15 min buys a limited second inflation; three hours is the ceiling.
  7. Under neuraxial anaesthesia, plan the density and duration of the block for the cuff, not the incision, and add an intrathecal opioid for a long thigh tourniquet.
  8. Before deflation: normovolaemia, vasopressor ready, warming on, ventilation up, one limb at a time.
  9. After deflation: expect 15 min of hypotension, a CO2 and potassium peak, a cold patient and a wet wound; stay at the bedside.
  10. Document inflation and deflation times, pressure, LOP, cuff site and padding, and any pre-existing neurological deficit in the limb before the cuff went on.

The cards that carry a tourniquet tag follow these rules without repeating them; where the operation changes the rule (a bilateral knee, a calf tourniquet for foot surgery, a forearm cuff for hand surgery) the card says so.

Part A

Bone cement and bone cement implantation syndrome

Bone cement implantation syndrome is an embolic event with a mediator tail: pressurising cement into a long bone forces marrow fat, air and debris into the femoral veins, the right heart receives it over a minute or two, and the pulmonary circulation answers with vasoconstriction, right ventricular dilatation and a fall in left-sided filling. Hypoxia, hypotension and loss of consciousness around cementation define it, and the Donaldson grading (1: SpO2 below 94% or systolic fall of 20-40%; 2: SpO2 below 88% or systolic fall over 40% or unexpected loss of consciousness; 3: collapse needing CPR) is what the cohorts are built on. Something scoreable happens in about a quarter of cemented arthroplasties and in a third of cemented hemiarthroplasties for hip fracture, severe grades carry a three- to sixteen-fold rise in early death, and the patients at risk are the old, the ASA III-IV, the renal and the pulmonary hypertensive, having a cemented stem for a fracture. The defence is a bundle, not a drug: canal lavage, a dry vented canal, a cement gun with vacuum-mixed cement and restrained pressurisation on the surgical side; a named moment, a normovolaemic patient, a vasopressor already running, oxygen up and the ventilator watched on the anaesthetic side. Cement still wins for hip fracture: the randomised and registry evidence shows a day-one mortality excess that is repaid within a week by fewer periprosthetic fractures and better function.

What the cement is and what it does to the canal

Polymethylmethacrylate bone cement is two parts mixed in theatre: a powder of pre-polymerised PMMA beads with a radio-opacifier (barium sulphate or zirconium dioxide), an initiator and often an antibiotic, and a liquid of methylmethacrylate monomer with an accelerator and a stabiliser. Mixing starts an exothermic free-radical polymerisation: a working phase of a few minutes in which the dough can be injected and pressurised, then setting over 8-15 min with a peak interface temperature that can exceed 70 degrees in a thick mantle. It is a grout, not a glue: it holds the implant by interdigitating with cancellous bone, which is why the surgeon wants a clean, dry, open trabecular bed and why pressure is applied to drive the dough into it.

That pressure is the problem. The femoral canal is a closed tube once the cement restrictor is in. Injecting cement retrograde, pressurising it with a seal over the calcar and then driving a stem into the column of dough raises intramedullary pressure to several hundred millimetres of mercury. Marrow fat, air, bone debris, cement particles and whatever lies in the canal are forced into the metaphyseal and diaphyseal venous sinusoids and from there into the femoral vein. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows the result in real time: in 20 hip fracture patients randomised to cemented or uncemented hemiarthroplasty, cemented stems produced greater and more prolonged cascades of echogenic material crossing the right atrium, some emboli over 3 cm long, with pulmonary hypertension, desaturation, and fat and marrow in blood aspirated from the right atrium. In 60 elective hip replacements randomised three ways, a severe embolic cascade was seen in 85% of conventionally cemented stems, in none of the uncemented stems and in 5% of stems cemented with suction applied to the canal; arterial saturation fell from 99.5% to 92.9% and the calculated shunt rose by about a quarter in the conventionally cemented group only. The emboli begin as the cement is injected and continue through stem insertion, with a second shower when the hip is reduced and the femoral vein, kinked during the exposure, straightens and empties.

The syndrome: embolic load, mediator release, right heart failure

Bone cement implantation syndrome is the clinical name for what the right heart and the lungs do with that load. The monomer was blamed for decades, and it does dilate vessels in vitro, but the plasma concentrations measured in patients are well below those that produce haemodynamic change, and the uncemented stem that embolises little produces little syndrome. The embolic theory fits the timing, the echocardiography and the dose-response with pressurisation.

 cement pressurised / stem driven in
            |
   intramedullary pressure rises
            |
   fat, marrow, air, debris into femoral veins
            |
   right atrium (seen on TOE within 30-60 s)
            |
   pulmonary vascular bed: mechanical obstruction
          + mediator release (thromboxane, complement,
            histamine, endothelin) + marrow thromboplastin
            |
   pulmonary vasoconstriction, PVR and PAP rise
            |
   RV dilates, septum shifts, LV filling falls
            |
   hypotension, V/Q mismatch and shunt (hypoxia),
   fall in end-tidal CO2, arrhythmia, loss of consciousness,
   PEA arrest in the extreme case

Two things turn an embolic shower into a syndrome. The first is quantity, set by the surgical technique and the canal: a fracture canal with its haematoma and loose marrow, a long stem, a wide pressurised mantle and a dry unvented column all raise the dose. The second is the pulmonary circulation’s response, which is both mechanical and chemical. Fat and marrow do not simply plug vessels; they activate complement, platelets and the clotting cascade and release vasoconstrictors, so the rise in pulmonary vascular resistance is out of proportion to the obstructed cross-section. Marrow thromboplastin also starts clot: in 130 cemented hip replacements, canal suction during cementing cut the embolic cascade from 91% to 15% of cases and day-4 deep vein thrombosis from 18% to 3%, which places part of the thrombotic burden of arthroplasty at the moment of cementation.

The right ventricle is the organ that fails. A thin-walled chamber used to an afterload of 20 mmHg is asked to push against double or treble that within a minute; it dilates, its wall tension rises, its coronary perfusion (which depends on the systemic pressure it is now helping to lower) falls, and the shifted septum takes the left ventricle’s filling with it. The patient who dies of BCIS dies of acute right heart failure with an empty left heart. That is the physiological logic behind every rule in this chapter: minimise the load, keep the right heart full and the systemic pressure up, and avoid the two things (hypovolaemia and a sympathectomy from an unsupported spinal) that leave it unable to cope.

The grading below counts the intraoperative event; a persistent oxygen requirement and confusion on the ward after a cemented hemiarthroplasty belong to the same process in milder form.

The severity grading and what the cohorts show

The published grading, proposed in the 2009 review and used by every cohort since, is:

  • Grade 1: moderate hypoxia (SpO2 below 94%) or hypotension (fall in systolic pressure of 20-40%).
  • Grade 2: severe hypoxia (SpO2 below 88%) or hypotension (fall in systolic pressure over 40%) or unexpected loss of consciousness.
  • Grade 3: cardiovascular collapse requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

Two cohorts give the numbers. In 1,016 cemented hemiarthroplasties for femoral neck fracture, grade 1 occurred in 21%, grade 2 in 5.1% and grade 3 in 1.7%; early mortality was 5.2% with no BCIS, 9.3% with grade 1, 35% with grade 2 and 88% with grade 3, and severe BCIS carried a 16-fold rise in mortality. Independent predictors of a severe event were ASA III-IV, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and treatment with diuretics or warfarin: a frail cardiopulmonary patient, possibly dry, possibly bleeding. In 3,294 cemented arthroplasties of every kind, something scoreable happened in 26%: 31% of hip hemiarthroplasties, 28% of knee replacements, 24% of hip replacements, 23% of revisions, 20% of unicompartmental knees and 16% of shoulder arthroplasties. Severe BCIS carried a hazard ratio of 3.46 for death within 30 days, and the independent risk factors were age over 75 (odds ratio 1.57), ASA III or IV (1.58) and renal impairment (3.32).

The fracture population is where it kills. The English and Welsh incident reporting system recorded 62 deaths or severe harms from cement in hemiarthroplasty between 2005 and 2012, one for every 2,900 hemiarthroplasties: 41 deaths, 14 cardiac arrests and seven peri-arrests, 89% of them during or within minutes of cement insertion, and 80% of the deaths on the table. Three quarters of the deaths came after a 2009 national alert, which is what produced the 2015 joint guideline. A reporting-system denominator undercounts, so the true rate of catastrophe is higher than one in 2,900, and the registry day-one mortality data below say the same.

Knee replacement sits in the same cohort at 28%. The cuts open cancellous bone on both sides of the joint, cement is pressurised into both, and in a tourniquet knee the load is held in the limb and delivered at deflation on top of the metabolic washout in the tourniquet chapter. It is usually mild and usually mistaken for deflation hypotension; in the patient with pulmonary hypertension it is neither.

Risk factors, in order of weight

The risk factors sort into those that increase the embolic dose and those that reduce the patient’s ability to absorb it.

Dose:

  • A fracture, because the canal contains haematoma and disrupted marrow and the surgery is urgent and often done by a less experienced team at an inconvenient hour.
  • A cemented hemiarthroplasty rather than a total hip, partly because of the patient it is done in and partly because hemiarthroplasty stems were historically long, monoblock and pressurised into an unprepared canal.
  • A long stem, a wide canal, osteoporotic bone with open trabeculae, a pathological fracture or a canal full of tumour.
  • Heavy pressurisation, no venting, no lavage, cement injected into a wet bloody canal.
  • A previously uninstrumented canal; a revision canal that has already been reamed and lined by cement embolises less.

Reserve:

  • Pulmonary hypertension of any cause, a dilated or impaired right ventricle, severe tricuspid regurgitation.
  • Severe aortic stenosis and any fixed-output state: the fall in left-sided filling cannot be met by a rise in stroke volume.
  • Age over 75, ASA III-IV, renal impairment, COPD, diuretic therapy, anticoagulation, and the hypovolaemia that a fracture patient brings to theatre after a day on a trolley with a litre of blood in the thigh.
  • A patent foramen ovale, which turns a pulmonary load into a paradoxical cerebral or coronary one. In the elderly it is present in about a quarter and almost never known about.
  • A spinal anaesthetic with an unopposed sympathectomy at the moment of cementation: not a contraindication, but a reason to have the pressure supported before the cement goes in rather than after.

The patient at the top of this list, an 85-year-old ASA IV with COPD, pulmonary hypertension, chronic kidney disease and a displaced intracapsular fracture, is the patient the guideline was written for.

The prevention bundle

The UK joint guideline sets out a bundle rather than a single measure, and the logic is to cut the dose with surgical technique and to prepare the patient and the team for the dose that remains. The components are:

Before the case:

  1. Identify the at-risk patient (the list above) and say so at the team brief. The surgeon decides on cemented or uncemented fixation with that information; in the extreme-risk patient the discussion is whether an uncemented stem or a different operation is safer, with the periprosthetic fracture cost in mind.
  2. Resuscitate: fracture patients arrive hypovolaemic and often with a haemoglobin that has not yet fallen to reflect the blood in the thigh. Fluid before the spinal, not after the cement.
  3. Decide on monitoring. An arterial line for the ASA III-IV patient, placed before induction, costs ten minutes and shows the fall in pressure at the moment it happens rather than when the cuff next cycles. A central line is rarely needed; a vasopressor infusion can run through a good peripheral cannula for the duration of the event.

Surgical technique, which is where most of the dose reduction lives:

  1. Thorough pulsed lavage of the canal and suction until it is dry, which removes the marrow and fat that would otherwise be injected into the veins.
  2. A distal cement restrictor and a vent or suction catheter in the canal during cement insertion, so that the pressure has somewhere to go other than the venous sinusoids. The bone-vacuum technique that abolished the embolic cascade in the randomised series used suction at -800 mbar through cannulae placed along the linea aspera.
  3. Vacuum-mixed cement delivered retrograde with a cement gun, which gives a uniform mantle with fewer voids at lower pressure than finger-packing.
  4. Restrained pressurisation and a steady, not forceful, stem insertion. The Dutch cohort’s authors ask for avoidance of excessive pressurisation in the high-risk patient; the surgeon can trade a few per cent of interdigitation for a smaller embolic load and will do so if asked.
  5. A spoken warning before the cement goes in. The guideline formalises what good teams do anyway: the surgeon says “cementing now”, the anaesthetist acknowledges it, and the next five minutes belong to the patient.

Anaesthetic readiness at the moment of cementation:

  1. The patient normovolaemic, with the systolic pressure at or near baseline, not drifting down under a spinal. If the pressure is already 20% below baseline when the cement goes in, the first grade of BCIS has been reached before the embolus arrives.
  2. A vasopressor drawn up and, in the at-risk patient, already running: metaraminol or noradrenaline for the sympathectomised spinal, with adrenaline drawn up for the right ventricle that fails.
  3. Inspired oxygen increased before the cement goes in and the pulse oximeter watched; under general anaesthesia, the capnograph is the earliest monitor, because a fall in end-tidal CO2 with unchanged ventilation means the pulmonary blood flow has fallen before the pressure does.
  4. The anaesthetist at the head of the patient, not writing the chart.

The guideline’s authors are explicit that the bundle rests on previously published advice and observational data rather than on a trial of the bundle itself. The surgical measures have randomised echocardiographic evidence behind them, the anaesthetic measures are physiology, and the whole package is cheap.

Cemented versus uncemented for hip fracture

The temptation after reading the cohorts is to abandon cement in the frail patient. The evidence does not support that as a general policy, and the reason is that the harm from cement is concentrated into the first day and the benefit is spread over the following year.

The Australian registry analysed about 25,000 hemiarthroplasties: cemented monoblock stems carried 1.7 times the day-one mortality of uncemented monoblock stems, and the relationship had reversed by one week and stayed reversed at one month and one year. The Norwegian register, 11,210 fractures, found a first-day relative risk of 2.9 with cement, a number needed to harm of 116 overall and 33 in patients worse than ASA 3, with the excess tracking comorbidity exactly as the BCIS cohorts predict. Then the WHiTE 5 trial randomised 1,225 patients aged 60 and over to cemented or modern uncemented hemiarthroplasty. Quality of life at four months was better with cement (EQ-5D 0.371 against 0.315, an adjusted difference of 0.055, at the lower edge of what patients notice), mortality at 12 months was 23.9% with cement and 27.8% without (odds ratio 0.80, confidence interval crossing one), and periprosthetic fracture occurred in 0.5% of cemented and 2.1% of uncemented hips (odds ratio 4.37). The uncemented stem in osteoporotic bone splits the femur, loosens and subsides, and the reoperation for a periprosthetic fracture in an 85-year-old is a bigger insult than the cement was.

The honest synthesis is this. Cement kills a small number of the frailest patients on the table, on day one, by the mechanism in this chapter. Uncemented fixation in the same population trades that for more fractures, worse function and no survival advantage by a week. The system-level answer is cement for hemiarthroplasty, with the bundle applied to every case and hardest to the patient at the top of the risk list. The individual-level answer, for the patient with severe pulmonary hypertension, a failing right ventricle or critical aortic stenosis, is a conversation between surgeon and anaesthetist before the list, in which an uncemented stem, a shorter stem, or in the moribund patient no operation, are all on the table. The neck of femur card carries the operation-level detail and the orthopaedic patient chapter the frailty context.

When it happens

The event declares itself within a minute or two of cement insertion or stem impaction, and under general anaesthesia the sequence is usually a fall in end-tidal CO2, then a fall in saturation, then a fall in blood pressure, then an arrhythmia. Under a spinal the patient becomes restless, dyspnoeic, confused or unconscious, and the pressure falls. The differential at that moment is short: BCIS, pulmonary thromboembolism from the fracture, anaphylaxis to the antibiotic or the cement, myocardial infarction, and a spinal that has climbed or a patient who was already empty. Timing to the cement, the absence of bronchospasm and rash, and a surgeon who has just pressurised a canal settle it.

The management is the treatment of acute right heart failure with a self-limiting cause:

  1. Say it out loud. The surgeon stops pressurising, does not reduce the hip until told, and holds the stem where it is if it is half in.
  2. 100% oxygen. Under general anaesthesia, confirm the airway and ventilation and read the capnograph as a cardiac output monitor. Under a spinal, oxygen by mask and prepare to intubate if consciousness is lost or saturation does not recover.
  3. Fluid: a 250-500 mL bolus to fill the right ventricle, then reassess rather than flood it; an over-distended right ventricle shifts the septum further and makes things worse.
  4. Vasopressor to restore systemic pressure, which is the right ventricle’s coronary perfusion pressure: metaraminol or noradrenaline first, adrenaline in 10-50 mcg increments if the pressure does not respond or the heart rate falls, and an adrenaline infusion if it is needed twice. Adrenaline is the right drug for the failing right ventricle because it adds contractility to the vasoconstriction; a pure alpha agonist supports the pressure but not the pump.
  5. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation at once if the pulse is lost. The rhythm is usually pulseless electrical activity; chest compressions move blood through a transiently obstructed pulmonary bed, and the cohort survivors of grade 3 events are those resuscitated immediately.
  6. Echocardiography if it is in the room: a dilated, poorly contracting right ventricle with a small left ventricle confirms the diagnosis, and a transoesophageal probe shows the embolic material itself.
  7. Do not reach for a pulmonary vasodilator in theatre. Inhaled nitric oxide or milrinone belongs in intensive care for the patient whose pulmonary pressure stays up; in the first ten minutes the problem is systemic pressure and right ventricular perfusion.
  8. Once stable, finish the operation with the least additional insult: the surgeon reduces the hip slowly, closes, and the patient goes to a high-dependency bed with oxygen, an arterial line and a low threshold for troponin, echocardiography and a CT pulmonary angiogram if the hypoxia persists past the first hour.

The event is usually over in 20-30 min as the pulmonary bed clears and the mediators are metabolised. Grade 1 needs nothing beyond the vasopressor already running; grade 2 needs the full sequence; grade 3 needs everything and a frank conversation with the family afterwards, because the mortality is high however well it is managed.

Edge cases and variants

  • Bilateral or two-stem cases: a revision with a long cemented stem, a periprosthetic fracture with a cemented revision stem, or a tumour prosthesis. The dose is larger, the canal is often open to the diaphyseal venous plexus, and the measures above apply with an arterial line as routine. Stage the two sides of a bilateral case if the first side produced an event.
  • The cemented revision knee and the cemented tumour endoprosthesis: a long intramedullary stem cemented into a reamed canal behaves like a hip stem, and in the knee the tourniquet holds the load until deflation.
  • Vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty: cement injected under pressure into a vertebral body escapes into the paravertebral and epidural veins and reaches the lungs; small cement emboli are common on CT and usually silent, but a large injection at several levels in a patient with a bad right ventricle is the same syndrome. The vertebroplasty card covers it.
  • Antibiotic-loaded cement is not the cause of BCIS, but anaphylaxis to an antibiotic given at induction can present in the same minutes; bronchospasm, flushing or rash separate the two.
  • Nitrous oxide expands the gas component of the embolus; avoid it during cementation in the at-risk patient.
  • The shoulder: cemented humeral stems embolise too (16% in the Dutch cohort), in the beach chair position where cerebral perfusion is already marginal (positioning chapter); an event here is usually mild, but a fall in pressure in a sitting patient needs treating at once.
  • Known patent foramen ovale: a cerebral embolus is the risk; the case for an uncemented stem and for avoiding the Valsalva-like rise in right atrial pressure at impaction is stronger than usual.

The rule set

  1. Name the at-risk patient at the brief: fracture, cemented stem, age over 75, ASA III-IV, renal impairment, COPD, pulmonary hypertension, a bad right ventricle, aortic stenosis, diuretics, anticoagulation.
  2. Fill the patient before the spinal; do not let the pressure drift down before the cement.
  3. Arterial line for the ASA III-IV patient; vasopressor running, adrenaline drawn up, oxygen up, capnograph watched.
  4. Ask for the surgical bundle: lavage to a dry canal, restrictor and vent, vacuum-mixed cement by gun, restrained pressurisation, a spoken “cementing now”.
  5. Stand at the head for the five minutes after the warning; grade what happens and write it down.
  6. Treat an event as acute right heart failure: oxygen, measured fluid, vasopressor then adrenaline, early CPR, surgeon paused.
  7. Keep cement for hip fracture as the default; reserve the uncemented discussion for the patient with severe pulmonary hypertension or right ventricular failure, and have it before the list, not in the canal.

Part A

Fat embolism

Fat embolism is marrow fat in the venous blood and it happens in almost every long bone fracture and in almost every reamed nail; fat embolism syndrome is the small fraction of patients in whom that fat produces lung injury, brain injury and a petechial rash 12-72 h later. Two mechanisms run in series: a mechanical obstruction of the pulmonary bed by fat and marrow at the moment of fracture or reaming, then a chemical injury as lipase turns the trapped neutral fat into free fatty acids that strip the capillary endothelium. The diagnosis is clinical, the Gurd, Schonfeld and Lindeque criteria are three unvalidated ways of saying so, and the treatment is supportive. The one intervention with consistent evidence is early fixation of the femur, within 24 h where the patient's physiology allows it, with external fixation as the damage-control alternative when it does not. The collapse during nailing is a different animal from the syndrome on the ward: it is acute right heart failure from an embolic shower, and the differential at that moment is blood loss, tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis and a paradoxical embolus through a foramen ovale.

Fat embolism and fat embolism syndrome are two different things

Fat embolism is a laboratory and echocardiographic fact: marrow fat in the venous blood, in the right heart and in the pulmonary vascular bed. It happens in almost every long bone fracture and in almost every operation that instruments a medullary canal. Transoesophageal echocardiography during 111 intramedullary procedures showed embolic material crossing the right heart in 97 of them; right atrial blood sampled during knee replacement contained fat in 46% of unilateral and 65% of bilateral cases; and post-mortem lung sections from trauma patients show fat in the pulmonary capillaries far more often than anyone was diagnosed with anything. Most of it is clinically silent.

Fat embolism syndrome is what happens when that fat injures the lung, the brain and the skin. It is a clinical diagnosis, usually declared 12-72 h after the fracture or the operation, in a patient who was fine when they left recovery. The incidence depends entirely on how hard you look and what you call it: 1-10% of long bone fractures in the older literature, under 1% in retrospective series, 0.03% in a coded trauma registry of 1.25 million isolated femoral and tibial fractures (which measures coding rather than disease), and 4.3% in a recent prospective single-centre series of 3,475 diaphyseal fractures that looked for it. The systematic review of femoral fractures shows the incidence falling across the decades, from 7.9% before 1980 to 4.8% in the next twenty years and 1.7% since 2000, which tracks the move from traction and delayed surgery to early nailing more closely than it tracks any drug.

Keeping the two apart matters in both directions. The fat embolism you see on the monitor during reaming is not the syndrome and does not predict it reliably; the syndrome you are asked about on the ward two days later is not an acute embolic event and will not respond to being treated as one.

Mechanism: an embolus, then a chemical burn

Two theories were argued over for fifty years and the honest reading is that they describe two phases of the same process.

The mechanical phase is quick. A fracture, or a reamer, breaches the venous sinusoids of the marrow while the intramedullary pressure is raised by haematoma, by the fracture ends being moved, by a reamer head advancing down a closed tube or by a nail being driven into one. Marrow fat, marrow cells and bone debris are forced into the metaphyseal veins, travel to the right heart and lodge in the pulmonary arterioles and capillaries. The load is proportional to the pressure and the volume of marrow disturbed: a femur produces more than a tibia, a pathological femur full of tumour more than either, and bilateral femoral fractures more than one. The immediate consequence is the same right-heart physiology described for cement in the cement chapter: a rise in pulmonary vascular resistance, a fall in end-tidal CO2 and in saturation, and in a large shower a dilated right ventricle and a falling systemic pressure. In the echocardiographic series the pulmonary response was proportional to the embolic load, and 24 of the 25 severe responses occurred during reaming of pathological lesions or cemented hemiarthroplasty, which is where the marrow is loosest and the pressure highest. Marrow is also thrombogenic: right atrial blood sampled during reaming showed activation of the clotting cascade, and in 12 of the 111 patients large coagulative masses were seen trapped in the heart.

Fat that reaches the pulmonary capillaries does not all stay there. Droplets small enough pass through the pulmonary bed, and a patent foramen ovale, present in about a quarter of adults and almost never known about, lets the larger ones cross directly. In the Edinburgh series paradoxical embolisation was seen in four patients, all with pathological femoral lesions, and two died; a separate case report with echocardiography documented a fulminant fatal syndrome from paradoxical embolism through a foramen ovale during nailing. Systemic fat was found at post-mortem in one patient without a foraminal defect, so transpulmonary passage is real as well. This is the route to the brain, the kidney, the retina and the skin.

The biochemical phase is slow, and it explains the latency. Neutral marrow fat is relatively inert. Over the following 24-72 h, tissue and plasma lipase hydrolyse it to free fatty acids, which are directly toxic to pneumocytes and capillary endothelium; the capillaries leak, the alveoli fill with protein-rich fluid and haemorrhage, platelets and fibrin deposit around the droplets, and the picture is one of acute lung injury rather than obstruction. Complement activation was found in every patient with the syndrome in the Schonfeld trial, but also in many without it, which is the usual finding for an inflammatory marker in trauma; the steroid trials that showed an effect were built on this phase, and the one that measured free fatty acids found that methylprednisolone stabilised them. The two phases together give the shape of the illness: a mechanical shower that is usually silent, then a chemical injury that declares itself a day or two later in the organs the fat reached.

 fracture / reamer / nail / broach / alignment rod
          |
   intramedullary pressure up, sinusoids open
          |
   fat + marrow + debris -> femoral veins -> right heart
          |                              \
   pulmonary capillaries                  PFO or transpulmonary
   (mechanical: PVR up, V/Q               passage -> brain, skin,
    mismatch, RV strain, minutes)         retina, kidney
          |
   lipase: triglyceride -> free fatty acids (hours to days)
          |
   endothelial injury, capillary leak, platelet and fibrin
   deposition: ARDS-like lung, encephalopathy, petechiae,
   thrombocytopenia, anaemia, fever   (12-72 h)

Who gets it

The risk factors sort into the dose of marrow released and the time it is left to be released.

  • A femoral fracture, which carried an adjusted odds ratio of 4.63 in the Bogota series; tibial and humeral fractures carry a smaller risk, pelvic fractures some, and closed fractures more than open ones in some series because the haematoma stays under pressure.
  • Multiple fractures and bilateral femoral fractures: 4.6% against 2.9% for a unilateral high-energy fracture in the systematic review, and in the German trauma registry bilateral femoral shaft fractures were an independent risk factor for pulmonary failure (34.7% against 20.6%).
  • Pathological fractures and tumour-filled canals, which produced the most severe embolic responses on echocardiography.
  • Young age. The syndrome is a disease of the young adult with a high-energy fracture: in 274 isolated femoral fractures there were no cases over the age of 35, and younger age was an independent predictor in the national registry. The usual explanation is that young marrow is more cellular and more fatty-fluid, and young patients sustain the high-energy injuries.
  • Obesity (adjusted odds ratio 2.63 in one series, independent in the registry) and diabetes.
  • Delay to fixation, which has its own section below.
  • Elective surgery that instruments the canal: cemented long-stem arthroplasty, long-stem revision stems, intramedullary alignment rods and bilateral knee replacement (marrow cells in right atrial blood in 12% of bilateral and 4% of unilateral cases, with neurological signs in six of the sixteen positive patients) all produce it in smaller amounts than a reamed fracture nail.

The clinical picture and the three sets of criteria

The classic triad is respiratory, neurological and cutaneous, in that order of frequency, appearing 12-72 h after the insult. Respiratory signs are near universal: tachypnoea, hypoxaemia, then bilateral infiltrates on the chest radiograph, from mild desaturation on the ward to full acute respiratory distress syndrome needing ventilation; in the Bogota series 94% of patients needed advanced ventilatory support. Neurological signs follow in most: restlessness, confusion and drowsiness that are easily mistaken for opioids, then focal deficits, seizures or coma; the MRI shows scattered diffusion-restricting lesions in the white matter, the so-called starfield pattern. The petechial rash is the least common and the most specific: a crop of petechiae on the conjunctivae, the oral mucosa, the neck, the axillae and the upper anterior chest, often lasting only a day or two, and in the Schonfeld trial the only finding that reliably predicted the syndrome. Fever, tachycardia, a falling haemoglobin and platelet count out of proportion to the bleeding, retinal exudates and fat in the urine round out the picture.

Three sets of criteria exist and none has been validated, because there is no gold standard to validate them against. Gurd’s criteria, from 1970 and revised with Wilson in 1974, are the most quoted:

  • Major: petechial rash; respiratory symptoms with bilateral radiographic changes; cerebral signs unrelated to head injury or other cause.
  • Minor: tachycardia above 110 per minute; fever above 38.5 degrees; retinal changes (fat or petechiae); jaundice; renal signs (anuria or oliguria); a sudden fall in haemoglobin or platelet count; a raised ESR; fat macroglobulinaemia.
  • Diagnosis: at least one major and four minor features.

Schonfeld’s score, written for a steroid trial, weights the findings: petechiae 5 points; diffuse alveolar infiltrates on the chest radiograph 4; hypoxaemia (PaO2 below 70 mmHg on room air) 3; and one point each for confusion, fever above 38 degrees, heart rate above 120 and respiratory rate above 30, with a score of 5 or more making the diagnosis. Lindeque’s criteria, from a femoral and tibial fracture trial whose authors judged Gurd’s criteria inadequate for early diagnosis, are respiratory only: a sustained PaO2 below 60 mmHg (8 kPa); a PaCO2 above 55 mmHg (7.3 kPa) or a pH below 7.3; a sustained respiratory rate above 35 despite sedation; or increased work of breathing shown by dyspnoea, accessory muscle use, tachycardia and anxiety. Any one of these in a patient with a long bone fracture satisfies the Lindeque definition.

The practical use of the three is as a checklist, not a test. Gurd’s list reminds you to look at the conjunctivae and the axillae, to send a platelet count and to think about the brain; Lindeque’s list reminds you that hypoxaemia on day two in a young man with a femoral fracture is the syndrome until proved otherwise. Investigations exclude the alternatives rather than confirm the diagnosis: a chest radiograph or CT, a CT pulmonary angiogram when thromboembolism is plausible, an MRI brain for the confused patient (CT is usually normal), bloods for the cytopenias, and an echocardiogram if the right heart is in question. Fat in the urine, sputum or lavage fluid is neither sensitive nor specific.

Reaming and nailing as the trigger

Reamed intramedullary nailing is the operation that produces the largest embolic load, and the anaesthetist’s interest is in three questions: whether reaming makes the lung injury worse, whether the timing matters, and what to do when a patient collapses on the table.

The echocardiographic evidence is clear that reaming embolises. In 24 reamed nailings of tibial and femoral fractures, 14 patients showed minimal emboli, six showed copious showers of small emboli, and four showed multiple emboli over 10 mm long; three of those four developed the syndrome and one died, and earlier nailing was associated with a smaller load. The showers come with each pass of the reamer and with nail insertion, and they are larger in a fresh fracture with a haematoma under pressure, in a pathological bone, and when the reamer is driven fast down a tight canal. The surgeon has levers: sharp reamers with deep flutes, advancing slowly, venting the canal, and the reaming systems with irrigation and suction that remove marrow as they cut and are designed to keep the intramedullary pressure down; the surgeon who is told the patient has a bad chest or a known shunt will usually use them.

Whether reaming makes the clinical outcome worse is a different question, and the answer from the randomised trials is that it does not. The meta-analyses of reamed against unreamed femoral nailing (eight trials, about 1,100 patients) show no difference in ARDS or mortality, with reaming producing faster union and fewer secondary operations; the sheep work that measured intramedullary pressure found it higher with an unreamed nail driven into an unprepared canal than with reaming, because an unreamed nail is a tight piston. Unreamed nailing to protect the lung is not supported, and the surgeon’s choice of a reamed nail should stand.

Early fixation: the one intervention that works

The femoral fracture left in traction keeps releasing marrow with every movement, and the intramedullary pressure stays raised by the haematoma. Fixation stops both. The randomised trial of 178 adults with femoral fractures, stabilised within 24 h or after 48 h, found that in the multiply injured, delay produced more pulmonary complications (adult respiratory distress syndrome, fat embolism and pneumonia), longer intensive care and hospital stays, and higher cost. The observational data point the same way with larger numbers: in 274 isolated femoral shaft fractures there were no cases of the syndrome among the 60 nailed within 10 h and 11 among the 109 nailed later; in the Japanese trauma registry, fixation itself was not an independent risk factor but delay to operation was (odds ratio 2.21); in the American registry fixation within 48 h was protective; and in the Bogota series fixation within 24 h carried an adjusted odds ratio of 0.42. Early fixation also produces the only reliable fall in incidence in the systematic review across sixty years.

The limit on early fixation is the second hit. In the severely injured patient, a reamed femoral nail at hour six is a second major insult laid on top of the first: the EPOFF randomised study measured a perioperative rise in interleukin-6 after primary nailing that did not occur after external fixation, and the larger observational series found a smaller and shorter systemic inflammatory response after damage-control external fixation despite worse injuries in that group. This is the basis of damage control orthopaedics: early stabilisation of the femur within 24 h in every patient, by definitive nail in the physiologically stable patient and by external fixation in the patient who is under-resuscitated, coagulopathic, hypothermic, acidotic, or has a severe chest or head injury, with conversion to a nail once the physiology has recovered, usually between day 3 and day 10. The decision is made with the trauma surgeon and the intensivist on the physiology in front of you, not on the fracture; the polytrauma card sets out the markers and the sequence, and the open fracture and damage control card the external fixation itself.

Bilateral femoral fractures are the case that most often forces the question. The embolic load is doubled and the pulmonary failure rate is higher, but leaving both femurs in traction is worse. The defensible default is to fix both early, the second only after the physiology has been reassessed following the first, and with external fixation of one or both if the patient is marginal.

Management of the syndrome

There is no specific treatment. The syndrome is self-limiting over three to seven days in most patients, and the management is the management of acute lung injury and encephalopathy from any cause.

  • Oxygen titrated to saturation, then continuous positive airway pressure or high-flow nasal oxygen, then intubation and lung-protective ventilation when the work of breathing or the gas exchange demands it. Around a third of patients in the older series needed ventilation; in the recent prospective series most did.
  • Fluid balance aimed at euvolaemia. Hypovolaemia worsens the right heart and the cerebral perfusion; overload worsens the leaky lung. A fracture patient is usually behind, and the first move is usually to fill, measured against the lung.
  • Vasopressors for the hypotension of the right-heart phase, as in the cement chapter.
  • Neuroprotection as for any encephalopathy: normoxia, normocapnia, normoglycaemia, seizure control, and an MRI to confirm the diagnosis and grade it. In a series of 34 patients with cerebral fat embolism, every death had onset within 24 h and a severe MRI grade, and 26 of the 27 survivors recovered completely over a mean of 4.7 weeks. The confused patient on day two who is otherwise stable will almost always recover; the comatose patient within hours of a pathological fracture may not.
  • Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for the refractory case, now reported in enough series to be a real option in a young patient with an otherwise survivable injury.
  • Corticosteroids are the only drug with trial evidence, all of it for prophylaxis and most of it old. The meta-analysis pooled seven trials and 389 patients: steroid prophylaxis reduced the syndrome by 78% and reduced hypoxia, with no effect on mortality and no excess of infection; the authors judged the trials poor and the confirmatory trial has not been done. Steroids given after the syndrome is established have no evidence. The author’s practice is not to use them; a unit that gives them prophylactically to the young patient with bilateral femoral fractures is not acting against the evidence.
  • Heparin, dextran, alcohol and aspirin have all been tried and none has evidence.
  • Fix the fracture if it has not been fixed. The syndrome is not a reason to delay stabilisation, which removes the source; it is a reason to do it with an arterial line, a plan for the right heart, and possibly an external fixator rather than a reamed nail.

Collapse during nailing: the differential

The patient who deteriorates on the table during reaming or nail insertion is a different problem from the ward syndrome. The event is acute, it is the embolic phase, and it looks exactly like cement implantation syndrome: a fall in end-tidal CO2, then saturation, then blood pressure, with a right ventricle that dilates on echocardiography if a probe is in. Fulminant fat embolism with collapse on the table is rare; the collapse during nailing more often has another cause, and the differential has to be run in seconds.

 collapse during reaming or nail insertion
   |
   |-- EtCO2 falls first, SpO2 then BP, surgeon reaming:
   |     embolic shower (fat, marrow, clot): stop reaming, O2, fill,
   |     vasopressor then adrenaline, TOE if available, CPR if PEA
   |
   |-- BP and EtCO2 fall together, HR up, pale, traction table,
   |   pelvis or second long bone: haemorrhage (femur 1-1.5 L,
   |   pelvis more): blood, TXA, surgeon packs, call for help
   |
   |-- airway pressure up, SpO2 down, BP down, chest trauma,
   |   positive pressure ventilation: tension pneumothorax:
   |   decompress, do not wait for the radiograph
   |
   |-- BP down with bronchospasm, flushing, rash, antibiotic
   |   or cement in the last 10 min: anaphylaxis: adrenaline
   |
   |-- new neurological signs or arrhythmia with a shunt
   |   known or suspected: paradoxical embolus through a PFO
   |
   |-- also: pulmonary thromboembolism from the fracture, a high
   |   spinal in the awake patient, myocardial ischaemia, cardiac
   |   contusion or tamponade in the polytrauma patient

The discriminators are the capnograph, the airway pressure, the skin and the timeline. An embolic event under general anaesthesia announces itself as a fall in end-tidal CO2 with unchanged ventilation, because pulmonary blood flow has fallen before the pressure does; haemorrhage produces a tachycardia and a falling pressure with the end-tidal CO2 following rather than leading; a tension pneumothorax produces a rising airway pressure and a falling saturation before the pressure; anaphylaxis produces bronchospasm and a rash. In the trauma patient more than one can be true.

What to do for the embolic case:

  1. Say it. The surgeon stops reaming and withdraws the reamer; a half-inserted nail stays where it is until the patient is stable.
  2. 100% oxygen, confirm the airway and the ventilation, and read the capnograph as the cardiac output monitor it now is.
  3. Fill the right ventricle with a measured bolus, then vasopressor to restore the systemic pressure that perfuses it; adrenaline in 10-50 mcg increments if the pressure does not respond or the rate falls, and an infusion if it is needed twice.
  4. Chest compressions at once if the pulse is lost; the rhythm is usually pulseless electrical activity and compressions move blood through a transiently obstructed pulmonary bed.
  5. Echocardiography if it can be had: a dilated right ventricle with a small, underfilled left ventricle confirms the diagnosis, and a transoesophageal probe shows the material crossing the atrium and a shunt if there is one.
  6. When stable, decide with the surgeon whether to finish. A nail that is nearly home should usually be completed, slowly, with the canal vented; a reaming that had barely begun in a patient who has just arrested should stop, and an external fixator applied. The second femur in a bilateral case waits.
  7. Intensive care, ventilated, with an arterial line, an echocardiogram and the expectation that the chemical phase follows in 24-72 h.

The preparation that makes this manageable is the same as for cement: the at-risk patient named at the brief, an arterial line before the reaming starts, normovolaemia, a vasopressor running in the frail or the under-resuscitated, and the anaesthetist at the head of the bed during the reaming rather than at the chart. The femoral nailing and tibial nailing cards carry the step at which this happens; the metastasis card and the periprosthetic fracture card cover the pathological and long-stem canals where the load is largest.

The rule set

  1. Fat embolism is near universal after a long bone fracture and during reaming; the syndrome is uncommon, delayed by 12-72 h, and diagnosed clinically. Do not treat the shower on the monitor as the syndrome, or the syndrome on the ward as an embolus.
  2. Name the high-risk patient: young, femoral fracture, bilateral or multiple fractures, pathological bone, obese, delayed to theatre, chest injury, known right-to-left shunt.
  3. Fix the femur within 24 h: a reamed nail in the physiologically stable patient, external fixation and later conversion in the under-resuscitated, coagulopathic, hypothermic or chest-injured one. Reaming itself does not worsen the lung in the trials; the decision is about the patient, not the reamer.
  4. For the nailing: arterial line in the at-risk patient, normovolaemia, vasopressor ready, anaesthetist present for the reaming, surgeon asked to ream slowly and vent in the pathological or bilateral case.
  5. Collapse during reaming is acute right heart failure until proved otherwise: stop, oxygen, measured fluid, vasopressor then adrenaline, early compressions, echocardiography, with haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis and paradoxical embolus run in parallel.
  6. On the ward, hypoxaemia, confusion or petechiae in the first three days after a long bone fracture is the syndrome until excluded. Use Gurd’s list as a checklist and image to exclude the alternatives.
  7. Treatment is supportive: oxygen and ventilation, euvolaemia, vasopressors for the right heart, neuroprotection, intensive care early, ECMO for the refractory young patient. Steroids have poor-quality prophylactic evidence and no treatment evidence; nothing else has any.
  8. Expect recovery in most. The patient who dies does so early, with a pathological or bilateral femur, a severe MRI grade, or a foramen ovale.
