Part A

Blood management and tranexamic acid

Orthopaedic bleeding comes from cut bone that cannot constrict and from fibrinolysis switched on by the surgery, so it continues for hours after the wound is closed and much of it never reaches the suction. The plan has three parts: arrive with enough red cells (find and treat anaemia and iron deficiency weeks before elective surgery), lose fewer (tranexamic acid for almost everyone, with position, temperature, pressure and cell salvage where the operation is big enough), and tolerate a lower haemoglobin afterwards (a restrictive threshold of about 80 g/L, or symptoms, is as safe as 100 g/L even in elderly hip fracture patients with cardiovascular disease). Tranexamic acid cuts transfusion by about two thirds in arthroplasty and by a third to a half in hip fracture and spine surgery, works by any route, and has not been shown to raise thrombotic risk in more than 125,000 randomised patients. The anticoagulant timing rules for neuraxial and deep blocks are the other half of the same subject, because the drug that prevents the clot is the drug that causes the haematoma.

Why orthopaedic operations bleed the way they do

Soft tissue bleeds from vessels that can be clipped, tied or cauterised, and that constrict when the pressure falls. Bone does neither. A cut cancellous surface is a sponge of venous sinusoids held open by trabeculae: it cannot contract, it cannot be coagulated effectively, and it keeps oozing until clot, cement or an implant seals it. That is why blood loss in this specialty tracks the area of raw bone (reamed acetabulum, osteotomised femoral neck, decorticated transverse processes, a medullary canal opened from end to end) more closely than the length of the incision, and why it continues into the drain, the joint and the thigh for 24 hours after closure.

Three consequences follow. First, a large share of the loss is hidden. After a knee replacement done under tourniquet the suction canister may hold 100 mL while the haemoglobin falls by 30 g/L over two days, because the blood went into the joint and the soft tissues after the cuff came down. A nailed extracapsular hip fracture has bled into the thigh before the patient reaches theatre and bleeds again from the reamed canal. The measured loss is the floor, not the estimate.

Second, surgery and tourniquet ischaemia both switch on fibrinolysis. Tissue plasminogen activator is released from injured endothelium, plasmin dissolves the clot that was plugging the bone surface, and the ooze restarts. This is the target of tranexamic acid, and it explains why an antifibrinolytic works so well in operations where the bleeding surface cannot be controlled mechanically.

Third, venous pressure at the wound matters more than arterial pressure. Cancellous bone and epidural veins bleed at venous pressure, so a prone abdomen that is compressed, a head-down lateral position or a coughing, straining patient raises the loss more than a systolic of 130 mmHg does. Positioning is blood management; the detail is in positioning and spine essentials.

The plan that follows from this has the three pillars of patient blood management: more red cells at the start, fewer lost, and a lower haemoglobin tolerated at the end.

  BEFORE                    DURING                     AFTER
  red cell mass             losses                     tolerance
  -------------             ------                     ---------
  find anaemia early        tranexamic acid            restrictive threshold
  ferritin, TSAT, CRP       position, warm, not        (about 80 g/L or
  iron (IV if <6 weeks)     hypertensive               symptoms)
  B12, folate, renal        neuraxial where it fits    single units, reassess
  stop or bridge the        cell salvage if >500 mL    iron after surgery
  anticoagulant on time     expected or likely         restart anticoagulant
                            tourniquet, cement         on a rule, not a guess

Before surgery: anaemia and iron

Pre-operative anaemia is the strongest predictor of transfusion that anyone can change. A patient who starts a hip revision at 105 g/L has no reserve for a 1.5 L loss; the same patient at 135 g/L will probably leave without a transfusion. The international consensus statement on perioperative anaemia makes the practical points that matter in a pre-admission clinic. Screen early enough to act, which means at listing rather than the week before. Treat a haemoglobin below 130 g/L as anaemia worth investigating in both sexes: the lower “normal” for women leaves them with a smaller red cell mass facing the same blood loss. Iron deficiency is the commonest cause and the most treatable: a ferritin below 30 micrograms/L is absolute deficiency, and in a patient with inflammation (a raised CRP, which includes most patients with inflammatory arthritis or an infected joint) a ferritin below 100 micrograms/L with a transferrin saturation below 20% means iron-restricted erythropoiesis even though the ferritin looks adequate.

Oral iron works if there are six to eight weeks and a gut that tolerates and absorbs it; a low dose on alternate days is absorbed as well as higher daily doses and is better tolerated. Intravenous iron is the choice when surgery is less than six weeks away, when oral iron has failed, or when inflammation is blocking absorption. A single infusion of ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose replaces the deficit in one visit and the haemoglobin response is evident from about two weeks. The honest reading of the evidence is that intravenous iron reliably raises haemoglobin and that the benefit for hard outcomes is less certain; the argument for it in elective arthroplasty rests on the size of the transfusion effect and the fact that the operation can wait. Anaemia without iron deficiency needs its cause found (B12, folate, renal disease, marrow, occult gastrointestinal loss) before the joint is replaced, not after.

Elective arthroplasty in an anaemic patient is a postponable operation. Hip fracture surgery is not: there the anaemia is managed around the operation, with tranexamic acid, a restrictive threshold and iron afterwards.

Tranexamic acid

Tranexamic acid is a lysine analogue that occupies the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen and stops it docking onto fibrin. Clot that has formed on the bone surface stays there. It does not make blood clot where it otherwise would not, which is the mechanistic reason the thrombosis signal has been so hard to find.

Arthroplasty

The effect is large and consistent. In the United States cohort of 872,416 hip and knee replacements, transfusion fell from 20.1% to 7.7% with tranexamic acid, an odds ratio of roughly one third, at every dose category, with no increase in thromboembolic events, renal failure or a combined complication outcome. The multi-society arthroplasty guideline, built on a network meta-analysis of the randomised trials, reached four conclusions that have simplified practice: intravenous, topical and oral routes all work; no route is clearly better than another; higher doses and repeat doses add little that can be measured; and for the intravenous route, giving the dose before the incision (or before tourniquet inflation) is favoured.

The defensible default is therefore TXA 1 g IV (or 10-15 mg/kg) before incision. A second 1 g IV at closure or about three hours later is common, reasonable for the longer operations and revisions, and consistent with the POISE-3 regimen, although the arthroplasty network meta-analysis could not show that it adds to the first dose. Oral TXA 2 g about two hours before surgery is equivalent, cheap and awkward only for the logistics.

Topical versus intravenous

Topical tranexamic acid (1-3 g in 30-100 mL of saline, poured into the joint or injected through the drain after closure and left for a few minutes) puts the drug where the bleeding is, with plasma levels a fraction of those after an intravenous dose. In the meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials it cut transfusion as effectively as the intravenous route, with thromboembolic events no different from placebo. Its place is the patient in whom the surgeon or anaesthetist is unwilling to give a systemic dose: a coronary stent placed in the last few months, a recent stroke or pulmonary embolus, a seizure disorder, severe renal impairment. Combined intravenous and topical dosing is widely used; the evidence that it beats either alone is weak.

Does it cause thrombosis

The fear is intuitive and the data do not support it. In the meta-analysis of 216 randomised trials and 125,550 patients across all surgical disciplines, thromboembolic events occurred in 2.1% with intravenous tranexamic acid and 2.0% without, with no increase in venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction or stroke, and no increase in the trials that included patients with previous thromboembolism. POISE-3 is the necessary caveat: in 9,535 non-cardiac surgical patients, tranexamic acid reduced major bleeding (9.1% versus 11.7%) and the composite cardiovascular outcome was 14.2% versus 13.9%, a hazard ratio of 1.02 whose confidence interval ran to 1.14 and so narrowly failed the prespecified non-inferiority margin. The plain reading is that a small excess of arterial or venous events cannot be excluded, that if it exists it is much smaller than the bleeding benefit, and that the patient with a recent thrombotic event is a judgement, not a contraindication. The arthroplasty guideline says the same thing: the trials excluded most high-risk patients, the observational data in those who were given it anyway are reassuring, and the decision in a patient with a recent stent or embolus is individual.

Two harms are real. Seizures are dose-related and were described with the high doses once used in cardiac surgery; tranexamic acid is renally cleared, so reduce the dose in significant renal impairment and avoid repeat dosing in dialysis patients. And tranexamic acid given intrathecally by ampoule confusion with a local anaesthetic causes refractory seizures, ventricular arrhythmia and death. The ampoules can look alike. Keep tranexamic acid off the spinal tray and out of the drawer that holds heavy bupivacaine.

Hip fracture

The patient is older, already anaemic and has bled before theatre. Two meta-analyses of the randomised trials (13 trials and 1,194 patients; 12 trials and 1,397 patients aged over 65) give a transfusion risk ratio of 0.5 to 0.6 with intravenous tranexamic acid and no detectable increase in thromboembolic events, with the honest qualification that events were too few for certainty. The effect was clear in trials using a restrictive threshold and disappeared where patients were transfused at 100 g/L, which is a reminder that tranexamic acid and the transfusion trigger are one decision. The defensible default for neck of femur fracture surgery is TXA 1 g IV at induction (15 mg/kg in the very small patient), with a lower threshold to omit or go topical in the patient whose fracture followed a stroke or infarct.

Spine

Decorticated bone and epidural veins bleed in proportion to the number of levels. In 11 randomised trials tranexamic acid reduced total blood loss by about 200 mL and the proportion transfused by a third, without a thrombosis signal. Dosing in deformity surgery is typically a loading dose followed by an infusion for the length of the operation (10-50 mg/kg then 1-10 mg/kg/h in published protocols); the higher regimens bled less in one retrospective adult comparison, have not been shown to be better in a randomised trial, and carry the seizure risk. For one- and two-level surgery a single 1 g IV dose is enough. More in spine essentials.

Cell salvage

Cell salvage returns washed red cells at a haematocrit of 50-60% with no plasma, platelets or clotting factors. It earns its set-up cost when the expected loss is more than about 500-1,000 mL or when the loss is unpredictable and potentially large: revision hip arthroplasty, pelvic and acetabular fixation, deformity correction, multilevel fusion, periacetabular osteotomy, and any patient who refuses or cannot receive allogeneic blood. In revision hip arthroplasty the meta-analysis found allogeneic transfusion in 44% of patients with salvage and 65% without. In primary hip and knee replacement with tranexamic acid the loss is too small to make salvage worthwhile.

A collect-only set-up (reservoir and anticoagulated suction, with the processing bowl opened only if the reservoir fills) keeps the option cheap. The suction must be diverted to waste whenever the field contains something that should not be reinfused: povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine irrigation, topical haemostatic agents, antibiotic powder, and methylmethacrylate that has not yet cured. Infection and tumour are relative contraindications: for metastatic spine surgery a leucodepletion filter on the return line is the usual compromise. After a large reinfusion the patient has red cells and nothing else, so check coagulation and fibrinogen once the returned volume passes about half a blood volume.

Transfusion thresholds

FOCUS settled the question for the population this book is about. In 2,016 hip fracture patients aged 50 or over with cardiovascular disease or risk factors, transfusing to keep the haemoglobin above 100 g/L was no better than transfusing only below 80 g/L or for symptoms (chest pain, heart failure, tachycardia or hypotension unresponsive to fluid): death or inability to walk across a room at 60 days was 35.2% versus 34.7%, and coronary events and mortality did not differ. The restrictive group received a median of no units.

The working rule is a threshold of 70-80 g/L in a stable patient, 80 g/L in those with ischaemic heart disease, one unit at a time with reassessment, and symptoms overriding the number in either direction. A patient who is dizzy on standing, tachycardic and unable to do physiotherapy at 82 g/L is under-filled or under-transfused and deserves treatment, not a rule. A haemoglobin on day 1 underestimates the fall; the nadir after hip and knee replacement is on day 2 or 3, after the hidden loss has equilibrated. Postoperative intravenous iron is a reasonable alternative to a marginal transfusion in a patient who was iron deficient going in.

Anticoagulants, antiplatelets and the needle

A vertebral canal haematoma needs a needle or catheter and a patient who cannot clot. The ASRA guideline sets an interval for each drug between the last dose and the needle, and between the needle or catheter removal and the next dose. The intervals are built from the drug’s half-life (about five half-lives for full clearance, two for prophylactic doses) and its time to peak (the next dose must not peak while the puncture site is still fresh). The intervals in routine use, for normal renal function:

Drug Last dose to needle Catheter Next dose after needle or removal
Aspirin, NSAIDs No restriction No restriction No restriction
Unfractionated heparin 5,000 units SC two or three times daily 4-6 h Remove 4-6 h after a dose 1 h
Enoxaparin prophylactic (40 mg daily) 12 h Remove 12 h after a dose 4 h; first postoperative dose 12 h after the needle
Enoxaparin therapeutic (1 mg/kg twice daily, 1.5 mg/kg daily) 24 h Remove before the first therapeutic dose 4 h after removal and 24 h after the needle
Warfarin 5 days and INR in the normal range Remove with INR below 1.5 Restart after removal
Rivaroxaban, apixaban (treatment doses) 72 h Not while the catheter is in 6 h
Dabigatran 72-120 h by creatinine clearance Not while the catheter is in 6 h
Clopidogrel 5-7 days May stay 1-2 days if no loading dose At once without a load; 6 h after a loading dose
Ticagrelor 5-7 days Do not maintain a catheter At once without a load; 6 h after a loading dose
Prasugrel 7-10 days Do not maintain a catheter At once without a load; 6 h after a loading dose
Fondaparinux Single pass, atraumatic, no catheter Avoid 6 h

The fifth edition keeps the structure and refines it by dose: it separates low (prophylactic) from high (treatment) doses, with shorter intervals for the low doses of the direct oral anticoagulants than the 72 hours required after treatment doses. The intervals in the table below were checked against published summaries of the fourth edition; the fifth edition’s own tables were not available when this chapter was written, so read the low-dose intervals from the guideline itself. Renal impairment lengthens every interval for enoxaparin, dabigatran and, to a lesser degree, the factor Xa inhibitors, and the elderly hip fracture patient on a DOAC with a creatinine clearance of 35 mL/min is the common case in which the interval collides with the 36-hour surgical target. The practical resolution there is a general anaesthetic with a superficial, compressible block (fascia iliaca above the inguinal ligament is compressible; a lumbar plexus block is not) or, where the service measures them, a drug level or anti-Xa assay to show that the drug has gone.

For peripheral blocks the guideline divides by depth. Deep plexus and deep peripheral blocks at non-compressible sites (lumbar plexus, paravertebral, the deeper quadratus lumborum approaches, and by extension infraclavicular) follow the neuraxial intervals, because a haematoma there cannot be seen or pressed on and has caused major blood loss and nerve injury. Superficial blocks at compressible sites (femoral, adductor canal, popliteal, interscalene, axillary) are a risk-benefit judgement made under ultrasound with a small needle, and are usually done. Catheters carry the rule twice: once at insertion and once at removal, and the commonest error is a catheter pulled three hours after the evening enoxaparin. The timing of the postoperative thromboprophylaxis around a neuraxial block is taken up in venous thromboembolism prophylaxis.

Predicting the loss by operation

The figures are typical measured-plus-hidden totals with tranexamic acid in use; individual cards give the reasons.

Operation Expected total loss Plan
Primary THA 300-600 mL plus hidden loss TXA; group and screen; transfusion uncommon
Primary TKA 100-300 mL seen, as much again hidden TXA; nadir day 2-3
Anatomic and reverse TSA 200-500 mL TXA; transfusion uncommon unless anaemic or for fracture
Revision THA 1-2 L, more with acetabular reconstruction TXA two doses, cell salvage, crossmatch, arterial line
Revision TKA 500 mL-1.5 L after tourniquet release TXA; crossmatch for complex cases
Neck of femur fracture 300 mL (intracapsular) to more than 1 L (nailed extracapsular) TXA; restrictive threshold; recheck day 1-2
Femoral shaft nailing 1 L or more into the thigh before theatre Crossmatch; TXA
Pelvic and acetabular fixation 0.5-1.5 L single acetabular approach; 2 L or more combined Cell salvage, crossmatch, large-bore access, TXA
Periacetabular osteotomy 500 mL-1.5 L TXA, cell salvage
Posterior lumbar fusion 300-800 mL per one or two levels TXA; position the abdomen free
Adult deformity and scoliosis 1-3 L, more with osteotomies TXA load and infusion, cell salvage, crossmatch, viscoelastic testing
Spinal metastasis decompression Unpredictable; renal and thyroid deposits bleed torrentially Pre-operative embolisation where offered, crossmatch, TXA
Periprosthetic joint infection surgery 500 mL-2 L Anaemic at baseline; crossmatch; salvage relatively contraindicated

Edge cases

The patient who refuses blood. Establish before the day exactly which products and techniques are acceptable (many accept cell salvage in continuous circuit, and some accept fractions). Then use every pillar at full strength: iron and, with haematology, erythropoietin beforehand; tranexamic acid by both routes; salvage; meticulous positioning; staged surgery where the operation can be divided; minimal blood sampling afterwards.

The recent stent or thrombosis. Keep the aspirin going through arthroplasty: the bleeding cost is small and it does not restrict neuraxial block. For dual antiplatelet therapy within the mandatory period, elective surgery waits. For tranexamic acid, topical dosing is the middle path and a single intravenous dose remains defensible when the bleeding risk is high; the decision is author’s judgement on thin direct evidence.

The tourniquet and the cement. A tourniquet moves the loss from the operation to the recovery room without reducing the total, and cement on a femoral or tibial surface tamponades cancellous bone. Both change when the bleeding shows, covered in the tourniquet and bone cement.

Hypotensive anaesthesia. Deliberate hypotension reduces arterial bleeding and has no effect on venous ooze from bone. With tranexamic acid, neuraxial anaesthesia and good positioning there is little left for it to add in arthroplasty, and in the beach chair and the prone spine patient it is the direct cause of the rare catastrophic injuries. A normal pressure for that patient, a low venous pressure at the wound and an antifibrinolytic is the better combination.

Massive loss. The pelvic fracture, the revision hip with a torn iliac vein and the deformity correction that has passed a blood volume are managed by ratio-based or viscoelastic-guided replacement like any other major haemorrhage. Fibrinogen falls first; give it early (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate to keep it above 2 g/L), keep the patient warm and the ionised calcium normal, and remember that salvaged blood contains no clotting factors.

Part A

Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis

Hip and knee replacement, hip fracture and pelvic trauma combine all three limbs of Virchow's triad in one operation, which is why they sit at the top of every risk table; arthroscopy, upper limb and most day surgery sit at the bottom and need nothing beyond early walking unless the patient brings the risk. The agent question after arthroplasty is no longer open-ended: in the Australian CRISTAL trial aspirin alone gave more symptomatic thromboembolism than enoxaparin (3.45% versus 1.82%), almost all of the difference in below-knee thrombosis, with no difference in death or major bleeding, while a short course of rivaroxaban followed by aspirin matched continued rivaroxaban in EPCAT II. Guidelines therefore accept several regimens and differ mainly in how much weight they give to a calf thrombosis against a wound haematoma. The anaesthetist's part is timing: the first dose after a spinal, the dose before a catheter comes out, and the hip fracture patient whose evening enoxaparin must not sit inside the morning's needle. Mechanical prophylaxis and walking on the day of surgery are the constants under every regimen.

Why orthopaedic operations clot

Virchow’s triad is delivered in full by a hip or knee replacement. Stasis: the femoral vein is kinked for minutes at a time when the hip is dislocated, flexed and rotated for femoral preparation, a thigh tourniquet stops venous return completely for an hour, and the calf pump is idle during and after surgery. Endothelial injury: the same vein is stretched and twisted, and a segment of it sits against a retractor. Hypercoagulability: reaming and broaching a medullary canal pushes marrow fat and tissue thromboplastin into the venous blood, and the surgical stress response adds fibrinogen and platelet activation for a week or more. The link between marrow embolism and thrombosis is direct: in a randomised trial of cemented hip replacement, suction venting of the canal cut embolic cascades on echocardiography from 91% to 15% and day-4 deep vein thrombosis from 18% to 3%. The same embolic load is the subject of bone cement implantation syndrome and fat embolism.

Hip fracture adds the days of immobility and dehydration before the operation, so thrombus may already be present on arrival. Pelvic and acetabular fracture adds direct venous injury in the pelvis. At the other end of the scale, an arthroscopy or a hand operation injures no large vein, opens no canal and immobilises nobody, and the baseline risk is that of the patient.

The risk continues after discharge. The hypercoagulable state outlasts the hospital stay, which is why symptomatic events after arthroplasty cluster in the second and third weeks, and why every guideline’s duration (10-14 days at minimum, up to 35 days after hip replacement) is longer than the admission.

Risk by operation

Tier Operations Usual approach
High Hip fracture, THA, TKA, revision hip and knee, pelvic and acetabular fixation, polytrauma, femoral and tibial fracture fixation Mechanical plus pharmacological, extended beyond discharge
Intermediate Periacetabular and knee osteotomy, multiligament knee, ankle fixation with non-weight-bearing, Achilles repair, major spinal fusion and deformity, amputation Mechanical for all; pharmacological by patient risk and duration of immobilisation
Low Knee arthroscopy, ACL reconstruction, hip arthroscopy, microdiscectomy, shoulder arthroplasty and all upper limb surgery Early mobilisation; pharmacological only for patient risk factors

Patient factors move a patient up a tier: previous thromboembolism (the strongest), active cancer, known thrombophilia, oestrogen therapy, pregnancy and the puerperium, severe obesity, age, and anything that will keep the patient in bed. In the Danish fast-track cohort the independent predictors of thrombosis after hip and knee replacement were age over 85 and a BMI above 35, with odds ratios of 2.5 to 3.7.

For the low tier the trials are clear. In POT-KAST, eight days of low-molecular-weight heparin after knee arthroscopy gave symptomatic thromboembolism in 0.7% against 0.4% with nothing. In POT-CAST, heparin for the whole period of a lower-leg cast gave 1.4% against 1.8%. Routine anticoagulation does not work in unselected patients because the baseline risk is too low for it to show; that does not mean the patient with a previous embolus having an arthroscopy should go without.

The agent after arthroplasty

Four regimens are in common use and each has a trial behind it.

Low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily) is the reference agent against which everything else has been tested. It is the suggested first choice of the 2012 ACCP guideline, it has predictable timing around a neuraxial block, and it requires an injection every day for two to five weeks, which is the reason patients and surgeons look for alternatives.

Direct oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban 10 mg daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily) are oral, at least as effective as enoxaparin against all thrombosis, and are the agents the 2019 American Society of Hematology guideline conditionally prefers when an anticoagulant is chosen. The surgical objection is wound bleeding and haematoma, and they cannot be given while an epidural or deep catheter is in place.

Aspirin (100 mg daily in Australia) is cheap, oral, already taken by many of the patients and places no restriction on neuraxial technique. Both the ACCP and ASH guidelines list it as an acceptable option. CRISTAL is the direct test of aspirin as sole chemoprophylaxis and it is an Australian trial, nested in the national joint registry: 31 hospitals were randomised to give aspirin 100 mg or enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 35 days after hip replacement and 14 days after knee replacement, and the trial stopped early at 9,711 patients. Symptomatic thromboembolism within 90 days occurred in 3.45% with aspirin and 1.82% with enoxaparin. Aspirin failed the non-inferiority test and enoxaparin was superior. No secondary outcome differed, including death and major bleeding.

The plain reading has two halves. Aspirin alone prevents fewer clots than enoxaparin, and that question is closed. But of the 256 events, 174 were below-knee deep vein thromboses, 18 were above-knee and 79 were pulmonary emboli, and the trial was not powered to show a difference in embolism or death. How much a symptomatic calf thrombosis matters (it means weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation in a patient with a fresh joint, and some propagate) against the convenience and wound profile of aspirin is a value judgement, and surgeons continue to make it differently.

The hybrid regimen answers part of the objection. In EPCAT II every patient received rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for five days and was then randomised to aspirin 81 mg or continued rivaroxaban, for a total of 14 days after knee and 35 days after hip replacement. Symptomatic thromboembolism was 0.64% with the switch to aspirin and 0.70% with continued rivaroxaban, with bleeding no different. An anticoagulant for the first days, when the risk is highest and the patient is in or near hospital, followed by aspirin for the tail, is the structure NICE recommends for hip replacement (low-molecular-weight heparin for 10 days then aspirin for 28 days) alongside the alternatives of 28 days of heparin with stockings or rivaroxaban (duration set by the NICE technology appraisal, not NG89); for knee replacement NICE accepts 14 days of aspirin alone, 14 days of heparin with stockings, or rivaroxaban.

  Regimen                     Clots prevented    Wound/bleeding    Neuraxial timing
  --------------------------  -----------------  ----------------  -----------------
  Enoxaparin 40 mg daily      reference          reference         12 h rule
  DOAC (rivaroxaban 10 mg)    at least as good   surgeon's worry   no catheter in situ
  Aspirin 100 mg alone        fewer (CRISTAL)    least             no restriction
  Anticoagulant 5-10 days,    as good as DOAC    middle            as for the first
    then aspirin              (EPCAT II)                           agent

The Australian position is a framework, not a prescription. The national Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard requires that every admitted patient has thrombotic risk and bleeding risk assessed and documented, is offered prophylaxis appropriate to both, is told what it is for, is reassessed when the clinical picture changes, and leaves with a plan that states the agent and the stop date. It does not name an agent for arthroplasty. Practice among Australian arthroplasty surgeons has varied in agent and duration, and since CRISTAL the defensible default for a standard-risk patient is an anticoagulant in hospital with a switch to aspirin, or enoxaparin throughout, with aspirin alone reserved for the low-risk, rapidly mobilising patient after an informed conversation. That sentence is author’s judgement from the trials above.

For fracture surgery in younger patients the evidence points the same way with a different emphasis. PREVENT CLOT randomised 12,211 patients with operatively treated limb fractures or pelvic and acetabular fractures (mean age 45) to aspirin 81 mg twice daily or enoxaparin 30 mg twice daily. Death at 90 days was 0.78% against 0.73%, pulmonary embolism was 1.49% in each group, and deep vein thrombosis was 2.51% against 1.71%. Aspirin is a legitimate choice after isolated limb fracture fixation in a patient who will be up quickly. It was not a trial of the elderly hip fracture patient, for whom low-molecular-weight heparin from admission, timed around surgery and continued for about a month, remains the standard, and for whom the ACCP guideline specifically does not list the direct oral anticoagulants.

Mechanical prophylaxis and movement

Intermittent pneumatic compression empties the calf veins, replaces the idle muscle pump and stimulates endothelial fibrinolysis, with no bleeding cost. The ACCP guideline accepts a compression device as sole prophylaxis in a patient at high bleeding risk and suggests adding one to drug prophylaxis during the hospital stay; the ASH guideline prefers pneumatic compression to graduated stockings. The practical rules: put the sleeve on the non-operated leg before induction and on both legs in recovery, keep it running whenever the patient is in bed (a device hanging on the bed end has no effect), and leave it off a limb with critical ischaemia, a fresh skin graft or fragile, ulcerated skin. Stockings add little to a working compression device and injure skin in arterial disease and oedematous limbs.

Early walking is the most powerful mechanical prophylaxis and the reason the modern event rates are a fraction of the historical ones. In the Danish fast-track cohort of 17,582 hip and knee replacements with a median stay of two days and prophylaxis during the admission only, 90-day symptomatic thromboembolism was 0.40% and pulmonary embolism 0.16%. The anaesthetic contributes directly: a technique that has the patient standing within hours of surgery (short-acting spinal, motor-sparing blocks, no urinary catheter, treated nausea) is thromboprophylaxis. See enhanced recovery and day-case arthroplasty.

Timing around neuraxial anaesthesia and catheters

The full interval table is in blood management. The rules that govern the postoperative chart are these.

  Enoxaparin 40 mg daily and a single-shot spinal

  needle                       first dose
    |------------ 12 h -----------|-------- 24 h --------| next dose
  09:00                         21:00                   21:00

  With an epidural or deep catheter in place

    dose ------ 12 h ------ remove catheter --- 4 h --- next dose

Prophylactic enoxaparin: the needle goes in at least 12 hours after a dose and the first postoperative dose is given at least 12 hours after the needle. An evening dosing time achieves both without anyone doing arithmetic: a morning or afternoon spinal is followed by a dose at 20:00-22:00, and a pre-operative dose for a hip fracture patient given the evening before leaves a clear 12 hours by the morning list. A catheter is removed at least 12 hours after a dose and the next dose waits four hours. Twice-daily and therapeutic regimens do not coexist with a neuraxial catheter. In renal impairment (creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min) the dose is halved and the intervals lengthen.

Direct oral anticoagulants: the first prophylactic dose is given no sooner than six hours after the needle or after catheter removal, and not while an epidural or deep plexus catheter is in place. A patient who needs a catheter for two days has enoxaparin for those two days and switches when the catheter is out.

Aspirin: no restriction at any dose, alone. The risk rises when it is combined with another agent, which is exactly the hybrid regimen, so the catheter comes out under the anticoagulant’s rule.

Bloody or difficult tap: delay the first dose to 24 hours and write it on the chart, because the person giving the evening dose was not in theatre.

Peripheral catheters: for superficial, compressible sites (adductor canal, femoral, popliteal, interscalene) prophylactic anticoagulation is not a barrier and the catheter is removed without special timing, though removal at the trough is sensible. Deep sites follow the neuraxial rule.

The day-case and short-stay patient

The patient who goes home the same day has shown, by doing so, the mobility that protects against thrombosis, and has also left the building where the injections and the compression device were. The plan has to work at home.

For day-case hip and knee replacement, selection has already removed most high-risk patients. The usual regimens are an oral agent for the guideline duration: a direct oral anticoagulant, or an anticoagulant for the first days followed by aspirin, with aspirin alone for the lowest-risk. Enoxaparin requires teaching the injection before the day of surgery, not in recovery. The discharge document states the agent, the dose, the stop date and the symptoms that should bring the patient back (calf swelling or pain, breathlessness, pleuritic pain, and a wound that is leaking more on day five than on day two).

For arthroscopy, upper limb surgery and minor foot surgery, nothing beyond walking unless the patient carries a risk factor. For a lower-limb operation that ends in a cast or boot and weeks of non-weight-bearing, risk-stratify: POT-CAST showed no benefit in unselected patients, and the patient with a previous clot, cancer, oestrogen therapy or an Achilles rupture is the one who is given low-molecular-weight heparin or a direct oral anticoagulant for the period of immobilisation.

Edge cases

Already anticoagulated. The patient on a therapeutic direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin for atrial fibrillation or previous thrombosis needs prophylaxis from the evening of surgery (prophylactic enoxaparin, or the prophylactic dose of their own agent) and returns to the treatment dose when the surgeon is content with the wound, typically at 48-72 hours after arthroplasty. Restarting a full dose on the first evening is how a haematoma becomes a periprosthetic infection. Bridging with therapeutic heparin is reserved for mechanical valves and very recent thrombosis.

Recent thromboembolism. Elective surgery within three months of a deep vein thrombosis or embolus should wait. When a fracture cannot wait and anticoagulation must stop, a retrievable vena cava filter is considered for a proximal thrombosis within the previous month; as primary prevention filters are recommended against by both ACCP and ASH.

Spine. The bleeding complication is an epidural haematoma with cord compression, so the balance tips toward mechanical prophylaxis alone for decompressions and short fusions, with low-molecular-weight heparin started 24-48 hours after surgery for long fusions, tumour, trauma with neurological deficit and combined anterior-posterior procedures. This is consensus practice, not trial evidence.

Polytrauma and pelvic fracture. Start low-molecular-weight heparin as soon as bleeding is controlled, usually within 24-48 hours, and time the doses around repeat trips to theatre. Compression devices go on any limb that can take one.

Obesity and extremes of weight. Fixed-dose enoxaparin under-doses at 140 kg and over-doses at 45 kg. Weight-banded dosing (40 mg twice daily or about 0.5 mg/kg above 120 kg, 20 mg below 50 kg) is widely used and rests on anti-Xa levels, not outcome trials.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Any heparin is contraindicated, including flushes. A direct oral anticoagulant or fondaparinux replaces it, and fondaparinux brings its own neuraxial restriction.

Tranexamic acid. It does not replace or interfere with thromboprophylaxis, and across the randomised trials it has not increased thrombosis; give both.

Part A

Positioning: beach chair, lateral, prone and the traction table

Each orthopaedic position buys the surgeon access and charges the patient somewhere else, and the charge is predictable from the geometry. The beach chair lifts the brain 20-30 cm above the cuff, so the brain sees 15-25 mmHg less than the number on the screen (Cullen quotes 20-40 mmHg at the brainstem, depending on height and angle), cerebral desaturation is the rule when that is ignored, and the rare strokes in this position have followed uncorrected or deliberate hypotension. Lateral and prone positions move the risk to the brachial plexus, the dependent eye and the abdomen: arm position changes account for most upper limb evoked potential changes in spine surgery, and a compressed abdomen turns epidural veins into the surgeon's bleeding problem. The traction table trades a perineal post against the pudendal nerve in proportion to force and time, and a raised well leg against its own calf perfusion. The defence in every case is the same: refer the pressure to the organ at risk, pad and align so that no nerve is stretched or pressed, limit the time, and write down what was done.

What a position costs

Positioning injuries have four mechanisms, and each position in this chapter is a different mix of them.

Gravity acts on a column of blood. Any organ lifted above the heart is perfused at a pressure lower than the one measured at the heart, by 0.77 mmHg for every centimetre of height (about 2 mmHg for every 2.5 cm). Any limb lifted above the heart drains well and fills poorly. This is the beach chair problem for the brain and the hemilithotomy problem for the calf.

Stretch acts on nerves. A peripheral nerve tolerates only a small elongation before its intraneural blood flow stops; the brachial plexus, fixed at the vertebral foramina and the axillary sheath and slung over the first rib and under the clavicle, is stretched by abduction beyond 90 degrees, by external rotation with extension, by the head turned or tilted away, and by a shoulder that sags backwards off a support.

Pressure acts on nerves and skin where they lie between bone and a hard surface: the ulnar nerve in its groove, the common peroneal nerve on the fibular neck, the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve under an iliac bolster, the pudendal nerve against a perineal post, the eye against a headrest.

Compression acts on compartments and cavities. A belly pressed on by a bolster transmits pressure to the vena cava and from there to the epidural veins. A calf resting in a support has its compartment pressure raised from outside.

General anaesthesia and regional blocks both remove the warning. The awake patient shifts an arm that has gone numb; the anaesthetised or blocked patient cannot. Duration multiplies everything.

Beach chair

Used for anatomic and reverse shoulder arthroplasty, rotator cuff repair, stabilisation and most other shoulder arthroscopy, proximal humerus and clavicle surgery. The surgeon gains a shoulder in its anatomical orientation, an arm that hangs free for manipulation, less traction on the plexus than the lateral position, and easy conversion to an open approach.

The hydrostatic gradient

            external auditory meatus  --------  brain sees: cuff MAP - 15 to 23
                  |
                  |  20-30 cm   x 0.77 mmHg/cm
                  |
            arm cuff at heart level   --------  displayed MAP (say 65)
                  |
                  |  60-80 cm
                  |
            calf cuff                 --------  reads 45-60 mmHg HIGHER than heart

With the back raised 60-80 degrees the circle of Willis is 20-30 cm above the upper arm cuff. A displayed mean pressure of 65 mmHg is a cerebral perfusion pressure in the mid-40s before any allowance for venous or intracranial pressure. That is at or below the lower limit of autoregulation for many normal brains and well below it for the chronic hypertensive, whose curve is shifted to the right. A cuff moved to the calf because the other arm is unavailable makes the error far larger in the wrong direction: the reading is inflated by the height of the heart above the calf, so a calf reading of 90 mmHg may be a brain pressure of 30 mmHg.

General anaesthesia makes the position worse than it is in an awake volunteer. Sitting pools blood in the legs and splanchnic bed, anaesthesia blocks the sympathetic response that would normally compensate, cardiac output falls, and positive pressure ventilation with hypocapnia adds cerebral vasoconstriction. In 124 patients under a standardised general anaesthetic, cerebral desaturation events occurred in 80.3% of those in the beach chair and in none of those in the lateral position. In the APSF-funded study of 218 patients, the beach chair group had lower cerebral saturation and measurably impaired autoregulation, but no difference in cognition or injury biomarkers afterwards. Together these say that reduced cerebral oxygenation in the beach chair is common and usually harmless, which is the setting in which a rare catastrophe hides.

The catastrophes are real. The first case series described four patients with ischaemic brain and spinal cord injury after beach chair shoulder surgery, middle-aged, without the vascular risk factors that would have predicted a stroke; the authors attributed the injuries to the position and to how blood pressure was managed in it. The APSF advice that followed, restated by Cullen in 2020, is simple: think of the pressure at the brain, not at the cuff; calculate the gradient and correct for it; and do not use deliberate hypotension in the sitting patient. Cullen argues the 2009 APSF allowance of a 30% fall from baseline should go, and that cuff pressure be kept at or very near the awake baseline.

Practical rules

  1. Cuff on the non-operative upper arm at heart level. If an arterial line is used, level the transducer at the external auditory meatus so that the displayed number is the brain’s number.
  2. Set the target at the brain: a mean of at least 70 mmHg at the level of the meatus, which is a displayed arm-cuff mean of about 80 mmHg or more, and keep the corrected pressure within about 20% of the patient’s resting baseline. For the chronic hypertensive, the patient with carotid disease or a previous stroke, set it higher. These thresholds are consensus, not trial-derived.
  3. Never use a leg cuff uncorrected. If the calf is the only site, subtract the full height difference between calf and meatus.
  4. Refuse deliberate hypotension. A wet arthroscopic field is managed with pump pressure, adrenaline in the irrigation, and a systolic that is normal for the patient, not low.
  5. Run a vasopressor from the start: a phenylephrine or metaraminol infusion begun before sitting up, with the patient raised in stages and the pressure checked after each. Keep end-tidal CO2 normal or slightly high; hypocapnia narrows the margin.
  6. Expect the hypotensive bradycardic event. A sudden fall in heart rate and pressure 30-60 minutes after sitting up, classically in the awake or lightly sedated patient with an interscalene block containing adrenaline, is attributed to an underfilled, vigorously contracting ventricle triggering a vagal reflex. Treat with ephedrine or atropine and fluid, lower the back if it persists.
  7. Fix the head in neutral. Rotation, lateral flexion and extension each narrow a vertebral or carotid artery and stretch the plexus on the operative side; the head strap must not sit on the eyes, the ear or the greater auricular nerve. Check after every change of table position, because the head moves when the back is raised.
  8. Secure the airway for a position in which it cannot be reached. The head is draped and at the far end of the patient from the machine. A tracheal tube taped on the side away from the surgeon is the default for long or open procedures; a supraglottic airway is defensible for short arthroscopies when the head is fixed and access has been rehearsed.

Cerebral oximetry detects the desaturation and guides the vasopressor, but no trial shows that treating the number prevents injury. It is reasonable in the patient with cerebrovascular disease and unnecessary as routine if the pressure is managed at the brain. The alternative is a regional technique with light sedation, which preserves autoregulation and lets the patient report symptoms; the block menu covers the choice.

Lateral decubitus

Used for the posterior approach to the hip, revision hip, some shoulder arthroscopy and stabilisation, lateral lumbar fusion and some acetabular fixation.

The pelvis is clamped between an anterior support on the pubis or the anterior superior iliac spines and a posterior support on the sacrum. The anterior support is the hazard: set too low or too tight it compresses the femoral vessels and nerve of the dependent leg, or in an obese patient the abdomen and vena cava. Check the dependent foot pulse and that a hand slides between the support and the abdomen.

The dependent shoulder and plexus carry the weight of the chest. A roll under the chest wall just caudal to the axilla (not in it) lifts the thorax off the shoulder; the head is supported so the cervical spine is in line with the thoracic spine, because lateral flexion toward the table stretches the upper plexus and compresses the lower. The dependent arm lies forward on a board at no more than 90 degrees, the upper arm on a gutter or pillow at no more than 90 degrees and not pulled forward. The dependent eye and ear must be free of the headrest; the dependent common peroneal nerve is padded at the fibular neck and a pillow separates the knees.

For shoulder arthroscopy in the lateral position the arm is suspended in abduction and forward flexion with longitudinal traction. The plexus injuries reported in this position are traction neurapraxias, so the weight is kept as low as gives a view and the arm is not held in extreme abduction. Irrigation fluid tracks into the neck and chest wall in long cases; feel the neck and check airway pressures before extubating.

Physiologically, under general anaesthesia the dependent lung is well perfused and poorly ventilated, so shunt rises in the obese and in long cases. A dense block or a long operation on a heavy patient puts the dependent gluteal muscles and greater trochanter at risk of pressure necrosis; revision surgery beyond three or four hours in a large patient is the setting for dependent-side rhabdomyolysis.

For the lateral approach to the lumbar spine the table is broken to open the space between rib and iliac crest. The break stretches the upper-side psoas and lumbar plexus, and the retractor then sits within the psoas; time in the broken position is the modifiable variable.

Prone

Used for posterior lumbar and cervical surgery, deformity correction, decompression, sacroiliac fusion and coccygectomy, and some Achilles, calcaneal and posterior malleolar work. The physiology and the visual loss question are covered in spine essentials; what follows is the checklist logic.

Abdomen. The purpose of every prone frame is to let the abdomen hang free. A compressed abdomen raises caval pressure, diverts venous return through the vertebral plexus and makes the epidural veins bleed into the wound; it also splints the diaphragm and raises airway pressure. Supports belong on the chest and the iliac crests. Airway pressure after turning that is much higher than it was supine means the abdomen is not free or the tube has moved.

Eyes and face. The globe must carry no pressure at any point in the case: direct pressure causes central retinal artery occlusion, a different and more preventable injury than the ischaemic optic neuropathy of long spinal operations. Use a contoured foam head support with cut-outs or skull pins, keep the head neutral and at or above the level of the heart, and look at or palpate the eyes and nose at intervals and after any table movement, recording each check. A mirror or camera system makes this easy. The forehead, chin and nose are the pressure points; the tongue should be inside the teeth with a soft bite block.

Airway. The tube is fixed for a position in which re-intubation is nearly impossible: tape that will survive saliva, the tube depth noted, a reinforced tube where the neck will be flexed. After long prone cases with large fluid volumes the face, tongue and larynx swell; check for a cuff leak and consider delayed extubation. An operating trolley stays outside the room for emergency supination, and chest compressions can be started prone if it is not immediately available.

Brachial plexus and arms. Two options: arms tucked at the sides, palms in, or arms forward on boards with the shoulders abducted and the elbows flexed. The second gives access to lines and is the default, and it is the position that produces evoked potential changes. In 1,000 monitored spine operations, position-related upper limb SSEP changes occurred in 7.0% of prone patients with the arms abducted and 7.5% of lateral patients, against 1.8-3.2% in other positions; 92% reversed when the arm was moved and none of those patients woke with a deficit. Keep abduction under 90 degrees, the elbows lower than the shoulders, the forearms pronated on padding with nothing pressing in the ulnar groove or the axilla, and the head not turned. If SSEPs are being monitored, an upper limb change is a positioning alarm first.

Everything else. Breasts are placed medially and free of the chest support, genitalia free, the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve protected from the iliac bolster (meralgia paraesthetica is the commonest nerve complaint after prone spinal surgery), knees padded and slightly flexed, feet off the end of the table or on a bolster so the toes hang free. Check radial pulses after positioning the arms: a patient with thoracic outlet narrowing can lose the pulse in abduction.

The traction table

Used for hip fracture fixation, femoral nailing, hip arthroscopy and the anterior approach to the hip. The operative foot is bound into a boot and pulled; a padded post in the perineum provides the countertraction; the other leg is moved out of the way of the image intensifier.

Pudendal nerve and perineum

The pudendal nerve and the perineal skin are trapped between the post and the pubic ramus. In a prospective study of 106 femoral nailings with a strain gauge in the post, 10 patients (9.4%) had a pudendal palsy: nine sensory, one with erectile dysfunction. The palsied patients had more than twice the traction dose (73.3 against 34.9 kilogram-hours); duration alone did not separate the groups, and adduction of the hip and reduction manoeuvres were the moments of peak force. All but one had recovered by three months. Skin necrosis of the scrotum or labia is the same injury taken further.

The modifiable factors are force and time, and the anaesthetist controls part of the first. Traction is pulling against muscle tone; a dense spinal or full neuromuscular blockade at the time of reduction or joint distraction lets the surgeon achieve the same position with less force. The other measures are a large, well-padded post placed against the medial thigh of the operative side (not centred on the perineum), genitalia checked to be free before draping, traction released whenever it is not needed, and the traction time recorded like a tourniquet time. In hip arthroscopy the convention is to keep continuous traction under two hours, and post-less systems that use table tilt and friction are an alternative.

The foot in the boot can suffer too: pressure on the dorsum, a traction injury of the sciatic or peroneal nerve with the hip flexed and the knee extended, and a missed pressure injury in the insensate foot of a blocked or diabetic patient.

Well-leg compartment syndrome

When the non-operative leg is placed in hemilithotomy (hip and knee flexed, calf resting in a support), three things happen to that calf: it is raised above the heart, so its arterial pressure falls by the hydrostatic gradient; its compartment pressure is raised by the weight of the leg on the support; and it stays there for the length of a difficult nailing. Add hypotension and the perfusion gradient of the compartment can close. The result is a compartment syndrome in the uninjured leg, discovered late because nobody is looking at that leg and the patient may have a spinal or epidural.

Prevention: prefer the scissor position (well leg extended and lowered, hip slightly extended) where the image intensifier allows; if hemilithotomy is used, support the heel or foot and not the calf, keep the leg no higher than it needs to be, lower it if the operation runs long, and avoid hypotension. On emergence and in recovery, examine the well calf. How to keep a block from hiding the diagnosis is covered in nerve injury and compartment syndrome.

In the obese patient the post, the boot and the abducted well leg are all under more load and the reduction takes longer; a radiolucent flat-top table with manual traction is the alternative the trauma literature recommends.

Preventing and documenting nerve injury

Perioperative peripheral nerve injury is uncommon and not randomly distributed. In 380,680 anaesthetics there were 112 injuries (0.03%); hypertension, diabetes and smoking were associated with injury, as were general and epidural anaesthesia and orthopaedic surgery. The first three are markers of nerves with a poor microvascular reserve: the same position that a healthy nerve tolerates for three hours injures a diabetic one.

The ASA practice advisory turns the mechanisms into rules. Ask before surgery whether the patient can comfortably adopt the planned position, and try it awake where there is doubt (the stiff shoulder, the fixed spine, covered in the orthopaedic patient). Limit arm abduction to 90 degrees in the supine patient. Keep the forearm supinated or neutral on an armboard so the ulnar groove is off the surface, and avoid prolonged elbow flexion beyond 90 degrees (the author’s rule; the advisory sets no agreed angle), which tightens the cubital tunnel. Do not hyperextend the knee or elbow or flex the hip to the point of hamstring stretch. Pad the fibular head. Recheck during the case, particularly after any table movement.

Documentation is part of prevention because it forces the check. The record should state: the position and the supports used; head and neck alignment; the position of each arm, with the abduction angle; what was padded; that the eyes were free and when they were checked; the pulses checked after positioning; traction and tourniquet times; and any pre-existing deficit or paraesthesia, recorded before the anaesthetic. A deficit found afterwards is examined and mapped the same day, separated from residual block by its distribution and time course, and followed through the pathway in nerve injury and compartment syndrome.

Edge cases

The hypertensive patient with carotid stenosis listed for beach chair shoulder surgery. The lower limit of autoregulation is high and the collateral supply is poor. Options in order of preference: block with light sedation and a normal pressure; general anaesthesia with an arterial line levelled at the meatus and cerebral oximetry; or a request for the lateral position.

The ankylosed or severely kyphotic spine. The patient is positioned to the deformity, not to the table. Any attempt to straighten a fused spine under anaesthesia risks fracture and cord injury.

The shoulder that will not abduct. A frozen or arthritic shoulder on the non-operative side cannot go on an armboard at 90 degrees in the prone or supine position without stretching the plexus. Find out awake and tuck that arm.

The long case that changes position. Supine to lateral to prone in a single anaesthetic (combined anterior-posterior spine, pelvic fixation) repeats every risk at each turn. Re-run the whole check each time: tube, eyes, arms, abdomen, pulses.

The blocked limb. A limb with a dense block is positioned for the rest of the day by other people. Sling and protect the blocked arm, and tell the ward that the blocked leg will not report pressure on its heel or peroneal nerve.

  9. Welch MB, Brummett CM, Welch TD, et al. Perioperative peripheral nerve injuries: a retrospective study of 380,680 cases during a 10-year period at a single institution. Anesthesiology 2009;111:490-497

  10. Flierl MA, Stahel PF, Hak DJ, Morgan SJ, Smith WR. Traction table-related complications in orthopaedic surgery. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2010;18:668-675
    Review of perineal soft-tissue injury, pudendal and other nerve palsies and well-leg compartment syndrome on the traction table, with prevention by positioning, minimum traction time and a flat-top table for obese patients
  11. Brumback RJ, Ellison TS, Molligan H, et al. Pudendal nerve palsy complicating intramedullary nailing of the femur. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1992;74:1450-1455
    Prospective study of 106 femoral nailings with a strain gauge in the perineal post: 10 pudendal palsies (nine sensory, one with erectile dysfunction), associated with the magnitude of traction (73.3 versus 34.9 kilogram-hours) and not its duration alone; hip adduction and reduction manoeuvres raised the force; all but one resolved by three months

Part A

The block menu: regional anaesthesia keyed to the operation

Choosing a block is matching three maps: which nerves supply the tissue the surgeon will cut, which of those the block reaches, and which nerves it paralyses that the patient needs afterwards. The useful blocks are therefore defined as much by what they spare as by what they cover: a superior trunk or suprascapular block trades a little early analgesia for a working diaphragm, an adductor canal block trades the back of the knee for quadriceps that still lift the leg, and a block chosen for an injured tibia is the one that leaves ischaemic pain reportable. A single shot with dexamethasone 8-10 mg IV is the default for most operations; a catheter earns its logistics only where pain is severe beyond 24 hours, and in the shoulder a randomised trial found no added benefit once dexamethasone and multimodal analgesia were in place. Rebound pain affects about half of ambulatory block patients and is reduced by intravenous dexamethasone and by oral analgesia started before the block fades; liposomal bupivacaine does not solve it. Dose the local anaesthetic as one budget shared with the surgeon's infiltration, know where the lipid is, and record the limb's neurology before the needle goes in.

How to read the menu

A block is chosen by laying three maps over each other.

The first map is the innervation of what the surgeon cuts. Skin is the least of it. Joints are supplied by articular branches of every nerve that crosses them, bone by its periosteal and endosteal nerves, and the deep structures follow sclerotomes, not dermatomes: the shoulder joint is C5-6 whatever the skin over the incision says, and the back of the knee capsule is tibial and obturator even though the incision is anterior.

The second map is what the block reaches. Each block has a reliable core and an unreliable edge, and the edge is where a “failed” block is usually a correctly working block that was never going to cover that structure.

The third map is what else the block takes. Motor block and collateral nerve block are the price: the phrenic nerve with an interscalene injection, the quadriceps with a femoral block, the foot with a sciatic block, and in an injured limb the ability to feel ischaemic muscle.

The operation sets the first map and the patient sets the tolerance for the third. The pain model sets how long the block needs to last.

Shoulder

The joint, the cuff, the subacromial bursa and most of the capsule are supplied by the suprascapular nerve (posterior and superior, about two thirds of the joint) and the axillary nerve (anterior and inferior), with contributions from the lateral pectoral and subscapular nerves. All come from C5-6 through the superior trunk. The skin over the top of the shoulder is C3-4 (supraclavicular nerves) and the axilla and medial arm are T2.

Block Covers Spares or misses Cost
Interscalene Whole joint, C4 cape by spread Posterior portal and axilla (T2); ulnar side of hand Phrenic paresis near-universal at conventional volumes; Horner, hoarseness
Superior trunk As interscalene for the joint Supraclavicular nerves (add a superficial cervical plexus block for clavicle and superior incisions) Phrenic paresis less complete
Suprascapular plus axillary Most of the joint Anterior capsule (lateral pectoral, subscapular); skin No phrenic block; two injections; not a surgical block
Supraclavicular or infraclavicular plus suprascapular Joint by a different route Variable Lower phrenic risk; less evidence

The phrenic nerve lies on the anterior scalene a few millimetres from the C5 root. With the volumes once used, hemidiaphragmatic paresis occurred in every patient. Low volume, dilute solution and extrafascial injection reduce it, but no single measure brings it below about 20%. Moving distally to the superior trunk gave non-inferior analgesia at 24 hours with paresis in 76% against 98% and, more usefully, complete paresis in 5% against 73%. Suprascapular block avoids the phrenic nerve altogether: across 16 trials it matched interscalene block for 24-hour opioid use and for pain at every time after the recovery room, with fewer respiratory complications. PROSPECT accepts either for rotator cuff repair.

So the menu reads: interscalene or superior trunk block for arthroplasty, reverse arthroplasty, cuff repair and open stabilisation in a patient with normal lungs; superior trunk in the patient with moderate respiratory disease or obesity; suprascapular plus axillary under general anaesthesia when a 25% fall in vital capacity cannot be afforded (severe COPD, contralateral phrenic palsy or pneumonectomy); and for subacromial decompression, diagnostic arthroscopy and capsular release, a single shot or a suprascapular block is enough. Clavicle surgery needs C3-4 as well as C5-6. After a proximal humerus fracture or dislocation, test and record axillary nerve function before any block.

Elbow

All four terminal nerves cross the elbow and all supply the joint, and the medial skin is supplied by the medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm, so the block must be at the plexus: supraclavicular, infraclavicular or axillary with a separate musculocutaneous injection. Infraclavicular is the catheter site of choice because the pectoral muscles hold the catheter and the site is away from the field. Supraclavicular injection blocks the phrenic nerve in a substantial minority.

What the block hides matters more here than anywhere else in the upper limb. After distal humerus or olecranon fixation and ulnar nerve transposition the surgeon wants to know that the ulnar nerve works; after distal biceps repair the posterior interosseous and lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerves are the ones at risk; after humeral shaft fixation it is the radial nerve. Three workable answers: block after the surgeon has examined the patient in recovery; use a short-acting agent for surgery and accept oral analgesia afterwards; or place a catheter, leave it unloaded until the examination is done, then start it. For elbow arthroplasty and arthrolysis, where continuous passive motion is the point of the operation, a catheter has a strong claim.

Wrist and hand

Below the elbow the choice is between a plexus block that gives a numb, paralysed arm with tourniquet tolerance, and distal blocks that keep the elbow and shoulder working.

Operation Defensible default Reason
Distal radius ORIF, wrist fusion, scaphoid Axillary, infraclavicular or supraclavicular block, long-acting Bone surgery with an upper arm tourniquet; rebound pain is the trap
Carpal tunnel, trigger finger Surgeon’s local infiltration Pain score 1; a plexus block is a worse experience than the operation
Dupuytren’s, trapeziectomy Plexus block, or short-acting plexus block plus long-acting forearm blocks Anaesthesia from the first, analgesia from the second, without a flail arm overnight
Tendon repair where active movement is tested Wide-awake local with adrenaline, no tourniquet The patient moves the repair on request

A forearm tourniquet is tolerated for about 20 minutes with distal blocks alone. The combination of a short-acting proximal block for surgery and long-acting blocks of the median, ulnar and radial nerves in the forearm gives 12 hours of hand analgesia with a shoulder and elbow that work by the time the patient is home, which is the author’s preference for day-case hand surgery.

Hip

The anterior capsule, which carries most of the nociceptors, is supplied by articular branches of the femoral, obturator and accessory obturator nerves; the posterior capsule by the sciatic nerve, the nerve to quadratus femoris and the superior gluteal nerve. The skin of the lateral and posterior approaches is lateral femoral cutaneous, subcostal and cluneal.

Block Covers Spares or misses Cost
Fascia iliaca (suprainguinal) Femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, variable obturator Posterior capsule Quadriceps weakness
Femoral Anterior capsule in part, anterior thigh Obturator, lateral skin, posterior capsule Quadriceps weakness, falls
PENG Anterior capsule articular branches Skin, posterior capsule Motor-sparing in principle; femoral spread with larger volumes
Lumbar plexus Femoral, obturator, lateral femoral cutaneous Posterior capsule Deep block: neuraxial anticoagulant rules, epidural spread
Spinal Everything Nothing, for 2-4 h No analgesia after it wears off unless an opioid is added

PROSPECT for total hip arthroplasty recommends a fascia iliaca block or local infiltration analgesia on top of paracetamol, an NSAID and dexamethasone, and recommends against femoral block, lumbar plexus block and epidural because the weakness, falls and hypotension outweigh the analgesia in an operation whose pain is moderate and short. That fits the mechanism: THA is a pain score 2-3 bone operation and the patient needs to walk the same day. The defensible default is a spinal, surgeon infiltration, and no motor-blocking peripheral block; fascia iliaca or PENG is added for the patient in whom basic analgesics are contraindicated or pain is expected to be high.

For hip fracture the block is given on arrival, not in theatre: femoral or fascia iliaca block reduces pain on movement and opioid use while the patient waits, and quadriceps weakness matters less before fixation. The PENG block was described for exactly this purpose and is an alternative. For hip arthroscopy the pain is capsular and fluid-related and short-lived; a fascia iliaca block adds quadriceps weakness for a modest gain, and intra-articular or portal local anaesthetic is usually enough. Periacetabular osteotomy and revision arthroplasty are where an epidural, a lumbar plexus catheter or intrathecal morphine still have a place.

Knee

The anterior knee is supplied by the saphenous nerve and the nerves to the vasti (all in or near the adductor canal) with the anterior obturator; the posterior capsule by the tibial nerve and the posterior obturator through the popliteal plexus; the lateral side by genicular branches of the common peroneal nerve.

The quadriceps question is the centre of the knee menu. A femoral block gives excellent anterior analgesia and takes the quadriceps with it: in a randomised comparison of continuous blocks after knee replacement, quadriceps strength was 18% of baseline with a femoral catheter and 52% with an adductor canal catheter, with no difference in pain or morphine use. A patient who cannot lock the knee cannot walk safely on day 0, and a buckling knee is how inpatient falls after arthroplasty happen. PROSPECT for primary TKA therefore recommends a single-shot adductor canal block with surgeon periarticular infiltration and intravenous dexamethasone.

The adductor canal block misses the back of the knee. The options are surgeon infiltration of the posterior capsule under direct vision, an IPACK injection (between the popliteal artery and the capsule), or a sciatic block. Sciatic block gives the best posterior analgesia and has two costs: a foot drop that delays walking, and a foot drop that hides a common peroneal palsy, which is the nerve injury of knee replacement in a valgus or flexed knee and of high tibial osteotomy. The defensible default is infiltration or IPACK, with sciatic block reserved for revision and for patients with severe posterior pain after surgery.

ACL reconstruction: adductor canal block; the hamstring harvest site is posterior and medial and is not covered, and a femoral block is avoided because early quadriceps activation is the rehabilitation. Multiligament reconstruction and quadriceps or patellar tendon repair: pain score 4-5, catheter territory; for multiligament reconstruction an adductor canal catheter, because the braced knee still needs a quadriceps and the sciatic territory is kept examinable; for extensor mechanism repair the limb is braced in extension so quadriceps weakness costs less. Knee arthroscopy: portal infiltration only. Tibial plateau fixation and tibial nailing: the compartment syndrome question decides, below.

Ankle and foot

Everything below the knee is sciatic except a medial strip of skin to the medial malleolus and sometimes the medial midfoot, which is saphenous.

Operation Block Notes
Forefoot surgery Ankle block Ankle motor function kept; walks out in a stiff shoe; calf or ankle tourniquet tolerated for short cases
Ankle fracture fixation, Achilles repair Popliteal sciatic plus saphenous, single shot Bone surgery in the young: the highest rebound risk
Hindfoot fusion, calcaneal fixation, ankle replacement, pilon Popliteal catheter Among the most painful operations in the 179-procedure cohort; pain lasts beyond any single shot
Amputation Sciatic catheter, plus femoral or adductor canal for a below-knee stump Surgeon-placed perineural catheters are an alternative

A popliteal block does not cover a thigh tourniquet, so the anaesthetic is a spinal or general anaesthetic with the block for analgesia, or the surgeon uses a calf cuff. The blocked foot is insensate and the patient is on crutches: non-weight-bearing instructions, a protected heel and a warning about burns and pressure are part of the block.

Spine

Regional techniques for spinal surgery are fascial plane blocks (erector spinae, thoracolumbar interfascial plane), surgeon wound infiltration and intrathecal morphine placed by the surgeon or anaesthetist. The plane blocks reduce early opioid use in small trials and their effect is short; for fusion the stronger options are intrathecal morphine and a multimodal intravenous regimen, covered in spine essentials. No block should obscure the first postoperative neurological examination.

Single shot or catheter

A single shot of ropivacaine or bupivacaine lasts 10-16 hours and, with dexamethasone, 20-24 hours. A catheter is justified when the operation’s pain is severe for longer than that and movement-evoked (pain score 4-5 in this book’s scale), when the patient is opioid-tolerant, or when early forced movement is the purpose of the surgery.

The evidence is weaker than the logic. In the shoulder, a randomised trial of 60 arthroplasty and cuff repair patients who all received dexamethasone and multimodal analgesia found that adding a ropivacaine infusion to day 2 changed neither morphine use nor pain scores. The catheter’s advantage has shrunk as the single shot has lengthened, and the default in most operations has moved to a single shot with intravenous dexamethasone and a planned oral regimen, with catheters selective.

Ambulatory catheter logistics, where a service offers them: an elastomeric pump with ropivacaine 0.2% at 5-8 mL/h with or without a patient bolus; written and verbal instructions; a named 24-hour contact; a daily telephone call; a carer at home for the first night; catheter removal by the patient or carer at 48-72 hours with the tip checked. Large prospective series report few serious complications. The failure modes are leakage, dislodgement and secondary block failure, and for interscalene infusions continuous phrenic paresis, which excludes patients with limited respiratory reserve. Exclude patients who live alone, cannot be reached by telephone, or have significant renal or hepatic impairment.

Adjuncts

Dexamethasone. Intravenous and perineural routes were equivalent in a placebo-controlled interscalene trial: median analgesia 757 minutes with ropivacaine alone, 1,405 minutes with perineural and 1,275 minutes with intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg. Perineural dosing shows a ceiling at 4 mg and is off-label. Because the intravenous route also treats nausea, is recommended by every PROSPECT guideline cited here and is associated with less rebound pain, dexamethasone 8-10 mg IV at induction is the default and perineural use adds little. Expect a transient rise in glucose in diabetic patients.

Dexmedetomidine. Perineural dexmedetomidine 50-60 micrograms prolongs sensory block and analgesia by more than half, prolongs motor block by the same proportion, and causes bradycardia and hypotension. It is useful when dexamethasone is not wanted; the motor prolongation is a cost in day surgery.

Adrenaline marks intravascular injection and adds little duration to ropivacaine. Clonidine adds a modest prolongation with sedation and hypotension.

Liposomal bupivacaine. The plain reading of the evidence is that it does not deliver what the formulation promises. In nerve blocks, the pooled benefit over plain bupivacaine at 24-72 hours was 1.0 cm.h of area under the pain curve, clinically unimportant, and it vanished when the one industry-sponsored trial was removed. Infiltrated, it beat plain local anaesthetic in 4 of 36 trials, and a nerve block with plain bupivacaine beat infiltrated liposomal bupivacaine in 11 of 12. Positive results clustered in trials at high risk of bias. It is not a substitute for a catheter.

Rebound pain

Rebound pain is the abrupt arrival of severe pain when a dense block resolves, typically 12-24 hours after surgery, at night, at home, in a patient who has taken no analgesia because nothing hurt. In 972 ambulatory patients it occurred in 49.6%. The independent associations were bone surgery, female sex, younger age and the absence of intravenous dexamethasone.

The plan that follows: give dexamethasone 8-10 mg IV; start regular paracetamol and an NSAID before the block wears off, not after; tell the patient the hour at which the block is expected to fade and to take the first opioid dose at the first tingling or at bedtime, whichever comes first; and for bone surgery in a young patient (ankle fixation, distal radius ORIF) consider whether a shorter block that fades in daylight is kinder than a long one that fades at 2 am. For operations with a pain score of 1-2 a long-acting block can create a worse night than the operation would have.

Local anaesthetic dose and LAST

Conventional maximum doses, by lean body weight: bupivacaine and levobupivacaine 2 mg/kg, ropivacaine 3 mg/kg, lidocaine 3 mg/kg plain and 7 mg/kg with adrenaline. Reduce in the frail and elderly, in hepatic or cardiac failure and in pregnancy. The limits are crude and the site matters more than the number, but they are the budget, and in arthroplasty the budget is shared: surgeon infiltration of ropivacaine 300 mg in a knee plus an adductor canal block of 100 mg exceeds 3 mg/kg in any patient under 130 kg. Agree the total before the first syringe is drawn up.

For toxicity the ASRA checklist governs: stop injecting, call for help and the lipid, manage the airway and stop seizures with a benzodiazepine, then lipid emulsion 20%. Over 70 kg: 100 mL over 2-3 minutes then 200-250 mL over 15-20 minutes. Under 70 kg: 1.5 mL/kg then 0.25 mL/kg/min. Repeat the bolus or double the infusion if the circulation remains unstable, to a ceiling of about 12 mL/kg. Adrenaline in small boluses of 1 microgram/kg or less; avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, beta blockers and further local anaesthetic; avoid propofol when the circulation is unstable. Observe for at least two hours after a seizure and four to six hours after cardiovascular toxicity.

Before the needle: neurology and the compartment question

Record the limb’s neurology before the block: pre-existing numbness or weakness, the specific nerve at risk from the injury or operation, and the time and expected duration of the block so that a deficit persisting beyond it triggers action. The reasoning and the pathway are in nerve injury and compartment syndrome, as is the argument about blocking a limb at risk of compartment syndrome. The short version for the menu: in a tibial fracture, a high-energy forearm fracture or a crush injury, a dense, long block that outlasts surgery by many hours is avoided; a low-concentration block or catheter with structured surveillance is acceptable; and the decision is made with the surgeon and documented.
