Electrophysiology has two uses at two times. Done in the first few days, before Wallerian degeneration has reached the muscle, an abnormal study reveals a lesion that pre-dated the operation. Done at two to three weeks, it localises the lesion (root, plexus, nerve; at the block site or the surgical site or the tourniquet) and grades it. Most deficits are neurapraxias and resolve; the patient needs to be told that, given a named follow-up, and referred early for hand therapy or a foot-drop splint if function is affected. Disclosure and a contemporaneous record of the examination are part of the treatment.

Compartment syndrome: the mechanism and who gets it

A muscle compartment is a closed fascial envelope. Bleeding and oedema after injury or reperfusion raise the pressure inside it; when the pressure approaches the diastolic pressure the capillaries close, muscle and nerve become ischaemic, ischaemic tissue swells further, and the cycle runs to necrosis within hours. The perfusion pressure of the compartment is the diastolic pressure minus the compartment pressure, which is why a hypotensive patient develops the syndrome at a lower compartment pressure, and why an elevated limb fares worse than one at heart level.

The symptom is ischaemic muscle pain: severe, escalating, out of proportion to the injury, and provoked by passively stretching the muscles of the compartment. Paraesthesia follows. Paralysis and pulselessness are late and mean the muscle is already lost.

The patient at risk is a young man with a tibial fracture. In 164 cases, 69% had a fracture and about half of those were tibial shaft; most patients were men under 35, whose muscle bulk fills the compartment; high-energy distal radius and forearm fractures were the upper limb equivalent; soft-tissue injury without fracture was the second commonest cause; and one tenth of patients were anticoagulated or had a bleeding disorder. In orthopaedic lists the risk therefore sits with tibial nailing and plateau fixation, open and high-energy fractures, forearm and high-energy distal radius fractures, crush injury, revascularised limbs, calcaneal and Lisfranc injuries in the foot, and the uninjured leg held in hemilithotomy on a traction table. Elective surgery is not immune: tibial osteotomy and prolonged tourniquet cases produce occasional cases. The operation itself is described in compartment syndrome and fasciotomy.

Diagnosis is clinical, supported by pressure measurement. In 116 tibial fractures monitored continuously, a differential pressure below 30 mmHg as the threshold for fasciotomy missed no case, while an absolute pressure threshold of 30 mmHg would have sent 43% of patients for an unnecessary fasciotomy.

Does regional anaesthesia hide it: the actual evidence

There are no randomised trials and there will not be. The evidence is case reports, and a careful reading of them does not support the belief that blocks hide compartment syndrome.

The systematic review found 28 reports, 23 of them about epidurals. In 32 of 35 patients the classic symptoms and signs were present despite the epidural, and 18 had documented breakthrough pain. The delays in the reports were mostly failures to act on findings that were there. The reviewers concluded that there is no convincing evidence that patient-controlled opioid analgesia or regional analgesia delays diagnosis provided patients are adequately monitored, and made the point that is usually left out of the debate: pain is an unreliable sign with any analgesic technique, including an opioid PCA, and examination is unreliable too.

The physiological explanation for breakthrough is that ischaemic pain is an intense, summating stimulus that a low-concentration sensory block does not abolish. A patient whose block or epidural was working and who now has escalating pain, or rising opioid demand, has announced the diagnosis. That is the most useful sign available, and it is lost only if the block is dense enough to produce surgical anaesthesia of the whole limb for many hours, or if the response to the pain is a top-up.

The Association of Anaesthetists guideline for lower leg trauma, written with orthopaedic surgeons, turns this into practice. Avoid neuraxial or peripheral techniques that give dense blocks lasting well beyond the surgery. Single-shot or continuous peripheral blocks with lower concentrations of local anaesthetic and without adjuncts are not associated with delayed diagnosis provided surveillance is appropriate. Observations are made at set intervals by staff trained to recognise the syndrome, using an objective scoring chart. The patient is told the options and consents. And neither the surgeon nor the anaesthetist has a veto over a treatment recommended by the other: the decision is joint.

How to block when the risk exists

  1. Name the risk aloud at the briefing and agree the plan with the surgeon. Record the discussion and the patient’s consent.
  2. For the anaesthetic, use a general anaesthetic or a spinal that will have gone within two to three hours. Avoid long-acting intrathecal doses and avoid an epidural infusion at concentrations that give a motor block.
  3. For analgesia, use a sensory-weighted, low-concentration block: ropivacaine 0.2% or less. Leave out perineural adjuncts, and consider omitting intravenous dexamethasone on the day if its only purpose is to prolong the block; do not add dexmedetomidine or clonidine. A catheter that can be turned down or off is safer than a single shot that cannot be reversed.
  4. Choose the territory with the compartments in mind. For a tibial plateau or shaft fracture an adductor canal block treats the anterior knee and medial leg and leaves the deep and anterior compartments reporting; a dense sciatic block does not. For forearm fractures a low-dose block with early offset is preferred to a long, dense plexus block.
  5. Start scheduled surveillance in recovery and continue for 24-48 hours: pain score at rest and on passive stretch of the toes or fingers, analgesic consumption, compartment tenseness, sensation and movement, hourly at first, on a chart with a stated escalation trigger.
  6. Treat breakthrough pain as a diagnosis, not a failure of analgesia. Nobody boluses the catheter or increases the PCA until the limb has been examined by someone who can act.
  7. Split casts and dressings to skin at the first concern, keep the limb at heart level, and keep the blood pressure normal.
  8. Use continuous compartment pressure monitoring where it is available for the patient who cannot report: the obtunded, the intubated polytrauma patient, the child, and by extension the patient whose block is denser than intended.

Once a fasciotomy has been done and the post-release neurological examination is recorded, the masking argument is over; the fasciotomy card sets out when a block or catheter is added.

Edge cases

The intubated polytrauma patient. No block is hiding anything, and nobody is examining either. Pressure monitoring or scheduled clinical checks by the surgical team are the only surveillance; see polytrauma.

The anticoagulated patient with a minor injury. Bleeding into a compartment after a trivial fracture or a contusion is over-represented in the series. A low threshold for suspicion applies whatever the analgesia.

The elective osteotomy. The risk is low but real, and the peroneal nerve is also at risk. An adductor canal block and infiltration, no sciatic block, and a documented foot examination in recovery covers both.

The block that will not wear off. A single-shot block persisting beyond 24-36 hours with dexamethasone, or 48 hours at the outside, is investigated as a nerve injury, starting with the pathway above. Reassurance without examination is the error.

The patient who already has a deficit and needs a block. Document it in detail, explain the smaller margin, reduce concentration and volume, and proceed if the analgesic benefit is real. A carefully recorded pre-existing deficit protects the patient’s follow-up as well as the anaesthetist.

Part A

Opioid-tolerant and chronic pain patients

The opioid-tolerant patient has three separate problems that are easy to merge into one: a baseline requirement that must be supplied or withdrawal follows, a shifted dose-response so that acute doses need to be larger, and a sensitised nervous system that makes the same operation hurt more. The plan is built before admission with the pain service and the usual prescriber: verify and continue the baseline including methadone and buprenorphine, put the weight of the analgesia on techniques that do not act at the opioid receptor (a block or catheter, ketamine, an NSAID), size the rescue dose from the patient's own daily total, and watch sedation, because tolerance to respiratory depression is less dependable than tolerance to analgesia. Buprenorphine should not be routinely stopped. About a quarter of arthroplasty patients take opioids beforehand and do worse in absolute terms, but they still benefit from the operation, and those who taper before surgery do as well as patients who never took them. The discharge plan names a date for return to baseline and a single prescriber; pain catastrophising identifies who will struggle but has not been shown to be fixed by pre-operative coping-skills training.

Three problems, not one

A patient who has taken opioids every day for months arrives with three distinct changes, and each needs its own answer.

Dependence. The nervous system has adapted to the drug being present. Remove it and a withdrawal syndrome begins within 6-24 hours for short-acting opioids and later for methadone and buprenorphine: yawning, sweating, gooseflesh, restlessness, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, tachycardia, hypertension and pain everywhere. In a surgical ward this is misread as uncontrolled surgical pain, anxiety or delirium. The answer is to supply the baseline, every day, by some route.

Tolerance. Receptor desensitisation and downstream adaptation shift the dose-response curve to the right. A dose that would settle an opioid-naive patient does little. The answer is larger acute doses, calculated from what the patient already takes, on top of the baseline and not instead of it. Tolerance is uneven: it develops fully to nausea and largely to analgesia and sedation, but tolerance to respiratory depression is incomplete and unreliable, and it does not protect against the additive effect of benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids and alcohol. Large doses in a tolerant patient are necessary and are still dangerous.

Sensitisation. Long-term opioid exposure and chronic pain both prime the dorsal horn: NMDA receptor activity is up, descending inhibition is down, and the same incision produces more pain for longer. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia is the name when the opioid is the cause. More opioid does not fix it and may worsen it. The answer is analgesia that does not go through the opioid receptor: a block that stops the input arriving, ketamine at the NMDA receptor, an NSAID at the wound.

  Problem          What it looks like             Answer
  ---------------  -----------------------------  --------------------------------
  Dependence       withdrawal if a dose is missed  continue the baseline, any route
  Tolerance        usual doses do nothing          rescue sized from daily total
  Sensitisation    more pain, wider, longer        block or catheter, ketamine, NSAID

The usual working definition of tolerance is 60 mg or more of oral morphine equivalent a day for a week or more, but the plan is needed from well below that, and the buprenorphine patch and tramadol users in every arthroplasty clinic are on the same spectrum.

Who they are in an orthopaedic list

About a quarter of patients presenting for hip or knee replacement have been prescribed opioids for the joint. In the meta-analysis of six studies they had worse pain and function scores after surgery in absolute terms, with a standardised difference of about half a standard deviation, but their relative improvement was not significantly different: they start worse, improve by a similar amount, and finish worse. They should be counselled, not refused. The modifiable part is the dose. In matched cohorts, chronic opioid users who weaned successfully before arthroplasty improved as much as patients who had never taken opioids, and far more than those who did not wean.

The other groups: spinal surgery patients, in whom long-term opioid use is the norm and the operation is among the most painful; patients having repeated operations for infected joints or bone infection; those on methadone or buprenorphine for opioid use disorder; people with implanted intrathecal pumps; cancer patients with metastatic fractures; and amputees with months of ischaemic pain behind them.

Planning with the pain service

The plan is made at pre-admission, not in the anaesthetic bay.

  1. Establish the real baseline: every opioid, dose, formulation and time of last dose, cross-checked against the dispensing record or real-time prescription monitoring and, for methadone and buprenorphine maintenance, with the prescriber or dispensing pharmacy. Include gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, cannabis and alcohol.
  2. Decide whether there is time to taper. For elective arthroplasty weeks away, a reduction agreed with the general practitioner is worth attempting, on the cohort evidence above. Do not attempt a taper in the fortnight before surgery.
  3. Set expectations with the patient. Pain scores will be higher than the patient in the next bed. The target is function (coughing, sitting out, physiotherapy), not a number. The baseline will be continued. Extra opioid will be given and then withdrawn on a schedule. Agreeing this before surgery prevents most of the conflict afterwards.
  4. Choose the regional technique and book what it needs: a catheter, an epidural, a monitored bed for a ketamine infusion.
  5. Write the plan where the ward will find it: baseline, adjuncts, rescue dose, escalation, and who prescribes at discharge.
  6. Involve the acute pain service from recovery, with daily review.

Continuing the baseline

Oral modified-release opioids are taken as usual on the morning of surgery with a sip of water and restarted at the next due time. If the gut will not be available, the baseline is converted to an intravenous equivalent and given as the background of a PCA or a separate infusion. Conversion ratios are approximations: oral morphine 30 mg is about 10 mg intravenous morphine, oral oxycodone 20 mg is about oral morphine 30 mg, and a calculator is preferable to memory. When rotating to a different opioid, reduce the calculated dose by a quarter to a half for incomplete cross-tolerance; when continuing the same opioid, do not.

Transdermal fentanyl and buprenorphine patches stay on. Note the site, keep forced-air warming and heating pads off a fentanyl patch (heat increases absorption), and check it is still attached after positioning and skin preparation.

Intrathecal pumps keep running. Record the drug, the concentration, the daily dose and the pump site; keep the pump and catheter out of the surgical field and the diathermy path; and remember that the intrathecal dose does not prevent systemic withdrawal if the patient’s oral opioids are stopped.

Buprenorphine

Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with very high receptor affinity and a long duration. The old practice of stopping it days before surgery, so that full agonists could work, exchanged a theoretical problem for two real ones: withdrawal and uncontrolled pain in the gap, and relapse or overdose in patients treated for opioid use disorder. The multi-society consensus is unambiguous: do not routinely discontinue buprenorphine perioperatively.

In practice: low-dose patches (5-40 micrograms/h) are continued and ignored for dosing purposes. Sublingual maintenance doses are continued, and dividing the daily dose into three or four parts is a consensus option (low certainty), because analgesia lasts 6-8 hours while withdrawal suppression lasts 24 hours or more. Full agonists still work on top of buprenorphine, at higher doses than usual, and the potent high-affinity agonists (fentanyl, hydromorphone) are the logical choice for PCA. The consensus panel allows a taper to 16 mg to be considered for patients on higher doses facing very painful surgery, in centres with integrated addiction and acute pain services; that is expert opinion and is done with the prescriber, never unilaterally. Depot buprenorphine cannot be withdrawn and is managed the same way: regional technique, ketamine, and titrated full agonist.

Methadone

Maintenance methadone is continued at the verified dose. Verify before charting: the prescriber or pharmacy confirms the dose and the date last dispensed, because a patient who has missed several days has lost tolerance and a full dose can kill. Once-daily dosing suppresses withdrawal for 24 hours but gives only 6-8 hours of analgesia, so splitting the same total into two or three doses helps. If the patient cannot swallow, give it parenterally at about half to two thirds of the oral dose in divided doses. Check the QT interval before adding ondansetron, droperidol or other QT-prolonging drugs.

Methadone is also a useful intraoperative opioid in its own right, for tolerant and non-tolerant patients, because one dose lasts a day or more and it has NMDA antagonist activity. In a blinded trial in posterior spinal fusion, methadone 0.2 mg/kg IV at the start of surgery roughly halved hydromorphone use on day 1 compared with hydromorphone at closure, with lower use on days 2 and 3 and lower pain scores at most assessments. PROSPECT does not recommend it for complex spine surgery, on comparator and safety grounds. Dose on ideal body weight, reduce in the elderly and in sleep apnoea, and make sure the ward knows a long-acting opioid has been given.

Ketamine

Ketamine is the adjunct with direct evidence in this population. In 102 opioid-dependent patients having major lumbar surgery, ketamine 0.5 mg/kg IV at induction followed by 10 micrograms/kg/min until closure reduced morphine consumption at 24 and 48 hours and, unexpectedly, at six weeks, with lower pain intensity at six weeks and no excess of side effects. The mechanism fits the problem: NMDA antagonism opposes both central sensitisation and opioid-induced hyperalgesia.

The ASRA, AAPM and ASA consensus guideline supports subanaesthetic ketamine for acute pain with opioid-tolerant patients and painful surgery as the leading indications, bolus doses up to about 0.35 mg/kg and infusions generally no higher than 1 mg/kg/h outside intensive care. Ward practice is far lower than that ceiling: 0.1-0.2 mg/kg/h (typically 5-15 mg/h) continued for 24-72 hours gives most of the benefit with few psychotomimetic effects. Contraindications are poorly controlled cardiovascular disease, active psychosis, severe liver disease and pregnancy. Vivid dreams and dysphoria are dose-related; reduce the rate before abandoning the drug.

Regional and catheter techniques

A block is the most effective opioid-sparing measure available because it removes the nociceptive input instead of competing with it at a desensitised receptor. Throughout this book the opioid-tolerant patient is the standing indication to move one step up the ladder: from no block to a single shot, from a single shot to a catheter, from a catheter for two days to one for three or four. For knee replacement that means an adductor canal catheter with surgeon infiltration, and a low threshold for adding a sciatic or IPACK component; for cuff repair and shoulder arthroplasty an interscalene catheter; for revision knee and multilevel fusion, epidural or intrathecal opioid as part of the plan. The menu is in the block menu.

Two cautions. A perfect block does not treat withdrawal: the baseline opioid continues regardless. And the block ends: the rebound when a single shot wears off is worse in a sensitised patient, so the oral and ketamine components must already be running.

Intrathecal morphine works in tolerant patients with a blunted effect for a given dose; conventional doses (100-200 micrograms) are still used, the baseline systemic opioid is continued, and monitoring is as for any patient.

The non-opioid base is used at full strength: regular paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor unless truly contraindicated, and dexamethasone. Gabapentinoids are continued if the patient already takes them and are not started for the occasion, because the added sedation and respiratory depression outweigh a small analgesic gain. Clonidine treats the autonomic symptoms of withdrawal and adds modest analgesia.

Calculating the rescue dose

The rescue dose is derived from the patient’s total daily opioid, not from the standard chart.

  Baseline         oxycodone MR 40 mg twice daily = 80 mg oral oxycodone/day
                   = about 120 mg oral morphine equivalent/day
  Continue         40 mg MR twice daily, unchanged
  Breakthrough     one sixth of the daily total: 80 / 6 = about 13 mg
                   -> oxycodone IR 10-15 mg oral, 2-hourly as needed
  If nil by mouth  baseline = about 40 mg IV morphine/24 h (1.5-2 mg/h background)
                   PCA bolus 2-3 mg morphine, 5 min lockout, reassess at 4 h
  Review           total used in 24 h tells you tomorrow's dose

One sixth of the 24-hour total (some services use one tenth) as an immediate-release dose every two to three hours is the conventional breakthrough dose. For PCA, start with a bolus about double the standard and adjust it to the pattern of use: a patient pressing every lockout with good effect each time needs a bigger bolus, not a background. A background infusion is used only to replace a baseline that cannot be given by mouth. Expect total requirements two to three times those of an opioid-naive patient for the same operation, and expect them to fall more slowly.

Monitor sedation, not just respiratory rate. A rising sedation score in a tolerant patient on a high dose is the early sign of opioid-induced ventilatory impairment, and the fix is a dose reduction and a non-opioid, not naloxone by reflex. If naloxone is needed, titrate in 40 microgram increments: a full ampoule precipitates acute withdrawal and severe pain.

Opioid use disorder

On maintenance treatment. Covered above: continue methadone or buprenorphine, verify the dose, add analgesia on top, and tell the patient plainly that maintenance treatment is not analgesia and that their pain will be treated. Fear of being under-treated is the commonest reason these patients discharge themselves.

Untreated, active use. The baseline is unknown and often understated or overstated. Titrate to effect with a PCA, start ketamine, and use the regional technique. Treat withdrawal when it appears. The consensus panel supports starting buprenorphine during the admission in a patient who wants treatment, with the addiction medicine service; an orthopaedic admission is an opportunity as well as a problem.

In recovery and abstinent. The patient may ask for no opioids at all. A regional technique with ketamine and full non-opioid analgesia can achieve that for many operations. Where it cannot, untreated severe pain is itself a relapse risk; a short, supervised course agreed in advance, with the patient’s support person and general practitioner informed, is the defensible position.

On naltrexone. Oral naltrexone is stopped 72 hours before elective surgery. Depot or implanted naltrexone blocks opioid analgesia for weeks: time elective surgery for the end of the dosing interval, plan for regional and non-opioid analgesia, and be aware that opioid given in escalating doses against the blockade becomes an overdose as the blockade fades.

Discharge and weaning

The consensus statement on preventing opioid-related harm sets the general rules: judge analgesia by function, avoid modified-release and transdermal opioids for acute pain, limit the quantity supplied, give explicit instructions for stopping, no automatic repeats, and advice on storage and disposal. For the tolerant patient three additions apply.

Separate the two prescriptions. The baseline continues under its usual prescriber at its usual dose. The acute supplement is an immediate-release opioid with a quantity and an end date, and it is the only thing the hospital prescribes.

Write the reverse taper. The supplement comes down by about a fifth to a quarter of the starting dose every two to three days, reaching zero within one to two weeks after arthroplasty and two to four weeks after major spinal surgery. Put the schedule in the discharge summary and give the patient a copy.

Close the loop. The general practitioner or pain specialist receives the plan on the day of discharge, including the doses, the stop date and a named contact. Where the operation has removed the reason for the opioid (the arthritic hip has been replaced), the letter says so and proposes a taper of the baseline over the following months.

Pain catastrophising

Catastrophising is a measurable pattern of response to pain: rumination, magnification and helplessness. It predicts worse acute pain, higher opioid use and chronic postsurgical pain. In the meta-analysis of 29 studies, pre-operative anxiety or catastrophising raised the odds of chronic postsurgical pain by about 1.5 to 2 times, the association was most consistent in musculoskeletal surgery, and catastrophising predicted better than general anxiety.

The natural next step, treating it before surgery, has been tested and did not work. In 402 patients with high catastrophising scores having knee replacement, eight sessions of pain coping skills training gave no better pain or function at 12 months than arthritis education or usual care; all three groups improved substantially.

The plain reading is that catastrophising is a marker of risk and not, on current evidence, a target that pre-operative psychology removes. Its use is in triage. The high-scoring patient gets the strongest regional plan, an honest account of what to expect, function-based goals, early pain service review, and resistance to chasing pain scores with escalating opioid, which is the path by which such patients leave hospital on more than they came in with. For the patient with established chronic pain and high distress having an operation whose indication is pain alone, the expected gain is weighed with the surgeon against the risk of the roughly one in five who have persistent pain after knee replacement.

Edge cases

The patient who is drowsy and in severe pain. Sedation limits the opioid before pain is controlled. Stop escalating the opioid; add or increase ketamine, re-site or bolus the catheter, check for withdrawal from a missed baseline dose, and look for another cause of pain (compartment syndrome, haematoma, dislocation).

The tolerant patient for day surgery. Take the usual doses, use a long-acting block with dexamethasone IV, and send the patient home on the baseline plus a small, time-limited supplement. Do not convert a stable patient to a new long-acting opioid for a day-case procedure.

High-dose gabapentinoid or benzodiazepine users. Continue them, because withdrawal from either is dangerous, and reduce the opioid supplement accordingly, with sedation scoring at the higher frequency.

Renal impairment. Morphine and oxycodone metabolites accumulate. Fentanyl, hydromorphone (with care), buprenorphine and methadone are the safer choices for baseline and PCA.

The unknown dose at 02:00 for a fracture. Give no more than half the claimed methadone or buprenorphine dose until it is verified, cover the remainder with titrated short-acting opioid, block the limb, and verify in the morning.

Part A

Antibiotic prophylaxis and periprosthetic infection

An implant lets a handful of skin bacteria establish a biofilm that no later antibiotic will clear, so prophylaxis is a race to have a bactericidal tissue level in place from incision to closure: cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g at 120 kg or more) finished within 60 minutes before the knife and before any tourniquet goes up, repeated at four hours or after 1.5 L of blood loss, and stopped within 24 hours. A penicillin allergy label should almost never displace cefazolin: its side chain is shared with no penicillin, the measured rate of dual allergy is under 1%, and the usual substitute, vancomycin, was associated with nearly three times the rate of methicillin-sensitive staphylococcal infection in Australian surveillance data and added nothing but harm when given with cefazolin in the ASAP trial. Vancomycin, when it is indicated, needs an hour or more to infuse and so has to be started before the patient reaches theatre. In established periprosthetic infection a single prophylactic dose does not spoil the cultures and should not be withheld. For open fractures the antibiotic matters most in the first hour after injury, long before the anaesthetist meets the patient, so the job at induction is to find out what was given and when.

Why an implant changes the arithmetic

Every surgical wound is contaminated by the time it is closed. Skin organisms survive in hair follicles and sebaceous glands beneath any preparation, and more settle from the air and the team. In soft tissue the inoculum is small and host defences clear it. A foreign body changes the terms: bacteria that reach a metal or polyethylene surface before host cells do attach, multiply, and within days surround themselves with a biofilm in which they are metabolically slow, shielded from neutrophils and tolerant of antibiotic concentrations hundreds of times those that kill them free-floating. The number of organisms needed to establish infection falls by several orders of magnitude, and once the biofilm is mature the infection cannot be cured without removing or mechanically stripping the implant.

Prophylaxis therefore has one aim: a bactericidal concentration in blood, wound fluid and bone from the moment the skin is cut until it is closed, so that organisms are killed in the hours before they can attach. Everything about dose, timing and redosing follows from that sentence. An antibiotic given after the tourniquet is up, an hour too early, or allowed to fall below the inhibitory concentration in the fourth hour of a revision, has missed part of the window.

The organisms are predictable. Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci cause most infections of joint replacements and fracture implants, with streptococci, enterococci and gram-negative rods behind them, and Cutibacterium acnes in the shoulder and spine.

Cefazolin: dose, timing, redosing

Cefazolin is the agent of choice in every major guideline because it is bactericidal against methicillin-sensitive staphylococci and streptococci, reaches bone and synovial fluid, and can be given as a push.

Element Rule Reason
Dose 2 g IV; 3 g IV at 120 kg or more Tissue levels in obese patients fall below target with smaller doses
Timing Complete within 60 minutes before incision, in practice at induction Peak tissue level at the incision
Tourniquet Complete before inflation, ideally 5-10 minutes before The cuff isolates the limb from the circulation
Redose At 4 hours from the first dose; after about 1,500 mL blood loss Two half-lives; haemorrhage and fluid replacement dilute the drug
Renal failure Redose later or not at all Half-life is prolonged
Duration Single dose, or continued to 24 hours at most No benefit beyond 24 hours; resistance and Clostridioides difficile beyond it

Redosing is the element most often missed, because it falls in the middle of a difficult case: the revision hip at hour four, the deformity correction that has lost two litres, the pelvic fixation. Set a timer at the first dose. The four-hour clock starts when the pre-operative dose was given, not at incision.

Duration is contested at the margins. The guideline position is no more than 24 hours. The Norwegian registry analysis of 22,170 hip replacements found the lowest revision rates when four systemic doses were given on the day of surgery and antibiotic was also in the cement, with nothing gained from continuing for two or three days; that is observational and reflects an older era, but it is why many arthroplasty surgeons give two or three postoperative doses and few give more. Drains and urinary catheters are not reasons to continue.

The penicillin allergy label

About one patient in ten carries a penicillin allergy label, and nine in ten of those are not allergic when tested. The label matters in orthopaedics because of what it does to prophylaxis.

Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is determined mainly by the R1 side chain, not the shared beta-lactam ring. Cefazolin’s side chain is unlike that of any penicillin or any other cephalosporin in clinical use. The meta-analysis of 77 studies found dual allergy to penicillin and cefazolin in 0.7% of patients with a penicillin allergy history, 0.6% where the penicillin allergy was unconfirmed, and 0.1% among patients with an unconfirmed label who were given perioperative cefazolin. In those with a confirmed penicillin allergy the estimate was 3.0% with a credible interval running from near zero to 17%, which is the group in which more care is justified.

The alternative is worse for the joint. In Australian surveillance data from 22,549 cardiac and arthroplasty procedures, vancomycin in place of a beta-lactam carried an adjusted odds ratio of 2.79 for surgical site infection with methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, the commonest pathogen. Vancomycin is a slower, weaker killer of sensitive staphylococci and has no gram-negative activity; clindamycin is bacteriostatic and resistance is common.

The working rules:

  1. A history of a non-severe reaction to a penicillin, of any type, or an unverifiable childhood label: give cefazolin.
  2. A history of immediate severe reaction to a penicillin (anaphylaxis, angioedema): cefazolin is still the better drug on the numbers and is the author’s reading of the cross-reactivity data; give it with the patient monitored, intravenous access secure and adrenaline to hand, which describes induction of anaesthesia. Where local policy forbids it or the patient declines, use vancomycin, and add gram-negative cover if the operation warrants it.
  3. A history of a severe delayed cutaneous reaction to any beta-lactam (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug reaction with eosinophilia): avoid all beta-lactams.
  4. A history of reaction to cefazolin itself: avoid cefazolin; other beta-lactams are usually tolerated, on specialist advice.
  5. The elective patient with a penicillin label seen weeks ahead: refer for delabelling. It changes every future anaesthetic.

Cefazolin is itself among the commoner causes of perioperative anaphylaxis, in patients with and without a penicillin history. Giving it before induction, or at least separated by a few minutes from the muscle relaxant, makes the culprit easier to identify afterwards; that timing is author’s preference, not a guideline requirement.

Vancomycin

Vancomycin is indicated for patients known to be colonised or previously infected with MRSA, for units with a high MRSA rate where local policy dictates, and for the few who cannot have a beta-lactam. In the first two groups it is given in addition to cefazolin, because cefazolin is the better drug for the sensitive staphylococci that still cause most infections.

It should not be added routinely. The ASAP trial randomised arthroplasty patients without known MRSA colonisation across Australian centres to vancomycin or placebo on top of cefazolin. Surgical site infection occurred in 4.5% with vancomycin and 3.5% with placebo. In knee replacement the vancomycin group did worse (5.7% against 3.7%, relative risk 1.52), in hip replacement there was no difference, and hypersensitivity reactions doubled.

The practical problem is the infusion. The dose is 15 mg/kg of actual body weight, typically 1-1.5 g, given no faster than 10 mg/min, because rapid infusion releases histamine: flushing, hypotension, and occasionally cardiovascular collapse at exactly the moment of induction. At that rate 1 g takes 100 minutes and 1.5 g takes 150 minutes, so a 1.5 g dose cannot finish inside the 120-minute window: it is started first, and the tourniquet, not the incision, is the hard deadline. The guideline window is to begin within 120 minutes before incision, and the infusion should be complete, or nearly so, before incision and before a tourniquet is inflated. That means vancomycin is charted in advance and started on the ward or in the holding bay; a vancomycin infusion started in the anaesthetic room is finishing as the wound is being closed.

The tourniquet rule

A tourniquet seals the limb. Whatever antibiotic is in the tissue at inflation is all there will be until release, and none of a dose given after inflation reaches the wound. The rule is that the full dose is in before the cuff goes up, with a few minutes for distribution: for cefazolin, push it at induction and inflation will follow by more than five minutes in the ordinary course of positioning and preparation; for vancomycin, the infusion must have been started early enough to finish.

One randomised trial tested the opposite strategy. In 908 knee replacements, cefuroxime given 10 minutes before tourniquet release, so that the peak arrived with the reperfusion haematoma, was not inferior to the same dose before inflation (deep infection 1.9% against 3.4% at three months). This has not displaced the standard rule, but it supports a second dose before release when the first was mistimed or the tourniquet time is long. Regional administration of low-dose vancomycin by the intraosseous route after inflation is used in some centres and gives very high local concentrations; outcome evidence is limited. More on the cuff in the tourniquet.

Cutibacterium acnes and the shoulder

Cutibacterium acnes lives in the sebaceous glands of the dermis, most densely over the shoulder, chest and back, and most densely in men. Skin preparation sterilises the surface and does not reach the glands; the incision then cuts through them. In ten men having primary shoulder arthroplasty after correctly timed antibiotics and double skin preparation, 7 of 50 deep tissue specimens, from three of the patients, grew the organism.

The infection it causes is indolent. A shoulder replacement or cuff repair becomes painful and stiff months to years later with normal inflammatory markers, and cultures need to be held for up to 14 days to grow it. Cefazolin is active against the organism in the laboratory and remains the prophylactic agent; no systemic regimen has been shown to eliminate it from the wound. Many shoulder surgeons ask patients to apply topical benzoyl peroxide for several days beforehand to reduce the load in the skin. For the anaesthetist the points are that standard prophylaxis is given on time as for any arthroplasty, and that a revision shoulder for unexplained pain or loosening is an infection case until the extended cultures say otherwise.

Periprosthetic joint infection for the anaesthetist

Three operations are offered, chosen by the age of the biofilm and the state of the implant and soft tissues; the detail is on the periprosthetic joint infection card.

  Onset                      Biofilm      Operation
  -------------------------  -----------  ----------------------------------------
  Early postoperative or     immature     DAIR: debridement, antibiotics, implant
  acute haematogenous,                    retention, exchange of modular parts
  symptoms under 3-4 weeks
  Chronic, good tissues,     mature       One-stage exchange
  known sensitive organism
  Chronic, poor tissues,     mature       Two-stage: removal, antibiotic spacer,
  resistant or unknown                    weeks of antibiotics, reimplantation
  organism, sinus

Antibiotics or cultures first

The traditional request is to withhold antibiotics until deep samples have been taken, for fear of sterilising the cultures. The randomised trial does not support it: in 65 patients with culture-positive infection, intraoperative cultures grew the pre-operative organism in 82% of those given prophylaxis before incision and 81% of those in whom it was delayed. The yield depends on the patient having been off therapeutic antibiotics for two weeks beforehand and on taking multiple samples, not on a single dose at induction.

The defensible default is to give prophylaxis at induction when the organism is already known from an aspirate. When no organism has been identified and the surgeon asks to wait, have the dose drawn up and give it the moment the samples (usually five) are taken, which is within minutes of opening the joint, and before a tourniquet if at all possible. In a patient who is septic, antibiotics are not delayed for any reason. The same reasoning applies to septic arthritis and osteomyelitis.

The patient

The acutely infected patient may be bacteraemic and septic, and DAIR is urgent because the window before the biofilm matures is short. Resuscitate, give antibiotics after blood cultures, expect vasodilatation at induction, and treat a spinal as acceptable once antibiotics have been started in a patient who is not in septic shock; untreated systemic sepsis is the usual reason to avoid neuraxial block.

The chronically infected patient is depleted: anaemic from inflammation and repeated surgery, hypoalbuminaemic, often with a creatinine that has risen on weeks of vancomycin or an aminoglycoside, a long line in place, and tolerant of opioids after multiple operations (see opioid-tolerant patients). Revision for infection bleeds more than aseptic revision and cell salvage is relatively contraindicated; plan as in blood management. Rifampicin, used for staphylococcal biofilm, induces hepatic enzymes: it lowers the effect of oxycodone, methadone, midazolam, direct oral anticoagulants and warfarin within days of starting and the effect reverses over a fortnight after stopping.

Antibiotic-loaded cement

In primary arthroplasty, commercially premixed cement contains a low dose of gentamicin or tobramycin (0.5-1 g per 40 g of powder). The registry evidence favours it: systemic prophylaxis alone was associated with 1.8 times the rate of revision for infection compared with systemic plus cement antibiotic. At that dose there is no systemic toxicity.

Spacers are different. A spacer is hand-mixed with several grams of vancomycin and an aminoglycoside per packet so that it elutes high local concentrations for weeks. Enough reaches the circulation to cause acute kidney injury in a minority, particularly in patients with reduced renal reserve who are also receiving intravenous vancomycin. Record the spacer’s antibiotic load, avoid other nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, hypovolaemia, contrast) in the days after, and check the creatinine. Cementation physiology still applies: see bone cement implantation syndrome.

Open fractures

In an open fracture the contamination has already happened and the antibiotic is early treatment, not prophylaxis. Time from injury is what counts. In 137 type III open tibial fractures, antibiotics given more than 66 minutes after injury carried an odds ratio of 3.78 for deep infection and wound coverage later than five days an odds ratio of 7.39, while time to surgical debridement was not associated with infection. Where both were prompt the infection rate was 2.8%; where both were delayed it was 40.5%.

The EAST guideline gives the content:

Fracture Antibiotic Duration
Gustilo type I and II Gram-positive cover (cefazolin 2 g IV) as soon as possible Stop 24 hours after wound closure (1998 EAST guideline, carried forward)
Type III Add gram-negative cover 72 hours from injury, or no more than 24 hours after soft-tissue coverage, whichever is shorter
Farm, soil or faecal contamination Add high-dose penicillin for clostridia As above

The guideline found no advantage for fluoroquinolones and noted concern about fracture healing. Local protocols vary in how gram-negative cover is delivered (an aminoglycoside, a third-generation cephalosporin or piperacillin-tazobactam).

By the time the patient reaches theatre the first dose should have been given by paramedics or the emergency department. At induction establish what was given and when, redose cefazolin if four hours have passed, do not repeat a once-daily aminoglycoside, confirm tetanus cover, and remember that an aminoglycoside, hypovolaemia, contrast from the trauma scan and an NSAID are a reliable recipe for kidney injury. The surgery is on the open fractures card.

What else the anaesthetist controls

Antibiotic timing is the largest contribution, but not the only one. Hypothermia impairs neutrophil function and wound perfusion, so warm from the anaesthetic room. Keep glucose below about 10 mmol/L in diabetic and stressed patients, remembering the transient rise after dexamethasone. Avoid unnecessary transfusion. Keep theatre door openings and personnel to a minimum once implants are open. Treat injection ports and neuraxial technique as part of the sterile field: an epidural abscess or an infected regional catheter next to a new joint is an infection the anaesthetist owns.

Edge cases

The patient already on therapeutic antibiotics. If the regimen covers staphylococci and a dose was given within the redosing interval, no extra prophylaxis is needed; otherwise give cefazolin as usual. Therapeutic vancomycin by level does not need a top-up.

Morbid obesity. Give 3 g at 120 kg or more and keep to the four-hour redose; the obese patient is at higher risk of infection for reasons that go beyond tissue levels (wound tension, haematoma, diabetes).

Short procedures without implants. Arthroscopy, carpal tunnel release and simple soft-tissue surgery do not need prophylaxis unless an implant or graft is placed. Removal of metalwork is variable; many surgeons give a dose.

Known MRSA carrier for elective arthroplasty. Decolonise beforehand where the pathway exists, give vancomycin (started early) with cefazolin, and note that the guideline redosing interval for vancomycin is long enough that a second dose is rarely needed.

Cement and allergy. A patient with a documented aminoglycoside allergy needs plain cement requested in advance; it is not on the shelf in every theatre.

The antibiotic that was forgotten. If the incision has been made, give it immediately. If the tourniquet is up, give it immediately anyway so that it is in the blood at release, and consider asking for a brief deflation in a long case with an implant.

Part A

Spine essentials: neuromonitoring, prone physiology, blood loss and vision loss

Spinal surgery adds four things to an orthopaedic anaesthetic that the limb operations do not have: a patient turned face down for hours, a cord whose function is being watched electrically, a bleeding surface that scales with the number of levels, and an airway that the operation itself can swell. Prone positioning lowers cardiac index through reduced venous return and the size of the fall depends on the frame; a free abdomen is both haemodynamic and haemostatic. Ischaemic optic neuropathy is the visual loss of long, bloody prone operations, not of eye pressure: in the registry 96% of cases had six hours of anaesthesia or a litre of blood loss, and the independent risk factors are male sex, obesity, the Wilson frame, duration, blood loss and a low proportion of colloid. Motor evoked potentials require a propofol-opioid anaesthetic with no relaxant after intubation, and a signal change is managed by a rehearsed checklist that starts with pressure, haemoglobin, temperature and the anaesthetic before it reaches the implants. Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss in multilevel surgery; after anterior cervical surgery the commoner airway failure is pharyngeal oedema at about 36 hours, with haematoma the early one; and intrathecal morphine buys the first 24 hours after fusion at the price of itch and monitoring.

What turning prone does

Three things change when an anaesthetised patient is rolled from the trolley onto a spinal frame.

Venous return falls. Blood pools in the dependent legs, and any pressure on the abdomen narrows the inferior vena cava. Intrathoracic pressure rises where the chest rests on its supports, which reduces ventricular filling and compliance. The net effect is a fall in stroke volume and cardiac index with a compensatory rise in systemic resistance, so the blood pressure may look acceptable while the output has dropped by a fifth or more. The size of the fall depends on the support. In an echocardiographic comparison of five systems, cardiac index and stroke volume fell on the Andrews, Wilson and Siemens frames and changed least on the Jackson table and on longitudinal bolsters, and patients whose fluid deficit had been corrected before the turn had less hypotension. The practical reading: fill before turning, have the vasopressor running, and for the patient with limited cardiac reserve ask for the Jackson table.

The abdomen decides the bleeding. If the belly hangs free, caval pressure is low and so is the pressure in the epidural venous plexus, which drains to the cava through valveless veins. If the belly is compressed, caval blood diverts through the vertebral veins and the surgeon operates in a field that wells up from the epidural space. Checking that the abdomen is free is a haemostatic act. A free abdomen also lets the diaphragm descend: functional residual capacity and oxygenation in the prone anaesthetised patient are as good as or better than supine when the supports are on the chest and pelvis, and airway pressure rises when they are not.

The head becomes dependent or level. Venous pressure in the head and orbit rises with any head-down tilt and with abdominal compression, the face and airway accumulate oedema in proportion to time and crystalloid, and intraocular pressure rises. This is the background to the visual loss question below. The positioning checklist (eyes, tube, arms, pressure points) is in positioning.

Postoperative visual loss

Two different injuries share the name.

Central retinal artery occlusion is caused by pressure on the globe from a headrest, or occasionally by embolus. It is unilateral, the eye is often red, swollen or bruised, and it is prevented by keeping everything off the eye and checking that it stays off.

Ischaemic optic neuropathy is the one that matters after long spinal operations. In the ASA registry it accounted for 83 of 93 cases. The patients were not old or vasculopathic: mean age 50 and mostly healthy. The operations were long and bloody: mean anaesthetic duration 9.8 hours, median blood loss 2 L, and 96% had either six hours of anaesthesia or a litre of blood loss. It was bilateral in 55 of the 83, and 16 had the head held in pins with nothing touching the face, which rules out eye pressure as the cause. The patient wakes with painless visual loss, often complete, and there is no effective treatment.

The case-control study that followed, 80 cases against 315 matched spinal fusion controls, identified six independent risk factors:

Risk factor Odds ratio
Wilson frame 4.30
Obesity 2.83
Male sex 2.53
Anaesthesia duration, per hour 1.39
Estimated blood loss, per litre 1.34
Colloid as a share of non-blood fluid, per 5% 0.67 (protective)

The list points to a mechanism. The Wilson frame puts the head below the heart; obesity raises abdominal and therefore venous pressure when prone; long duration and large crystalloid volumes with little colloid produce interstitial oedema. The leading hypothesis is that raised venous pressure and oedema in the optic nerve, a structure in a tight sheath with a marginal blood supply, produce something like a compartment syndrome. Hypotension and anaemia, the factors most people would guess, did not emerge as independent predictors, though no one concludes from that that they are safe.

The ASA practice advisory converts this into practice, and it is consensus built on these observational data:

  1. Identify the high-risk case beforehand: prone surgery expected to be prolonged, with substantial blood loss, or both. Tell the patient that there is a small risk of visual loss. This is one of the few rare complications that belongs in every consent for long prone surgery.
  2. Position with the head neutral and level with or above the heart: slight reverse Trendelenburg, and a frame that does not drop the head. No pressure on the globe, checked and documented.
  3. Monitor blood pressure continuously in high-risk cases and decide case by case whether deliberate hypotension is used, and only when anaesthetist and surgeon agree it is essential.
  4. Crystalloid, colloid or both may be used to maintain intravascular volume; the advisory no longer directs colloid, and the colloid signal comes from the case-control study above.
  5. Monitor haemoglobin periodically; no transfusion threshold has been shown to prevent the injury.
  6. Consider staging very long procedures.
  7. Check vision as soon as the patient is alert. If there is any loss, obtain urgent ophthalmology review, correct haemoglobin, pressure and oxygenation, and image to exclude other causes.

The anaesthetist’s leverage is on four of the six risk factors: the frame, the fluid, the blood loss (tranexamic acid and a free abdomen) and, through staging, the duration; head height is the mechanism the frame stands for. The relevant operations are adult deformity correction, multilevel posterior lumbar fusion, posterior cervical fusion and long tumour and trauma cases.

Neuromonitoring

Monitoring exists because the surgeon cannot see cord function. Distraction, derotation, an osteotomy closing, a misplaced screw or a fall in perfusion can each stop conduction while the anatomy looks fine, and for a period of minutes the change is reversible.

Modality Pathway tested Sensitivity to anaesthesia What it detects
SSEP Peripheral nerve, dorsal columns, sensory cortex Volatile agents depress cortical responses in a dose-dependent way; relaxants help Dorsal cord, global perfusion, and limb positioning
Transcranial MEP Motor cortex, corticospinal tract, anterior horn, muscle Very sensitive to volatile agents and abolished by neuromuscular blockade Anterior cord and motor pathway; the modality that predicts motor outcome
Free-running EMG Nerve root to muscle Needs no relaxant Root irritation in real time
Triggered EMG Pedicle screw to root to muscle Needs no relaxant A screw that has breached the pedicle wall

SSEPs are averaged over hundreds of stimuli, so they report with a delay of a minute or more and test only the sensory half of the cord; a pure anterior cord injury can leave them intact. MEPs test the motor pathway directly and respond within seconds, and they are the modality the anaesthetic most easily destroys.

The anaesthetic that permits it

Responses that cross synapses are the vulnerable ones: the cortical SSEP and the muscle MEP both depend on synaptic transmission that inhalational agents suppress. The ASNM position statement is that intravenous anaesthesia with propofol and an opioid is optimal for muscle MEPs. The working recipe:

  1. Propofol and remifentanil by infusion, with processed EEG to keep the propofol dose no higher than it needs to be, because very deep propofol anaesthesia also suppresses MEPs.
  2. No volatile agent, or at most a low, constant fraction (under 0.5 MAC) agreed with the neurophysiologist where baseline signals are strong. No nitrous oxide.
  3. One intubating dose of relaxant and no more. Baselines are recorded once the train-of-four has returned; reversal with sugammadex is reasonable if the surgeon is ready before the relaxant has worn off.
  4. A soft bite block between the molars on both sides before the first stimulus. Transcranial stimulation activates the jaw muscles directly and tongue laceration is the commonest injury of the technique.
  5. Steady state. The neurophysiologist is comparing each response with a baseline, so a bolus of propofol, a change in infusion rate or a new drug is announced before it is given. Ketamine, lidocaine and low-dose dexmedetomidine infusions are compatible if started early and kept constant.
  6. A stable physiological milieu. Evoked potentials deteriorate with hypotension, hypothermia, anaemia and hypocapnia, so mean pressure, temperature, haemoglobin and carbon dioxide are kept where they were at baseline.

For lateral lumbar fusion, where the retractor passes through psoas among the roots of the lumbar plexus, EMG is the essential modality and any residual relaxant defeats it.

Responding to a signal change

A loss of MEPs, or a fall in SSEP amplitude of about half, is a shared emergency with a short window. The consensus checklist developed for deformity surgery organises the response under five headings, and the anaesthetist owns the second.

 1. GAIN CONTROL OF THE ROOM
    stop the operation, announce the change, quiet, call senior help

 2. ANAESTHETIC AND SYSTEMIC          <-- yours
    raise mean arterial pressure (above 80-90 mmHg)
    check haemoglobin, transfuse if low
    normalise temperature, CO2 and pH
    review the last 10 minutes: bolus, rate change, volatile, relaxant
    check train-of-four

 3. TECHNICAL
    electrodes, connections, stimulus; neck and limb position

 4. SURGICAL
    what was done just before; release distraction or correction,
    remove the rod, check screws, look for compression, irrigate warm

 5. IF NO RECOVERY
    wake-up test, further release, imaging, stage the operation

Raising the pressure is the single most effective anaesthetic intervention, because a cord under traction has a higher perfusion requirement than a cord at rest; it is done at once and not after the technical checks. An isolated upper limb SSEP change is a positioning problem until proved otherwise: in 1,000 monitored operations 92% of such changes reversed when the arm was moved.

The wake-up test remains the definitive check when signals do not return: the infusions are stopped, the patient is asked to move the feet, and anaesthesia is resumed. A propofol-remifentanil technique makes it possible within minutes. Mention it to the patient beforehand in any deformity case.

Blood loss and tranexamic acid

Spinal bleeding comes from decorticated bone, epidural veins and stripped muscle, and it scales with the number of levels and with osteotomies. A single-level decompression loses very little; a one- or two-level fusion a few hundred millilitres; a long deformity correction with a three-column osteotomy one to three litres or more; a vascular metastasis an unpredictable amount.

The measures, in order of effect: a free abdomen and a level or head-up table; tranexamic acid; normothermia; cell salvage for long constructs; and early attention to fibrinogen once the loss passes half a blood volume. Deliberate hypotension is not on the list. It reduces arterial bleeding in a field where the bleeding is venous and osseous, and it does so at the expense of cord and optic nerve perfusion in the two situations where those are most at risk.

Tranexamic acid has consistent evidence in spine surgery. The meta-analysis of 11 trials found about 200 mL less total blood loss and a third fewer patients transfused. The multicentre placebo-controlled trial in fusions of more than three segments found significantly less intraoperative and total bleeding, with transfusion avoided in 48% against 33% and a mean of 0.85 against 1.42 units, differences that sat on the edge of significance in a trial of 95 patients. No thrombotic signal has appeared. Published regimens for multilevel surgery use a loading dose of 10-50 mg/kg followed by an infusion of 1-10 mg/kg/h; a moderate regimen (10-15 mg/kg then 1-2 mg/kg/h) is the defensible default, and a single 1 g IV dose covers one- and two-level surgery. The wider picture is in blood management.

Anterior lumbar exposure is a different risk: the loss is small until an iliac vein tears, and then it is very fast. Large-bore access and blood available are the preparation for anterior lumbar fusion, and a pulse oximeter on the left foot shows when the retractor is occluding the left iliac artery.

The airway in cervical disease

Before the operation

The patient for ACDF or posterior cervical surgery may have a cord that is already compressed, and extension narrows the canal further. Three findings decide the plan: whether the spine is unstable (trauma, rheumatoid atlanto-axial disease, tumour); whether there is myelopathy, and whether symptoms appear when the patient extends or flexes the neck in clinic; and whether the airway is otherwise difficult (a fixed flexed neck, previous fusion, a halo).

No trial shows that one intubation technique gives better neurological outcomes than another. What the techniques share when they are done well is what matters: the neck is not moved beyond the range the patient tolerated awake, and the blood pressure does not fall. For most patients with stenosis and a stable spine, videolaryngoscopy with the head neutral and manual in-line stabilisation is appropriate. Awake tracheal intubation is the choice when instability is combined with a difficult airway, when symptoms are provoked by small movements, or when the surgeon wants a neurological examination after intubation and positioning. In severe myelopathy cord autoregulation is impaired, so induction hypotension is treated as seriously as neck movement, and a mean pressure at or above the patient’s baseline is maintained from induction to decompression. Rheumatoid and ankylosing spondylitis necks are covered in the orthopaedic patient.

After anterior cervical surgery

The surgeon retracts the trachea, oesophagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve to one side for the length of the operation, and the tissues respond like any tissue under a retractor. In 311 anterior cervical operations, 6.1% had an airway complication and 1.9% needed reintubation, with one death. The timing is the lesson: symptoms developed on average 36 hours after surgery, and all but two cases were due to pharyngeal oedema, not haematoma. The associations were exposure of more than three vertebral bodies, exposure involving C2, C3 or C4, blood loss over 300 mL and operating time over five hours.

So there are two different airway emergencies. Haematoma is early, within the first hours, with a tense, swelling neck: the wound is opened at the bedside to release it before or while the airway is secured, and the tray and the instruction to do so are at the bedside in recovery. Oedema is late, on the first or second night, with a changing voice, difficulty swallowing saliva and a patient who wants to sit forward; it is managed by early senior review, nebulised adrenaline and steroid as temporising measures, and reintubation before obstruction is complete, by the most experienced person available with a plan for a front-of-neck airway.

For the long, multilevel or high cervical case, and for combined anterior and posterior surgery, the defensible default is to leave the tube in until a cuff leak is present and the patient is awake, extubate over an exchange catheter, and nurse in a monitored bed for the first night. Dexamethasone is commonly given; evidence that it prevents airway compromise is limited. Hoarseness after surgery is usually a recurrent laryngeal neurapraxia; reducing the cuff pressure after the retractors are placed is a simple measure many units use, and a patient with previous surgery on the opposite side needs the cords examined beforehand.

Analgesia after fusion and intrathecal morphine

Fusion is a pain score 4 operation and deformity correction a 5: decorticated bone, stripped muscle over many segments, and patients who are frequently opioid-tolerant before they start. PROSPECT for complex spine surgery recommends paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, intraoperative ketamine and epidural analgesia, with opioids as rescue. It found only limited evidence for intrathecal opioid, wound infiltration, erector spinae and thoracolumbar interfascial plane blocks, lidocaine, dexmedetomidine and gabapentinoids, and did not recommend methadone despite trial evidence in its favour, because the comparator was a short-acting opioid and the safety margin is narrow.

Intrathecal morphine is therefore an option and not a guideline recommendation, and it is widely used because it is simple: the dura is in the field, and the surgeon can inject under direct vision before closure, or the anaesthetist can inject before induction. In the meta-analysis of eight trials it reduced opioid consumption and pain scores for the first 24 hours, with more pruritus and no difference in nausea, sedation or length of stay; respiratory depression occurred only in the morphine groups, too rarely to reach significance. The reading: a real benefit confined to day 0 and the first night.

Practical points. Doses in the trials varied widely; 100-200 micrograms is the range in current adult practice, with the lower end for the elderly and for sleep apnoea. It does not interfere with neuromonitoring. It requires sedation and respiratory monitoring for 24 hours and no concurrent sedatives or long-acting opioid beyond the patient’s established baseline. And it stops at about 24 hours, so the rest of the plan has to be running by then: regular paracetamol, an NSAID where the surgeon accepts one (PROSPECT recommends them; some surgeons restrict them over concern about fusion), and ketamine, which in opioid-dependent patients having lumbar surgery reduced morphine use at 24 hours, 48 hours and six weeks. The opioid-tolerant fusion patient is planned as in opioid-tolerant and chronic pain patients.

Edge cases

Acute spinal cord injury. Cord perfusion depends on pressure; maintain a mean of 85-90 mmHg through fracture fixation as far as bleeding allows, expect neurogenic hypotension and bradycardia with lesions above T6, and avoid suxamethonium from about 48-72 hours after injury because of hyperkalaemia.

Vertebroplasty and cemented screws. Cement can leak into the vertebral veins and the canal; the embolic physiology is that of bone cement implantation syndrome, and a new deficit on waking needs immediate imaging.

The stimulator or pump implant. Spinal cord stimulator paddle placement may need the patient to report paraesthesia coverage, which sets the depth of sedation.

Monitoring that never had baselines. In severe myelopathy, neuropathy or obesity, signals may be absent from the start. Establish that before the incision so that their absence later is not misread, and agree whether a wake-up test will be the check.

The prone cardiac arrest. Compressions can begin prone over the thoracic spine while the wound is covered and a trolley is brought. Defibrillation pads placed before draping in the high-risk patient save minutes.

  8. Vitale MG, Skaggs DL, Pace GI, et al. Best practices in intraoperative neuromonitoring in spine deformity surgery: development of an intraoperative checklist to optimize response. Spine Deform 2014;2:333-339
    Consensus checklist of 26 items under five headings for responding to a neuromonitoring change in a patient with a stable spine, promoting a team approach
  9. Kamel IR, Drum ET, Koch SA, et al. The use of somatosensory evoked potentials to determine the relationship between patient positioning and impending upper extremity nerve injury during spine surgery: a retrospective analysis. Anesth Analg 2006;102:1538-1542

  10. Cheriyan T, Maier SP, Bianco K, et al. Efficacy of tranexamic acid on surgical bleeding in spine surgery: a meta-analysis. Spine J 2015;15:752-761

  11. Colomina MJ, Koo M, Basora M, et al. Intraoperative tranexamic acid use in major spine surgery in adults: a multicentre, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Br J Anaesth 2017;118:380-390

Part B. Why operations hurt

Part B

Why operations hurt: a first-principles pain model

Post-operative pain is predictable from four things: which tissue was cut, what was left under tension, what will be loaded afterwards, and who the patient is. Bone hurts hard and briefly; a tendon pulled onto bone under tension hurts for as long as it is loaded; a joint that has been re-tensioned aches for weeks; arthroscopic surface work barely registers. The early peak is a poor guide, because the shape of the curve after day 2 is what decides whether a single-shot block, a catheter or nothing is the right plan. Every card in Part C carries a 1-5 score and a day 0 to 7 trajectory built on this model, and this chapter defines them.

The claim

Pain after an orthopaedic operation is not a property of the operation’s name. It is a property of what was done to which tissue, what that tissue is now doing, and who it was done to. A surgeon who says “this is the least painful operation I do” is reporting the first of those four, filtered through the patients who complained to him. A registrar who says “cuff repairs are agony” is reporting the same thing from the other end of the corridor. Both are right about the days they saw and wrong about the days they did not.

The model in this chapter has four questions. Ask them in order and the block, the catheter decision and the oral regimen follow.

  1. TISSUE      what was cut, reamed, stripped or detached
                 (bone, tendon, capsule, muscle, periosteum, nerve, skin and portals)
                        |
  2. TENSION     what was left pulled tight, lengthened or re-tensioned
                 (a repaired tendon, a lengthened arm, a balanced knee, a corrected osteotomy)
                        |
  3. LOAD        what will be loaded in the days after, and how soon
                 (weight-bearing, hand use, physiotherapy, rolling over in bed)
                        |
  4. PATIENT     who it was done to
                 (age, sex, pre-operative pain, opioid exposure, catastrophising, what they expect)
                        |
                        v
            pain SCORE, pain SHAPE over day 0-7, and the PLAN that fits the shape

Tissue: what each kind of cut feels like

Nociceptors are not evenly distributed. Periosteum is dense with them; cancellous bone marrow is sensitive to pressure and inflammation; tendon and ligament carry mechanoreceptors that fire with stretch; synovium and capsule are richly innervated; muscle belly is comparatively quiet unless it is torn or ischaemic; cartilage has no nerves at all, which is why a bone-on-bone joint hurts and a cartilage-covered one does not. The surgeon’s choice of what to cut therefore sets the baseline.

Mechanism tag What the surgeon did How it hurts How long
bone osteotomy, reaming, broaching, drilling for anchors, decorticating a footprint, cement interface hard, deep, inflammatory; responds to NSAIDs; worse with the first loading peaks day 1-2, falls fast once nothing is loaded through it
tendon-tension a tendon or ligament repaired or reattached under tension, or a graft fixed in a tunnel sharp with every movement that loads it; night pain because the patient cannot find a position; aching between plateau for one to two weeks, then slow decline over the healing period
retension the joint re-tensioned or the limb lengthened: reverse shoulder, knee balancing, osteotomy correction, leg length change at the hip deep ache and stiffness pain, worse with range-of-motion exercises, a feeling of the limb being “too tight” weeks, improving as the soft tissues creep
capsule capsular release, labral repair, synovectomy, joint distension sharp with movement in the released direction, settles once the joint is moved regularly days
muscle a muscle split, released, lengthened or widely dissected aching, position-dependent, worse on contraction days to a week
periosteum subperiosteal stripping or plating along a long bone raw and incisional along the whole length of the plate, worse than the fracture it fixed days, then the bone takes over
nerve nerve handling, traction, decompression or transposition burning, dysaesthetic, in the territory rather than the wound unpredictable; may be the longest
tourniquet ischaemia and reperfusion plus cuff-site pressure dull thigh or arm ache after a long tourniquet, separate from the wound 24-48 h
surface arthroscopic portals and irrigation only minimal; swelling more than pain hours
visceral a retroperitoneal or anterior approach to the spine or pelvis abdominal wall and visceral, ileus, referred pain days

Two of these tags do most of the work in the atlas. Bone explains why an anatomic shoulder replacement, a distal radius plate and a primary hip hurt hard for two days and then stop. Tendon-tension explains why a rotator cuff repair, a quadriceps tendon repair and a multiligament knee reconstruction hurt for two weeks, at night, every time the patient moves.

Tension: what was left pulled tight

The surgeon’s second decision is what the tissues are left doing. A replaced humeral head sized to the one that was removed leaves the cuff and capsule at their original length: nothing pulls except the repaired subscapularis, so after the bone settles there is little left to hurt. That exception matters: in the one direct comparison the anatomic replacement, with its subscapularis repair and younger patients, needed opioids for longer than the reverse, which the folklore calls the more painful of the two. A reverse shoulder deliberately lengthens the arm and tensions the deltoid so that it can lift the arm without a cuff; the deltoid and the capsule spend weeks creeping to the new length and the patient feels every centimetre. A knee replacement is balanced by releasing tight ligaments and choosing insert thickness until the gaps match; the collateral ligaments and the posterior capsule are then held at a new tension through every flexion exercise. An osteotomy that corrects an alignment deformity leaves the soft tissues on the lengthened side stretched. A repaired tendon is the extreme case: by design it is pulled back to bone under enough tension to hold, and the tension is then tested by every movement until it heals.

This is the single most useful question to ask a surgeon who says an operation is painless or painful: what have you left under tension? The answer predicts the shape of the curve better than anything else they can tell you.

Load: what the patient will do to it

A cut bone that is not loaded is quiet by day 3. The same cut bone loaded by weight-bearing is not, which is why the Gerbershagen cohort, 50,523 patients ranked by their worst pain on the first day after 179 different operations, put open reduction of a calcaneal fracture at the top of the whole list, above every major abdominal and thoracic operation, and put foot arthrodesis, metacarpophalangeal arthrodesis and hand resection arthroplasty in the top eleven. Small bones that have to bear the body’s weight or do the hand’s work from day 1 hurt out of all proportion to the size of the incision. Twenty-two of the forty most painful procedure groups in that cohort were orthopaedic or trauma operations on the limbs. Spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery held ranks 2, 3 and 6, with no epidural analgesia used.

The same cohort delivered the finding that should keep every anaesthetist honest: appendicectomy, cholecystectomy, haemorrhoidectomy and tonsillectomy all ranked in the 25 most painful procedures, and laparoscopic appendicectomy patients reported pain equal to knee replacement and sternotomy patients, while receiving almost no opioid because nobody expected them to need it. Expectation sets the regimen, and the regimen sets the pain. “Minor” is a description of the surgeon’s effort, not the patient’s.

Load also explains the gap between pain at rest and pain on movement, which most of the published trials never measured: an updated systematic review of 944 post-surgical analgesic trials found that 53% did not assess movement-evoked pain at all. Blocks and catheters earn their keep on movement-evoked pain, which is the pain that stops physiotherapy, sleep and discharge; a trial that reports only rest pain understates what a continuous technique does for a tendon repair and overstates what it does for a bone cut.

The shape of the curve, not the height of the peak

Put tissue, tension and load together and each operation has a characteristic trajectory. The cards record it as the expected worst pain (0-10) on the evening of surgery, day 1, day 2, day 3 and day 7, with the card’s recommended plan in place.

pain
 8 |
 7 |          B.......B
 6 |        . :       :  B
 5 |    A   :  A      :      B        A = bone (THA, distal radius, hemiarthroplasty):
 4 |   . .  :    .    :          B        peaks as the block recedes, falls fast
 3 |  .   . :      A  :              B
 2 | .      .        .A . . . . . . A   B = tendon under tension (cuff repair, quads):
 1 |.        .                            same peak, then a plateau for a week or two

   D0        D1       D2       D3       D7
