  12. Cullen DJ. Why worry about blood pressure during surgery in the beach chair position? APSF Newsletter 2020
    Hydrostatic correction of about 2 mmHg per inch between cuff and external auditory meatus; strokes reported after shoulder surgery in beach chair with cuff systolics in the 80s-90s; no deliberate hypotension

Upper limb › Shoulder

3 Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair

With or without subacromial decompression, biceps tenodesis and distal clavicle excision

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Tendon under tension. A retracted, degenerate tendon pulled back onto a decorticated, bleeding footprint under tension and loaded by every movement for weeks; plus raw bone from acromioplasty, an inflamed bursa stripped out, and arthroscopic fluid in the soft tissues

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Interscalene brachial plexus block with intravenous dexamethasone; continuous catheter favoured by PROSPECT, single shot plus a written night plan the defensible day-case default
Catheter: selective Catheter for large or massive tears, revision repairs, opioid-tolerant or poorly coping patients, and any unit that cannot guarantee the oral regimen overnight; single shot with dexamethasone for small and medium tears in a counselled day-case patient
Alternatives: Superior trunk block (phrenic sparing, equivalent at 24 h); Suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks (phrenic sparing, PROSPECT grade B, inferior to interscalene); Liposomal bupivacaine interscalene where available, which pushes the peak to day 2
Position
Beach chair in most Australian practice; lateral decubitus with 5-7 kg of arm traction in some hands, which changes the airway access and the plexus traction but not the pain
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal into the wound; the fluid you see is irrigation. Haemoglobin is unchanged
Duration
60-150 min; small tears at the short end, massive tears with releases, tenodesis and decompression at the long end, and the irrigation clock runs the whole time
Length of stay
Day case or one night. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); anchors are implants and Cutibacterium acnes is the shoulder organism
Tranexamic acid
Not routinely needed for blood loss; some surgeons use TXA 1 g IV for arthroscopic visibility, which is a reasonable request
VTE
Mechanical only in most units; chemoprophylaxis only for the patient's own risk factors
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and heavy for most of the first day; the shoulder then hurts, especially at night, for one to two weeks, and the sling is what protects the repair, not a sign that something has gone wrong.
The trap
The block wears off at 2 am: rebound pain after a single-shot interscalene block is the rule after bone-and-tendon surgery, and the plan has to be written for the first night at home, not for the recovery room

What the surgeon is doing and why

A rotator cuff tear is a tendon that has pulled off bone. Supraspinatus is the usual victim, because it runs under the acromion and over the humeral head at the point of maximum load and minimum blood supply. Once the tendon end is off the greater tuberosity it retracts medially, the muscle behind it atrophies and fills with fat, and the humeral head loses the depressor that kept it centred under the acromion, so the patient gets weakness, night pain, and a head that rides up and impinges. The tissue the surgeon is working with is not healthy tendon that happened to tear; it is a degenerate, retracted, poorly vascular structure that has to be dragged back to where it came from and persuaded to heal to bone over about twelve weeks. Re-tear rates after repair are substantial and rise with tear size and age, which is why the protection afterwards is so cautious and why the surgeon cares about every detail of fixation.

The operation has a fixed logic:

  1. See the problem: diagnostic arthroscopy of the joint, then the subacromial space. The long head of biceps is often cut or tenodesed on the way because it is a pain generator and anchors nothing useful.
  2. Clear the workspace: the subacromial bursa, thick and inflamed, is stripped out so the tendon and the acromion can be seen. Many surgeons then shave the undersurface of the acromion (acromioplasty) and some excise the distal clavicle. The randomised trials show acromioplasty adds nothing to re-tear or function, but it is still common and it leaves a raw bleeding bone surface.
  3. Free the tendon: releases of the capsule and the coracohumeral ligament above and below the tendon so that it can be pulled laterally without excess tension. The more retracted the tear, the more release, the longer the case.
  4. Prepare the footprint: the cortical surface of the greater tuberosity where the tendon used to insert is decorticated with a burr to bleeding bone, because tendon heals to raw bone and not to cortex.
  5. Fix it: suture anchors are placed in the tuberosity (one row at the medial edge, or two rows in a “transosseous-equivalent” bridge), sutures are passed through the tendon, and the tendon is reduced onto the footprint and tied or locked under tension. The tension is the point: a lax repair does not heal and a tight one re-tears, and the surgeon judges it with the arm in a set position.
  6. Protect it: a sling, often with an abduction pillow, for six weeks, with no active use of the repaired tendon. Every movement that loads the tendon in those weeks is pain and risk.

The pain logic is the mirror image of an anatomic shoulder replacement. There the dominant mechanism is bone, with one repaired tendon resting in a sling, and the pain fades once nothing is being loaded through the cut. Here the dominant mechanism is tendon-tension: a repaired, poorly vascular tendon that is pulled onto bone and then loaded, however gently, by every reach and every roll in bed for weeks. Underneath it is bone (the decorticated footprint and the acromioplasty, which hurt like any osteotomy for two or three days), capsule (the releases), and arthroscopy itself (portals, irrigation fluid in the deltoid and subcutaneous tissues, and a shoulder that has been held in traction or abduction for an hour and a half). The early peak is no higher than after arthroplasty: in the one prospective comparison both groups peaked on day 2, at a mean of 4.4 for cuff repair and 5.1 for arthroplasty under long-acting interscalene blocks. The difference is afterwards. Cuff repair patients were still using more opioid at a week, and the night pain that defines this operation runs for one to two weeks. A plan that only covers the first night has covered the easy part.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Block, airway and the night plan before the patient is asleep

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The whole operation is done through 5 mm portals under irrigation; nothing about it needs your attention as much as the hours after it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the operation PROSPECT wrote its shoulder guideline for: interscalene block first choice, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg with it, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started pre-operatively and continued. Decide the catheter question now with the surgeon’s tear size in front of you (see the pain plan). Airway: a tracheal tube is the author’s default in beach chair, because the head is behind a screen and the neck may swell with irrigation fluid over a long case; a second-generation supraglottic device is reasonable for a short repair in a slim patient. Cuff on the non-operative arm, awake baseline pressure recorded, eyes taped and padded, because the surgeon’s arm and the camera cable will be passing over the face.

  2. 2 Positioning: beach chair or lateral decubitus

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Beach chair gives a familiar anatomy and easy conversion to open; lateral decubitus with the arm in longitudinal traction opens the joint and the subacromial space wider and some surgeons will not operate any other way.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Beach chair: the cuff overstates brain perfusion pressure by roughly 1 mmHg per 1.25 cm of height between cuff and ear, so keep the cuff reading near the awake baseline with a vasopressor infusion and treat the bradycardia-hypotension episodes that the sitting position plus interscalene block provoke. Lateral: the airway is now accessed from the side with the patient’s face in a cradle, the dependent arm and eye need padding, the traction (5-7 kg) is a sustained pull on the plexus that you cannot see, and hypotension is less of a problem but a shift in the patient’s position mid-case is harder to correct. In either position, check that the head is neutral once the surgeon has set the arm, because they will move it.

  3. 3 Portals, irrigation pump and the request for a low pressure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Visibility in the subacromial space depends on the balance between irrigation pump pressure (typically 40-60 mmHg) and the patient’s systolic pressure; bleeding from the bursa and the acromion fogs the view. Surgeons raise the pump, add adrenaline to the irrigation bags, or ask you to lower the pressure.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The request for a systolic of 90 is the central conflict of this operation. In beach chair it is a request for a brainstem perfusion pressure in the 50s, and PROSPECT lists controlled hypotension as not recommended on exactly those grounds. The honest answer is that you will keep the pressure near baseline, that adrenaline in the irrigation (1 mL of 1:1000 per 3 L bag is a common recipe) and a higher pump pressure are the surgeon’s tools, and that a patient with a working interscalene block and an adequate depth of anaesthesia will not be hypertensive. Adrenaline absorbed from the irrigation can produce transient tachycardia and hypertension; a sudden pressure rise shortly after a new bag goes up is that, not light anaesthesia.

  4. 4 Diagnostic arthroscopy, biceps and labrum

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The glenohumeral joint is inspected for the things that change the plan (a subscapularis tear, a SLAP lesion, cartilage loss that would make repair pointless) and the long head of biceps is tenotomised or tenodesed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing to do but note the time. A tenodesis into the bicipital groove adds an anchor and twenty minutes; a tenotomy adds nothing.

  5. 5 Subacromial bursectomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The inflamed bursa is thick, vascular and obscures everything. It is resected with a shaver and radiofrequency device until the acromion, the coracoacromial ligament and the tendon edge can be seen.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is where the fluid starts to go. Irrigation extravasates into the deltoid and the subcutaneous tissues, the shoulder swells, and over a long case in a heavy patient the swelling tracks to the neck. Watch the neck and the airway pressures as a matter of routine from this point, and warm the irrigation or the patient, because 20 L of room-temperature saline through the shoulder is a cooling system.

  6. 6 Acromioplasty and distal clavicle excision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The undersurface of the acromion is burred flat to remove a spur or a hooked morphology and to make room for the repaired tendon; the coracoacromial ligament is released. Some surgeons excise the distal 5-10 mm of the clavicle if the acromioclavicular joint is arthritic.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Bone work with a burr: bleeding, bone dust, and the pump going up. The pain contribution is a raw cancellous surface under the deltoid that behaves like a small osteotomy for two or three days. Nothing about the step needs intervention, but it is the step most likely to produce the low-pressure request.

  7. 7 Tendon mobilisation and releases

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A retracted tendon will not reach its footprint without releasing the adhesions, the capsule beneath it and the coracohumeral ligament above it. Massive tears need extensive releases, sometimes a margin convergence (side-to-side sutures to bring the tear edges together), and some get a patch or a superior capsular reconstruction instead of a repair.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The length of this step is the length of the case. A tear that the surgeon describes as “retracted to the glenoid” means releases, more anchors, more fluid, more traction, and a pain course at the top of the range. This is the information you need for the catheter decision, and it arrives now if it did not arrive in the pre-operative note.

  8. 8 Footprint preparation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The greater tuberosity is decorticated with a burr to a bleeding bed, because tendon heals to marrow and not to cortical bone. Some surgeons add bone marrow vents (small drill holes) to bring in a healing response.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Raw bleeding bone, the second of the three bone surfaces this operation creates. It is the reason that cuff repair qualifies as bone surgery for rebound pain purposes, with the higher odds that carries.

  9. 9 Anchors, suture passage and tendon reduction under tension

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Anchors go into the tuberosity, sutures are passed through the tendon with a dedicated instrument, and the tendon is reduced onto the footprint and fixed with knots or a knotless locking mechanism, in single-row or double-row configurations. The surgeon sets the tension with the arm in a specific degree of abduction and rotation and will want it held exactly there for the tying.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The arm position is set by the surgeon or an assistant and must not drift; a shift of 10 degrees changes the tension on a repair that is about to be locked. This is not a request for neuromuscular block (a working interscalene block already provides a flail arm) but for a steady patient and a steady table. The tendon pulled onto bone under tension here is what the patient will feel for the next fortnight; the moment the knots go down, the mechanism this card is built around exists.

  10. 10 Closure, sling and the swollen shoulder

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals are closed with a stitch or a strip, a bulky dressing goes on, and the arm goes into a sling, usually with an abduction pillow that takes the tension off the repair.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Put the sling on before the patient lightens; an awake patient with a dense block will otherwise lift the dead arm by the wrist and load the repair. Examine the neck before extubation after a long case in beach chair: subcutaneous fluid tracking from the deltoid to the supraclavicular fossa and anterior neck is common, usually harmless, and occasionally enough to compromise the airway. A patient with a visibly swollen neck, a long case and a difficult airway earns a longer wait and a careful look rather than a reflex extubation.

  11. 11 Recovery and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The repair is protected by the sling and nothing else; the surgeon wants pendular movements only, cryotherapy and sleep.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first paracetamol and NSAID dose goes in before the patient leaves recovery. The block lasts 12 to 24 hours with dexamethasone, longer with liposomal bupivacaine, and when it recedes the pain rises over an hour or two to its day 1 and 2 level; half of ambulatory block patients describe exactly this, more often after bone surgery. The written night plan (what to take at bedtime, what to take when the fingers start to tingle, when the opioid is for) is the single intervention that decides whether this patient telephones at 3 am. Night pain persists for one to two weeks because the patient cannot lie on either side without loading the shoulder; sleeping propped up and the sling worn in bed are surgical advice worth repeating. Day case is the norm for small and medium tears with a single-shot block; a catheter patient can also go home if the unit runs ambulatory infusions, or stays a night if it does not.

Pain plan

The mechanism is tendon under tension plus two raw bone surfaces, loaded by movement for weeks, so this is the shoulder operation where a continuous technique has the strongest claim and the operation PROSPECT’s guideline was written for. The guideline recommends interscalene block as first choice, with single-shot and continuous both graded A and the continuous technique favoured; intravenous dexamethasone (grade B) and preferred over perineural; paracetamol with an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before surgery; and suprascapular with or without axillary nerve block as a phrenic-sparing alternative that is inferior to interscalene. It recommends against subacromial or intra-articular infusions, stellate ganglion and cervical epidural blocks, gabapentinoids, and controlled hypotension.

Against that stands the randomised trial that added a ropivacaine 0.2% infusion to day 2 on top of dexamethasone, magnesium, paracetamol and ketorolac, in a mixed arthroplasty and cuff repair population, and found no difference in morphine at any time point or in pain scores, with four of thirty catheters falling out. The two are reconcilable: the catheter’s advantage shows when the alternative is a bare single shot, and shrinks when the single shot is prolonged with dexamethasone and backed by a regimen that is actually taken.

The defensible default, then, is a single-shot interscalene block (15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%, or a superior trunk block with the same volume when the patient cannot afford a hemidiaphragm, which matches it at 24 h), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID started before the block recedes, oral opioid for the nights of the first week, and a night plan written down for the patient. The catheter is the right call for the large or massive tear with extensive releases, the revision repair, the opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, the patient who has had a catastrophic rebound night before, and the unit that cannot guarantee a 2 am dose on a ward. If a catheter is placed, it needs a fixation that survives a sling and a patient who knows what a leaking dressing looks like, because the common failure is the catheter in the bed rather than the catheter in the patient.

Rebound pain is the planning target: in 972 ambulatory block patients it occurred in half, with bone surgery (OR 1.82), female sex (OR 1.52) and younger age raising the odds and intravenous dexamethasone lowering them (its absence OR 1.78). Every cuff repair involves bone. Escalation triggers: pain above 7 after the block has gone, with a sling correctly fitted and the hand warm and moving, is treated with the oral opioid that is already charted and a check that the regular analgesia was actually given; pain with a tense, hugely swollen shoulder in the first hours is extravasated irrigation fluid and settles; new severe pain days later with a hot joint is an infection until proven otherwise.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Tear size is the variable that matters. Small tears with one anchor and no releases run 60 minutes and behave like a decompression with a sore tuberosity; massive tears with margin convergence, patches or a superior capsular reconstruction run over two hours and sit at the top of this card’s range. The pre-operative MRI report, not the booking slip, tells you which you have.
  • Open and mini-open repair. Still used for some massive tears and by some surgeons: a deltoid split, more muscle pain, more bleeding, and PROSPECT’s recommendation to prefer the arthroscopic approach is on pain grounds.
  • Lateral decubitus. Changes airway access and brings sustained plexus traction; the dependent brachial plexus and peroneal nerve need padding and the eye on the pillow needs checking. Hypotension matters less, head position matters more.
  • The request for hypotension in beach chair. The reported strokes happened at cuff systolics in the 80s and 90s. Adrenaline in the irrigation and the pump are the surgeon’s levers; the vasopressor infusion is yours.
  • Fluid extravasation. Long case, high pump pressure, heavy patient, lateral position: the neck swells. Inspect before extubation; if in doubt, wait.
  • Hypothermia. Litres of room-temperature irrigation through the shoulder; forced-air warming from the start.
  • Phrenic palsy. Near-universal after interscalene block; use a superior trunk block for the patient with COPD, obesity with poor reserve, or a contralateral problem, and expect slightly less from a suprascapular plus axillary combination.
  • Chronic pain and opioid-tolerant patients. This operation is the one where their course is worst; a catheter and a pre-agreed plan with the pain service are both reasonable.
  • Day-case discharge criteria. A working block is not a reason to delay discharge, but a patient going home with a dense block needs the sling, written instructions, someone at home, and oral analgesia already started.
  • Infection. Cutibacterium acnes and anchors; presentation is late and indolent.

Key sources

This is the best-evidenced shoulder operation for analgesia, because PROSPECT built its guideline on it. The guideline’s preference for a continuous interscalene technique predates the 2024 randomised trial showing no added benefit from an infusion once dexamethasone and multimodal analgesia are in place, and the 2025 prospective comparison showing early pain equal to arthroplasty; the card’s catheter advice is the author’s reconciliation of the three, not a guideline statement. The acromioplasty meta-analysis is cited for the surgical variant, not for pain.

  1. Toma O, Persoons B, Pogatzki-Zahn E, Van de Velde M, Joshi GP. PROSPECT guideline for rotator cuff repair surgery: systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Anaesthesia 2019;74:1320-1331
    Interscalene block first choice (single shot and continuous both grade A, continuous favoured); IV dexamethasone grade B and preferred over perineural; paracetamol plus NSAID or COX-2; suprascapular with or without axillary block as an alternative (grade B); arthroscopic technique recommended; subacromial or intra-articular infusion, stellate ganglion, cervical epidural, gabapentinoids and controlled hypotension not recommended
  2. Lopez R, Schiffman C, Singh J, et al. Early postoperative pain is similar after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair vs. short-stay shoulder arthroplasty: a prospective study. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2025;34:1199-1207
    50 cuff repairs and 52 arthroplasties, all with liposomal bupivacaine interscalene block: peak mean VAS on day 2 of 4.4 and 5.1, no difference over 14 days; cuff repair used more opioid on days 7 and 8
  3. Rhyner P, Cachemaille M, Goetti P, et al. Single-bolus injection of local anesthetic, with or without continuous infusion, for interscalene brachial plexus block in the setting of multimodal analgesia: a randomized controlled unblinded trial. Reg Anesth Pain Med 2024;49:313-319
    60 arthroplasty and cuff repair patients with dexamethasone, magnesium, paracetamol and ketorolac: continuous ropivacaine 0.2% to day 2 did not change morphine use at 12, 24, 36 or 48 h or pain scores; four catheters fell out
  4. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    Rebound pain (NRS 3 or less rising to 7 or more within 24 h) in 49.6% of 972 ambulatory block patients; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, no IV dexamethasone OR 1.78
  5. Kang R, Jeong JS, Chin KJ, et al. Superior trunk block provides noninferior analgesia compared with interscalene brachial plexus block in arthroscopic shoulder surgery. Anesthesiology 2019;131:1316-1326
    Arthroscopic shoulder surgery, 15 mL ropivacaine 0.5%: pain at 24 h 1.4 vs 1.2, maximum pain 4.7 vs 4.8; complete hemidiaphragmatic paresis 5% vs 73%
  6. Cullen DJ. Why worry about blood pressure during surgery in the beach chair position? APSF Newsletter 2020
    Cuff pressure overstates brain perfusion by about 2 mmHg per inch of height; strokes reported after shoulder surgery with cuff systolics in the 80s-90s; deliberate hypotension should not be used
  7. Song L, Miao L, Zhang P, et al. Does concomitant acromioplasty facilitate arthroscopic repair of full-thickness rotator cuff tears? A meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis of randomized controlled trials. SpringerPlus 2016;5:685
    Randomised trials of repair with and without acromioplasty show no difference in re-tear or function; acromioplasty remains common and adds a raw bone surface

Upper limb › Shoulder

4 Subacromial decompression and ACJ excision

Arthroscopic subacromial decompression, acromioplasty and distal clavicle excision without cuff repair

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A burred acromial undersurface and, if the clavicle is excised, a raw distal clavicle end: two small cancellous bone surfaces under the deltoid that hurt like a minor osteotomy for two or three days; the bursectomy and portals add surface pain; nothing is repaired, tensioned or loaded

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Interscalene or superior trunk block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone, chosen for the anaesthetic and the first night as much as for the pain
Catheter: no No mechanism to justify one: no repair, no tension, no loaded tissue, and the pain is largely over by day 3
Alternatives: Suprascapular nerve block (anterior approach) with or without axillary nerve block, phrenic sparing and near-equivalent after the recovery room; General anaesthesia with surgeon-delivered subacromial local anaesthetic infiltration and an oral regimen, which is adequate for an isolated decompression in a patient who declines a block; Liposomal bupivacaine interscalene where available, of no proven benefit over plain bupivacaine with dexamethasone here
Position
Beach chair in most Australian practice; lateral decubitus with arm traction in some hands, which changes airway access and plexus traction but not the pain
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal; the fluid in the drapes is irrigation and the haemoglobin does not move
Duration
30-60 min skin to skin; the distal clavicle adds 15-20 min, a biceps tenotomy adds five
Length of stay
Day case. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg) if any anchor or implant is placed; for a pure decompression with no implant surgeons vary, and the author gives it because Cutibacterium acnes is the shoulder organism and the cost of omission is a septic joint
Tranexamic acid
Not needed for blood loss; some surgeons ask for TXA 1 g IV for arthroscopic visibility, which is a reasonable request
VTE
Mechanical only; the operation is short, the patient walks out, and chemoprophylaxis is for the patient's own risk factors
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (also the block adjunct) and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and heavy for the rest of the day; the shoulder is sore for two or three days, mostly at night, and most people are on simple painkillers only by the end of the first week.
The trap
This is the operation the CSAW trial could not separate from placebo arthroscopy: the block, the dexamethasone and the written night plan are the only things on the table that reliably change what the patient feels, so do not under-treat a short case because it is a short case, and do not over-treat it with a catheter it cannot use

What the surgeon is doing and why

Subacromial pain with an intact cuff was explained for forty years by impingement: a hooked or spurred acromion and a thickened coracoacromial ligament rubbing the supraspinatus tendon on elevation, so remove the roof and the tendon stops being abraded. The operation built on that idea is a bursectomy, release of the coracoacromial ligament and a burring of the anterior-inferior acromion to a flat surface. The mechanical story has not survived well. The CSAW trial randomised 313 patients with at least three months of subacromial pain, an intact cuff and a failed course of physiotherapy and injection to decompression, to arthroscopy with bursal inspection and no bone or ligament work, or to no treatment, and at six months the Oxford Shoulder Score was 32.7 after decompression and 34.2 after placebo arthroscopy; both surgical groups scored three to four points better than no treatment, below the threshold the trial defined as clinically important. The Cochrane review pooling both placebo-controlled trials reached the same conclusion. The operation is still done, in smaller numbers, for the patient who has exhausted everything else, for a large spur in a shoulder with a partial-thickness tear, and as a component of other arthroscopic procedures, where it adds a raw bone surface (see rotator cuff repair).

Distal clavicle excision is a different operation with a better mechanical rationale. The acromioclavicular joint is a small, incongruent, heavily loaded joint that wears, develops osteolysis in weightlifters, and hurts on cross-body adduction. Resecting the lateral 5-10 mm of the clavicle takes the two bone ends out of contact while leaving the coracoclavicular and the superior and posterior acromioclavicular ligaments intact, so the joint stays stable and stops hurting. Done arthroscopically, from the subacromial space or directly through the joint, it is an extension of the same portals; a prospective series of 59 isolated excisions saw pain fall from 8.2 to 3.4 by six months. Resecting too much destabilises the clavicle and produces a pain that does not go away, which is why the surgeon measures with the burr.

What actually happens to tissue, in order:

  1. Arthroscopy of the glenohumeral joint through a posterior portal, to look for the things that would change the operation: a partial or full cuff tear, labral pathology, a biceps lesion, cartilage loss. Many surgeons tenotomise a frayed long head of biceps on the way through.
  2. The scope goes into the subacromial space. The bursa, thick and vascular in these shoulders, is resected with a shaver and radiofrequency ablation until the acromion, the coracoacromial ligament and the cuff surface can be seen.
  3. The coracoacromial ligament is released off the acromion or ablated. This is the step that bleeds, because the acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery runs with it.
  4. The anterior-inferior acromion is burred flat from front to back to remove the hook or spur, typically 5-8 mm of bone. Raw cancellous bone, bleeding into the field, is the pain generator of the operation.
  5. If the clavicle is going, the acromioclavicular joint is opened from below, the inferior capsule resected, and the distal clavicle burred back by measured increments with the superior capsule and ligaments left alone.
  6. Portals closed with a stitch or a strip, local anaesthetic into the subacromial space by many surgeons, a sling for comfort only.

The pain logic: bone, small and short. Two raw cancellous surfaces under the deltoid behave like a small osteotomy, peaking on the first night and the first day and falling fast, because nothing is loaded through them. There is no repair, no tendon under tension, no lengthened muscle, no capsule tightened. The bursectomy and the irrigation add the surface pain of any shoulder arthroscopy, and a shoulder that was held in abduction or traction for 45 minutes aches. Patients are allowed to move from day 0, which is why the fall is quick. The honest caveat is the Gerbershagen cohort’s finding that “minor” procedures produce unexpectedly severe first-day pain, and that 22 of the 40 most painful operations in 50,000 patients were orthopaedic extremity procedures in which regional anaesthesia had been used in only 15%. A decompression under general anaesthesia alone, sent home with paracetamol, is on the wrong side of that curve. The score is 2 because, with a block and a written regimen, the patient copes without a catheter and is on simple analgesia by day 3; the day 1 figure of 4 is the rebound, not the operation.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative check, block and the anaesthetic decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon’s list is fast and the operation is one of the few in this book whose benefit over a placebo is unproven, so the patient in front of you has usually had a long conversation and a lot of physiotherapy already, and will often have an arthroscopy that finds more than the booking said.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The decision is whether the block is the anaesthetic or the analgesic. A single-shot interscalene or superior trunk block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg covers the operation, the recovery room and the evening, and it is the author’s default because the alternative (general anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration) is the combination that produces the Gerbershagen day 1 curve. The block can be the sole anaesthetic with sedation in a slim, calm patient and a surgeon who works quickly, which spares the airway in beach chair; general anaesthesia on top is the commoner arrangement because a 45-minute case in beach chair with a camera cable over the face is a poor place to manage a patient who becomes restless. If the patient’s chest cannot take a hemidiaphragm, a superior trunk block matches interscalene at 24 h with complete phrenic paresis in 5% rather than 73%, and an anterior suprascapular block is a further step down with no meaningful difference after the recovery room in two meta-analyses. Airway: a second-generation supraglottic device is reasonable for a short case in a slim patient; a tube for the obese patient, the long list and the surgeon who may convert to a cuff repair. Awake baseline pressure before any drug.

  2. 2 Beach chair, head fixation and pressure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Beach chair gives the surgeon a vertical humerus and a free arm for the assistant to abduct and rotate while they work in the subacromial space; some surgeons use lateral decubitus with 5-7 kg of traction to open the space.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The same physiology as every beach chair card: the cuff overstates brain perfusion by about 1 mmHg per 1.25 cm between cuff and ear, pressure falls as the chair goes up and the block adds a sympathetic effect, and the strokes reported after shoulder surgery happened at cuff systolics in the 80s and 90s. The short case is the dangerous one, because the vasopressor infusion that would be started for a two-hour replacement gets skipped for a 40-minute decompression and the pressure is chased with boluses instead. Start it anyway. Head neutral and strapped, eyes taped and padded, checked again after the arm is positioned.

  3. 3 Portals, pump pressure and the request for hypotension

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Visibility in the subacromial space is the balance between pump pressure (40-60 mmHg) and the patient’s systolic pressure; the bursa and the acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery bleed into the field and the surgeon’s levers are the pump, adrenaline in the irrigation and asking you to lower the pressure.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The request for a systolic of 90 is the central conflict of this operation and it comes at the bursectomy. The answer is the same as for a cuff repair and PROSPECT says so: no deliberate hypotension in beach chair. A patient with a working block and an adequate depth of anaesthesia will not be hypertensive, adrenaline in the bag (1 mL of 1:1000 per 3 L is a common recipe) and a higher pump pressure are the surgeon’s tools, and a sudden rise in pressure and heart rate shortly after a new bag goes up is the adrenaline, not light anaesthesia. Warm the patient or the irrigation; 10 L of room-temperature saline through a 40-minute case is enough to drop the core temperature in a small patient.

  4. 4 Diagnostic arthroscopy and the biceps

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon inspects the glenohumeral joint for the pathology that would change the operation. A partial-thickness cuff tear may be debrided or, if deep, repaired; a full-thickness tear turns this into a cuff repair; a frayed biceps is tenotomised.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The one moment of this case that changes your plan. A tenotomy adds five minutes and nothing to the pain. A conversion to cuff repair adds an hour, anchors, a decorticated footprint and a tendon under tension, and moves the patient to the rotator cuff repair card: a longer case, a tube rather than a laryngeal mask if the airway allows a swap, and a night plan written for a 5 rather than a 2. Ask what was found; the surgeon will tell the assistant before they tell you.

  5. 5 Bursectomy and coracoacromial ligament release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The inflamed bursa obscures everything and is resected with shaver and radiofrequency; the coracoacromial ligament is released from the acromion so that the undersurface can be burred and the arch is no longer rubbing the cuff.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The bleeding step, and the step where the fluid starts to go into the deltoid. In a short case the extravasation is modest; it still makes the shoulder tense and swollen for a few hours and the patient should be told that the swelling is fluid, not bleeding. Watch the pump pressure creep; a surgeon who has raised it to 80 mmHg to see through blood is a surgeon who will shortly ask about the blood pressure.

  6. 6 Acromioplasty

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The anterior-inferior acromion is burred flat, removing the hook and the spur, until the surgeon is satisfied with a flat undersurface; some use a cutting-block technique with the burr from the lateral portal, some work freehand from the posterior portal. The amount of bone is small (5-8 mm), but it is cancellous, raw and bleeding at the end.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the pain generator being created, and it is the reason a decompression counts as bone surgery for rebound pain purposes, with the higher odds that carries (OR 1.82 in the ambulatory cohort). Nothing to do but note the time and expect the low-pressure request.

  7. 7 Distal clavicle excision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    If the acromioclavicular joint is arthritic or the clavicle has osteolysis, the joint is entered from below through the subacromial space (or directly through a superior portal), the inferior capsule and the meniscus are removed, and the distal clavicle is burred back 5-10 mm in measured passes with the superior and posterior capsule and the coracoclavicular ligaments left intact. Too much resection destabilises the clavicle and produces a new pain that does not settle.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A second raw bone surface, superior and medial to the first, under the trapezius and deltoid origins. It roughly doubles the bone contribution and the night pain in the author’s experience, which is why a decompression with excision sits at the top of this card’s range and an isolated decompression at the bottom. The clavicle end bleeds from its medullary bone; the surgeon’s view goes and the pump goes up again. The dermatome matters: the acromioclavicular joint and the skin over it are supplied by the supraclavicular nerves from C3 and C4, which an interscalene block covers by spread and a superior trunk or suprascapular block often does not; if you have placed one of those, expect the patient to describe pain on top of the shoulder when the subacromial pain is gone, and consider a few millilitres of local anaesthetic under the skin over the joint or a superficial cervical plexus block (see ACJ reconstruction and clavicle fixation).

  8. 8 Closure, local anaesthetic and sling

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals are closed, many surgeons instil 10-20 mL of local anaesthetic into the subacromial space, and a sling goes on for comfort only; there is nothing to protect and the patient is encouraged to move from the first day.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The subacromial local anaesthetic is a supplement, not a substitute; PROSPECT recommends against continuous subacromial infusions and the single instillation has a small, short effect. Give the antiemetic. Put the sling on before the patient lightens so that the blocked arm is not swung off the table. Emergence is quick; the wound is three portals.

  9. 9 Recovery, the written plan and discharge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the patient home the same day, moving the shoulder through a comfortable range from day 1 and back to physiotherapy within the week, because the operation does nothing without the exercise programme that follows it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block lasts 12-24 hours with dexamethasone and the worst pain arrives on average 14-15 hours after it, which is the middle of the first night; the first rescue dose was needed at a mean of 11 hours in the one trial that timed it. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID start in recovery, not when the arm tingles, and the patient leaves with an oral opioid for two or three nights and a written plan that says what to take at bedtime and what to take when the fingers wake up. Pre-emptive opioid given at six hours did not reduce the worst pain in the one randomised trial that tried it, so the plan is a regular regimen and a rescue, not a prophylactic dose. A dense block is not a reason to delay discharge: sling, someone at home, the first doses already in, and a phone number. Day-case failure on this list is nausea or a block that was not placed, not pain.

Pain plan

The mechanism is two small raw bone surfaces that hurt for two or three days and are not loaded, so the plan is a single-shot block that covers the operation and the first night, a regular oral regimen that starts before the block recedes, and no catheter. There is no procedure-specific PROSPECT guideline; the rotator cuff repair guideline is the nearest and its skeleton (interscalene block first choice, intravenous dexamethasone preferred over perineural, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, suprascapular block as the phrenic-sparing alternative, no subacromial infusion, no controlled hypotension) applies with the catheter recommendation removed.

The defensible default is an interscalene block with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%, or a superior trunk block with the same volume in the patient who cannot afford a hemidiaphragm, with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg. The suprascapular block, anterior approach, with or without an axillary nerve block, is the next step down: in 16 trials it matched interscalene for 24 h opioid use and lost only in the recovery room, by 1.5 cm on a 10 cm scale, with fewer respiratory and block-related complications, and a second meta-analysis of six trials found the same. For an isolated decompression, where the mechanism is small and short, that trade is often worth making; the recovery room difference is covered by a dose of intravenous opioid. General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration alone is the author’s floor, acceptable only when the patient declines a block and understands that the first night will be worse.

The catheter decision is no, for any patient, because there is no mechanism for one: nothing is repaired, nothing is under tension, nothing is loaded, and by the time an infusion would be doing its work the pain has gone. The opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient having this operation is the exception that proves it: their course is worse for patient reasons, and the answer is a pre-agreed oral plan with their usual opioid continued, not a catheter in a day-case patient.

Rebound is the planning target because this is an ambulatory bone operation in a population that skews young and active, which is two of the four risk factors in the 972-patient cohort (bone surgery OR 1.82 and younger age; the others are female sex and no dexamethasone), and the fourth (no intravenous dexamethasone, OR 1.78) is the one you control. The curve on this card has the rebound on day 1 and the fall by day 3. Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone, with the hand warm and moving and the sling comfortable, is treated with the charted oral opioid and a check that the regular doses were given; a tense, hugely swollen shoulder in the first hours is irrigation fluid and settles; new severe pain with fever days later is a septic joint until proven otherwise, and C. acnes grows slowly. A frozen shoulder after decompression is a recognised outcome (two per arm in CSAW) and presents weeks later as stiffness, not to you.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The operation that is not a decompression. The booking says decompression; the arthroscopy finds a full-thickness tear and the surgeon repairs it. The pain plan, the airway and the length of the case all change, and the time to find out is before the block, by asking the surgeon what they will do if they find a tear.
  • Isolated decompression versus decompression with distal clavicle excision. The second bone surface roughly doubles the night pain and brings in the C3-C4 territory over the top of the shoulder that a superior trunk or suprascapular block will not cover; an interscalene block usually does by spread, and a superficial cervical plexus block is the honest supplement if you have chosen a phrenic-sparing technique.
  • Open distal clavicle excision. Still done by some surgeons and for revision: a 3-4 cm incision over the joint, deltotrapezial fascia divided and repaired, more muscle pain and a sling worn for comfort for longer. Same block, same day case.
  • Block as sole anaesthetic. Works for a short decompression in a cooperative patient with a surgeon who does not convert, and spares the airway in beach chair. The C3-C4 skin on top of the shoulder and the posterior portal in the axillary nerve territory are the gaps; surgeon infiltration of the portals closes them.
  • Lateral decubitus. Airway from the side, face in a cradle, dependent arm and peroneal nerve padded, and 5-7 kg of traction on the plexus for the duration. Hypotension matters less, head position more.
  • The request for hypotension. In a 40-minute case it is tempting to say yes. The strokes happened at systolics in the 80s and 90s in beach chair and the case being short does not change the hydrostatics.
  • Chronic pain, opioid tolerance and the patient who has had several injections and years of symptoms. The CSAW population is this population, and their pain after a procedure of unproven benefit can be out of proportion to the tissue. Pre-agree the plan, continue the usual opioid, and do not read the first night as a complication.
  • Diabetes. Dexamethasone 8 mg raises the glucose for a day; it is still worth giving for the block, and the discharge advice should say so.
  • Phrenic palsy. Near-universal after interscalene block; for the COPD or obese patient use a superior trunk or suprascapular block, which costs almost nothing in this operation.

Key sources

The evidence that matters most on this card is surgical, not anaesthetic: CSAW and the Cochrane review that followed it show no clinically important benefit of decompression over placebo arthroscopy for the classic indication, which changes who is on the list and why. The analgesic evidence is extrapolated from the PROSPECT rotator cuff repair guideline and from mixed arthroscopic shoulder populations in which decompression is a minority; the two meta-analyses comparing suprascapular and interscalene blocks and the superior trunk trial are the basis for offering a phrenic-sparing block here more readily than on the arthroplasty cards. The pain score and trajectory are the author’s calibration against the Part B scale, not a measured cohort, and the claim that distal clavicle excision roughly doubles the night pain is author’s judgement.

  1. Beard DJ, Rees JL, Cook JA, et al. Arthroscopic subacromial decompression for subacromial shoulder pain (CSAW): a multicentre, pragmatic, parallel group, placebo-controlled, three-group, randomised surgical trial. Lancet 2018;391:329-338
    313 patients with intact cuffs after failed non-operative care: Oxford Shoulder Score at 6 months 32.7 after decompression versus 34.2 after arthroscopy only (difference -1.3, not significant); both surgical groups 3-4 points better than no treatment, below the threshold of clinical importance; six frozen shoulders
  2. Karjalainen TV, Jain NB, Page CM, et al. Subacromial decompression surgery for rotator cuff disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;1:CD005619
    Eight trials, 1,062 participants with impingement and no full-thickness tear; two placebo-controlled trials (506 participants) found no clinically important benefit of decompression over arthroscopy alone
  3. Toma O, Persoons B, Pogatzki-Zahn E, Van de Velde M, Joshi GP. PROSPECT guideline for rotator cuff repair surgery. Anaesthesia 2019;74:1320-1331
    The nearest procedure-specific guideline: interscalene block first choice, IV dexamethasone preferred over perineural, paracetamol plus NSAID, suprascapular block as an alternative, controlled hypotension not recommended
  4. Hussain N, Goldar G, Ragina N, Banfield L, Laffey JG, Abdallah FW. Suprascapular and interscalene nerve block for shoulder surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Anesthesiology 2017;127:998-1013
    16 trials, 1,152 patients: no difference in 24 h morphine consumption; interscalene better in the recovery room by 1.5 cm on a 10 cm scale and not thereafter; suprascapular block had fewer block-related and respiratory complications
  5. White L, Reardon D, Davis K, Velli G, Bright M. Anterior suprascapular nerve block versus interscalene brachial plexus block for arthroscopic shoulder surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. J Anesth 2022;36:17-25
    Six trials, 709 patients: interscalene pain scores lower by 0.4 in recovery only, no difference in opioid use or in pain at 6-24 h; anterior suprascapular block had far less Horner's syndrome, hoarseness and respiratory impairment
  6. Kang R, Jeong JS, Chin KJ, et al. Superior trunk block provides noninferior analgesia compared with interscalene brachial plexus block in arthroscopic shoulder surgery. Anesthesiology 2019;131:1316-1326
    80 arthroscopic shoulder patients, 15 mL ropivacaine 0.5%: pain at 24 h 1.4 vs 1.2; complete hemidiaphragmatic paresis 5% vs 73%
  7. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, and absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78
  8. Uppal V, Barry G, Ke JXC, et al. Reducing rebound pain severity after arthroscopic shoulder surgery under general anesthesia and interscalene block: a two-centre randomized controlled trial of pre-emptive opioid treatment compared with placebo. Can J Anaesth 2024;71:773-783
    73 arthroscopic shoulder patients: hydromorphone 2 mg at six hours did not reduce worst pain in 24 h (6.5 vs 5.9); mean time to worst pain 14.6 h and to first rescue analgesia 11.3 h after the block
  9. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJ, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients; 22 of the 40 most painful procedures were orthopaedic or trauma operations on the extremities, with regional anaesthesia used in only 15.5% of those; minor procedures produced unexpectedly high day 1 pain
  10. Leon JV, Hermans D, Venkatesha V, Duckworth DG. Patient outcomes following arthroscopic distal clavicle excision: a prospective case series. JSES Int 2023;7:2400-2405
    59 isolated arthroscopic distal clavicle excisions: VAS from 8.2 before surgery to 3.4 at six months; return to work at a mean of 1.7 months
  11. Cullen DJ. Why worry about blood pressure during surgery in the beach chair position? APSF Newsletter 2020
    Hydrostatic correction of about 2 mmHg per inch between cuff and external auditory meatus; strokes reported after shoulder surgery in beach chair with cuff systolics in the 80s-90s; no deliberate hypotension

Upper limb › Shoulder

5 Shoulder stabilisation: Bankart, remplissage, Latarjet

Arthroscopic labral repair with or without remplissage; open coracoid transfer and free bone block for glenoid bone loss

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Bone. For the Latarjet: an osteotomised coracoid screwed onto a decorticated glenoid neck through a split subscapularis, with the conjoint tendon pulled through the split under tension; for the arthroscopic Bankart: anchors in the glenoid rim and a capsulolabral complex re-tensioned onto it, plus an infraspinatus tenodesis into the humeral head if remplissage is added; a young male population with the highest rebound odds in the book

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Interscalene brachial plexus block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone, and a night plan written for a young patient
Catheter: selective Not for the arthroscopic Bankart. For the open Latarjet the catheter is a reasonable choice, not a necessary one: the mechanism is bone and muscle rather than a loaded tendon, the pain settles by day 3, and in a 25-year-old day-case athlete a single shot with dexamethasone, magnesium and a written regimen is the author's default; the catheter is for the revision Latarjet, the bone block with iliac crest harvest, and the patient with a previous catastrophic rebound
Alternatives: Superior trunk block (phrenic sparing, equivalent at 24 h); Suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks for the arthroscopic Bankart, which is inferior in the recovery room and adequate afterwards; not for the Latarjet, where the anterior wound and the musculocutaneous territory are not covered; Intravenous magnesium 50 mg/kg at induction as a rebound adjunct
Position
Beach chair for both; lateral decubitus with arm traction for the arthroscopic Bankart in some hands, especially for posterior labral work
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Arthroscopic: minimal, irrigation only. Open Latarjet: 100-300 mL from the coracoid osteotomy, the split subscapularis and the decorticated glenoid neck, with the axillary vessels close; transfusion rare
Duration
Arthroscopic Bankart 60-90 min, plus 20-30 min for remplissage; open Latarjet 90-150 min; arthroscopic Latarjet longer than open in most hands; free bone block with iliac crest harvest adds a second site and 30 min
Length of stay
Arthroscopic Bankart: day case. Latarjet: day case or one night, surgeons vary. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg): anchors, screws or buttons are implants and Cutibacterium acnes is the organism in this young male population with sebaceous skin
Tranexamic acid
Not needed for the arthroscopic Bankart; TXA 1 g IV is reasonable for the open Latarjet and for arthroscopic visibility
VTE
Mechanical only; young, mobile, day case
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (also the block adjunct) and ondansetron 4 mg IV; young males vomit less than the beach chair average, but a dense block with an opioid rescue at home is still the setting for it
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and useless until the small hours; the shoulder then hurts hard for two or three days, worse after the open operation, and the pain is the healing bone and muscle, not the repair failing; the sling is for the repair, not the pain.
The trap
The Latarjet is open surgery on a 25-year-old: the rebound at 2 am after a single-shot block is the worst in the shoulder chapter because the ambulatory cohort's risk factors (bone surgery, young age) are present and dexamethasone is the one you can remove, and the patient is at home; the block is the easy part and the night plan is the operation

What the surgeon is doing and why

An anterior dislocation in a young person tears the anterior-inferior labrum off the glenoid rim with its capsule and inferior glenohumeral ligament (the Bankart lesion), and the posterolateral humeral head is dented against the rim on the way out (the Hill-Sachs lesion). Each further dislocation stretches the capsule and chips the rim. The surgeon’s problem is therefore three things in one joint: a detached, lax soft-tissue restraint; a glenoid that has lost bone from its front edge and is shaped like an inverted pear; and a humeral defect that can engage the front of the glenoid in abduction and external rotation and lever the head out. The operation chosen depends on how much bone has gone, and the two main operations create pain by completely different mechanisms.

The arthroscopic Bankart repair treats the soft tissue. The labrum and capsule are mobilised off the glenoid neck, the rim is lightly decorticated, three or four suture anchors are placed in the glenoid face at the edge of the cartilage, and the capsulolabral complex is sutured back up onto the rim with a deliberate shift, so that the capsule is tighter than it was. If the Hill-Sachs lesion is large enough to engage, a remplissage is added: the infraspinatus tendon and posterior capsule are sutured down into the humeral defect with anchors, filling it so that the dent can no longer catch the rim. The tissues created are a re-tensioned capsule, three or four small anchor holes in cortical bone, and in remplissage a tenodesis under tension. Recurrence in contact athletes runs about 15% after a Bankart alone and is reduced by remplissage to the point where, in subcritical bone loss, the pooled comparisons find no difference from a Latarjet, with fewer complications.

The Latarjet treats the bone. The coracoid process is osteotomised at its base, with the conjoint tendon (short head of biceps and coracobrachialis) still attached, rotated, and screwed flat onto the decorticated anterior-inferior glenoid neck through a horizontal split in the subscapularis. That does three things at once: the coracoid widens the glenoid arc so the head has further to travel before it falls off; the conjoint tendon, now running through the subscapularis split, becomes a sling that tightens across the front of the joint exactly when the arm is abducted and externally rotated; and the inferior half of the subscapularis is tensioned over the graft. It is the better operation for critical bone loss, for the collision athlete and for the failed Bankart (recurrence 3.5% against 14.4% for a revision Bankart), at the cost of a 30% complication rate in the pooled open series, more late pain, less external rotation, and the two nerves that run within a centimetre of the work: the musculocutaneous nerve entering the conjoint tendon 3-8 cm below the coracoid tip, and the axillary nerve crossing the inferior subscapularis on its way under the joint. In the hands of a surgeon who keeps the split muscular and does not pull the conjoint tendon hard, the clinical nerve injury rate is under 1%; in the pooled literature it is higher, and the transferred tendon changes the course of both nerves permanently, so that electrodiagnostic changes appear in most patients when the arm is tested in the dislocating position. The free bone block (iliac crest or distal tibial allograft) is the Latarjet without the sling, fixed with screws or suture buttons, and the comparative data show the same recurrence; it adds a harvest site when autograft is used.

The pain logic separates the two operations. The arthroscopic Bankart is capsule and small bone: anchors in cortical bone and a re-tensioned capsule that hurts sharply with movement for a few days and settles. Remplissage adds a tenodesis under tension on the back of the joint, which is a small version of the cuff repair mechanism and extends the night pain. The Latarjet is bone and muscle: an osteotomy of the coracoid, a decorticated glenoid neck, two screws, a split and re-tensioned subscapularis, and a conjoint tendon that has been pulled through a muscle and now takes load every time the arm goes out to the side. That is why the Latarjet hurts more, bleeds more and is a 4, and why the pooled comparisons show worse early pain after Latarjet than after Bankart with remplissage, converging later. What both share is the population: young and having bone surgery, which is two of the four rebound risk factors in the ambulatory cohort before you have done anything. The trajectory on this card is for the Latarjet. The arthroscopic Bankart runs a point lower at every time and the remplissage adds a day to its tail.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Assessment, block, magnesium and the night plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has usually decided between Bankart and Latarjet on the CT measurement of glenoid bone loss, the Hill-Sachs size and the sport, and the plan does not change on the table except that an arthroscopic Latarjet converts to open in a few per cent. The patient is young, fit, and has had the shoulder out several times.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is a healthy patient and the whole anaesthetic conversation is about the night. Interscalene block (or superior trunk block if there is a reason to protect the diaphragm, which in this population is rare) with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, placed before induction. For the open Latarjet the author adds intravenous magnesium 50 mg/kg before induction: in the one randomised trial in exactly this operation it reduced the rebound pain on block resolution from 6.2 to 4.0 and lowered pain at 24 h. The catheter decision is made now (see the pain plan). Airway: a second-generation supraglottic device for a short arthroscopic Bankart in a slim patient; a tracheal tube for the open Latarjet and for any case that might run long. Awake baseline pressure before any drug; these are patients with low resting pressures and the chair will take them lower. The written night plan is drafted now, because the patient will be home by the time it matters.

  2. 2 Beach chair or lateral decubitus

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Beach chair for the open Latarjet and for most arthroscopic Bankarts; lateral decubitus with 5-7 kg of longitudinal and lateral traction opens the anterior-inferior joint wider for the labral work and some surgeons prefer it, especially for posterior labral repairs.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Beach chair: the cuff overstates brain perfusion by about 1 mmHg per 1.25 cm between cuff and ear, and a 22-year-old with a resting systolic of 105 and an interscalene block can sit in the chair at a cuff systolic of 80 without anyone being alarmed; that is a brainstem pressure in the 50s and the strokes in the literature happened in this range. Start the vasopressor early and treat the bradycardia-hypotension episodes. Lateral: airway from the side, face in a cradle, dependent arm and peroneal nerve padded, and the traction is a sustained pull on the plexus for 90 minutes that a block will conceal.

  3. 3 Antibiotic and examination under anaesthesia

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon examines the relaxed shoulder for the direction and degree of translation, which confirms the diagnosis and sometimes finds a posterior or multidirectional component that changes the repair.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV finished before the knife, 3 g over 120 kg; sebaceous young male skin carries the highest Cutibacterium acnes load and the anchors or screws are implants. The examination needs a relaxed patient and no muscle tone, so the surgeon may ask for the depth that a block alone does not provide; it is the one moment a short-acting relaxant is reasonable if the airway is a tube.

  4. 4 Arthroscopy, labral mobilisation and glenoid preparation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The joint is inspected, the Hill-Sachs lesion is assessed for engagement with the arm abducted and externally rotated, and the Bankart lesion is mobilised with an elevator off the glenoid neck until the capsulolabral complex floats freely and can be brought up to the rim. The rim and neck are rasped or burred to bleeding bone so the labrum will heal.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Irrigation starts to go into the tissues. The arm is moved repeatedly into abduction and external rotation to test engagement, which pulls on the plexus and will dislocate the shoulder on the table in a relaxed patient; the surgeon expects this. In the arthroscopic Latarjet this is also where the coracoid is exposed from inside, through the rotator interval, with a much longer instrument time.

  5. 5 Anchors and labral repair

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Three or four anchors go into the glenoid face at the cartilage edge from 5:30 to 3 o’clock, sutures are passed through the capsule and labrum with a deliberate inferior-to-superior shift so the capsule ends up tighter, and the complex is tied or locked onto the rim. The tension is set with the arm in a specific rotation and the surgeon will want it held exactly there.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The anchor holes are the bone component and the shift is the capsule component. Position is set by the assistant and must not drift; this is not a request for relaxant but for a still table. In a young patient without a working block the pressure and heart rate will tell you this step has started.

  6. 6 Remplissage

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    If the Hill-Sachs lesion engages, one or two anchors are placed in the floor of the defect from a posterior portal and the infraspinatus tendon and posterior capsule are tied down into it, converting the dent into an extra-articular surface that cannot catch the rim. It costs a few degrees of external rotation and adds 20-30 minutes.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A tenodesis under tension on the back of the shoulder, loaded by every external rotation. It is a small cuff repair, and the patient will describe a posterior ache that outlasts the anterior pain by a few days. The posterior portal and the anchor sit in axillary nerve and suprascapular territory, both covered by an interscalene block.

  7. 7 Open Latarjet: deltopectoral approach and coracoid osteotomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A short deltopectoral incision, the conjoint tendon identified and the coracoid exposed by releasing pectoralis minor from its medial border and the coracoacromial ligament from its lateral. The coracoid is osteotomised at the knee with a saw or osteotome, with the conjoint tendon attached, and prepared with two drill holes and a decorticated undersurface. The musculocutaneous nerve enters the conjoint tendon 3-8 cm below the tip and is at risk from traction on the graft, not from the saw.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first real blood of the operation, from the coracoid and from the branches of the thoracoacromial artery along the pectoralis minor edge. Retraction on the conjoint tendon with the coracoid attached is traction on the musculocutaneous nerve; the surgeon knows and keeps it gentle. A patient in a light plane will tense the pectoralis and the surgeon will say so. Deepen rather than relax, because the subscapularis split that follows is easier to judge in a muscle with tone.

  8. 8 Subscapularis split, glenoid neck preparation and graft fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The subscapularis is split horizontally at the junction of its upper two-thirds and lower third, in the muscular portion rather than at the tendon, which is the step that protects the axillary nerve running across its inferior edge. The capsule beneath is opened vertically, the anterior-inferior glenoid neck is cleared of soft tissue and decorticated to bleeding bone, and the coracoid is laid flat on it, flush with the glenoid face, and fixed with two screws (or suture buttons in some techniques). A graft that sits proud makes arthritis; one that sits medial does not stabilise. The capsule is then repaired to the native glenoid, leaving the graft extra-articular.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is where the Latarjet earns its pain score: an osteotomised bone screwed onto a decorticated bed through a muscle that is being levered open with retractors in the axillary nerve’s territory, with the arm in external rotation to open the split. The glenoid neck bleeds from cancellous bone and the subscapularis from muscle; this is the 200 mL of the operation. Levers under the subscapularis sit on the axillary nerve and the posterior lever on the plexus; a 90-minute Latarjet in a muscular athlete produces plenty of retractor force. The axillary vessels and the plexus are a finger’s breadth medial to the field, which is why surgeons are careful with the medial retractor and why arterial injury, though rare, is on the consent form.

  9. 9 Closure, sling and emergence

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The subscapularis split closes itself when the arm returns to neutral and is not sutured by most surgeons; the deltopectoral interval is closed in layers; the skin is a 5 cm scar. For the arthroscopic Bankart the portals are closed with a stitch or a strip. A sling goes on and stays for four to six weeks, with external rotation limited to protect the repair, and the patient is told not to reach behind.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the antiemetic. The sling before the patient lightens, because the first thing a young patient with a dead arm does is pick it up by the wrist and swing it, and the position that does it loads the repair. Emergence is unremarkable. Examine and document hand function and regimental badge sensation as far as the block allows and write down what could not be tested; the Latarjet is the shoulder operation most likely to produce a real musculocutaneous or axillary nerve problem, and the block makes it invisible for 16 hours.

  10. 10 Recovery, discharge and the first night at home

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The repair is protected by the sling and nothing else. The surgeon wants the patient home, elbow and wrist moving, and back at the first follow-up with a radiograph showing the graft in place.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block lasts 12-24 hours with dexamethasone, 17 hours in the Latarjet trial, and the worst pain comes on average 14-15 hours after it was placed, which is 2-4 am for a morning list. The first regular paracetamol and NSAID dose goes in before the patient leaves recovery, the oral opioid is dispensed with a written instruction for the first two nights, and the patient and whoever is taking them home are told that the arm coming back to life brings a sharp rise in pain over an hour that is treated by the regimen, not a reason to attend the emergency department. Pre-emptive opioid at six hours did not help in the one trial that tested it; regular non-opioid analgesia started on time and a rescue dose taken at the first tingle is the plan. A dense block is not a reason to keep the patient in. For a Latarjet done as a day case, surgeons vary, and the honest default in a patient without home support is one night.

Pain plan

The arthroscopic Bankart is capsule and small bone and runs a point below the trajectory on this card at every time; a single-shot interscalene or superior trunk block with intravenous dexamethasone, regular paracetamol and NSAID, and two nights of oral opioid is the defensible default and nothing more is needed. The remplissage adds a tenodesis under tension and a posterior ache that lasts a few days longer; it does not change the plan. There is no procedure-specific PROSPECT guideline; the rotator cuff repair guideline is the nearest and its skeleton applies.

The open Latarjet is the operation this card is scored for. The mechanism is bone (coracoid osteotomy, decorticated neck, screws) and muscle (a split and re-tensioned subscapularis, a conjoint tendon that now takes load with every abduction), which is severe for three days and then settles, because nothing is being loaded through healing tendon. That is a 4 with a quick fall, not a 5. The defensible default is a single-shot interscalene block with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, intravenous magnesium 50 mg/kg before induction, regular paracetamol and an NSAID started in recovery, and oral opioid for three nights, with a written plan. The author’s practice is that this is enough for a primary Latarjet in a counselled young patient, and that a catheter is the right call for the revision Latarjet, the bone block with iliac crest harvest (a second painful site that the interscalene block does not touch), the patient with a chronic pain history or opioid tolerance, and the patient who describes a catastrophic rebound after a previous shoulder operation. A catheter in a 24-year-old going home with a sling needs a fixation that will survive a weekend and a phone number that answers; the common failure is the catheter in the bed by the second morning.

The suprascapular plus axillary combination is adequate for the arthroscopic Bankart and wrong for the Latarjet: the anterior wound, the coracoid and the conjoint tendon sit in musculocutaneous and lateral pectoral territory that neither block covers.

Rebound is the enemy on this card more than on any other in the shoulder chapter. In the 972-patient ambulatory cohort the independent risk factors were bone surgery (OR 1.82), younger age, female sex (OR 1.52) and no intravenous dexamethasone (OR 1.78); a Latarjet in a 22-year-old has the first two before you start and the fourth is your choice. Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone with the hand warm, the fingers moving and the sling on is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were taken; pain with a tense, swelling deltopectoral wound in the first hours is a haematoma and the surgeon’s problem; weakness of elbow flexion or numbness of the lateral forearm once the block has receded is the musculocutaneous nerve and needs documenting and the surgeon told the same day.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Arthroscopic versus open Latarjet. Arthroscopic Latarjet has a long learning curve, longer operating times (110-170 minutes in a recent series), a conversion rate to open of a few per cent in early hands, and the same nerves at risk from a different direction. The pain is somewhat less; the block choice is the same.
  • Free bone block. Iliac crest autograft brings a second wound in a territory no shoulder block covers; it hurts as much as the shoulder for the first days and is the strongest argument for a catheter or at least local infiltration at the crest. Distal tibial allograft avoids the harvest.
  • Posterior labral repair and posterior bone block. Lateral decubitus more often, the posterior portals in axillary and suprascapular territory (both covered by interscalene), and a sling in neutral rather than internal rotation; the same capsule and small bone mechanism.
  • Capsular shift for multidirectional instability. Plication of a lax capsule without a labral tear, usually in a hyperlax young woman; capsule mechanism, settles in days, and a population with a higher rebound and anxiety profile than the collision athlete.
  • Revision surgery. A failed Bankart going to Latarjet, or a failed Latarjet going to a bone block, is scar, retained metal, more bleeding and a longer case; the catheter earns its place.
  • The nerves. Interscalene block makes the musculocutaneous and axillary nerves untestable for 16 hours after the one shoulder operation that does injure them. Document before, document what could not be tested after, and examine the next morning.
  • Beach chair in the young hypotensive patient. A resting systolic of 100 and a cuff systolic of 75 in the chair is the brainstem pressure the literature’s strokes happened at; youth is not protection, and the short case tempts people to skip the vasopressor infusion.
  • Epilepsy. Seizure-related dislocations are an indication for the Latarjet and the patient will dislocate again with the next seizure; anticonvulsant timing and a plan for a seizure in recovery are part of the anaesthetic.
  • Pain catastrophising and kinesiophobia. In Bankart patients followed beyond two years, pain intensity tracked with unhelpful thinking rather than with bone loss or the operation; the pre-operative conversation about what the pain will be, and that it is not the repair failing, is analgesia.

Key sources

The surgical evidence is strong on recurrence and weak on pain: the meta-analyses compare Bankart, remplissage and Latarjet on redislocation and return to sport and mention pain only as a late VAS score. The Latarjet complication rate of 30% is pooled from level IV series across four decades and overstates modern open practice, where a single-surgeon series of 164 cases had no clinical musculocutaneous or axillary deficit. The one analgesic trial specific to the Latarjet is the magnesium study, small and single-centre but randomised and blinded. The block evidence is extrapolated from the PROSPECT rotator cuff repair guideline. The pain scores and the catheter advice are the author’s calibration against the Part B scale and the mechanism.

Upper limb › Shoulder

6 SLAP repair and biceps tenodesis

Superior labral repair; long head of biceps tenotomy, arthroscopic suprapectoral tenodesis and open subpectoral tenodesis

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Tendon under tension. A tenodesis fixes the biceps tendon into a drill hole in the humerus under a set tension and the muscle pulls on it with every elbow flexion; a SLAP repair re-anchors the superior labrum and biceps root onto decorticated glenoid under tension. Both are small versions of the cuff repair mechanism: low peak, but a tendon that is loaded by movement for weeks. A tenotomy has no mechanism beyond the arthroscopy

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Interscalene or superior trunk block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone
Catheter: no No mechanism large enough to justify one; the peak is low, the patient is at home, and the tendon pain that persists is managed by the sling and the oral regimen, not an infusion
Alternatives: Suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks for the arthroscopic procedures (phrenic sparing, inferior in the recovery room only); For the open subpectoral tenodesis, interscalene is the better choice because the incision and the drill hole sit in axillary, musculocutaneous and medial brachial cutaneous territory, with surgeon infiltration of the wound; General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration for an isolated tenotomy
Position
Beach chair for most; lateral decubitus with arm traction for SLAP repair in some hands because traction opens the superior joint; the open subpectoral tenodesis needs the arm abducted and externally rotated on a support
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
