Minimal for the arthroscopic procedures; the open subpectoral tenodesis bleeds from the drill hole and the pectoralis edge, under 100 mL
Duration
Isolated tenotomy 20-30 min; arthroscopic tenodesis or SLAP repair 45-75 min; open subpectoral tenodesis 45-60 min as a stand-alone, 20 min added to an arthroscopy
Length of stay
Day case. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg): anchors and interference screws are implants and Cutibacterium acnes is the shoulder organism; for a pure tenotomy with no implant surgeons vary
Tranexamic acid
Not needed; TXA 1 g IV is a reasonable request for arthroscopic visibility
VTE
Mechanical only; day case, mobile from the first day
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (also the block adjunct) and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm is numb and heavy until the small hours; after that the shoulder aches for a few days and the front of the upper arm stays sore for a week or two where the tendon has been fixed, which is the tendon healing and not a problem.
The trap
The tenodesis looks like a small operation and is: the trap is the patient, not the procedure. SLAP and biceps surgery is done for pain rather than instability, the population carries more chronic pain, more pre-operative opioid use and more disappointment than the Bankart population, and the first night after a single-shot block in a day case is where it shows

What the surgeon is doing and why

The long head of biceps is a tendon that runs from the supraglenoid tubercle and the superior labrum, over the top of the humeral head inside the joint, and out through the bicipital groove under the transverse ligament. It is a pain generator out of proportion to its function. Inside the joint it frays, inflames and becomes unstable in the groove when the subscapularis or the biceps pulley is damaged; at its root it can peel the superior labrum off the glenoid (the SLAP lesion, superior labrum anterior to posterior), classically in the throwing athlete whose late-cocking position winds the biceps root up and pulls the labrum back, and commonly in the middle-aged patient as a degenerative finding of uncertain significance. Nothing in the arm needs the long head: the short head and brachialis flex the elbow, and a tenotomised long head loses a few per cent of supination strength and nothing measurable in daily life. The surgeon’s choice is therefore not whether to sacrifice the tendon but what to do with the stump.

Three operations, in ascending order of tissue:

  1. Tenotomy. The tendon is cut at its root with a radiofrequency device through the arthroscope. It retracts down the groove and scars where it stops. Five minutes; no implant; no protection needed. The costs are a Popeye deformity (the belly of the muscle drops; 23% in the pooled level I trials against 7% after tenodesis) and cramping pain in the biceps in the first months (three times the odds). Across 11 randomised trials and 860 patients, function and pain at follow-up were the same as tenodesis.
  2. Arthroscopic suprapectoral tenodesis. The tendon is cut at its root, pulled out of the joint, and fixed into a drill hole at the top of the bicipital groove or just below it with an interference screw or anchor, at a length that keeps the muscle at its native tension. The diseased intra-articular portion is removed; the groove portion stays. The surgeon adds 20-30 minutes and an implant, and the patient keeps the contour of the arm. Stiffness afterwards is a little commoner than with the open technique.
  3. Open subpectoral tenodesis. A 3 cm incision in the axillary fold at the inferior border of pectoralis major, the tendon retrieved from below, the groove segment excised with it (which is the argument for the technique: the groove is where the tendon is most diseased), and the tendon fixed into a drill hole in the humeral shaft under the pectoralis tendon with a screw or button. The wound sits over the musculocutaneous nerve as it enters coracobrachialis, with the axillary and brachial vessels medial and the radial nerve a drill length posterior; nerve complications were 1.1% in the pooled open series against 0.2% arthroscopic, and the open wound carries a small infection rate. It is a stand-alone operation for the young patient with isolated biceps pathology and the preferred technique of many surgeons for the SLAP tear in a patient over 30, where the pooled data show a higher chance of a good outcome from tenodesis (88%) than from repair (63%) and the same return to sport in the under-40 cohorts.

The SLAP repair itself is reserved by most surgeons for the young overhead athlete with an acute type II lesion: the superior labrum and biceps root are mobilised, the superior glenoid is decorticated, one or two anchors are placed at the biceps root and the labrum is sutured back down under tension. The cost is stiffness, a long rehabilitation and a reoperation rate of around 10% in the pooled cohorts, which is why the indications have narrowed.

The pain logic. A tenotomy has no mechanism beyond the arthroscopy: portals, irrigation, a bursal or joint inspection, and perhaps a biceps cramp in the second week when the muscle settles into its new length. A tenodesis is a small tendon-tension operation: a tendon fixed into a drill hole under set tension and pulled on by every elbow flexion for the six weeks it takes to heal to bone. The peak is low, because the drill hole is small and nothing else is cut, but the anterior arm stays sore for a week or two and lifting a kettle hurts. The open subpectoral adds a wound through the axillary fold and a drill hole in cortical shaft bone, which is the bone component and the reason it sits at the top of this card’s range. The SLAP repair is capsule and labrum under tension on decorticated glenoid with the arm immobilised in a sling; it hurts sharply on movement for a few days and the stiffness afterwards is a surgical rather than an analgesic problem. All of it is a 2 with a block: the day 1 figure of 4 is the rebound, and the tail is a small tenodesis in a rested arm, which is why it falls to 1 by a week for most.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative assessment, the patient and the block

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Biceps and SLAP surgery is done for pain, usually after injections and physiotherapy have failed, in a population that includes manual workers, throwing athletes and patients with years of anterior shoulder pain and a scan that may or may not explain it. The surgeon’s plan is usually “arthroscopy, tenodesis or tenotomy depending on findings, and whatever else is there”, so the operation that arrives is not always the one booked.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The patient matters more than the procedure. Pre-operative opioid use, a long pain history, and a diagnosis that is “a SLAP tear” on a scan in a 45-year-old all predict a worse first night than the tissue justifies, and these are commoner here than on the instability list. Ask, and write the night plan accordingly. The block: a single-shot interscalene or superior trunk block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg covers the arthroscopy and the first evening; for the open subpectoral tenodesis the interscalene is preferred because the wound and drill hole sit in territory (axillary, musculocutaneous) that a suprascapular block does not reach. Airway: a supraglottic device is reasonable for a short arthroscopic case in a slim patient; a tube for the open procedure with the arm abducted away from you and for any case likely to find a cuff tear. Awake baseline pressure before any drug.

  2. 2 Beach chair or lateral, and the arm position for the open tenodesis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Beach chair for most; lateral decubitus with traction opens the superior joint for SLAP work. For the subpectoral incision the arm is abducted and externally rotated on a support to bring the axillary fold forward and lift the pectoralis edge.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The usual beach chair arithmetic (about 1 mmHg per 1.25 cm between cuff and ear; strokes at cuff systolics in the 80s and 90s; vasopressor infusion started early, no deliberate hypotension). The abducted, externally rotated arm for the open tenodesis is held for 30-45 minutes and puts the plexus on stretch; check the position before the drapes go on and keep the abduction under 90 degrees.

  3. 3 Antibiotic and diagnostic arthroscopy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The joint is inspected: the biceps root and labrum, the tendon pulled into the joint with a probe to see the groove portion, the pulley, the subscapularis, the cuff and the cartilage. The findings decide tenotomy versus tenodesis and whether a SLAP repair is warranted, and often reveal the cuff tear that is the real pain generator.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV finished before the knife, 3 g over 120 kg. The one moment that changes your plan is here: a full-thickness cuff tear turns this into a rotator cuff repair with its own card and a different night, and the surgeon will tell the assistant before they tell you. Ask.

  4. 4 Tenotomy or intra-articular release of the tendon

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tendon is cut at its root with radiofrequency, flush with the labrum, so that it retracts down the groove. If a tenodesis is planned, the tendon is first tagged with a suture or held with a clamp through an anterior portal so it cannot retract, then released.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing to do. A released tendon in a tenotomy patient means the operation is over bar the portals; a tagged tendon means 20-45 minutes more.

  5. 5 Arthroscopic suprapectoral tenodesis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tendon is brought out through an anterior portal, the diseased intra-articular part excised, the groove opened or the subacromial space used to reach the top of the groove, a drill hole made in the humerus and the tendon fixed with an interference screw or anchor at a length that sets the muscle tension. The surgeon judges the tension with the elbow at a set angle; too tight limits elbow extension, too loose gives a Popeye.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A drill hole in metaphyseal bone and a tendon under set tension: the two mechanisms of this card created in a few minutes. The arm is held still in the position the surgeon sets, and the elbow angle matters, so the assistant will hold it. This is bone surgery for rebound purposes, in a small way.

  6. 6 Open subpectoral tenodesis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A 3 cm incision along the inferior border of pectoralis major in the axillary fold, the pectoralis tendon retracted upwards, the tendon found in the groove under it and delivered into the wound, the groove segment excised, and a unicortical drill hole made in the shaft at the inferior pectoralis border for a screw or a button. The musculocutaneous nerve lies medial as it enters coracobrachialis and the axillary and brachial vessels are medial again; the surgeon keeps retractors lateral and avoids drilling through the far cortex. The pectoralis tendon is not cut.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A wound in the axillary fold and a drill hole in cortical shaft bone. The incision bleeds from the pectoralis edge and the hole from the medullary canal, under 100 mL. Arm abduction is held throughout. Retraction medially is traction on the musculocutaneous nerve and the vessels; the surgeon will want the arm relaxed, which the block provides. Surgeons infiltrate the wound with local anaesthetic at the end, which is worth encouraging because the medial arm skin is intercostobrachial territory that the block does not cover.

  7. 7 SLAP repair

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For the young athlete with an unstable biceps root: the labrum is mobilised off the superior glenoid, the bone is decorticated, one or two anchors are placed posterior to the biceps root (anterior anchors stiffen the shoulder), sutures pass through the labrum and the complex is tied down. The arm goes into a sling for four to six weeks with no active biceps use.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Capsule and small bone, under tension, immobilised. The peak is a point higher than a tenodesis on day 1 and the stiffness afterwards is the surgeon’s problem rather than yours. Traction in the lateral position for this step is sustained and the plexus is already blocked, so position checks are the only safeguard.

  8. 8 Closure, sling and emergence

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals closed with a stitch or a strip, the subpectoral wound in layers with a subcuticular suture, and a sling: for comfort only after a tenotomy, for four to six weeks after a tenodesis (no lifting, no resisted elbow flexion) and after a SLAP repair.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the antiemetic. The sling on before the patient lightens, because the first thing a patient with a dead arm does is flex the elbow against the weight of the forearm, which is the one movement the tenodesis should not see. Emergence is quick. Document hand and forearm sensation and elbow flexion as far as the block allows after an open subpectoral tenodesis, and write down what could not be tested, because a musculocutaneous neurapraxia from the retractor is the recognised complication and the block hides it until tomorrow.

  9. 9 Recovery, discharge and the first fortnight

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Day case. The surgeon wants the elbow and wrist moving, the shoulder resting, and no biceps load for six weeks after a tenodesis.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block lasts 12-24 hours with dexamethasone and the worst pain arrives on average 14-15 hours after it, in the middle of the first night; first rescue was needed at a mean of 11 hours in the one trial that timed it. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID start in recovery, the oral opioid is dispensed for two nights with a written plan, and the patient is told that the anterior arm will stay sore for a week or two after a tenodesis and that a cramp in the biceps in the second week after a tenotomy is the muscle settling at its new length, not a tear. Pre-emptive opioid at six hours did not reduce the worst pain in the one randomised trial; a regular regimen started on time and a rescue dose at the first tingle is the plan. A dense block is not a reason to keep the patient.

Pain plan

The mechanism is a small tendon-tension operation with a drill hole, in a day-case patient, so the plan is a single-shot block that covers the operation and the evening, a regular oral regimen that starts before the block recedes, two nights of oral opioid, and no catheter. There is no procedure-specific PROSPECT guideline; the rotator cuff repair guideline is the nearest and its skeleton (interscalene first, intravenous dexamethasone preferred over perineural, paracetamol and NSAID, suprascapular block as the phrenic-sparing alternative, no controlled hypotension) applies with the catheter recommendation removed.

The defensible default is an interscalene block with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% or a superior trunk block with the same volume, with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg. For the arthroscopic procedures the suprascapular plus axillary combination is adequate: in 16 trials it matched interscalene for 24 h opioid use and lost only in the recovery room, which a dose of intravenous opioid covers. For the open subpectoral tenodesis the author’s practice is interscalene, because the incision and the drill hole sit in axillary and musculocutaneous territory with the medial arm skin in intercostobrachial territory, and the surgeon’s wound infiltration closes the last gap. General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration alone is acceptable for an isolated tenotomy, which has no mechanism to block.

The catheter is no for all three operations. The tendon pain that persists for a fortnight after a tenodesis is low-grade, movement-related and protected by the sling, which is exactly the kind of pain an infusion does not help and an oral regimen does. The patient who would seem to justify one (the opioid-tolerant, the chronic pain patient, the one with three previous shoulder operations) is better served by a pre-agreed oral plan with the usual opioid continued and the pain service told, than by a catheter in a day case.

Rebound is the planning target because this is an ambulatory operation with a drill hole in a population that skews towards two of the four risk factors in the 972-patient cohort (bone surgery OR 1.82, younger age), with the absence of intravenous dexamethasone (OR 1.78) the one you control. Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone, with the hand warm and moving and the sling comfortable, is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were taken; a swollen tense shoulder in the first hours is irrigation fluid; a swollen, bruised upper arm after a subpectoral tenodesis is a haematoma from the drill hole and settles unless it is expanding; numbness of the lateral forearm or weak elbow flexion after the block has receded is the musculocutaneous nerve and is documented and reported the same day; a biceps that is suddenly lower in the arm a week after a tenodesis is a failed fixation, which is the surgeon’s conversation.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The operation that arrives is not the one booked. A biceps procedure is often “arthroscopy plus whatever is found”, and the finding that matters is a full-thickness cuff tear, which changes the card. Ask before the block what the surgeon will do if they find one.
  • Tenotomy versus tenodesis. The randomised evidence shows the same pain and function with more Popeye deformity and cramping after tenotomy and 15 minutes more operating time for tenodesis. Surgeons vary by patient age, occupation and preference; the anaesthetic is the same except that a tenotomy needs no sling and no protection.
  • Arthroscopic suprapectoral versus open subpectoral. The open technique excises the groove segment, has slightly less stiffness, and carries a small wound infection and nerve complication rate that the arthroscopic technique does not; its wound and drill hole are the reason the interscalene is preferred over a suprascapular block for it.
  • Tenodesis as part of a cuff repair or decompression. The commonest setting in which a biceps is tenodesed is as a step in another operation; the pain plan belongs to the larger procedure and the tenodesis adds a sore anterior arm for a fortnight.
  • The SLAP repair in a patient over 35. Most surgeons now tenodese rather than repair in this group on the pooled outcome data; a surgeon who still repairs is committing the patient to a long stiff recovery and a 10% reoperation rate, and the analgesic plan is the same as the tenodesis with a point more on day 1.
  • Chronic pain, pre-operative opioid use and the uncertain diagnosis. This is the population in which “SLAP tear” on a scan is being treated in a 45-year-old with years of pain, and the first night can be out of proportion to the tissue. The pre-operative conversation about what the pain will be, and that a sore anterior arm for two weeks is the tendon healing, is analgesia.
  • Bilateral or repeated surgery. Patients who have had one shoulder done know what their rebound was like; ask, and plan the second night around the first.
  • Phrenic palsy. Near-universal after interscalene block; for the obese or COPD patient a superior trunk or suprascapular block costs nothing in this operation.
  • Beach chair hypotension in a short case. The temptation is to skip the vasopressor infusion for a 40-minute case; the strokes happened in short cases too.

Key sources

The evidence on this card is surgical and good on the choice of operation: 11 randomised trials show tenotomy and tenodesis give the same pain and function, with cosmetic deformity and cramping the only consistent differences, and the pooled cohorts favour tenodesis over SLAP repair for all but the young overhead athlete. There is no analgesic evidence specific to biceps or SLAP surgery; the block recommendations are extrapolated from the PROSPECT rotator cuff repair guideline and the suprascapular versus interscalene meta-analyses in mixed arthroscopic populations, and the rebound data come from a general ambulatory block cohort and a mixed arthroscopic shoulder trial. The pain score, the trajectory, the claim that a tenodesed arm stays sore for a fortnight and the preference for interscalene over suprascapular block for the open subpectoral technique are the author’s judgement from the mechanism and the anatomy, not measured outcomes.

  1. Hartland AW, Islam R, Teoh KH, Rashid MS. Clinical effectiveness of tenotomy versus tenodesis for long head of biceps pathology: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open 2022;12:e061954
    11 randomised trials, 860 patients: no difference in patient-reported function or pain; tenodesis reduced Popeye deformity (OR 0.29); tenotomy was 15 minutes shorter
  2. Zhang C, Yang G, Li T, et al. Biceps tenodesis better improves the shoulder function compared with tenotomy for long head of the biceps tendon lesions: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. J Clin Med 2023;12:1754
    10 randomised trials, 787 patients: small Constant score advantage for tenodesis; tenotomy had more Popeye deformity (OR 3.34) and cramping pain (OR 3.36); no difference in pain, ASES, strength or external rotation
  3. Belk JW, Kraeutler MJ, Houck DA, Chrisman AN, Scillia AJ, McCarty EC. Biceps tenodesis versus tenotomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of level I randomized controlled trials. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2021;30:951-960
    Five level I trials, 468 patients, mean age 60: cosmetic deformity 6.8% after tenodesis versus 23.3% after tenotomy; no difference in pain or function
  4. Hurley ET, Baker R, Danilkowicz RM, et al. Similar outcomes between biceps tenodesis and SLAP repair for SLAP tears in younger patients: a meta-analysis. J ISAKOS 2024;9:79-83
    Five cohort studies of type II SLAP tears under 40: return to play 78.5% after tenodesis versus 67.7% after repair, not significant; no difference in ASES, pain or reoperation (2.9% vs 10.8%)
  5. Recker AJ, Waters TL, Bullock G, et al. Biceps tenodesis has greater expected value than repair for isolated type II SLAP tears: a meta-analysis and expected-value decision analysis. Arthroscopy 2022;38:2887-2896
    23 studies, 908 patients: probability of a good outcome 87.8% after tenodesis versus 62.9% after SLAP repair; reinjury 1.5% versus 6.4%
  6. Lee TY, Touhey DC, Perugini JM, et al. Outcomes following arthroscopic suprapectoral and open subpectoral biceps tenodesis at short- to midterm follow-up: a systematic review. Am J Sports Med 2026;54:2341-2353
    43 studies, 11,113 tenodeses, mean age 54: complications 5.6% overall; stiffness commoner after arthroscopic suprapectoral (2.5% vs 1.4%), wound infection (1.1% vs 0.5%) and nerve complications (1.1% vs 0.2%) commoner after open subpectoral
  7. Toma O, Persoons B, Pogatzki-Zahn E, Van de Velde M, Joshi GP. PROSPECT guideline for rotator cuff repair surgery. Anaesthesia 2019;74:1320-1331
    The nearest procedure-specific guideline: interscalene block first choice, IV dexamethasone preferred over perineural, paracetamol plus NSAID, suprascapular block as an alternative, controlled hypotension not recommended
  8. Hussain N, Goldar G, Ragina N, Banfield L, Laffey JG, Abdallah FW. Suprascapular and interscalene nerve block for shoulder surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Anesthesiology 2017;127:998-1013
    16 trials, 1,152 patients: no difference in 24 h morphine; interscalene better in the recovery room only; suprascapular block had fewer block-related and respiratory complications
  9. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, and absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78
  10. Uppal V, Barry G, Ke JXC, et al. Reducing rebound pain severity after arthroscopic shoulder surgery under general anesthesia and interscalene block: a two-centre randomized controlled trial of pre-emptive opioid treatment compared with placebo. Can J Anaesth 2024;71:773-783
    73 arthroscopic shoulder patients: hydromorphone 2 mg at six hours did not reduce worst pain in 24 h; worst pain at a mean of 14.6 h and first rescue at 11.3 h after the block
  11. Cullen DJ. Why worry about blood pressure during surgery in the beach chair position? APSF Newsletter 2020
    Hydrostatic correction of about 2 mmHg per inch between cuff and external auditory meatus; strokes reported after shoulder surgery in beach chair with cuff systolics in the 80s-90s; no deliberate hypotension

Upper limb › Shoulder

7 Frozen shoulder: MUA, hydrodilatation, capsular release

Manipulation under anaesthesia, hydrodilatation under block, and arthroscopic capsular release for adhesive capsulitis

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Capsule. A contracted, fibrotic capsule torn (MUA), ruptured by fluid (hydrodilatation) or cut (arthroscopic release); sharp pain with movement that is deliberately provoked by physiotherapy from day 0 because the released capsule re-scars within days if the range is not used; settles over a week in most, but the pre-operative pain and the diabetic phenotype can run longer

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Interscalene brachial plexus block with intravenous dexamethasone as the anaesthetic for MUA and hydrodilatation, and as the analgesic for arthroscopic release; a continuous interscalene catheter for the release when the unit can run one into day 2-3 of physiotherapy
Catheter: selective The one shoulder operation on this list where the catheter's logic is physiotherapy rather than pain intensity: a release that is not moved through its full range on days 0-3 re-scars, and a working block on the physiotherapy table is what makes that possible. The author's practice is a catheter for the arthroscopic release in the stiff diabetic or post-surgical shoulder and after a failed MUA, and a single shot with a day 1 physiotherapy session timed inside the block for the uncomplicated primary
Alternatives: Superior trunk block (phrenic sparing, same anaesthetic quality for the shoulder); Suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks, adequate for hydrodilatation and a gentle MUA, inferior as a sole anaesthetic for a forceful manipulation or an arthroscopic release; Cervical nerve root block (C5-C6) as used in some units for awake MUA; General anaesthesia alone for MUA, which is the historical technique and leaves the first night uncovered
Position
Supine or semi-sitting on the trolley for MUA and hydrodilatation; beach chair or lateral for the arthroscopic release
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
None for MUA and hydrodilatation; minimal irrigation-only loss for the release, though the released capsule bleeds into the joint
Duration
MUA 5-10 min; hydrodilatation 15-20 min including the injection; arthroscopic release 30-60 min, longer with a subacromial decompression or a posterior release added
Length of stay
Day case for all three. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
None for MUA or hydrodilatation; cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g over 120 kg) for the arthroscopic release in most units, though there is no implant and surgeons vary
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
Mechanical only; the patient walks out and uses the arm from the first day
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (also the block adjunct) and ondansetron 4 mg IV if a general anaesthetic is given; the intra-articular steroid the surgeon injects at MUA or hydrodilatation is a separate dose and raises the diabetic's glucose for days
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb for most of the day and the physiotherapist will move it while it is numb; after that the shoulder is sore for a few days every time it is stretched, and it has to be stretched, because a shoulder that is rested after this procedure stiffens again.
The trap
The manipulation breaks the capsule by force through a long lever in a patient who is often a woman in her fifties with diabetes and thin bone: a humeral shaft or surgical neck fracture, a glenoid rim avulsion or a dislocation is the surgeon's slip, but a patient who is deeply relaxed and insensate gives no warning, and the sound of the capsule tearing and the sound of bone are not always distinguishable

What the surgeon is doing and why

A frozen shoulder is a capsule that has become inflamed, then fibrotic, then contracted. The rotator interval and the coracohumeral ligament thicken first, which takes away external rotation; the anterior and inferior capsule follow, which takes away abduction and elevation; the axillary pouch, which should let the head drop into it on abduction, is obliterated. The joint volume falls from 15-20 mL to a few millilitres. The disease is self-limiting over one to three years in most people, which is the fact every treatment has to be measured against, and it runs longer and harder in diabetics, who make up a third of the surgical population. Nothing about the humeral head, the glenoid or the cuff is wrong; the whole problem is a few millimetres of contracted collagen, and all three procedures on this card exist to tear, burst or cut it.

Manipulation under anaesthesia tears it. With the patient relaxed and insensate, the surgeon holds the scapula down with one hand and takes the humerus through forward elevation, then abduction, then external and internal rotation, using the forearm as the lever and the elbow as the grip, feeling and hearing the capsule give. The inferior capsule tears on abduction and the anterior capsule on external rotation. It takes five minutes. Most surgeons inject steroid into the joint at the same time. The costs are a fracture of the humeral shaft or surgical neck through a long lever in osteoporotic bone, a glenoid rim avulsion, a dislocation, a cuff tear or a plexus traction injury, each uncommon and each reported; the two recent series that counted found a glenoid avulsion in one of 68 and one of 110 manipulations, and a plexus injury in the second.

Hydrodilatation bursts it. Under image guidance, often by a radiologist rather than a surgeon, 20-40 mL of saline with local anaesthetic and steroid is injected into the joint until the capsule ruptures, usually into the subscapularis bursa, and the arm is then moved. It is done awake with local anaesthetic in many units, under a block in some, and is the least invasive of the three; the pooled trials find a small effect on pain and range over steroid injection alone that may not be clinically important, and the UK FROST team named it as the comparator their trial lacked.

Arthroscopic capsular release cuts it. Through a posterior portal in a joint with almost no room, the surgeon divides the rotator interval and coracohumeral ligament with a radiofrequency device, then the anterior capsule down to the subscapularis, then, in most hands, the inferior capsule round the axillary pouch, with the axillary nerve a few millimetres below it, and sometimes the posterior capsule. The arm is then manipulated through the released range, which is now easy. Many surgeons add a subacromial decompression. In UK FROST, 503 patients were randomised between release, MUA and structured physiotherapy with steroid injection, and at 12 months the release beat MUA by two Oxford Shoulder Score points and physiotherapy by three, which the trial had pre-defined as below clinical importance; MUA did not beat physiotherapy; serious adverse events were commoner after release (eight against two); and MUA was the most cost-effective arm while the release was not cost-effective at all. The honest summary is that all three treatments work, the release works slightly more and costs and risks more, and the physiotherapy afterwards is doing much of the work in every arm.

The pain logic. The mechanism is capsule: a torn, burst or cut fibrotic capsule that is sharply painful on movement and settles over days, with no bone cut, nothing repaired and nothing under tension. That would make a 1 if the patient were allowed to rest. They are not. The released capsule re-scars within days unless the new range is used, so the physiotherapy starts on the day of the procedure and is deliberately painful, and the patient’s pain in the first week is physiotherapy-evoked capsule pain on a background of the pre-existing inflamed joint. The diabetic shoulder is stiffer, bleeds more into the joint and re-scars faster, and the patient who comes to a release after a failed MUA has had two insults. That is why the card is a 2 rather than a 1, why the trajectory has a day 1 peak that is the physiotherapy rather than the rebound, and why the block on this card is as much a physiotherapy tool as an analgesic.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The patient, the procedure and the block as the anaesthetic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has usually chosen between MUA, hydrodilatation and release on the duration of symptoms, the diabetic status, the previous treatment and their own habit; a post-surgical or post-traumatic stiff shoulder is more likely to get a release because the adhesions are extracapsular and a manipulation alone will not free them.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For MUA and hydrodilatation the block is the anaesthetic. An interscalene block with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% and intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg gives a flail, insensate arm within 20 minutes and lasts into the evening; the surgeon manipulates with the patient awake or lightly sedated, which has the advantage that the patient sees the arm move through a range they have not had for a year, and the disadvantage that they hear the capsule tear. Units that do MUA under general anaesthesia alone are running the historical technique and leave the first night and the day 1 physiotherapy uncovered. For the arthroscopic release the block is the analgesic and a general anaesthetic goes on top because the beach chair and the camera make an awake patient hard work; the catheter decision is made now (see the pain plan). This population is in its fifties, a third diabetic, and the diabetic frozen shoulder patient is the one whose glucose the steroid and the dexamethasone will disturb for days; the ward and the patient need to know. A supraglottic airway is adequate for a release in a slim patient; a tube for the obese diabetic with reflux. Awake baseline pressure before any drug if a chair is involved.

  2. 2 Positioning for MUA and hydrodilatation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    MUA is done on the trolley, supine or semi-sitting, with the surgeon standing on the affected side holding the scapula down with one hand and the arm with the other; hydrodilatation is done supine or seated under ultrasound or fluoroscopy, usually in the radiology department.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    No chair, no head holder, no pressure problem. The block itself is the risk: a seated or semi-sitting patient with a fresh interscalene block has a vagal reflex waiting (two of 68 patients in one series had a vasovagal episode during the block, and one a panic attack), and the hoarseness and Horner’s syndrome that follow a high-volume interscalene are worth warning about before they are noticed. Monitoring and a cannula for the whole of the procedure, because the manipulation that follows is not pleasant to watch and the patient’s pressure will tell you how good the block is.

  3. 3 Examination under anaesthesia and the manipulation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon measures the range with the patient relaxed, then holds the scapula and takes the arm through forward elevation first (the safest direction, tearing the inferior capsule), then abduction, then external rotation at the side and in abduction, then internal rotation and cross-body adduction, feeling and hearing the capsule give. The elbow is the grip and the forearm the lever, kept short to limit the torque on the humerus. Each direction is held until the give is felt. Steroid is then injected into the joint by most surgeons.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the step the trap is about. The torque that tears a fibrotic capsule is transmitted through the humeral shaft, and in a thin-boned diabetic woman the shaft or the surgical neck can go first; glenoid rim avulsions and dislocations are the other reported failures. The anaesthetised or blocked patient gives no warning. Your contribution is a patient who is fully relaxed (a working block provides it; a general anaesthetic needs enough depth and, in some surgeons’ hands, a relaxant for the few seconds of the manipulation, because muscle tone resisting the lever is what transfers the force to bone) and a surgeon who is not fighting. A loud crack with a sudden loss of resistance is the capsule; a crack followed by a change in the shape of the arm or crepitus on the next movement is bone, and the procedure stops for a radiograph. A plexus traction injury from a forceful manipulation in a blocked patient presents the next day as a block that did not wear off; document the pre-block neurology for exactly that reason.

  4. 4 Hydrodilatation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Under ultrasound or fluoroscopy, the joint is entered posteriorly or through the rotator interval, position is confirmed with contrast or a visible distension, and local anaesthetic, saline and steroid are injected under pressure in increments until the capsule ruptures, which the operator sees as a sudden loss of resistance and leakage into the subscapularis bursa; 20-40 mL usually does it and some operators stop short of rupture. The arm is then moved through the range.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Done awake with local anaesthetic in many units, under a suprascapular or interscalene block in some, and under sedation in a few. The injection against a contracted capsule is intensely painful without a block, and a patient who moves at the moment of rupture can lose the needle position. Under a block, the procedure is quiet and the physiotherapy that follows can start at once. Nothing else to do; the steroid is the surgeon’s and the glucose consequence is yours to warn about.

  5. 5 Beach chair and portals for the arthroscopic release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Beach chair or lateral decubitus, as for any shoulder arthroscopy. The joint has almost no volume, so the posterior portal is placed by feel into a tight space, the capsule is distended with the pump as far as it will go, and the surgeon works in a few millilitres of room until the first releases open it up.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The usual beach chair arithmetic: the cuff overstates brain perfusion by about 1 mmHg per 1.25 cm between cuff and ear, a vasopressor infusion started early, no deliberate hypotension. The tight joint means a high pump pressure from the start, which with a long case means fluid in the deltoid; the release itself is short. Cefazolin 2 g IV before the knife in most units, though there is no implant.

  6. 6 Rotator interval, coracohumeral ligament and anterior release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The rotator interval between supraspinatus and subscapularis is opened with radiofrequency and the coracohumeral ligament divided at the base of the coracoid, which restores external rotation; the anterior capsule is then divided from the superior glenohumeral ligament down to the top of the subscapularis, with the tendon itself preserved. Each cut gives a visible gain in range and more room to work.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Radiofrequency in a small, bleeding, fibrotic joint; the view is poor and the surgeon may ask for the pressure to come down. The answer is the same as on every beach chair card. In the diabetic the capsule is thicker, more vascular and bleeds more.

  7. 7 Inferior and posterior release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The inferior capsule round the axillary pouch is released from the glenoid side, where the axillary nerve lies a few millimetres below the capsule as it crosses under the joint; surgeons vary in how far round they go, and some release the posterior capsule for lost internal rotation. The arm is then manipulated through the full range, which is now easy and quiet. Some surgeons add a subacromial decompression, which adds a raw bone surface and changes the pain mechanism (see subacromial decompression).

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The axillary nerve is the structure at risk from the inferior release and the block hides a deficit until tomorrow; document regimental badge sensation and deltoid power before the block. The manipulation at the end of a release is gentle, because the capsule has been cut rather than torn, and carries far less fracture risk than a primary MUA. A decompression added at the end adds bone to the mechanism and a point to the day 1 figure.

  8. 8 Closure, the physiotherapist and the first session inside the block

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals are closed; no sling, or a sling for comfort only, and the surgeon’s instruction is movement from today. A release that is not taken through its full range in the first days re-scars, and the whole rationale of the operation is lost.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the step that separates frozen shoulder from every other shoulder card: the surgeon wants the arm moved, hard, while the block is working. The first physiotherapy session is timed for the recovery room or the ward on day 0, inside the block, and the patient is shown the range they now have. For MUA and hydrodilatation the session happens the same afternoon. If a catheter has been placed, the day 1 and day 2 sessions happen with a top-up or a running infusion; if not, the day 1 session is timed for the morning after the regular analgesia and a rescue dose, and the patient is told in plain words that the session will hurt and that the hurt is the point.

  9. 9 Discharge, the diabetic and the following week

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Day case for all three procedures. The surgeon wants daily physiotherapy for two weeks and home exercises several times a day, and the steroid in the joint is doing its anti-inflammatory work over that time.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block lasts 12-24 hours with dexamethasone. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID start in recovery, oral opioid is dispensed for two or three nights and, unlike the other shoulder cards, the rescue dose is timed before the physiotherapy session rather than waited for. The diabetic has had intra-articular steroid and intravenous dexamethasone on the same day and will see the glucose rise for several days; insulin-treated patients need to know what to do with it. A dense block is not a reason to delay discharge; a catheter patient goes home with an ambulatory pump if the unit runs one and stays a night if it does not. Hoarseness and a droopy eyelid after the block are expected and resolve with it.

Pain plan

The mechanism is capsule, provoked deliberately by physiotherapy from day 0, in a population with a painful, inflamed joint before the procedure and a third of it diabetic. The plan therefore has two purposes that the other shoulder cards do not combine: to make the procedure painless, and to make the physiotherapy possible. There is no PROSPECT guideline for any of the three procedures; the rotator cuff repair guideline is the nearest and its skeleton (interscalene first, intravenous dexamethasone preferred over perineural, paracetamol and NSAID, suprascapular block as the phrenic-sparing alternative) applies.

For MUA and hydrodilatation the defensible default is an interscalene block with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% and intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg as the sole anaesthetic, with sedation to taste, a physiotherapy session the same afternoon inside the block, regular paracetamol and an NSAID started before the block recedes, and two nights of oral opioid timed before the sessions. A superior trunk block gives the same anaesthetic quality with far less phrenic palsy. A suprascapular plus axillary combination is adequate for hydrodilatation and a gentle manipulation but is a weaker anaesthetic for a forceful MUA, where the patient needs to be insensate and flail.

For the arthroscopic release the catheter question is different from every other card in this chapter, because the argument for it is not the pain intensity, which is modest, but the physiotherapy. A release that is not moved through its range on days 0-3 re-scars, and the sessions on those days are the difference between the operation working and not. The one series that ran a continuous interscalene-type catheter with an ambulatory pump for two to three weeks after 123 releases, with physiotherapy from day 1, reported no post-operative opioid use and transient Horner’s and recurrent laryngeal palsies that settled with dose reduction; it is uncontrolled and the duration is longer than most units would accept, but the logic is sound. The author’s practice is a catheter for the release in the diabetic or post-surgical stiff shoulder and after a failed MUA, with the infusion run into day 2 or 3 and the physiotherapy timed to it, and a single shot with the day 1 session timed inside the regular analgesia for the uncomplicated primary release. In a unit that cannot run an ambulatory infusion, a single shot with a written plan and a daily rescue dose before physiotherapy is the honest fallback.

Rebound is less of a problem here than on the bone cards, because there is no bone, but the pre-existing joint pain returns when the block recedes and in a female population in its fifties two of the four risk factors in the ambulatory cohort are present. Escalation: pain above 7 that stops the physiotherapy is a failure of the plan and needs a rescue dose and a re-timed session, not a cancelled one; new severe pain in the arm rather than the shoulder after an MUA is a fracture until the radiograph says otherwise; a block that has not worn off by the next morning after a forceful manipulation is a plexus traction injury until proven otherwise and is documented and the surgeon told.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Primary versus secondary stiffness. A primary frozen shoulder is capsule only and a manipulation frees it; a post-surgical or post-traumatic stiff shoulder has extracapsular adhesions and retained metal, needs a release, bleeds more and re-scars faster. The catheter is for the second group.
  • The diabetic. A third of the surgical population: stiffer capsule, more bleeding, faster re-scarring, a worse outcome in every series, and a glucose that the intra-articular steroid plus intravenous dexamethasone will push up for days. Warn the patient and write it down.
  • MUA fracture. Roughly one bony injury per 70-110 manipulations in the series that count, mostly glenoid avulsions, with humeral fractures reported as cases; thin bone, a long lever, a forceful surgeon and muscle tone resisting the lever are the contributors. The blocked patient gives no warning. A short lever, full relaxation and a surgeon who stops at the first unexpected sound are the defences.
  • Awake MUA under block. Some surgeons prefer the patient to see the arm move; some patients cannot bear the sound of the capsule tearing. Sedation to the patient’s taste, and a conversation beforehand about what they will hear.
  • Hydrodilatation in radiology. Often done without an anaesthetist, under local anaesthetic, and tolerated poorly by some; where an anaesthetist is involved a suprascapular or interscalene block converts a miserable procedure into a quiet one and lets the physiotherapy start at once.
  • Release with decompression. Adds a raw acromial surface and a bone mechanism, a point on the day 1 figure and the rebound odds of a bone operation.
  • Phrenic palsy. Near-universal after interscalene block; the superior trunk block gives the same anaesthetic for a manipulation with complete paresis in 5% rather than 73%, and this is the one card where the block is often the whole anaesthetic in an awake patient who will notice the dyspnoea.
  • Horner’s syndrome and hoarseness. Common after a 20 mL interscalene block, frightening to an awake patient who has not been warned, and gone by the evening.
  • Bilateral disease. Common, especially in diabetics; one side at a time, because a bilateral interscalene block is a bilateral phrenic palsy.
  • Thyroid disease and Dupuytren’s. Associations rather than anaesthetic problems, but a patient with a frozen shoulder and an untreated thyroid is worth a thyroid function test.

Key sources

The surgical evidence is unusually good: UK FROST randomised 503 patients between all three treatments and found no clinically important difference, with MUA the most cost-effective and the release the riskiest and most expensive, and the hydrodilatation meta-analyses find a small effect of uncertain clinical importance. The anaesthetic evidence is thin: the fracture and nerve injury figures come from case series of awake manipulation under block, and the only study of a continuous block after capsular release is a single-centre uncontrolled series with a two-to-three-week infusion. The pain score, the trajectory, the physiotherapy-on-day-0 logic for the catheter and the preference for the block as the sole anaesthetic for MUA are the author’s judgement from the mechanism, not measured outcomes.

  1. Brealey S, Northgraves M, Kottam L, et al. Surgical treatments compared with early structured physiotherapy in secondary care for adults with primary frozen shoulder: the UK FROST three-arm RCT. Health Technol Assess 2020;24:1-162
    503 patients, mean age 54, 63% female, 30% diabetic: at 12 months arthroscopic release beat MUA by 2.0 and physiotherapy by 3.1 Oxford Shoulder Score points, MUA did not beat physiotherapy, and none of the differences reached the pre-set clinical importance threshold; serious adverse events in 8 release and 2 MUA patients; MUA the most cost-effective option
  2. Corbacho B, Brealey S, Keding A, et al. Cost-effectiveness of surgical treatments compared with early structured physiotherapy in secondary care for adults with primary frozen shoulder: an economic evaluation of the UK FROST trial. Bone Jt Open 2021;2:685-695
    Arthroscopic release cost £1,734 more than physiotherapy and £1,457 more than MUA with no better quality-adjusted life years; MUA had an 86% probability of being cost-effective at the £20,000 threshold
  3. Saltychev M, Laimi K, Virolainen P, Fredericson M. Effectiveness of hydrodilatation in adhesive capsulitis of shoulder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Scand J Surg 2018;107:285-293
    12 studies, seven pooled: small, clinically insignificant effects on pain and range; the volume injected made no difference
  4. Poku D, Hassan R, Migliorini F, Maffulli N. Efficacy of hydrodilatation in frozen shoulder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br Med Bull 2023;147:121-147
    Hydrodilatation gives at least transient improvement in disability and passive external rotation over steroid injection alone; its clinical relevance remains unclear
  5. Inglese F, Montemagno M, Brigo A, et al. High satisfaction rate and range of motion can be expected in frozen shoulder after awake manipulation with brachial plexus block. J Orthop Traumatol 2024;25:3
    110 awake manipulations under brachial plexus block: pain fell by 5.4 points at four months; three complications needing treatment, including a brachial plexus injury and a glenoid flake fracture
  6. Takahashi R, Iwahori Y, Kajita Y, et al. Clinical results and complications of shoulder manipulation under ultrasound-guided cervical nerve root block for frozen shoulder: a retrospective observational study. Pain Ther 2019;8:111-120
    68 manipulations under C5-C6 root block: one inferior glenoid avulsion fracture in a 72-year-old woman, two vasovagal episodes and one panic attack during the block
  7. Surendran S, Patinharayil G, Karuppal R, et al. Arthroscopic capsular release and continuous upper arm brachial block in frozen shoulder: a midterm outcome analysis. J Orthop 2020;21:459-464
    123 arthroscopic releases with a continuous interscalene-type catheter and ambulatory pump for two to three weeks, physiotherapy from day 1: no post-operative opioid needed; transient Horner's syndrome and recurrent laryngeal palsy in a few, resolving with dose reduction; an uncontrolled series
  8. Kang R, Jeong JS, Chin KJ, et al. Superior trunk block provides noninferior analgesia compared with interscalene brachial plexus block in arthroscopic shoulder surgery. Anesthesiology 2019;131:1316-1326
    80 arthroscopic shoulder patients, 15 mL ropivacaine 0.5%: pain at 24 h 1.4 vs 1.2; complete hemidiaphragmatic paresis 5% vs 73%
  9. Toma O, Persoons B, Pogatzki-Zahn E, Van de Velde M, Joshi GP. PROSPECT guideline for rotator cuff repair surgery. Anaesthesia 2019;74:1320-1331
    The nearest procedure-specific guideline: interscalene block first choice, IV dexamethasone preferred over perineural, paracetamol plus NSAID, suprascapular block as an alternative, controlled hypotension not recommended
  10. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, and absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78

Upper limb › Shoulder

8 ACJ reconstruction and clavicle fixation

Acromioclavicular joint stabilisation with hook plate, suture button or graft; midshaft and distal clavicle plating

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Periosteum. A subcutaneous bone stripped of periosteum along its length and plated, or drilled through from top to bottom for buttons, under skin with almost no soft tissue between; the fracture haematoma and the reduction of displaced ends; for a hook plate, a metal hook sitting under the acromion that pushes on the subacromial bursa and cuff with every elevation until it is removed

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Superficial or intermediate cervical plexus block (C3-C4 supraclavicular nerves) combined with an interscalene or superior trunk block, with intravenous dexamethasone; the cervical plexus component is the one an interscalene block alone omits
Catheter: rarely Periosteal and fracture pain that settles over three days does not justify a catheter, and no single catheter covers both the C3-C4 skin and the C5-C6 bone; the exception is the nonunion revision with bone graft or the patient with chronic pain, where an interscalene catheter plus a single-shot cervical plexus block is the author's compromise
Alternatives: Clavipectoral fascial plane block plus superficial cervical plexus block, which is motor and phrenic sparing and in one small randomised trial gave longer analgesia than interscalene plus cervical plexus for midshaft fixation, while another found the reverse; Selective C3-C5 root block (fast, phrenic sparing in one trial, operator dependent); General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration along the plate, which is the historical default and leaves the first night uncovered
Position
Beach chair at 30-45 degrees with the head turned slightly away for the clavicle, or supine with a bump under the scapula; the neck and the block site are in the surgeon's field and the tube is taped to the opposite side
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
100-250 mL for a midshaft plate; more for a nonunion with bone graft; the subclavian vessels and the apex of the lung are a drill depth below the inferior cortex and the rare catastrophic bleed is from them
Duration
Midshaft or distal clavicle plate 60-90 min; ACJ suture button, open or arthroscopically assisted, 60-90 min; hook plate 45-60 min; ligament reconstruction with graft 90-120 min; nonunion with graft longer
Length of stay
Day case or one night. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); plates, buttons and grafts are implants and the skin over the clavicle is thin, so infection means exposed metal
Tranexamic acid
TXA 1 g IV for a nonunion or a graft reconstruction; optional for a simple plate
VTE
Mechanical only in the elective and the young trauma patient; the clavicle fracture patient who is also a polytrauma patient follows the trauma pathway
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (also the block adjunct) and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The top of the shoulder and the collarbone will be numb into the evening if both blocks have worked; the plate then aches for a few days and the skin over it stays tender for weeks because there is nothing between the metal and the skin.
The trap
The clavicle is not in the brachial plexus: its skin and periosteum are supplied by the supraclavicular nerves from C3 and C4, so an interscalene block alone leaves the patient awake to the incision and sore on the top of the shoulder afterwards, and the combined block that fixes this adds a second phrenic insult in a patient who may already have rib fractures and a pneumothorax on the same side

What the surgeon is doing and why

The clavicle is the only bony strut between the arm and the trunk: a subcutaneous S-shaped bone that holds the shoulder girdle away from the chest, with the subclavian vessels, the brachial plexus and the apex of the lung running under its middle third and nothing but skin and platysma over it. It breaks in the middle third when a cyclist or a rugby player lands on the point of the shoulder, and the acromioclavicular joint at its lateral end dislocates when the same fall drives the acromion down while the clavicle stays up, tearing the acromioclavicular capsule first (Rockwood I-II) and then the coracoclavicular ligaments (III and above), so that the clavicle rides high and the arm hangs away from it. The surgeon’s problem in both injuries is the same: a displaced bone with no muscle envelope to hold it, under thin skin, that heals adequately without surgery in most people and badly in some, and that has the great vessels and the lung immediately beneath it.

For the midshaft fracture, a sling unites most fractures and operative fixation reduces nonunion and shortens the time to function at the cost of a plate under the skin that many patients want removed. For the displaced distal fracture, the one randomised trial found the same function at a year with fixation but union in 95% against 64% without, and 44% of the plated patients had a second operation to take the metal out. For the acromioclavicular joint, grades I and II are left alone, grade III is argued over, and IV and above are reconstructed with a hook plate, a suture button construct or a ligament reconstruction with graft, depending on the surgeon and the chronicity.

What the surgeon does to tissue:

  1. Midshaft and distal clavicle plating. An incision along the clavicle, platysma and the supraclavicular nerves (which cross the bone and are preserved or sacrificed, giving the numb patch below the scar that most patients have), the periosteum stripped from the fracture ends, the fracture reduced with clamps, and a precontoured plate laid on the superior or anterior surface and fixed with screws drilled from top to bottom, with the drill tip emerging a few millimetres from the subclavian vein. Some surgeons use an intramedullary device, with less stripping and a smaller scar.
  2. Hook plate for the acromioclavicular joint or the distal fracture. A plate along the distal clavicle with a hook that passes under the acromion and levers the clavicle down into reduction. Quick and strong, but the hook sits in the subacromial space pushing on the bursa and the cuff with every elevation, erodes the acromion, and is removed at three to six months in a second operation; it bleeds less than a button construct and hurts more while it is in.
  3. Suture button construct. Open or arthroscopically assisted, a drill hole from the top of the clavicle through the base of the coracoid, a button under the coracoid and one on the clavicle with a high-strength suture loop between them, tensioned to pull the clavicle down. Nothing is left under the acromion. The drill passes 30-40 mm with the plexus and vessels medial to the coracoid base. The pooled comparisons give the button lower late pain scores and the hook plate less bleeding, with no clear winner in function.
  4. Ligament reconstruction. For chronic dislocations, a tendon graft (hamstring autograft or allograft) is looped under the coracoid and through the clavicle to rebuild the coracoclavicular ligaments; a graft harvest adds a second site.

The pain logic. The dominant mechanism is periosteum: a subcutaneous bone stripped along its length and plated, or drilled through from top to bottom, under skin with almost nothing between the metal and the surface. It is raw, incisional and deep at once, peaks on day 1 and settles over three days as a fracture does, but the skin over the plate stays tender for weeks and the hook plate adds an irritation under the acromion that lasts until the plate comes out. No tendon is under tension and no joint re-tensioned, so the tail is short. That makes a 3: a block is expected, opioids are needed for two or three days, and the fall is quick.

The anaesthetic logic is about anatomy rather than intensity, and it is why this card exists separately. The clavicle is not in the brachial plexus. Its skin and periosteum are supplied by the supraclavicular nerves, which come off the cervical plexus at C3 and C4 and descend over the bone; the acromioclavicular joint and the lateral end receive a C5 contribution through the suprascapular and lateral pectoral nerves, and the inferior surface from the nerve to subclavius. An interscalene block at C5-C6 covers the joint and the lateral end but leaves the C3-C4 skin and periosteum of the shaft untouched, which is why clavicle fixation under interscalene block alone produces a patient who flinches at the incision and a first night the block did not cover. The combined approach, a superficial or intermediate cervical plexus block for C3-C4 plus an interscalene or superior trunk block for C5-C6, is the technique the scoping review of 44 studies names as reliable surgical anaesthesia; the motor-sparing alternatives (clavipectoral fascial plane block plus supraclavicular nerve block, or a selective C3-C5 root block) are the subject of small randomised trials described in the pain plan.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The patient, the injury and which nerves to block

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon is fixing a fracture in a cyclist who fell last week, reconstructing a joint in a rugby player, or removing a hook plate from either; the elective nonunion and the chronic dislocation with graft are the long versions. The injury that matters to you is the one next to the clavicle: rib fractures, a pneumothorax or a scapular fracture on the same side are common in the cyclist and the motorcyclist, and the polytrauma patient’s clavicle is fixed when the rest allows.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Decide the block by territory. The cervical plexus component (superficial or intermediate) covers the C3-C4 skin and periosteum of the shaft; the interscalene or superior trunk component covers the C5-C6 contribution to the lateral end and the joint. For a midshaft plate the cervical plexus block does most of the work and a small-volume superior trunk block completes it; for an acromioclavicular reconstruction the interscalene component matters more. Intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg with the block. The combined block carries one phrenic palsy, and a patient with same-side rib fractures and a chest drain cannot afford it: use a low-volume superior trunk block, or the clavipectoral plus supraclavicular nerve combination, which spared the diaphragm in the trials. The block site is the surgical field, so the cervical plexus injection goes in before the skin preparation and is noted to the surgeon. Airway: a tracheal tube taped to the opposite side, because the surgeon’s hands, the drill and the retractor are all at the root of the neck; a supraglottic device is reasonable for a quick hook plate removal.

  2. 2 Positioning

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Beach chair at 30-45 degrees with the head turned slightly away brings the clavicle into the surgeon’s line and lets the arm be moved to reduce the fracture or the joint; some surgeons work supine with a bump under the scapula to push the clavicle forward.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The usual beach chair arithmetic at a lower incline: a smaller hydrostatic gradient, but the same strokes in the same literature and the same vasopressor logic. The head turned away puts the tube and the circuit on the far side and the neck in slight rotation; check the ear and the eye on the dependent side. The cervical plexus block site is now in the field and the drapes will be over the face and the tube; secure both before the surgeon starts. The arm is draped free so that it can be lifted to reduce the fracture, which moves the shoulder girdle and the neck with it.

  3. 3 Incision, platysma and the supraclavicular nerves

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A longitudinal incision along the clavicle (or a transverse one in some hands), platysma divided, and the supraclavicular nerve branches crossing the bone identified and preserved or sacrificed, which the surgeon decides by whether they can be swept aside; most patients have some numbness below the scar whatever is done.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The skin incision is the test of the cervical plexus component: a patient under light general anaesthesia who responds to the knife here has a working interscalene block and no cervical plexus block, and the lesson is for next time. Cefazolin 2 g IV finished before the knife, 3 g over 120 kg; the skin is thin and infection means exposed metal.

  4. 4 Exposure, periosteal stripping and reduction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The periosteum is elevated from the fracture ends and far enough along the shaft to seat the plate, the haematoma and interposed soft tissue are cleared, and the fracture is reduced with pointed clamps, often with a lag screw across an oblique fracture line first. The reduction of a week-old displaced fracture in a muscular patient takes force, and the arm is lifted and pushed by the assistant to bring the lateral fragment up.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the mechanism of the card being created: a stripped bone, raw along its length. It bleeds from the periosteal surface and the fracture ends, which is the 100-250 mL of the operation. The reduction manoeuvre moves the shoulder girdle and the neck, and the pressure on the neck from a retractor levering the medial fragment up is pressure on the structures beneath the clavicle. A pneumothorax on the same side, if present, is at its most relevant now: positive pressure ventilation and a surgeon leaning on the chest wall.

  5. 5 Plating, drilling and the structures beneath

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A precontoured plate is laid on the superior (or anterior) surface and fixed with screws, three bicortical screws each side of the fracture. Each superior-to-inferior drill hole passes through the inferior cortex a few millimetres above the subclavian vein, the subclavian artery, the brachial plexus and the pleura; the surgeon protects them with a retractor or a finger under the bone and drills with a stop, and the anteriorly placed plate exists partly because its screws point away from the vessels.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The one catastrophe of the operation happens here: a drill or a long screw into the subclavian vein or artery, which presents as sudden, uncontrolled bleeding from the depths of a wound the surgeon cannot see into, and a pneumothorax from the pleura, which presents as a rise in airway pressure and a fall in saturation during or after the drilling. The second is commoner and is diagnosed on the recovery room radiograph. Note the time of each drill hole in a difficult reduction; if the surgeon says “that one went deep”, the post-operative chest radiograph is not optional.

  6. 6 Acromioclavicular reconstruction: hook, button or graft

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For the hook plate, the plate is laid along the distal clavicle and the hook slid under the acromion from the posterior edge, then the plate is pushed down to reduce the joint and screwed. For the button construct, a drill passes from the top of the clavicle through the base of the coracoid, which is found by palpation or by arthroscopy from the joint, the button is flipped under the coracoid, the suture loop is tensioned and the clavicle is pulled down and held. For the graft reconstruction the tendon is passed under the coracoid and through tunnels in the clavicle.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The coracoid drill is aimed at the base of a bone that has the plexus and the axillary vessels on its medial side; a drill that skids off the coracoid medially is the complication, and the arthroscopically assisted techniques exist to watch the drill emerge. The hook under the acromion sits on the subacromial bursa and the cuff and is the reason hook plate patients hurt more in the weeks after than button patients, a difference the pooled data put at half a point on the pain scale and a plate removal later. A graft harvest from the hamstring is a second site in a different block territory, and it needs its own infiltration or block.

  7. 7 Closure, sling and the skin

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Platysma is closed over the plate as the only soft-tissue cover, then skin, and a sling supports the arm for two to six weeks depending on the fixation; the patient is told not to lift the arm above shoulder height until the surgeon allows, and a hook plate patient is told the hook will catch.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the antiemetic. The sling before the patient lightens. The skin over a clavicular plate is the thinnest cover of any orthopaedic implant and the surgeon will want the dressing left alone; the numb patch below the scar from the sacrificed supraclavicular nerves is permanent in many and is not the block.

  8. 8 Recovery, the chest radiograph and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Day case or one night. The surgeon wants a radiograph of the fixation and, after any difficult drilling, of the chest, and a patient who moves the elbow and hand from the first day.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A chest radiograph in recovery after any midshaft plate where the drilling was difficult or the patient had rib fractures; a pneumothorax that was not there before the operation is a surgical complication and presents late if it is not looked for. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID start in recovery, and the block recedes over 10-15 hours depending on the technique, with the cervical plexus component usually wearing off before the interscalene. The first night is the periosteal ache along the bone plus the pre-existing fracture pain, treated with oral opioid for two or three nights. A dense arm block from the interscalene component is not a reason to keep the patient; a weak diaphragm in a patient with rib fractures is.

  9. 9 Hook plate removal and the second operation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The hook plate is removed at three to six months, once the joint or the fracture has healed, because the hook erodes the acromion and irritates the cuff for as long as it stays; the button construct and the simple plate are removed only if they bother the patient, which under thin skin they often do.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A short operation through the old scar: the plate comes out, the hook is slid back out from under the acromion, and the wound is closed. It hurts less than the insertion and a cervical plexus block alone, with surgeon infiltration, is often enough; a patient who has had a bad first night the first time will tell you. Day case.

Pain plan

The mechanism is periosteal and fracture pain along a subcutaneous bone that settles over three days, so the plan is a single-shot combined block that covers the operation and the first night, a regular oral regimen started before it recedes, and no catheter; the complexity is anatomical, not pharmacological. There is no PROSPECT guideline for clavicle surgery; the scoping review of 44 studies is the nearest synthesis and names the intermediate cervical plexus block as the technique of choice, reliable for surgical anaesthesia when combined with an interscalene block, and the rotator cuff repair guideline’s skeleton of intravenous dexamethasone, paracetamol and NSAID applies.

The defensible default is a superficial or intermediate cervical plexus block with 5-10 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% for the C3-C4 skin and periosteum, plus a superior trunk block with 10-15 mL for the C5-C6 contribution to the lateral clavicle and the joint, with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, regular paracetamol and an NSAID started in recovery, and oral opioid for two or three nights. The superior trunk rather than the interscalene for the second component because the diaphragm matters more here than in any other shoulder group: the clavicle patient often has rib fractures on the same side. Where the diaphragm cannot be touched at all, the clavipectoral fascial plane block plus a supraclavicular nerve block is the phrenic-sparing combination; in one randomised comparison of 60 fixations it gave longer analgesia (14.6 against 10.3 hours) and less 24 h analgesic use than cervical plexus plus interscalene, with hemidiaphragmatic paralysis only in the interscalene group, while a second trial found the upper trunk combination gave two hours more analgesia than the clavipectoral combination at the cost of motor block and diaphragmatic excursion. Both are small single-centre trials; the honest reading is that any combination covering both territories works, and the chest decides which.

The catheter is rarely justified. The pain is periosteal and short, and no single catheter position covers both the C3-C4 skin and the C5-C6 bone. The exception is the nonunion revision with bone graft, the chronic reconstruction with a hamstring harvest and the patient with chronic pain or opioid tolerance, where an interscalene catheter plus a single-shot cervical plexus block is the author’s compromise and the harvest site gets its own infiltration.

Rebound is moderate: bone surgery in a young population, but a plate rather than an osteotomy, and the cervical plexus component wears off earlier and more gently than the interscalene. Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has receded with the hand warm and moving is treated with the charted opioid; pain on the top of the shoulder with a numb arm is a working interscalene block and a missed cervical plexus block, fixed with a superficial cervical plexus block in recovery; new dyspnoea or a fall in saturation after a midshaft plate is a pneumothorax until the radiograph says otherwise; a swelling wound with a rising pulse is a vascular injury and the surgeon is called before anything else.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The missed territory. An interscalene block alone is the commonest error on this list: the patient is awake to the incision and sore on the top of the shoulder all night, and the fix is a five-minute superficial cervical plexus block that was not placed. Place it first, before the skin preparation, and tell the surgeon it is there.
  • Rib fractures and pneumothorax on the same side. The cyclist and the motorcyclist with a clavicle fracture often have both; a phrenic palsy from an interscalene block on top of a flail segment is the combination to avoid. Superior trunk, clavipectoral plus supraclavicular nerve, or a selective C3-C5 root block in hands that do it.
  • The polytrauma clavicle. Fixed when the rest allows, under the trauma pathway’s anaesthetic, with the block decision made on the chest and the head injury, not on the clavicle.
  • Hook plate versus button. The hook plate bleeds less, is quicker, hurts more while it is in and comes out in a second operation; the button construct is longer, drills next to the plexus, and is left in. The pooled comparisons find no clear winner in function; the pain difference favours the button by half a point.
  • Nonunion and the chronic dislocation. Scar, a plate to remove, bone graft from the iliac crest or a hamstring harvest, and a second painful site in a different block territory that needs its own plan; the one setting where a catheter is reasonable.
  • Intramedullary fixation. Less stripping, a smaller scar and less pain than a plate, with the same territory to block.
  • The subclavian vessels and the lung. A drill depth below the inferior cortex. A sudden bleed from the depths or a rising airway pressure during drilling is the surgeon’s catastrophe presenting to you; the chest radiograph in recovery after difficult drilling is not optional.
  • Adolescents. Most displaced midshaft fractures in adolescents are treated without surgery; the ones that reach theatre are the open, the shortened and the athlete’s, and the combined block works under general anaesthesia as it does in an adult.
  • Plate removal. Common, elective, short, and under-blocked because it looks minor; the cervical plexus block alone with surgeon infiltration is usually enough.

Key sources

The surgical evidence on operative versus non-operative treatment and on hook plate versus button is reasonable and is cited for the variants, not for pain. The anaesthetic evidence is the point of this card and it is thin but consistent: a scoping review of 44 heterogeneous studies establishes that no single block covers the clavicle and that cervical plexus plus interscalene is the combination that reliably works, and the small randomised trials of 2025-2026 compare motor-sparing combinations with each other and with interscalene, mostly in single centres and with analgesia duration rather than pain trajectory as the outcome. The innervation argument is standard anatomy. The pain score, the trajectory and the catheter advice are the author’s calibration against the Part B scale and the mechanism.

Upper limb › Shoulder

9 Proximal humerus fracture: ORIF versus reverse TSA

Locking plate fixation, fracture reverse arthroplasty, fracture hemiarthroplasty and the non-operative decision in the elderly

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A fractured, osteoporotic metaphysis, days old, with its haematoma, either plated through a deltoid-splitting or deltopectoral approach with periosteal stripping and screws into soft bone, or resected and replaced with a cemented stem, with the tuberosities and their cuff attachments sutured back around the implant under tension.
