The ulnar nerve is checked for kinking at its new entry or along its native course, the tourniquet released, bleeding dealt with, a drain placed by many surgeons, and thin posterior skin closed in layers. An anterior splint holds the elbow in extension so the wound is not folded.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Release here brings a reperfusion dip in pressure, a rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide and a bleeding field the surgeon must now control; after a full-length inflation the pressure takes minutes to recover. The repair wants a still patient and a held arm, not neuromuscular block. Give the antiemetic. The splint goes on before the patient lightens: an awake patient with a dense block and a repaired triceps will otherwise bend the elbow with the other hand.

  10. 10 Recovery, the first night and the nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the wound dry and flat, the elbow extended for a few days, no resisted extension for six weeks if the triceps was reflected, and to know that the ulnar nerve works.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The hand is examined when the block recedes, at the time agreed in step 1. The oral regimen starts in recovery: paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor if renal function and the rheumatoid drug list allow it, and an oral opioid for the first three nights. In the 972-patient ambulatory cohort half of block patients had rebound pain, with bone surgery (OR 1.82) and no intravenous dexamethasone (OR 1.78) raising the odds; this is bone surgery. A numb little finger and a rising elbow at 2 am is the block wearing off; a tense, swollen posterior wound is bleeding into a closed space over a nerve and needs the surgeon. Length of stay is one to three nights, longer for slow rheumatoid skin.

  11. 11 Radial head replacement: the lateral approach and the ligament

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Usually a trauma patient. Through the Kocher interval the surgeon removes the head fragments, checks the coronoid and ligaments, sizes the implant against the removed head, reams the neck and seats the stem. If the lateral collateral complex has come off the epicondyle (it usually has in a dislocation) it is repaired with anchors or tunnels, and in a terrible triad the coronoid is fixed first through the same wound.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Supine on an arm table with a standard tourniquet, 60-120 min, the same block with dexamethasone. The posterior interosseous nerve runs through supinator a few centimetres distal to the head and is protected by pronating the forearm; a wrist drop afterwards is retraction or an over-long reamer, and another reason to document before the block. The ligament repair is the tendon-tension element and the reason the elbow is splinted. Sizing is the surgical trap: an over-long head (up to about 20% of implants) erodes the capitellum, stiffens the elbow over months and causes 13-23% of revisions.

  12. 12 The radial head patient and discharge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Early protected motion in a hinged brace, because a stiff elbow after a terrible triad is the usual bad outcome, with the ligament repair protected from varus stress.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Most isolated radial head replacements go home the same day with a working block, oral analgesia started and a written night plan; a terrible triad with coronoid fixation and a ligament repair stays one night. The pain course behaves like a 2 after the first night, because the bone work is small and the early motion is passive.

Pain plan

The dominant mechanism is bone with cement, which argues for a single-shot block with dexamethasone to carry the first night and an oral regimen for the next three days; the two secondary mechanisms (a repaired triceps or ligament, and a handled nerve) argue for a regimen that expects movement-evoked pain in week 2 and a neuropathic flavour in the hand. There is no procedure-specific guideline for the elbow; the nearest PROSPECT evidence is for the shoulder, and this plan is author’s judgement built on the mechanism and on the general ambulatory block data.

The defensible default is an infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (equivalent for elbow surgery in the randomised comparison; infraclavicular gave fewer paraesthesiae), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg at induction, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before the block recedes, and oral opioid for the first three nights. The NSAID decision is harder than usual: rheumatoid patients are often on methotrexate, have renal function that will not tolerate a week of NSAID, and may already be on a COX-2 inhibitor. When the NSAID is off the table the opioid requirement rises and the catheter argument strengthens.

The catheter question has two parts. On pain grounds a primary total elbow sits where the anatomic shoulder sits: a single shot with dexamethasone and a reliable oral regimen is enough for most, and a continuous infraclavicular or retroclavicular catheter (described for total elbow replacement as a technique report, without a trial behind it) earns its place for a revision, an opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, or the rheumatoid patient who cannot take an NSAID. On nerve grounds a catheter means no ulnar nerve examination for two days, and that is the surgeon’s call as much as yours. The author’s practice is a single shot for a primary total elbow and for every radial head replacement, and a catheter only after a conversation with the surgeon about the nerve.

Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone, with a soft wound, a warm hand and the splint on, is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were given. Pain out of proportion in a tense posterior wound is a haematoma over the ulnar nerve and is surgical. Ring and little finger numbness that was absent when the block wore off, or that worsens over days, is a nerve under pressure in its new bed and also surgical. Burning dysaesthesia present from the start and stable is traction neuritis and settles over weeks; a gabapentinoid for it is author’s judgement, not evidence.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Triceps-reflecting versus triceps-on. The reflected sleeve gives the best exposure and the most movement-evoked pain in weeks 1-2, with a repair that fails in about 3%; triceps-on is favoured for fractures and leaves an elbow that extends from day 1. Ask which was done.
  • Unlinked designs. Kept by some surgeons for the rheumatoid elbow with good bone and intact collaterals: less loosening, more instability, and a still arm wanted while the ligaments are balanced.
  • Fracture total elbow. The frail patient over 70 with a comminuted distal humerus, often converted on the table from a planned fixation: the position and tourniquet of the elbow fracture card, a cement step in the frailest patient of the week, and the hip-fracture medical problems.
  • Rheumatoid airway, neck and drugs. Atlantoaxial instability, a stiff temporomandibular joint and cricoarytenoid arthritis, so an airway plan that does not involve extension; a steroid supplement; methotrexate continued in most units and biologics paused by most rheumatologists.
  • Infection and periprosthetic fracture. Infection 2-4% in the Mayo review, up to 8% in some series, 19% of revisions; fracture in 5-30% of primary elbows over their life, usually the thin humeral shaft above the stem, and the revision is a long case with a strut graft.
  • Ulnar nerve. Transposed by most, released in situ by some; symptoms in 3-11%, mostly transient. Document before the block, agree when the nerve will be examined, treat a worsening deficit as surgical.
  • Radial head overstuffing. Sized against the removed head, and 2 mm too long is enough to erode the capitellum; the stiffness presents months later as a revision.
  • Essex-Lopresti. The head must be replaced, not excised, and the wrist may be stabilised under the same anaesthetic, which lengthens the case and moves the tourniquet.
  • Posterior interosseous nerve. At risk in the lateral approach; a wrist drop in recovery needs the block excluded (document before) and then the surgeon.

Key sources

An uncommon operation with a complication literature far larger than its analgesia literature. The failure data come from the 9,308-elbow systematic review and the Mayo narrative review; the ulnar nerve figures from the same review and an 83-patient series that argues against routine transposition; the fracture indication from the single randomised trial of fixation against replacement in the elderly. The block recommendation rests on a randomised comparison of infraclavicular and supraclavicular approaches for ambulatory elbow surgery and on the general rebound-pain cohort; the catheter advice is author’s judgement. Radial head figures come from the 727-patient systematic review and the overlengthening review. The pain score is calibrated against the elbow fracture anchor in the Part B scale, since procedure-specific pain data do not exist.

  1. Sanchez-Sotelo J. Total elbow arthroplasty. Open Orthop J 2011;5:115-123
    Mayo review: triceps-reflecting Bryan-Morrey approach preferred, triceps-sparing where possible; routine subcutaneous ulnar nerve transposition by most surgeons; both components cemented with antibiotic-loaded cement; severe ulnar neuropathy about 5%, infection 2-4%, aseptic loosening 5-10%, triceps insufficiency 3%
  2. Prkic A, Welsink C, The B, van den Bekerom MPJ, Eygendaal D. Why does total elbow arthroplasty fail today? A systematic review of recent literature. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2017;137:761-769
    70 studies, 9,308 primary elbows, 13.5% revised: aseptic loosening 38% of revisions, deep infection 19%, periprosthetic fracture 12%; loosening less common with linked implants; revision more common after rheumatoid arthritis than after trauma
  3. McKee MD, Veillette CJ, Hall JA, et al. A multicenter, prospective, randomized, controlled trial of open reduction-internal fixation versus total elbow arthroplasty for displaced intra-articular distal humeral fractures in elderly patients. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2009;18:3-12
    42 patients over 65 randomised; five of 21 allocated to fixation were converted to arthroplasty on the table for comminution; operative time 108 versus 140 min; DASH better after arthroplasty at six weeks (43 versus 77) and six months (31 versus 47); reoperation 12% versus 27%, not significant
  4. Dachs R, Chivers D, Du Plessis JP, Vrettos B, Roche S. The ulnar nerve in total elbow arthroplasty: outcomes after in-situ release. Orthopaedic Proceedings 2014;96-B(Supp 19):22
    83 consecutive primary total elbows: in-situ release in 78, transposition in four for abnormal tracking; ulnar symptoms in 7.7% after in-situ release, four early-resolving neuropraxias and two (2.6%) needing later transposition; systematic reviews quoted at 3-11%
  5. Orthobullets. Elbow total arthroplasty
    Indications, linked versus unlinked designs, supine or lateral positioning, lifelong lifting restriction of 2-5 kg; infection 8%, periprosthetic fracture 5-30%, survivorship free of revision 92.4% at ten years for rheumatoid arthritis with a 14% complication rate
  6. Heijink A, Kodde IF, Mulder PGH, et al. Radial head arthroplasty: a systematic review. JBJS Rev 2016;4(10):e3

    150 ambulatory elbow operations with ropivacaine: supplementation 4.2% versus 4.1%, conversion to general anaesthesia 4.2% versus 5.5%, sensory onset 20 versus 19 min; paraesthesia during the block 8.3% infraclavicular versus 23.2% supraclavicular; both equally effective for the elbow
  9. Megaw K, Johnston DF. Continuous infraclavicular brachial plexus block using retroclavicular approach for total elbow replacement. J Clin Anesth 2020;60:111-112

Upper limb › Elbow

12 Elbow arthroscopy, release and tennis elbow surgery

Diagnostic and therapeutic elbow arthroscopy, arthroscopic and open capsular release for stiffness, and open, arthroscopic or percutaneous lateral epicondylar release

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Capsule. Capsular distension, debridement and (in a release) excision, with the joint then pushed through a range it has not had for months; irrigation in the periarticular tissues; a small raw bone surface after osteophyte or capitellar work. Tennis elbow surgery is a tendon origin debrided and sometimes repaired, a surface-and-periosteum operation. Open release adds a muscle split and an ulnar nerve that is handled

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration for diagnostic and loose body arthroscopy and for tennis elbow surgery; a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with intravenous dexamethasone added for arthroscopic or open release, where the surgeon wants the arm moved through its new range from day 1
Catheter: rarely A continuous infraclavicular catheter for the formal release of a severely stiff elbow is a defensible author's-judgement option when the surgeon runs an early movement programme and will accept not examining the nerves for two days; it is not needed for arthroscopy or tennis elbow surgery
Alternatives: Local infiltration alone for percutaneous or open tennis elbow release, with or without sedation; Axillary block (misses the posterior elbow unless the musculocutaneous and intercostobrachial nerves are added); Block as the sole anaesthetic in supine or lateral, impractical in prone
Position
Prone or lateral decubitus with the arm over a padded bolster and the elbow flexed to 90 degrees for arthroscopy; supine on an arm table with the arm across the chest for some surgeons and for most open tennis elbow and open release surgery
Tourniquet
Yes. Routine for arthroscopy and open release; 60-120 min. Tennis elbow surgery is 20-40 min under a tourniquet or, percutaneously, none at all
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal; the fluid in the drapes is irrigation. Open release bleeds modestly after tourniquet release into a drain
Duration
30-60 min for diagnostic arthroscopy and loose bodies; 90-150 min for arthroscopic or open release of a stiff elbow; 20-40 min for a lateral epicondylar release
Length of stay
Day case for arthroscopy and tennis elbow; day case or one night for a release, depending on the surgeon's movement programme. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV at induction (3 g over 120 kg) for arthroscopy and open release; many surgeons omit it for a percutaneous or open tennis elbow release with no implant
Tranexamic acid
Not needed; some surgeons ask for tranexamic acid 1 g IV for arthroscopic visibility in a vascular synovitis
VTE
Mechanical only; upper limb day surgery carries a negligible baseline risk
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 4-8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The elbow will be swollen and stiff for a few days from the fluid used to see inside it; the pain is worst on the first day and settles over a week, and for a release the movement exercises are the operation, not an optional extra.
The trap
The nerves sit millimetres from the anterior portals and a stiff or rheumatoid elbow pulls them closer: a transient palsy after arthroscopy is common enough that the surgeon may want the hand examined before any block, and a dense block in recovery after a release can hide both a nerve injury and the forearm that is swelling from extravasated irrigation

What the surgeon is doing and why

Three operations share this card because they share a joint, a position and a pain mechanism, and because the hazards they carry for you are the same: nerves that sit within millimetres of the instruments, a forearm that fills with irrigation fluid, and a surgeon who wants the arm moved afterwards.

The elbow is a tight, congruent joint with a capsule that scars readily. Any insult (a fracture, a dislocation, a haemarthrosis, weeks in a splint, rheumatoid synovitis) produces a thickened anterior capsule that blocks extension and a thickened posterior capsule and olecranon fossa osteophytes that block flexion; the patient loses the functional arc of 30-130 degrees and cannot reach their face or their pocket. Loose bodies, osteophytes on the coronoid and olecranon tips, synovitis and osteochondritis of the capitellum in a young thrower are the other reasons to look inside. Elbow arthroscopy is the way in. The joint is distended with 20-30 mL of saline through the lateral soft spot, which pushes the anterior neurovascular bundle away from the capsule, and portals are made above and below the medial and lateral epicondyles with the elbow flexed to 90 degrees, because flexion relaxes the anterior structures and extension brings the radial nerve 3-7 mm closer to the joint. The distances are small whatever is done: the proximal anteromedial portal sits about 4 mm from the ulnar nerve and 7-20 mm from the median nerve, and the proximal anterolateral portal a mean 13.7 mm from the radial nerve. A stiff elbow pulls the nerves onto the capsule and a rheumatoid elbow has a thin, friable capsule with no safe plane, which is why those two diagnoses predicted transient nerve palsy in the 473-case Mayo series (p less than 0.001 and p less than 0.05), where 12 palsies occurred in 10 patients, all temporary, alongside four deep infections (0.8%) and a minor complication rate of 11%, most of it portal drainage. The pooled modern figure across 14,213 arthroscopies is a total complication rate of 8% and a nerve injury rate of 1.95%, mostly transient.

A release for stiffness takes the same route and goes further. Arthroscopically, the surgeon excises the anterior capsule off the humerus (a capsulectomy, not a capsulotomy, because an incised capsule rescars), clears the coronoid and olecranon fossae of osteophytes and scar, releases the posterior capsule, and often decompresses or releases the ulnar nerve through a small medial incision, because an elbow regaining flexion will stretch a nerve that has been sitting in a scarred cubital tunnel. In the 30-patient arthroscopic series the arc went from 68 to 123 degrees with three transient nerve palsies. An open release does the same through a lateral column incision, a medial over-the-top approach, or both: a muscle interval is split, the capsule excised under direct vision, heterotopic bone removed if there is any, and the ulnar nerve transposed. In the 52-patient open series the arc went from 57 to 116 degrees, but 27% needed a manipulation under anaesthesia in the early weeks and five needed a second release, which is the honest description of what the surgeon is fighting: a capsule that wants to scar back, and a movement programme that has to beat it.

Tennis elbow is a degenerate tendon origin, not an inflamed one. The extensor carpi radialis brevis origin on the lateral epicondyle develops angiofibroblastic degeneration and microtears under repetitive load, and after a year of failed non-operative treatment the surgeon excises the degenerate tissue and either decorticates the epicondyle and repairs the origin (the open Nirschl-type procedure), releases it arthroscopically from inside the joint, or simply divides it percutaneously through a 1 cm stab. The three give the same pain relief and function in the pooled 1,622 elbows (VAS 1.45 open versus 1.62 arthroscopic), with more minor complications after open surgery (57% versus 33%, mostly stiffness, haematoma and superficial infection), and percutaneous release under infiltration alone returned 87% of patients to complete pain relief in a 30-elbow series with a three-week return to work.

The pain logic: the dominant mechanism for arthroscopy and release is capsule, which is sharp with movement and settles over days, and in a release it is made worse by the fact that the joint is then deliberately pushed through a range it has not had for months, so the movement-evoked component is the whole point of the operation rather than a side effect. Irrigation fluid in the periarticular tissues adds a tight, swollen elbow for 48 hours. Osteophyte removal and capitellar drilling add a small bone surface. Open release adds a muscle split and a handled ulnar nerve with a neuropathic edge. Tennis elbow surgery is a surface-and-periosteum operation, a decorticated epicondyle and a debrided tendon origin, and it hurts in the way a decompression does: a few bad days, then a sore elbow for weeks that responds to simple analgesia. None of these operations produces the deep bone pain of an arthroplasty or the prolonged tendon-tension pain of a cuff repair; a score of 2 fits all three, with the release at the top of that band.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative neurology, the block decision and the position

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon is about to put instruments within millimetres of three nerves, in a stiff or rheumatoid elbow that has pulled them closer, and will want to know afterwards whether a weak hand is the block or the operation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Document ulnar, median, radial and posterior interosseous function before anything is given. For a diagnostic or loose body arthroscopy and for tennis elbow surgery the author’s practice is general anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration and no block: the pain is a 2, the case is short, and a dense block buys nothing but a delay in the nerve check. For a release, where the surgeon wants the new range used from the first day, a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg is placed before induction, after the surgeon has agreed to examine the hand when it recedes rather than in recovery. The position decides the airway: prone and lateral need a tracheal tube and the usual care of the dependent eye, plexus and the face in a cradle; supine with the arm across the chest accepts a supraglottic airway in a short case.

  2. 2 Positioning and the tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Prone or lateral with the arm over a bolster and the elbow hanging at 90 degrees gives the surgeon access to the posterior compartment, gravity working for them, and the forearm free to move; supine with the arm across the chest is quicker but the arm has to be held. The tourniquet keeps the view clear.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    In prone, the bolster is under the mid-humerus and the shoulder is abducted to 90 degrees and the elbow flexed; check that the shoulder is not forced and that the bolster does not press the radial nerve against the shaft of the humerus, because a radial palsy from a bolster is indistinguishable from one from a portal. The tourniquet goes high on the arm, inflated after exsanguination. In lateral, the same hazards as a shoulder in lateral, with the dependent arm on a board and the head neutral. Tourniquet pain under general anaesthesia is a slow rise in pressure and heart rate from 45 min onwards that will not answer opioid; a release can run to 120 min, an arthroscopy for loose bodies to 45.

  3. 3 Antibiotic and the first distension

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The joint is filled through the lateral soft spot with 20-30 mL of saline before any portal is made; a distended joint moves the brachial artery and median nerve away from the anterior capsule and makes the capsule taut enough to pierce cleanly. Deep infection is 0.4-0.8% and most surgeons give an antibiotic for an arthroscopy that may become a release.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV before inflation. Nothing else at this step, but note the pump pressure the surgeon sets and the irrigation volume at the start, because this joint holds far less than a shoulder and extravasates earlier.

  4. 4 Anterior compartment: portals, loose bodies, synovectomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon enters through a proximal anteromedial or anterolateral portal with the elbow flexed, inspects the coronoid, the radial head and capitellum, removes loose bodies and synovitis with a shaver, and clears coronoid osteophytes with a burr. The trocar is kept flexed and aimed at the centre of the joint because extension brings the radial nerve closer.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The shaver and burr are the moments of risk for the posterior interosseous and median nerves, and a sudden request to stop the patient moving is a request for depth, not neuromuscular block: the surgeon cannot see the nerves and is relying on the elbow not shifting on the bolster. A retractor may be put through a second portal to hold the capsule off the nerves. Irrigation now begins to leave the joint; the forearm and the anterior elbow swell steadily from this point.

  5. 5 Capsulectomy and the formal release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For a stiff elbow the anterior capsule is excised from its humeral attachment, with a retractor holding the brachialis and the bundle away; the posterior capsule is released from the posterior compartment and the olecranon fossa cleared of bone and scar. The surgeon then extends and flexes the elbow on the table to confirm the gain and to tear whatever adhesions are left. A medial incision is often added to decompress or transpose the ulnar nerve, because regained flexion stretches a nerve trapped in scar.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the capsule mechanism being created and the step that fixes the pain course. The manipulation at the end is forceful; in a patient without a block it is the most stimulating moment of the operation, and in an osteoporotic post-traumatic elbow it is when a supracondylar fracture happens. The ulnar nerve work means a neuropathic element in the hand afterwards and another reason the surgeon wanted the pre-operative documentation.

  6. 6 Posterior compartment and the olecranon

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through a posterior and posterolateral portal the surgeon clears the olecranon fossa, trims the olecranon tip, removes posterior loose bodies and releases the posterior capsule; this is what restores flexion. The ulnar nerve is a few millimetres medial to the posteromedial gutter.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    In prone the surgeon is now working with gravity, the view is good and the step is quick. Check the forearm: by now a release has run 60-90 min of irrigation, and a forearm that is tense and hard rather than soft and swollen has a compartment filling with saline. The surgeon will usually stop the pump and wait; it resolves within hours and the reported experience is that it does not progress to a compartment syndrome, but a forearm that is still tense after the drapes come off is examined and documented before any block, and the block that was placed for a release is the one circumstance in which you cannot use pain to follow it.

  7. 7 Tennis elbow: the lateral epicondylar release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A different operation, usually supine on an arm table. Open: a 3-5 cm incision over the lateral epicondyle, the interval between extensor carpi radialis longus and the common extensor origin opened, the degenerate grey tissue at the extensor carpi radialis brevis origin excised, the epicondyle decorticated to bleeding bone to provoke a healing response, and the origin repaired or left. Arthroscopic: the same origin released from inside the joint, which avoids the skin incision and the extensor repair. Percutaneous: a stab and a division of the origin, under local infiltration alone, no tourniquet. The lateral collateral ligament is a few millimetres posterior and the surgeon stays anterior to the equator of the radial head to protect it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    20-40 min under a tourniquet for the open and arthroscopic versions, and the author’s practice is general anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration, or infiltration with sedation for the percutaneous release, because the pain is a 2 that simple analgesia covers. The posterior interosseous nerve is at risk only if the surgeon dissects distally; a wrist drop afterwards is surgical. The decorticated epicondyle is a raw bone surface and the reason the elbow aches for weeks.

  8. 8 Closure, dressing and the splint or no splint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals are closed with a suture rather than a strip because the elbow extravasates and leaks; a bulky dressing goes on. After a release the surgeon decides between a splint in extension overnight, a hinged brace, or nothing, and some use continuous passive motion from day 1. After tennis elbow surgery a sling for comfort and no immobilisation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the antiemetic. The elbow is swollen and the forearm full; a dressing that is already tight will be tighter in two hours. If a release patient has a block, the arm goes into whatever the surgeon wants before the patient wakes, and the forearm is examined one more time at the end.

  9. 9 Recovery and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the arm elevated, the swelling down, the nerves checked, and for a release, movement started within 24 h, because the capsule begins to scar back from the first day.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For the unblocked arthroscopy and tennis elbow patient, paracetamol and an NSAID started in recovery with a few doses of oral opioid for the first two nights; the pain peaks on the evening of surgery and day 1 and settles over a week. For the blocked release patient, the hand is examined when the block recedes at 12-24 h, at the time agreed with the surgeon, and the oral regimen is started in recovery, not when the block wears off. Half of ambulatory block patients describe rebound pain when the block goes, with bone surgery and no intravenous dexamethasone raising the odds; a release has a small bone component and the dexamethasone was given for that. Nearly every patient on this card goes home the same day; a release may stay a night where the surgeon runs a supervised movement programme.

Pain plan

The mechanism is capsule for arthroscopy and release, surface and periosteum for tennis elbow surgery, and neither is a mechanism that a long-acting block changes much after the first night. There is no PROSPECT guideline for any of the three and the analgesia literature is thin, so the plan is author’s judgement built on the mechanism, on the general rebound-pain data and on what the surgeon needs afterwards.

For a diagnostic or loose body arthroscopy and for tennis elbow surgery, the defensible default is general anaesthesia (or sedation for a percutaneous release), surgeon infiltration of the portals or the wound with 10-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% or bupivacaine 0.25%, paracetamol and an NSAID started pre-operatively and continued for a week, intravenous dexamethasone 4-8 mg at induction, and an oral opioid for two nights. No block: it would hide the nerve check for the one complication that matters, and it would not change the day 1 pain in an operation whose peak is reached with simple analgesia.

For a release the calculation changes, because the operation only works if the elbow is moved from the first day, and movement through a freshly excised capsule is the one thing a single-shot block makes possible on day 0 and the oral regimen makes tolerable from day 1. The defensible default is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% and intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, placed after the surgeon has agreed to a delayed nerve check, with the same oral regimen. A catheter is author’s judgement for the severely stiff elbow (arc under 60 degrees), the revision release, the patient who had a manipulation after a previous release, and the unit that runs continuous passive motion or a twice-daily physiotherapy programme in hospital, provided the surgeon accepts two days without a nerve examination and the forearm is examined by eye and by hand rather than by pain. The catheter’s cost is a flail arm during the exercises that it exists to make possible; the surgeon decides whether the trade is worth it.

Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has receded, or on day 1 in an unblocked patient, is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were given. Pain with a tense forearm, pain on passive finger extension, or a hand that is cooler than the other is a compartment filling, and after an arthroscopy it is usually saline rather than blood, but it is examined by a surgeon, not treated with more opioid. Pain that is better on day 1 than on day 3, in a hot swollen joint, is one of the 0.4-0.8% of deep infections.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Prone versus lateral versus supine. Prone and lateral mean a tracheal tube and the bolster hazards; supine with the arm across the chest means an assistant holding the arm and a surgeon who finds the posterior compartment harder. Ask which, because it decides the airway.
  • The rheumatoid elbow. Thin friable capsule, no safe plane, the strongest predictor of nerve palsy in the Mayo series, plus the neck, airway and steroid questions of every rheumatoid patient.
  • The post-traumatic stiff elbow with retained metal or heterotopic bone. The nerves are in scar and may be adherent to the capsule; the surgeon may convert to open, the case lengthens to two hours, and the ulnar nerve is transposed. A supracondylar fracture during the end-of-case manipulation is the disaster that turns a day case into a fixation.
  • Fluid extravasation. The elbow holds 20-30 mL and leaks from the first portal; a release with a high pump pressure fills the forearm. It resolves, but a tense forearm is examined before any block or discharge, and the block placed for a release removes pain as a sign.
  • Nerve palsy. 1.95% pooled, mostly transient, ulnar commonest; documented before the case, examined after the block recedes, and treated as the surgeon’s problem if it is a posterior interosseous or median palsy after an anterior portal.
  • The ulnar nerve in a release. Decompressed or transposed by most surgeons when flexion is being regained; dysaesthesia in the ring and little fingers afterwards is expected for weeks and is not the block.
  • Osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum. A young thrower, a short arthroscopy with drilling or a graft, day case; the bone surface adds a little to the first two days.
  • Tennis elbow: open versus arthroscopic versus percutaneous. Same outcome, fewer minor complications arthroscopically, and the percutaneous release needs nothing but infiltration. Iatrogenic lateral collateral instability is the complication that presents late and to the surgeon, not to you.
  • Continuous passive motion and early physiotherapy after a release. Where the surgeon uses it, the block and the regimen have to be matched to a programme, and the catheter question is decided by the programme, not by the operation.
  • Day-case discharge with a block after a release. A flail arm, a splint or brace, written instructions, oral analgesia already started and a named person for the night; the same list as any ambulatory block patient, with the forearm examined and documented before the patient leaves.

Key sources

The complication data for elbow arthroscopy are good: a single-institution series of 473 cases and a meta-analysis of 14,213, agreeing on a transient nerve palsy rate of about 2% and a deep infection rate under 1%. The stiffness data are small single-surgeon series, one arthroscopic and one open, that show the same 50-60 degree gain and the same tendency to recur. The tennis elbow data come from a systematic review of 1,622 elbows showing no difference between open and arthroscopic release and a small series of percutaneous release under local anaesthesia alone. There is no analgesia trial for any of these operations and no PROSPECT guideline; the block, catheter and day-case advice is author’s judgement from the mechanism and from the general ambulatory block literature.

    52 open releases, mean age 35: arc improved from 57 to 116 degrees; 27% needed a manipulation under anaesthesia in the early weeks; five needed a second release; three wound infections, three cubital tunnel syndromes, one complex regional pain syndrome
  6. Moradi A, Pasdar P, Mehrad-Majd H, Ebrahimzadeh MH. Clinical outcomes of open versus arthroscopic surgery for lateral epicondylitis, evidence from a systematic review. Arch Bone Jt Surg 2019;7:91-104
    34 studies, 1,622 elbows: no difference in pain (VAS 1.45 versus 1.62), DASH, satisfaction or return to work (8.9 versus 6.3 months, not significant); complications 57.3% open versus 33.4% arthroscopic, mostly minor (stiffness, haematoma, superficial infection, transient paraesthesia)
  7. Nazar M, Lipscombe S, Morapudi S, et al. Percutaneous tennis elbow release under local anaesthesia. Open Orthop J 2012;6:129-133
    30 elbows released percutaneously as day cases under 5 mL lidocaine 1% and 5 mL bupivacaine 0.5% with adrenaline, no tourniquet: 87% complete pain relief, return to work at a mean of three weeks, one haematoma, no infection or stiffness
  8. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of intravenous dexamethasone OR 1.78

Upper limb › Elbow

13 Distal biceps repair; ulnar nerve decompression and transposition

Acute and chronic distal biceps tendon repair by single or double incision; in situ cubital tunnel decompression, subcutaneous and submuscular anterior transposition

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A drilled and decorticated radial tuberosity, with a retracted biceps tendon pulled back 2-5 cm and fixed to it under tension in a young, muscular patient; the brace holds the forearm flexed and supinated, so the tendon component is protected and the course is bone-shaped, with a tendon flavour whenever the patient tries to turn the hand. Ulnar nerve surgery is a different and smaller mechanism: a nerve freed from its bed, with a neuropathic flavour, plus a muscle split and a medial epicondyle stripped of flexor origin in a transposition

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular brachial plexus block with intravenous dexamethasone, under general anaesthesia, for a distal biceps repair; general anaesthesia or sedation with surgeon infiltration, and no block, for ulnar nerve decompression and most transpositions
Catheter: rarely Not for a primary biceps repair in a counselled day-case patient; the defensible exception is a chronic reconstruction with a graft and a tendon that has been pulled hard, or the patient who has had a bad night after a previous block. Never for ulnar nerve surgery, where the surgeon wants the nerve examined in recovery
Alternatives: Axillary block with musculocutaneous and intercostobrachial supplementation for a biceps repair when the supraclavicular region is unavailable; Surgeon infiltration with sedation for in situ decompression as a sole technique; General anaesthesia with infiltration and no block for a biceps repair when the surgeon insists on an immediate posterior interosseous nerve check
Position
Supine with the arm on a table, forearm supinated for the anterior incision and pronated for the posterior one in a double-incision repair; supine with the arm on a table and the shoulder externally rotated for the medial elbow in ulnar nerve surgery
Tourniquet
Yes. Routine for both; 45-90 min for a biceps repair, 20-45 min for a decompression and longer for a submuscular transposition. Some surgeons release the tourniquet before the final tensioning of the biceps so the muscle is at its true resting length
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal under tourniquet; a haematoma in the antecubital fossa after release is the bleed that matters, and the brachial artery and its recurrent radial branches sit in the field
Duration
60-90 min for an acute biceps repair, 90-150 min for a chronic reconstruction with graft; 20-45 min for in situ decompression, 45-90 min for a transposition
Length of stay
Day case for both; a chronic reconstruction may stay a night. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV at induction (3 g over 120 kg) for a biceps repair with an implant; many surgeons omit it for an in situ decompression
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
Mechanical only; the baseline risk is negligible for upper limb day surgery
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (given anyway for the block) and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb into the night and the elbow will hurt most on the first and second days when the feeling comes back; the repair is protected by the splint and the no-lifting rule for six weeks, and a patch of numbness on the thumb side of the forearm is common and usually fades.
The trap
The posterior interosseous nerve wraps around the radial neck exactly where the surgeon is drilling, retracting and tying the biceps down; document wrist and finger extension before the block, and agree with the surgeon that a dense block will hide a wrist drop until the next day

What the surgeon is doing and why

Two operations on the front and the inside of the elbow, paired because they share a position, a tourniquet and a day-case pathway, and because they sit at opposite ends of the question this book keeps asking: whether a block helps, and whether it hides something the surgeon needs to see.

The distal biceps tendon inserts on the radial tuberosity, a bump on the medial side of the radius 2 cm below the radial head, and it ruptures in one setting: a man in his forties or fifties, often heavily built or a weight trainer, takes an eccentric load on a flexed elbow and feels a pop. The tendon retracts into the arm, the muscle belly rides up, and the forearm loses much of its supination strength and some flexion strength if nothing is done. Non-operative treatment is reasonable in a sedentary patient; everyone else is repaired within two or three weeks, before the tendon shortens, scars to the brachialis, and can no longer reach the tuberosity without a graft.

The surgeon’s problem is that the tuberosity faces posteriorly and medially and the only ways to it pass the radial nerve. The single anterior incision goes through the antecubital fossa, between brachioradialis and pronator teres, retracts the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve laterally (it is injured, usually transiently, in about 9% of repairs, and more often through a small incision than an extensile one), finds the recurrent radial vessels and ties them, and reaches the tuberosity with the forearm fully supinated to roll the bone towards the surgeon and the posterior interosseous nerve away. The nerve wraps around the radial neck inside the supinator a finger’s breadth from the tuberosity, and a retractor on the lateral side of the neck, a drill that exits the far cortex, or a cortical button flipped on the wrong side of it, are the mechanisms of a palsy; it happens in about 1.6-2.7% of repairs and mostly resolves. The double-incision technique, which the trial of 91 men found gave a 10% advantage in flexion strength for the same function scores, retrieves the tendon through a small anterior incision, passes it between radius and ulna, and fixes it through a second posterolateral incision with a muscle split of the extensor mass and bone tunnels in the tuberosity; it trades the nerve risk (lateral antebrachial cutaneous neuropraxia 2.2% versus 9.8%, posterior interosseous palsy 0.2% versus 2.7%) for heterotopic ossification and, rarely, a radioulnar synostosis (ossification or synostosis 9.8% versus 3.2%), because the ulnar periosteum and the interosseous membrane are disturbed on the way through.

Whichever route, the fixation is the same idea: the tuberosity is decorticated or a socket drilled into it, the tendon end is whip-stitched, and it is pulled down and fixed with a cortical button, an interference screw, suture anchors, or sutures through bone tunnels. The arm is flexed and supinated to get the tendon to reach; a tendon that has retracted for weeks has to be dragged, and a chronic rupture over about six weeks gets a graft because it will not reach at all. After the repair the forearm is immobilised in flexion and supination, then moved early but unloaded for six weeks, with a no-lifting rule that the patient population finds hard to keep: re-rupture (1.4-2.5%) clusters in the first three weeks and is attributed to non-compliance.

Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow is a nerve compressed or stretched in a tunnel that narrows with flexion. The nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle under the cubital tunnel retinaculum, between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, and is tethered proximally by the arcade of Struthers and the medial intermuscular septum. The surgeon has three choices and the randomised evidence says they are equivalent: simple in situ decompression (open the roof of the tunnel and the fascia of flexor carpi ulnaris and leave the nerve where it is), anterior subcutaneous transposition (free the nerve over 15 cm, divide the septum, move it in front of the epicondyle into a fat pocket), or submuscular transposition (the same, with the flexor-pronator origin detached from the epicondyle and repaired over the nerve). In the 152-patient randomised trial decompression and subcutaneous transposition gave the same proportion of good results at a year (49 of 75 versus 54 of 77), with complications in 9.6% after decompression and 31.1% after transposition, and the meta-analyses agree that there is no difference in outcome. Decompression is therefore the modern default, with transposition kept for a nerve that subluxes over the epicondyle, a revision, or a nerve that has to be moved for an elbow operation.

The pain logic follows. A biceps repair is tendon-tension in its purest form: a strong, retracted tendon fixed to drilled bone under tension in a young muscular patient, then loaded by every attempt to supinate or flex for weeks. The early peak is a bone-and-tendon peak and the course is prolonged by movement, the shape of a cuff repair but in a joint that is easier to rest, so it earns a 3 rather than a 5; the patient demographic (young, male, opioid-naive) puts rebound risk high. Ulnar nerve decompression is a nerve mechanism: a neuropathic ache and dysaesthesia often better the next morning than the day before surgery, with an incision that hurts for a few days. A transposition adds muscle (the flexor-pronator origin taken down and repaired, in the submuscular version) and a bigger wound, and sits at a 2. The card carries the biceps score because the biceps is the operation that needs a plan.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Documenting the nerves and deciding the block

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon is about to work within a centimetre of the posterior interosseous nerve, retract the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve for an hour, and in the ulnar case operate on the nerve itself; they will want to know afterwards which deficit is new.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Before any drug, examine and write down wrist and finger extension (posterior interosseous), sensation over the lateral forearm (lateral antebrachial cutaneous), and for the ulnar case little finger sensation, first dorsal interosseous power and a Froment’s sign. For a biceps repair, the author’s practice is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, placed awake before induction, after the surgeon has agreed that the nerve check will wait for the block to recede. For an ulnar nerve decompression or a subcutaneous transposition, no block: the operation is short, the pain is a 2 that infiltration covers, and the surgeon wants the little finger examined in recovery. A submuscular transposition is the author’s exception, where a block is reasonable if the surgeon accepts the delay.

  2. 2 Position, tourniquet and the airway

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with the arm on a table, the forearm supinated for the anterior approach. The tourniquet goes high on the arm. For the ulnar nerve, the shoulder is externally rotated and the elbow flexed on the table to present the medial side; some surgeons prefer the arm across the chest.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A supraglottic airway and spontaneous ventilation are reasonable for every operation on this card; a tracheal tube for the reflux-prone or the heavily built biceps patient. Cefazolin 2 g IV before inflation for the implant case. The external rotation needed for the medial elbow strains a stiff shoulder and is the position to check after the surgeon has set it. Tourniquet time runs 45-90 min for a biceps repair and under 45 min for a decompression; a submuscular transposition is longer.

  3. 3 Anterior incision and the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A transverse or S-shaped incision in the antecubital crease, then the interval between brachioradialis and pronator teres. The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve runs in the subcutaneous fat lateral to the biceps tendon and is retracted laterally for the rest of the case; the recurrent radial vessels cross the field and are ligated.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The nerve retracted here is the commonest complication of the operation (9.2% in 3,091 repairs), and it is a sensory nerve: a numb patch over the lateral forearm that usually resolves. It is also the nerve whose distribution a patient will describe the next day as “the block has not worn off”, which is why the pre-operative sensory map matters. Nothing to do at this step but note the time.

  4. 4 Retrieving the tendon

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tendon end is found, often retracted into the arm and scarred to the brachialis; the surgeon milks it distally with the elbow flexed, excises the frayed end, and whip-stitches it. A tendon more than a few weeks old may need a separate proximal incision or a graft.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The elbow is flexed hard and the muscle belly pulled on; in an unblocked patient this is a stimulating moment, and in a blocked patient it is the moment the surgeon finds out whether the tendon will reach. If it will not, the case lengthens by an hour for a graft and the pain course shifts up.

  5. 5 Exposing the tuberosity and protecting the posterior interosseous nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With the forearm in maximal supination, the radial tuberosity rotates into the wound and the posterior interosseous nerve, in the supinator on the far side of the neck, rotates away. A retractor is placed carefully, never levered against the lateral side of the neck. In the double-incision technique the surgeon instead passes a clamp between radius and ulna from the anterior wound to the posterolateral skin and makes the second incision there, splitting the extensor mass with the forearm pronated and staying off the ulna.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the step the trap is about. A posterior interosseous palsy presents as a finger and thumb drop with preserved wrist extension that drifts into radial deviation (extensor carpi radialis longus is spared) and no sensory loss; the mechanisms are retraction, a drill exiting the far cortex, and a cortical button that flips into the nerve. The surgeon will want the forearm held in full supination and still; a request for stillness is a request for depth or for a hand on the forearm, not neuromuscular block. In the double-incision technique the pronation and supination of the forearm between the two wounds is where the arm board and the tourniquet get dislodged.

  6. 6 Preparing the tuberosity and fixing the tendon under tension

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tuberosity is decorticated with a burr, or a socket drilled to the far cortex for a button or a screw, or bone tunnels made for a double-incision repair. The tendon is pulled down with the elbow flexed and the forearm supinated and fixed with a cortical button through the far cortex, an interference screw into the socket, suture anchors, or sutures tied over a bone bridge. Some surgeons let the tourniquet down before the final tensioning so that the muscle is at its resting length and the repair is not set too tight.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The mechanism this card is built around exists from the moment the tendon is fixed: bone drilled and a tendon tied to it under tension in a young patient. The bone component (socket, decortication) is the reason the rebound-pain odds are those of bone surgery. If the surgeon drops the tourniquet before tensioning, expect the reperfusion dip and a bleeding antecubital fossa in the middle of the critical step rather than at the end.

  7. 7 Closure, the splint and the position of the forearm

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Haemostasis after tourniquet release (the recurrent radial vessels and the brachial artery are in the field), layered closure, and a posterior splint with the elbow at about 90 degrees and the forearm supinated so the repair is unloaded. Early protected motion starts at one to two weeks; no lifting for six.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the antiemetic. The splint goes on before the patient lightens; a young man with a dense block will otherwise flex and supinate the arm with the other hand to look at it. A tense antecubital fossa in recovery is a haematoma from a recurrent branch and is surgical; it compresses the median nerve and the brachial artery, so a hand that is cooler than the other or a new numb thumb is examined rather than observed.

  8. 8 Ulnar nerve: the medial approach and in situ decompression

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A 4-8 cm incision behind the medial epicondyle, protecting the branches of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve that cross it (the usual cause of a painful scar), then division of the cubital tunnel retinaculum, the fascia between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris and, proximally, the arcade of Struthers. The nerve is left in its bed and the elbow is flexed on the table to check that it does not subluxate forward over the epicondyle; if it does, the surgeon moves to a transposition.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Surgeon infiltration with 10-15 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% or bupivacaine 0.25% along the wound and a general anaesthetic or sedation; the operation is 20-45 min. The nerve itself should not be stimulated in a decompression, but a tug on it in a lightly sedated patient produces a jolt into the little finger that the patient will remember. A medial antebrachial cutaneous branch cut here gives a numb or painful patch on the medial forearm that outlasts the nerve symptoms.

  9. 9 Ulnar nerve: anterior transposition

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    When the nerve subluxes, or at revision, the nerve is freed over about 15 cm with its vessels where possible, the medial intermuscular septum is excised so the nerve does not kink over it, and it is moved in front of the epicondyle. Subcutaneous: a fascial sling or a fat pocket holds it. Submuscular: the flexor-pronator origin is lifted off the epicondyle, the nerve laid on the muscle bed next to the median nerve, and the origin repaired over it. A medial epicondylectomy is a third option that removes the bone the nerve was riding over.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The submuscular version is the one with a muscle mechanism, a repaired flexor origin protected for a few weeks, and a 90 min tourniquet; it is the one ulnar operation where a block is reasonable, and even here the surgeon usually wants the hand examined in recovery because a nerve devascularised in the move declares itself early. Complications were three times more frequent after transposition than decompression in the randomised trial (31.1% versus 9.6%); a transposition patient in recovery with a new dense ulnar deficit is examined by the surgeon, not attributed to infiltration.

  10. 10 Recovery, the first night and discharge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the biceps repair protected and the nerve patient’s hand working, and both patients home the same day.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For the biceps patient, the oral regimen starts in recovery: paracetamol and an NSAID, and an oral opioid for the first three nights. The block recedes at 12-24 h and this patient is the rebound-pain phenotype of the 972-patient cohort (bone surgery OR 1.82, younger age, and the dexamethasone given to blunt it); the pain rises over an hour or two to its day 1 level, the worst of the course, and the written night plan is what keeps him from the emergency department. The nerve check happens when the block is gone, at the agreed time, and a wrist drop then is a call to the surgeon. For the ulnar patient, paracetamol and an NSAID with a few opioid doses for two nights; the little finger is examined before discharge and the patient told that the tingling may be better tomorrow or may take months, depending on how long the nerve was compressed.

Pain plan

Two mechanisms, two plans. The biceps repair is tendon-tension on a drilled bone in the patient most likely to have rebound pain, and the plan has to cover the first night and expect a hard day 1 and 2. The ulnar nerve operation is a nerve mechanism with a small wound, where the plan has to not hide the hand.

For the biceps repair the defensible default is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID started before the block recedes and continued for a week, and an oral opioid for the first three nights, with a written night plan. The patient is young, male and will be at home with a flail arm; he needs the splint explained, the no-lifting rule explained with the re-rupture figure attached to it, and someone with him on the first night. A catheter is rarely justified: the operation is a day case, the joint is splinted and rested rather than moved, and a flail arm for two days in a patient who will not keep still outweighs the gain. The exceptions are author’s judgement: a chronic reconstruction with a graft, a bilateral or revision case, and a patient who has had a catastrophic rebound night before. There is no procedure-specific guideline and no randomised analgesia trial for distal biceps repair; the plan is the mechanism and the general ambulatory block data.

For the ulnar nerve the defensible default is surgeon infiltration, general anaesthesia or sedation, paracetamol and an NSAID for a few days, and a couple of opioid doses for the first two nights, with no block, because the operation’s only serious complication is a nerve that is worse, and that is found by examining the hand in recovery. A submuscular transposition is the exception where a block is reasonable if the surgeon agrees. A patient already on a gabapentinoid or an antidepressant for neuropathic pain continues it.

Escalation for the biceps patient: pain above 7 on the first night with a soft antecubital fossa, warm fingers and the splint on is the block wearing off and is treated with the charted opioid; pain with a tense fossa, a cool hand or a new numb thumb is a haematoma on the median nerve and brachial artery and is surgical; a wrist drop after the block has gone is a posterior interosseous palsy and is the surgeon’s to follow. For the ulnar patient, pain is rarely the problem; a dense new motor deficit is.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Single versus double incision. Same function; the double incision gives more flexion strength, fewer nerve injuries and more heterotopic ossification, and adds a posterolateral muscle split and the pronation-supination shuffle during the case. The anaesthetic is the same.
  • Chronic rupture and graft. Over about six weeks the tendon will not reach; an allograft or autograft is woven in, the case runs to 150 min, the tourniquet is let down and re-inflated, and this is the patient for whom the catheter question is worth asking.
  • Heterotopic ossification. Mostly after double-incision repairs; some surgeons give an NSAID for prophylaxis, which is the regular NSAID you were charting anyway.
  • The weight trainer. Anabolic steroid use is over-represented in distal biceps ruptures; ask, because it changes the airway, the cardiovascular risk and the opioid tolerance.
  • The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. Numb lateral forearm in 9% of repairs, more with small incisions; it looks like a residual block to the patient and the ward, and the pre-operative sensory map is what separates them.
  • Posterior interosseous palsy. 1.6-2.7%; retraction, drill and button. Document before, examine after the block, and treat a persisting palsy as the surgeon’s to image and explore.
  • Ulnar nerve decompression versus transposition. Equivalent outcomes, a third of the complications with decompression; transposition for a subluxing nerve or a revision, submuscular for the thin patient whose subcutaneous nerve would sit on the desk edge.
  • The nerve decompressed as part of an elbow operation. Transposition is bundled with total elbow arthroplasty, distal humerus fixation and some releases; there the nerve plan belongs to the main operation’s card.
  • Pre-existing neuropathic pain. A long-compressed nerve with wasting does not recover its motor function and may not lose its pain; set the expectation before surgery and continue the neuropathic agents.

Key sources

The complication data for distal biceps repair are consistent across two systematic reviews and the randomised single-versus-double-incision trial, and they are what the trap and the nerve documentation rest on. The ulnar nerve evidence is better still: one adequately sized randomised trial and two meta-analyses agreeing that decompression and transposition give the same result and that transposition carries more complications. There is no analgesia trial for either operation and no PROSPECT guideline; the block and catheter advice is author’s judgement from the mechanism and the general ambulatory block literature, and the score of 3 for a biceps repair is calibrated against the Part B anchors rather than against measured pain data, which do not exist for this operation.

  1. Amarasooriya M, Bain GI, Roper T, Bryant K, Iqbal K, Phadnis J. Complications after distal biceps tendon repair: a systematic review. Am J Sports Med 2020;48:3103-3111
    72 studies, 3,091 primary repairs: complications 25% overall, 4.6% major; lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve injury the commonest at 9.2% (9.7% with a limited anterior incision versus 5.2% extensile); posterior interosseous nerve injury 1.6%, unaffected by fixation method; superficial radial nerve injury 6% extensile versus 2.1% limited; re-rupture 1.4%; synostosis 0.1%, only after double incision; most nerve injuries resolved
  2. Amin NH, Volpi A, Lynch TS, et al. Complications of distal biceps tendon repair: a meta-analysis of single-incision versus double-incision surgical technique. Orthop J Sports Med 2016;4(10)
    87 studies, 1,283 patients: complications 28.3% single incision versus 20.9% double; lateral antebrachial cutaneous neuropraxia 9.8% versus 2.2%; posterior interosseous palsy 2.7% versus 0.2%; heterotopic ossification 3.2% versus 7.2% and combined ossification or synostosis 3.2% versus 9.8%; re-rupture 2.5% versus 0.6%
  3. Grewal R, Athwal GS, MacDermid JC, et al. Single versus double-incision technique for the repair of acute distal biceps tendon ruptures: a randomized clinical trial. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2012;94:1166-1174

Prospective randomized controlled study comparing simple decompression versus anterior subcutaneous transposition for idiopathic neuropathy of the ulnar nerve at the elbow: part 1. Neurosurgery 2005;56:522-530
    152 patients randomised, one-year follow-up: excellent or good in 49 of 75 after decompression and 54 of 77 after transposition, not different; complications 9.6% versus 31.1% (risk ratio 0.32); the authors advise simple decompression even when the nerve subluxes
  5. Zlowodzki M, Chan S, Bhandari M, Kalliainen L, Schubert W. Anterior transposition compared with simple decompression for treatment of cubital tunnel syndrome: a meta-analysis of randomized, controlled trials. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2007;89:2591-2598
    Four randomised trials, 335 patients: no difference in motor conduction velocity or clinical scores between transposition (submuscular or subcutaneous) and simple decompression
  6. Macadam SA, Gandhi R, Bezuhly M, Lefaivre KA. Simple decompression versus anterior subcutaneous and submuscular transposition of the ulnar nerve for cubital tunnel syndrome: a meta-analysis. J Hand Surg Am 2008;33:1314.e1-12
    Ten studies, 449 simple decompressions, 342 subcutaneous and 115 submuscular transpositions: odds of improvement with decompression versus transposition 0.75 (95% CI 0.54-1.04), not significant
