Upper limb › Elbow

14 Elbow fractures: olecranon, distal humerus, radial head

Olecranon tension band and plate fixation; distal humerus two-column ORIF with or without olecranon osteotomy; radial head screw and plate fixation

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Fractured bone reduced and compressed with metal, drilled and plated along two columns in a distal humerus with periosteal stripping; a triceps either split, reflected or an olecranon osteotomy added; the ulnar nerve mobilised in every distal humerus; a tourniquet. The olecranon and radial head are small versions of the same, and the dislocated elbow adds a ligament repair

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
General anaesthesia with a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block and intravenous dexamethasone for olecranon and radial head fixation; for distal humerus ORIF the same block only after the surgeon has agreed to a delayed nerve examination, otherwise general anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration and a block offered the next morning
Catheter: selective A continuous infraclavicular catheter for a distal humerus fixation is defensible when the surgeon runs early motion and has seen the ulnar nerve intact and untethered; the author's practice is a single shot for olecranon and radial head fixation and a case-by-case decision for the distal humerus, with the nerve examination timing written in the notes
Alternatives: Axillary block with a musculocutaneous supplement for radial head and olecranon fixation; General anaesthesia alone with surgeon infiltration and a rescue block in recovery or the next day for the distal humerus where the surgeon wants an immediate nerve check; Low-concentration block (ropivacaine 0.2%) without adjunct where a compartment or nerve concern exists, on the lower-leg guideline's logic
Position
Lateral decubitus or prone with the arm over a padded post for the distal humerus and most olecranon fixations; supine with the arm across the chest for some surgeons; supine on an arm table for the radial head
Tourniquet
Yes. Sterile tourniquet high on the arm; an olecranon fixation sits inside 60 min, a distal humerus runs to the limit and beyond it, with release and re-inflation or completion without it
Cement
No
Blood loss
100-300 mL for a distal humerus after tourniquet release; under 100 mL for the olecranon and radial head
Duration
45-90 min for olecranon tension band or plate; 120-240 min for a distal humerus two-column fixation, longer with an osteotomy and an osteoporotic bone; 60-120 min for radial head fixation, longer in a terrible triad
Length of stay
Day case or one night for the olecranon and radial head; 1-3 nights for the distal humerus. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); an open fracture has its own antibiotic pathway and its own card
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction for a distal humerus; not needed for the olecranon or radial head
VTE
Mechanical for the inpatient; chemoprophylaxis only for the patient's own risk factors
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb into the night if a block is used; the elbow hurts most on the first two days and then settles, the metal may be felt under the skin at the point of the elbow, and the little finger side of the hand may tingle for some weeks because the nerve was moved out of the way.
The trap
The block that hides the nerve: the ulnar nerve is mobilised in every distal humerus fixation and gives post-operative symptoms in anything from one in twenty to one in three patients depending on how they are counted, the posterior interosseous nerve sits against the radial neck, and a surgeon who wants to examine the hand in recovery has a legitimate claim; the decision is made with the surgeon before the block, written down, and never defaulted

What the surgeon is doing and why

Three fractures of one joint, grouped because the surgeon’s logic is the same for all of them: the elbow tolerates neither an incongruent joint surface nor six weeks in a cast, so an intra-articular fracture is reduced anatomically, fixed rigidly enough to move within days, and the price is paid in exposure. What differs is how much exposure. An olecranon is subcutaneous and takes 45 min; a distal humerus is a three-dimensional puzzle behind the triceps and takes three hours; a radial head is a small bone on the lateral side with a nerve wrapped around its neck. The anaesthetic question they share is the one in the trap: a block is the best analgesic for all three, and each has a nerve the surgeon may want to examine before the block would allow.

The olecranon is the triceps’ lever arm. A fall onto the point of the elbow breaks it across, the triceps pulls the proximal fragment up, and the joint surface gapes. A tension band (two Kirschner wires down the shaft and a figure-of-eight wire over the dorsal surface) converts the pull of the triceps into compression at the joint line, which is elegant, cheap and works for a simple transverse fracture; it also leaves wires under thin skin that migrate and irritate, and in the pooled comparisons it needed removal in 79 of 236 cases against 41 of 332 after plating, with a complication rate twice that of a plate (RR 0.48 in favour of the plate). A precontoured dorsal plate is used for comminuted, oblique and osteoporotic fractures and is now the commoner choice. In a frail patient a displaced olecranon fracture can be left alone; surgeons vary.

The distal humerus is two columns of bone, medial and lateral, joined by the articular spool of the trochlea and capitellum, and an intercondylar fracture separates the columns from each other and from the shaft. The surgeon has to see the joint surface, reconstruct it, and fix each column with its own plate (parallel or perpendicular, a matter of preference). Seeing the joint from behind means getting past the triceps: a paratricipital approach works on either side of it and gives a limited view; a triceps split or reflection gives more; an olecranon osteotomy (a chevron cut through the olecranon, swung up with the triceps attached) gives the whole articular surface, at the cost of a second fracture that needs its own fixation and fails to unite in a few percent, with complications of 46-55% in comparative series against 27-41% for the paratricipital approach. The ulnar nerve is found and mobilised in every case, because the medial plate goes where the nerve lives; it gives post-operative symptoms in 5% of patients in the pooled olecranon osteotomy data and in a quarter to a third in one 134-patient trauma centre cohort that counted any symptom (26.8% with an osteotomy and 33.3% without, not different), mostly transiently, and many surgeons transpose it. In an osteoporotic patient over 65 with comminution the fragments may not hold screws, and the surgeon converts to a total elbow on the table; the randomised trial of that decision is on the total elbow card. Everything about this operation is long: a tourniquet that runs past its limit, an exposure that strips the periosteum off both columns, and a joint that will be stiff if it is not moved early.

The radial head is the lateral pillar of the elbow and the secondary stabiliser against valgus. A fall on the outstretched hand drives it into the capitellum and splits it (Mason type II, two pieces, displaced) or shatters it (type III). Two or three large fragments are fixed with headless screws or a small plate through a lateral approach, with the forearm pronated to carry the posterior interosseous nerve away from the field; more than three fragments are replaced rather than fixed, because in the one adequate trial replacement gave a better score (92 versus 72) and fewer adverse events (6 of 36 versus 15 of 31). A radial head fracture with a dislocation and a coronoid fracture is a terrible triad: the same lateral approach then fixes the coronoid, replaces or fixes the head and repairs the lateral collateral ligament, which turns a 60 min case into two hours and adds a ligament under tension.

The pain logic is bone, and the trajectory is the Part B anchor for a 3: a hard peak on day 1 and 2 from fractured and drilled bone, compressed with metal, falling quickly because nothing is loaded through the fixation. Behind it are contributors that scale with the operation: periosteal stripping along two columns and a reflected or osteotomised triceps in the distal humerus, which put that operation at the top of the band with a week-2 movement-evoked component; a handled ulnar nerve with a neuropathic edge; a tourniquet; and a ligament repair in the terrible triad. The olecranon and the isolated radial head are small versions, and in a counselled patient they are day cases.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Neurology, the fasting state and the block conversation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a documented hand before the nerve is moved, an elbow fixed within a few days of the injury before it stiffens, and to know whether the hand will be examinable in recovery.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Before any drug, examine and write down ulnar (little finger sensation, first dorsal interosseous), median, radial and posterior interosseous (wrist and finger extension) function; a fracture-dislocation often has a deficit already, and that is the fact that protects everybody later. Then the block conversation, which this card exists for. Olecranon and radial head: the author’s practice is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, under general anaesthesia, with the surgeon’s agreement that the hand will be examined when the block recedes. Distal humerus: the surgeon decides whether they want the ulnar nerve examined in recovery; if they do, the operation runs under general anaesthesia with infiltration and a block is offered once the hand has been seen; if they do not, the block goes in before induction with the agreement written down. The lower-leg guideline’s principle transfers: dense, long blocks that far outlast the surgery are the ones that delay a diagnosis, neither surgeon nor anaesthetist vetoes the other, and the patient’s consent to the chosen technique is documented. A low-concentration block (ropivacaine 0.2%) without adjunct is the compromise that keeps the analgesia and shortens the blind window. The unfasted emergency patient is on the hand trauma card.

  2. 2 Position: lateral or prone with the arm over a post

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The posterior elbow is reached with the patient lateral or prone and the upper arm supported on a padded post so that the forearm hangs at 90 degrees and the surgeon looks down onto the olecranon; the image intensifier comes in from the opposite side. Supine with the arm across the chest is the alternative for an olecranon and for some surgeons’ distal humerus; the radial head is supine on an arm table.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Lateral and prone mean a tracheal tube, the dependent eye, plexus and peroneal nerve padded, the head neutral in a cradle, and a tube that will not be reached once the drapes and the image intensifier are in place. The post under the humerus is the thing to check: it must sit under the mid-shaft, not in the axilla (plexus) and not at the distal shaft where the radial nerve runs in the spiral groove, because a radial palsy from the post looks exactly like one from the surgery. The high sterile tourniquet goes on before the final positioning. A distal humerus runs long enough that a second check of pressure points at 90 min is worth doing.

  3. 3 Tourniquet, antibiotic and tranexamic acid

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The field is bony and the surgeon wants it dry to see the joint surface; the tourniquet is inflated after exsanguination and will be up for the whole of an olecranon fixation and for as long as the surgeon can manage in a distal humerus.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV finished before inflation; tranexamic acid 1 g IV for a distal humerus, on borrowed evidence. The distal humerus is the elbow operation that overruns the tourniquet. Say the time at 90 and 120 min; the surgeon’s choices are a release and re-inflation after 10-15 min of reperfusion, or completion of the second column in a bleeding field. Under general anaesthesia the slow rise in pressure and heart rate from 45 min is tourniquet pain and does not answer opioid.

  4. 4 Olecranon: reduction and tension band or plate

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A posterior incision curved around the point of the elbow, the fracture cleaned of haematoma, the joint surface reduced under direct vision and held with a clamp, then either two wires and a figure-of-eight tension band or a dorsal plate with screws into the shaft and the proximal fragment. The joint is moved under the image intensifier to check that nothing crosses the articular surface.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The quick one, 45-90 min, inside a single tourniquet. The ulnar nerve is a centimetre medial to the plate and is protected rather than mobilised in a simple olecranon fracture. Day case in a fit patient with a working block and an oral regimen started; the wires under thin skin are the complaint at six weeks, not the pain on day 1.

  5. 5 Distal humerus: the ulnar nerve and the approach

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A long posterior incision, the ulnar nerve identified proximally and freed from the arcade of Struthers to the flexor carpi ulnaris, held on a sling for the rest of the case and usually transposed at the end. Then the choice: paratricipital windows either side of the triceps for an extra-articular or simple fracture, a triceps split or reflection, or an olecranon osteotomy for the comminuted articular fracture, which gives the whole joint but adds a fracture that will not unite in about 2-4%.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The nerve work is the first hour and the reason for the pre-operative examination. The osteotomy is the step that changes the pain course: a cut olecranon fixed with a tension band or a plate is a second bone operation inside the first, with its own hardware under thin skin, and ulnar neuropathy after a screw-fixed osteotomy ran to 21% in the pooled series. Ask which approach was used before writing the discharge plan: an osteotomy or a reflected triceps means more movement-evoked pain in weeks 1-2 than a paratricipital window.

  6. 6 Distal humerus: articular reconstruction and two-column plating

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The joint surface is rebuilt first, fragment by fragment, held with wires and then compressed with a screw across the trochlea; the reconstructed spool is then attached to the shaft with a plate on each column, parallel (medial and lateral) or perpendicular (medial and posterolateral), with as many screws into the distal fragments as the bone will take. The periosteum is stripped along both columns to seat the plates. The elbow is then moved through its arc under the image intensifier.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The long middle of the operation, usually 90-150 min on its own. Warm the patient, because a long case in lateral with an open joint loses heat steadily. The periosteal stripping is the mechanism that makes this fixation hurt more and for longer than its bone volume suggests. In an osteoporotic patient this is the step at which the surgeon finds that the screws will not hold and converts to a total elbow: cement, a frail patient, and the total elbow card’s cement step in a patient who has already been under anaesthesia for two hours. If the tourniquet has been released, bleeding from the cancellous surfaces is steady rather than brisk, and the blood loss on this card is mostly accrued now.

  7. 7 Radial head: the lateral approach and the posterior interosseous nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A lateral incision over the radial head through the Kocher interval (anconeus and extensor carpi ulnaris) or a common extensor split, the forearm pronated to swing the posterior interosseous nerve away from the radial neck, the fragments reduced and fixed with headless compression screws placed in the safe zone (the 90 degree arc that does not articulate with the ulna) or a low-profile plate. In a terrible triad the coronoid is reached through the same wound before the head is dealt with, and the lateral collateral ligament is repaired to the epicondyle at the end.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Supine on an arm table, 60-120 min, standard tourniquet. The posterior interosseous nerve is the nerve of this operation; a wrist drop after a radial head fixation is a retractor or a plate that is too distal, and another reason the hand was examined before the block. An isolated radial head fixation is a day case; a terrible triad with a ligament repair stays a night and has a tendon-tension element the isolated fracture does not.

  8. 8 Ulnar nerve transposition, tourniquet release and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    At the end of a distal humerus fixation most surgeons move the ulnar nerve into an anterior subcutaneous pocket so that it does not lie on the medial plate, checking that it is not kinked at the septum or the new entry. The tourniquet comes down, bleeding is dealt with, a drain goes in, and the posterior wound over the olecranon is closed in layers. An olecranon fixation is closed over the wires or plate with no drain. A splint holds the elbow at 90 degrees for comfort.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tourniquet release after a long inflation brings the reperfusion dip and the washout; after a distal humerus the pressure takes minutes to recover. Give the antiemetic. If a block has been placed, the splint and sling go on before the patient lightens.

  9. 9 Recovery: the hand, the first night and the rescue block

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a working hand, a dry wound, and movement started within days, because a fixed elbow that is not moved becomes a stiff elbow that needs a release.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The hand is examined at the time that was agreed: in recovery if no block was placed, or when the block recedes at 12-24 h if it was. A new ulnar deficit after a distal humerus is in the expected 25-33% and is usually traction; a dense new palsy that was not there before the block is the surgeon’s to see. If the surgeon wanted an unblocked recovery, this is where the block is offered: a single-shot block in recovery once the hand has been documented, or the next morning, gives the patient the first night. Oral paracetamol and an NSAID start in recovery; an oral opioid is charted for the first three nights. In the 972-patient ambulatory cohort half had rebound pain, with bone surgery (OR 1.82) and no intravenous dexamethasone (OR 1.78) raising the odds; every operation on this card is bone surgery and the dexamethasone was given for it. The olecranon and radial head patient go home the same day or the next morning; the distal humerus stays one to three nights, longer with an osteotomy, an older patient or a conversion.

Pain plan

The dominant mechanism is bone, which is moderate, short and NSAID-responsive, so the analgesic shape is a block for the first night and an oral regimen that carries the next three days, with the catheter kept for the long, stripped, early-moved distal humerus. The complication that argues against the block is nerve injury, and the plan has to answer both. There is no procedure-specific guideline for any elbow fracture and no randomised analgesia trial; the plan is the mechanism, the general ambulatory block data, and the principle borrowed from the lower-leg compartment syndrome guideline that a dense block far outlasting the surgery delays a diagnosis and a low-concentration one with good surveillance does not.

The defensible default for an olecranon or radial head fixation is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (or 0.2% when the surgeon wants a shorter blind window), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID started before the block recedes, and an oral opioid for the first three nights with a written night plan. The nerve examination is before the block and again when it recedes, and the surgeon has agreed to that sequence.

For a distal humerus fixation the default is decided with the surgeon, case by case, and written down. If the surgeon has seen the nerve intact and untethered and runs an early motion programme, a single shot or a continuous infraclavicular catheter is reasonable, and the catheter earns its place for the osteotomy, the reflected triceps, the opioid-tolerant patient and the stiff elbow that will need physiotherapy twice a day; the author’s practice is a single shot in most and a catheter after that conversation. If the surgeon wants the hand examined in recovery, the operation runs under general anaesthesia with infiltration of the wound, and the block is offered as a rescue once the hand is documented. A ropivacaine 0.2% block without adjunct is the middle path: most of the analgesia with a shorter, lighter block that lets a dense motor deficit show through.

Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone, with a soft wound, warm fingers and the splint on, is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were given. Pain out of proportion in a tense posterior wound after a distal humerus is a haematoma over a transposed nerve and is surgical. A tense forearm with pain on passive finger extension is a compartment syndrome until proven otherwise; it is rare after elbow fixation, but the high-energy fracture-dislocation is the patient it happens to and the reason the lower-leg guideline’s logic was applied. Stable ring and little finger dysaesthesia is traction neuritis and settles over weeks; a deficit that worsens over days is a nerve under pressure and is also surgical.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Tension band versus plate for the olecranon. Same fixation principle, twice the complication rate and twice the removal rate with wires; the anaesthetic is identical.
  • Osteotomy versus paratricipital for the distal humerus. The osteotomy gives the view and adds a fracture; complications in comparative series 46-55% against 27-41%, with the same ulnar neuropathy rate, and more movement-evoked pain in weeks 1-2.
  • Conversion to total elbow. The osteoporotic patient over 65 whose fragments will not hold a screw; five of 21 in the randomised trial. Position and tourniquet stay, cement arrives, and the frailest patient of the day gets the longest case.
  • The ulnar nerve. Mobilised in every distal humerus, transposed by most, symptomatic afterwards in one in twenty to one in three depending on the definition, mostly transiently. Documented before, examined at the agreed time, and the timing is the surgeon’s decision as much as yours.
  • The posterior interosseous nerve. The radial head’s nerve; pronation protects it, a distal retractor or plate injures it, and a wrist drop after a block has gone is surgical.
  • Terrible triad. Radial head, coronoid, lateral collateral ligament, sometimes the medial; two hours, a ligament under tension, a hinged brace and one night.
  • The high-energy elbow. A fracture-dislocation with a swollen forearm is the patient in whom a compartment syndrome is possible and a dense long block is the wrong choice; a low-concentration block without adjunct, hourly observations and a documented decision are the guideline’s answer.
  • The post under the arm. A radial palsy from a post at the spiral groove is indistinguishable from a surgical one; check the post sits under the mid-shaft before draping.
  • Heterotopic ossification. Common after distal humerus fixation, more after a head injury; some surgeons give an NSAID for prophylaxis, which is the NSAID you were charting.
  • The open fracture. Its own antibiotic pathway, its own timing and its own card (open fractures).

Key sources

The surgical evidence is reasonable: a meta-analysis of tension band against plate for the olecranon, a systematic review of 1,700 olecranon osteotomies, a 134-patient cohort comparing osteotomy with the paratricipital approach for ulnar neuropathy, a Cochrane review of radial head fixation against replacement, and the single randomised trial of fixation against arthroplasty for the elderly distal humerus. The anaesthetic evidence is not procedure-specific: the block-versus-nerve-check question is answered by analogy with the Association of Anaesthetists’ lower-leg compartment syndrome guideline and by the general data on nerve injury after blocks and on rebound pain, and the catheter advice is author’s judgement. The pain score is the Part B anchor for elbow fracture fixation.

    41 studies, 1,700 osteotomies: ulnar neuropathy 5.5% overall, 6.4% with tension band and 21% with screw fixation of the osteotomy; wound infection 4.2%; osteotomy non-union or delayed union 3.7%; hardware failure 1.1%; comparative studies show complications 46-55% with osteotomy versus 27-41% with the paratricipital approach
  3. Orthobullets evidence summary. Inclusion of olecranon osteotomy with the paratricipital approach for distal humerus fractures: ulnar neuropathy, non-union and infection. Retrospective cohort, level 1 trauma centre, 2007-2017
    134 distal humerus fixations, 64 with osteotomy and 70 without: ulnar neuropathy 26.8% versus 33.3%, not different; no difference in infection or non-union; more complex fractures got an osteotomy

    42 patients over 65: five of 21 allocated to fixation converted to arthroplasty on the table; operative time 140 min for fixation versus 108 for arthroplasty; function better after arthroplasty at six weeks and six months

Upper limb › Wrist and hand

15 Distal radius ORIF

Volar locking plate through the flexor carpi radialis approach; dorsal plating, fragment-specific fixation, K-wires and external fixation as the variants

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A fractured metaphysis reduced, held with a plate and drilled for locking screws, with periosteum lifted off the volar surface and pronator quadratus divided; the fracture itself is the pre-operative pain generator and fixation removes it. Short, bone-dominant, NSAID-responsive, and the rebound at the end of a dense block is the worst moment of the course

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Supraclavicular, infraclavicular or axillary brachial plexus block as the sole anaesthetic, with intravenous dexamethasone and light sedation, in the day-case patient; the same block under general anaesthesia where the patient or the surgeon prefers it
Catheter: rarely A single shot with dexamethasone and a written night plan is the defensible default; a continuous infraclavicular catheter did not reduce opioid consumption in the one randomised comparison and is reserved for the bilateral, revision or opioid-tolerant patient, or the one for whom rebound pain on a previous occasion was unmanageable
Alternatives: General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration and no block, which gives more pain at two hours and less at 12-24 h; Block plus general anaesthesia for the anxious patient or the long fragment-specific fixation; Haematoma block or Bier's block for closed reduction and K-wires, not for plating
Position
Supine with the arm on a radiolucent arm table, forearm supinated for the volar approach, the image intensifier at the end of the table; the shoulder abducted to 90 degrees and no further
Tourniquet
Yes. Routine; 45-90 min on the upper arm. A block that covers the wrist does not cover the tourniquet, so the sedation or the general anaesthetic has to
Cement
No
Blood loss
Under 100 mL
Duration
45-90 min for a volar plate; 90-150 min for fragment-specific, dorsal plus volar or an intra-articular reconstruction; 20-40 min for K-wires
Length of stay
Day case. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV at induction or before inflation (3 g over 120 kg); a plate is an implant
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
Mechanical only; negligible baseline risk in upper limb day surgery
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV with the block; ondansetron 4 mg IV if a general anaesthetic is given
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and useless for most of the day and into the night; when the feeling returns the wrist will hurt, worst on the first night and the first day, and the tablets started before the numbness wears off are what control it; after that it settles quickly.
The trap
The block wears off at 2 am and the patient who was comfortable at discharge is the one who telephones: rebound pain after a bone operation under a dense block is the rule, not the exception, and the oral analgesia has to be started in recovery and timed to the block, not to the first complaint

What the surgeon is doing and why

The distal radius is the commonest fracture an anaesthetist meets, and it comes in two patients: the older woman who falls on an outstretched hand onto osteoporotic metaphyseal bone and gets a dorsally angulated, impacted, extra-articular fracture, and the younger patient with a high-energy injury who gets an intra-articular fracture with a displaced lunate facet and a die-punch fragment. The bone is cancellous, it bleeds, and it crushes rather than snaps; the problem the surgeon is solving is that a radius that heals short and dorsally tilted shifts the load onto the ulna and the dorsal lip, and the wrist is weak and painful for life. The thresholds for operating are arguments about millimetres of shortening and degrees of tilt, and in the older patient the honest evidence is that the function at a year is about the same whether the fracture is plated or pinned (the DRAFFT trial, 461 patients, no difference in the patient-rated wrist score at 12 months, with K-wires cheaper) or, in the over-65s, whether it is operated on at all. Surgeons vary, and the volar locking plate is what most of them do.

The volar locking plate exists because the volar cortex is thick, flat and well covered by muscle, and because a plate with screws that lock into it at a fixed angle acts as a scaffold under the subchondral bone and holds a reduction in osteoporotic bone that a conventional screw would pull out of. The surgeon’s sequence is fixed:

  1. Get to the volar surface through the flexor carpi radialis sheath (the “FCR approach”), retracting the tendon and the radial artery laterally and the median nerve and the flexor tendons medially. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve runs along the ulnar side of the tendon and is the nerve that gets cut.
  2. Lift pronator quadratus off the radius from its radial edge to expose the fracture. This is the muscle mechanism, small but real, and some surgeons repair it at the end.
  3. Reduce the fracture: traction, volar pressure on the dorsal fragments, and often a lever (a periosteal elevator through the fracture) to tease the impacted dorsal cortex and the articular fragments back out to length. Intra-articular fragments are checked with the image intensifier or, in some hands, an arthroscope.
  4. Apply the plate proximal to the watershed line (the ridge where the volar cortex turns distally towards the joint), fix it to the shaft with a cortical screw, confirm the position on the image intensifier, then place the distal locking screws under the subchondral bone, with care that none of them protrudes through the dorsal cortex into the extensor tendons or into the joint.
  5. Check the screws on a tilted lateral view, close pronator quadratus if the surgeon does, close the skin, and put the wrist in a volar slab or a removable splint. Fingers move from the first day; the wrist moves at two weeks.

The complications that present to you are tendon ones: a plate that sits distal to the watershed, or a long screw through the dorsal cortex, irritates and then ruptures a tendon (flexor pollicis longus on the volar side, extensor pollicis longus dorsally) months later; a median nerve that is swollen in the carpal tunnel from the fracture haematoma presents as numbness the next morning and is the surgeon’s to decompress. Complex regional pain syndrome is the other late complication and the distal radius is its commonest cause.

The variants matter less to you than the volar plate. Dorsal plating is used for dorsal shear fractures and dorsal comminution that the volar plate cannot hold, through an incision between the extensor compartments, with more tendon irritation and a longer case. Fragment-specific fixation uses several small plates and pins for a shattered articular surface and takes twice as long. A dorsal and volar combination is the long, intra-articular reconstruction in a younger patient. K-wires are percutaneous, quick, and cheaper, with a cast afterwards. An external fixator spans the wrist for an open or grossly comminuted fracture and is the bridge to definitive surgery. None of them changes the block; the fragment-specific and combined cases change the tourniquet time and the duration of sedation.

The pain logic is bone, and this is the Part B anchor for a 2: a cancellous metaphysis reduced and drilled, a small muscle lifted and sometimes repaired, periosteum raised over a few centimetres, and nothing under tension afterwards. The fracture was the pre-operative pain generator and fixing it removes it, so by day 3 most patients are more comfortable than they were the day before surgery. The course is short and NSAID-responsive. What makes the card worth writing is the shape of the first 24 h under a block: a patient with a dense brachial plexus block has a pain score of 0 at discharge and the worst pain of the whole course at 2 am, and in the 972-patient ambulatory cohort half of block patients had exactly that pattern (a score of 3 or less rising to 7 or more within 24 h), with bone surgery (OR 1.82), younger age and female sex raising the odds and intravenous dexamethasone lowering them. The one randomised comparison of block against general anaesthesia for this operation showed the same thing from the other direction: the block group had less pain and used less opioid at two hours and went home sooner, the general anaesthesia group had lower pain at 12 and 24 h, and total analgesic use and satisfaction were the same. The block does not reduce the pain of a distal radius fixation; it moves it.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The patient, the fasting state and the block as the anaesthetic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Most distal radius fixations are semi-elective trauma on a day-surgery list within a week or two of injury; the surgeon wants a fixed wrist, a moving hand and a patient who goes home the same day.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block is the anaesthetic. A supraclavicular, infraclavicular or axillary block with 20-30 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% or an equivalent, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, light sedation, and no airway is the author’s default for the fasted day-case patient, and the operation is then 45-90 min of an awake patient listening to drilling, which some patients want and some do not. The axillary block needs a separate musculocutaneous injection for the lateral forearm and does not cover the tourniquet; the supraclavicular and infraclavicular blocks cover more of the arm and leave the intercostobrachial area to an intercostobrachial injection or the sedation. For the patient who refuses to be awake, the anxious patient, the fragment-specific case over two hours, or the surgeon who wants a still patient for an arthroscopically assisted reduction, the same block goes under a general anaesthetic with a supraglottic airway. The patient having general anaesthesia alone, with infiltration, will have more pain at two hours and less at 2 am, and that trade is worth explaining. Examine and document median, ulnar and radial function before the block; acute carpal tunnel symptoms from the fracture haematoma are common and the surgeon will want to know they predate the block.

  2. 2 Position, arm table and the image intensifier

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with the arm on a radiolucent table, abducted to 90 degrees and supinated, and the image intensifier either at the end of the table or over the arm; the surgeon sits on the axillary side of the arm and the assistant opposite. The tourniquet goes on the upper arm.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    In an awake patient, the position has to be tolerable for 90 min: the shoulder abducted to 90 and no more, the head on a pillow turned slightly away from the field, the drape held off the face on a screen, and the contralateral arm free for the pulse oximeter and the cannula. The image intensifier swings over the arm repeatedly; a sedated patient who turns towards the noise moves the arm. Lead for the patient’s trunk and for you. An awake patient feels the tourniquet from about 30-45 min as a deep ache that the block does not cover, and that is where the sedation is spent.

  3. 3 Tourniquet, antibiotic and the awake patient's first minutes

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The field is small and the surgeon wants it dry for the reduction and the plate position; the tourniquet is inflated after exsanguination and stays up for the fixation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV before inflation. Test the block before the tourniquet goes up, not after: pinprick over the volar wrist in the median and radial territories, and a check that the patient cannot flex the fingers against resistance. A block that is patchy at this point is supplemented now, with a distal median or radial nerve injection at the elbow or a surgeon’s infiltration, rather than discovered at the skin incision.

  4. 4 The FCR approach and pronator quadratus

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A 6-8 cm incision over flexor carpi radialis, the sheath opened, the tendon retracted radially with the radial artery, the floor of the sheath divided, and pronator quadratus elevated off the radius from its radial border to show the fracture. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve is on the ulnar side of the tendon and is the nerve that the retractor finds.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The dissection is not stimulating under a working block. In an awake patient the first sensation that breaks through is usually the retractor pulling on the proximal forearm, which is musculocutaneous territory in an axillary block without a supplement, or the tourniquet. The pronator quadratus elevation is the muscle mechanism; small, but it is why the forearm aches for a few days.

  5. 5 Reduction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Traction, direct pressure, and an elevator through the fracture to lever the dorsal and articular fragments back out to length and tilt, checked on the image intensifier in two planes. An impacted osteoporotic fracture that has been there for two weeks is harder to disimpact and may need the dorsal cortex broken through to get the length back.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Traction on the hand is traction on the shoulder in an awake patient; a sedated patient will tense the arm and the surgeon will say so, and the answer is a little more sedation and a hand on the elbow, not a deeper plane than the airway can tolerate. The reduction is the one moment at which a patchy block declares itself. This is also the step that lengthens the case: a fracture that will not come out to length is the one that becomes a fragment-specific or a combined dorsal-volar fixation.

  6. 6 Plate, shaft screw and the distal locking screws

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The plate is positioned proximal to the watershed line and fixed to the shaft through an oval hole so it can be slid before the first screw is tightened; then the image intensifier confirms the position, and the distal locking screws are placed under the subchondral bone in the row that supports the articular surface. Screw length is measured and checked on a tilted lateral view, because a screw that protrudes dorsally will rupture an extensor tendon in months, and a plate distal to the watershed will rupture flexor pollicis longus.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Drilling through the far cortex and the locking of screws is the bone mechanism of this operation and the reason the rebound odds are those of bone surgery. The awake patient hears and feels the drill as vibration and may find it the hardest part. Nothing to do except keep the arm still and the sedation steady; the image intensifier checks are the pauses.

  7. 7 Tourniquet release, closure and the splint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Pronator quadratus is repaired over the plate by surgeons who believe it protects the flexor tendons, the tourniquet is released, bleeding points are controlled, the skin is closed and a volar slab or removable splint is applied with the fingers free. Some surgeons infiltrate the wound.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reperfusion after a 60-90 min tourniquet is unremarkable in a fit patient. Ask the surgeon to infiltrate the wound even under a block, because it will outlast nothing but it costs nothing. The splint goes on before any sedation lightens; a patient with a flail arm will otherwise reach for it with the other hand.

  8. 8 Recovery, the rebound and the night plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the fingers moving from the first hour, the hand elevated, and the patient home with a plan for two weeks until the wrist starts to move.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This step decides the operation. The patient leaves recovery with a dense block and a pain score of 0, and the block recedes 12-24 h later, at night. The first dose of oral paracetamol and an NSAID goes in before discharge, not at the first tingle; the opioid is for the first two nights and is explained as the drug for when the hand comes back to life, with a written plan that says what to take at bedtime, what to take when the fingers tingle, and who to telephone. The one randomised trial that compared a single infraclavicular shot with a continuous infraclavicular catheter and with an opioid PCA found that the catheter cut the pain at 9 and 12 h (median 0 versus 2, and 0.5 versus 3) without reducing total opioid use; the single shot with a plan is what most units do and the catheter is for the exception. Intravenous dexamethasone lengthens the block and lowers the pain at 4 and 8 h in the randomised comparison, raises the glucose for a day, and its absence carried an OR of 1.78 for rebound pain in the ambulatory cohort; it is given. Discharge is the same day; a patient who had a general anaesthetic alone is the one who needs more opioid in recovery and less at 2 am.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone, short and NSAID-responsive, with a muscle lifted and nothing under tension; the whole problem is timing. The block is the best anaesthetic for the operation and the worst possible teacher of what the operation feels like, because the patient’s first experience of their wrist is at 2 am with no one to ask. The plan is built around that.

The defensible default is a supraclavicular, infraclavicular or axillary block with 20-30 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (or an equivalent long-acting agent), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started in recovery and continued for five to seven days, and an oral opioid for the first two nights, with a written night plan. The patient and the carer are told in plain words that the hand will come back to life between bedtime and the early morning, that the pain will rise over an hour or two to the worst of the week, that the tablets taken before bed are what blunt it, and that this is expected and not a complication. Sedation rather than general anaesthesia for the fasted day-case patient is the author’s practice; a general anaesthetic with the block for the patient who wants it or the long case.

The catheter question has a randomised answer for this operation, and it is nuanced: a continuous infraclavicular block abolished the rebound window at 9 and 12 h without reducing opioid consumption at all, and the single-shot group’s total opioid was modest (a median of 37.5 opioid-equivalent units against 30 with the catheter, not different). That is a catheter that does one thing well and nothing else, and for a day case it brings a flail arm for two days and a pump to manage at home. The author’s practice is a single shot for nearly all, and a catheter for the bilateral fracture, the revision or malunion osteotomy, the opioid-tolerant patient, and the one who has had an unmanageable rebound night before. The alternative that answers the same problem differently is general anaesthesia with infiltration and no block, which the randomised comparison found gave more pain at two hours and less at 12 and 24 h with the same satisfaction; for a patient who lives alone and will have no one to help at 2 am, that is a defensible choice and not a failure of regional anaesthesia.

Score calibration: this is a 2, the Part B anchor for distal radius ORIF, and the trajectory on the card (1 on the evening under the block, 4 on day 1 when it has gone, then 3, 2, 1) is the shape of a short bone operation with a dense block in front of it. The first-day figure is honest about the rebound; in a patient who had a general anaesthetic alone the evening figure is higher and the day 1 figure a little lower, and the curve meets by day 2. Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone with warm, moving fingers and a splint that is not tight is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the paracetamol and NSAID were actually taken; pain with numb fingers in the median distribution that was not there before the block is an acute carpal tunnel syndrome and is surgical; pain out of proportion at a week, with a swollen shiny hand and allodynia, is the start of complex regional pain syndrome and is referred, not reassured.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Volar plate versus K-wires versus nothing. The function at a year is similar for a dorsally displaced fracture in the DRAFFT trial; the K-wire patient has no incision, a cast, and the same block question; the older patient managed in plaster is not on your list.
  • Fragment-specific and combined dorsal-volar fixation. The intra-articular fracture in a younger patient; two hours, a tourniquet that may need a break, and a block under general anaesthesia rather than sedation.
  • Dorsal plating. A longer case through the extensor compartments, more tendon irritation, more swelling; the same block.
  • The axillary block’s gaps. The musculocutaneous nerve (lateral forearm, where the retractor sits) and the intercostobrachial territory under the tourniquet; both are supplemented or the patient is sedated through them.
  • Block for the awake patient. The patient who hears the drill; a headset, a screen and a steady level of sedation are the tools, and a patchy block is converted to a general anaesthetic before the incision, not after.
  • Acute carpal tunnel syndrome. Median numbness from the fracture haematoma, present before surgery in some and appearing the next morning in others; documented before the block, and decompressed by the surgeon if it is progressive.
  • Tendon rupture. Flexor pollicis longus months later from a plate distal to the watershed, extensor pollicis longus from a long dorsal screw; late, surgical, not yours.
  • Complex regional pain syndrome. The distal radius is its commonest precipitant; a swollen, shiny, allodynic hand at one to three weeks is referred early.
  • The older patient on anticoagulants. The commonest patient on the list; the block is a superficial one with a compressible site, and the usual rules apply.
  • The patient who lives alone. The rebound night is the argument for a general anaesthetic with infiltration, or for an overnight stay, not for a weaker block.
  • The unfasted patient on the trauma list. An isolated distal radius fracture in an unfasted patient can wait for fasting or have the block as the sole anaesthetic with no sedation; the urgent unfasted hand is on the hand trauma card.

Key sources

This is the best-evidenced operation in the wrist and hand section for the anaesthetic question, and the evidence is specific: a randomised comparison of brachial plexus block against general anaesthesia for distal radius fixation showing the block moves the pain from two hours to 12-24 h without changing total analgesic use or satisfaction; a three-arm randomised trial showing a continuous infraclavicular catheter removes the rebound window at 9-12 h without reducing opioid consumption; a randomised trial of dexamethasone with the block showing a longer block and lower early pain; and the 972-patient ambulatory cohort that defines rebound pain and its risk factors, of which this operation has most. The surgical evidence (DRAFFT, the complication review) is cited for the variants and the complications, not for pain. There is no PROSPECT guideline for distal radius fracture, and the day-case advice and the catheter exceptions are author’s judgement.

  1. Galos DK, Taormina DP, Crespo A, et al. Does brachial plexus blockade result in improved pain scores after distal radius fracture fixation? A randomized trial. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2016;474:1247-1254
    36 patients randomised to general anaesthesia or brachial plexus block for distal radius fixation: block gave less pain and less opioid at two hours and a shorter recovery stay; general anaesthesia gave lower pain at 12 and 24 h; total analgesic use, satisfaction and function at six and 12 weeks the same
  2. Lee JH, Kim HJ, Kim JK, Cheon S, Shin YH. Does intravenous patient-controlled analgesia or continuous block prevent rebound pain following infraclavicular brachial plexus block after distal radius fracture fixation? A prospective randomized controlled trial. Korean J Anesthesiol 2023;76:559-566
    66 volar plate patients in three arms of 22: single infraclavicular block, block plus opioid PCA, or continuous infraclavicular block; median pain at 9 h 2 with the single shot versus 0 with the catheter, at 12 h 3 versus 0.5; total opioid equivalents 37.5 single shot versus 30 catheter, not different; the catheter controlled the rebound window without reducing opioid use
  3. Kim MK, Park YH, Lee JS, Jung HS. Addition of dexamethasone to brachial plexus block after distal radius fracture surgery. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2023;481:1966-1974
    69 unstable distal radius fractures randomised to block with or without dexamethasone: longer block and lower pain at 4 and 8 h with dexamethasone, higher post-operative glucose, and no difference the authors judged clinically important thereafter
  4. Kasper AA, Plusch K, Voskerijian A, et al. Efficacy of direct versus peripheral adjuvant dexamethasone on duration and rebound pain in regional anesthesia for outpatient distal radius fracture fixation: a prospective randomized controlled blinded study. Hand (N Y) 2025;20:1132-1137
    50 volar plate patients with supraclavicular ropivacaine blocks, dexamethasone 4 mg perineural (27) or intravenous (23): the perineural route gave a shorter block in this trial, with no demonstrated difference in pain scores or opioid consumption at 24 h
  5. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871

    461 adults with dorsally displaced fractures: no clinical difference in the patient-rated wrist evaluation at 12 months between K-wires and a volar plate; K-wires cheaper

  8. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
