    439 adults with waist fractures displaced 2 mm or less: no difference in patient-rated wrist evaluation at 52 weeks between early fixation and cast with fixation of confirmed non-unions; potentially serious surgical complications in 14% of the surgery group versus 1%, cast complications in 18% of the cast group; the trial behind the current preference for casting undisplaced waist fractures
  2. Duncumb JW, Robinson PG, Williamson TR, et al. Bone grafting for scaphoid nonunion surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Bone Joint J 2022;104-B:549-558
    78 studies, 7,671 patients, mean age 28, 88% male: union 88.7% with non-vascularised and 87.5% with vascularised grafts, no difference; distal radius and iliac crest graft sources united equally (86.9% versus 87.6%); studies excluding proximal pole fractures and avascular necrosis reported 96.5% union against 86.8% in the rest
  3. Zhang H, Gu J, Liu H, Yuan C. Pedicled vascularized versus non-vascularized bone grafts in the treatment of scaphoid non-union: a meta-analysis of comparative studies. ANZ J Surg 2021;91:E682-E689
    Seven comparative studies, 413 patients: pedicled vascularised grafts united 1.13 times as often and 1.7 weeks earlier, with no difference in range of motion, grip, Mayo wrist score or re-operation; the authors note the greater technical difficulty and counsel caution
  4. Pulos N, Kollitz KM, Bishop AT, Shin AY. Free vascularized medial femoral condyle bone graft after failed scaphoid nonunion surgery. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2018;100:1379-1386
    49 patients with proximal pole osteonecrosis after failed non-union surgery: 41 (84%) united at a mean of 16 weeks after a free medial femoral condyle graft; 29 had further procedures, most of them planned wire removal
  5. Dimitriou R, Mataliotakis GI, Angoules AG, Kanakaris NK, Giannoudis PV. Complications following autologous bone graft harvesting from the iliac crest and using the RIA: a systematic review. Injury 2011;42 Suppl 2:S3-S15
    92 studies, 6,449 iliac crest harvests: overall complication rate 19.4%; the anterior crest carried more infection, haematoma, fracture and hypertrophic scar than the posterior crest and less chronic donor-site pain and sensory disturbance
  6. van de Wall BJM, Beeres FJP, Rompen IF, et al. RIA versus iliac crest bone graft harvesting: a meta-analysis and systematic review. Injury 2022;53:286-293
    Five comparative studies: chronic donor-site pain after iliac crest harvest 14.2% versus 0% with reamer-irrigator-aspirator harvest (OR 0.08), with lateral femoral cutaneous neuropraxia and scar numbness specific to the crest
  7. Boehm KS, Al-Taha M, Morzycki A, Samargandi OA, Al-Youha S, LeBlanc MR. Donor site morbidities of iliac crest bone graft in craniofacial surgery: a systematic review. Ann Plast Surg 2019;83:352-358
    44 studies, 2,801 craniofacial patients: mean donor-site pain 6.3 out of 10 on day 1 and 1.3 at day 14; acute gait disturbance 45.7%, chronic pain 3.1%, chronic nerve change 1.4%, crest fracture 1.2%
  8. Liu EH, Suen K, Tham SK, Ek ET. Surgical repair of triangular fibrocartilage complex tears: a systematic review. J Wrist Surg 2021;10:70-83
    27 studies of Palmer 1B peripheral and foveal repairs: residual pain scores 2.1 and 1.7 out of 10, DASH about 16, grip 80-93% of the other hand; transosseous sutures slightly better than capsular sutures or anchors; arthroscopic repair better than open; low complication rates
  9. Ma HH, Wang JP, Yang CY. Effectiveness of suture anchor and transosseous suture technique in arthroscopic foveal repair of the triangular fibrocartilage complex: a systematic review. J Orthop Surg Res 2024;19:72
    26 studies, 904 patients aged 21-41: both techniques gave clinically meaningful improvement in function, pain and grip; most complications self-limiting; re-operation 0-20% with anchors and 0-27% with transosseous sutures
  10. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain (NRS 3 or less rising to 7 or more within 24 h) in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of intravenous dexamethasone OR 1.78
  11. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: 22 of the 40 most painful procedures were orthopaedic or trauma operations on the extremities, and many minor procedures produced unexpectedly high first-day pain because little analgesia was prescribed for them

Upper limb › Wrist and hand

19 Trapeziectomy and CMC arthroplasty; wrist fusion and arthroplasty

Simple trapeziectomy, ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition, suture-button suspension and implant arthroplasty of the thumb base; total wrist arthrodesis and total wrist arthroplasty

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A whole carpal bone removed, leaving bleeding cancellous surfaces on the scaphoid, trapezoid and metacarpal base, a drilled metacarpal tunnel and a harvested forearm tendon (trapeziectomy); or three or four carpal joints decorticated, packed with graft and clamped under a dorsal plate from radius to metacarpal (wrist fusion). Small, richly innervated bone in a cast: a high day 1 peak that falls fast because nothing is loaded through it

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Supraclavicular, infraclavicular or axillary brachial plexus block with intravenous dexamethasone, as the sole anaesthetic with sedation or under general anaesthesia; WALANT for trapeziectomy in units that run it
Catheter: rarely A single shot with dexamethasone, the oral regimen started in recovery and a written night plan is the defensible default; a continuous infraclavicular catheter is for the revision or bilateral case, the opioid-tolerant patient and the one whose last block ended in an unmanageable night
Alternatives: Short-acting axillary block for the operation plus low-concentration distal radial and median nerve blocks at the elbow for the night, which cut moderate-to-severe day 1 pain from 92% to 33% in the one randomised trial; WALANT: tumescent lidocaine with adrenaline 25-30 min before incision, no tourniquet, no sedation, patient preference high in the series that asked; General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration alone, which trades a comfortable recovery room for a sorer first six hours and no rebound; Forearm tourniquet with a distal block for a short trapeziectomy in surgeons who use one
Position
Supine with the arm on a radiolucent arm table, shoulder abducted no further than 90 degrees, tourniquet on the upper arm; the thumb base is approached with the forearm in mid-pronation and the wrist fusion with it fully pronated, and the image intensifier comes in for the plate
Tourniquet
Yes. Upper arm, 45-90 min for the thumb and 90-150 min for a wrist fusion; a block that anaesthetises the hand does not anaesthetise the cuff, so sedation or the general anaesthetic carries the tourniquet. WALANT uses none
Cement
Sometimes. None for trapeziectomy, suture-button suspension, CMC implants or wrist fusion; a total wrist arthroplasty is press-fit in most current designs and cemented in some, a few millilitres with no cement implantation syndrome significance
Blood loss
Under 100 mL for the thumb; 100-250 mL for a wrist fusion with a local bone graft, more if iliac crest is harvested
Duration
Simple trapeziectomy 45-60 min; with ligament reconstruction, suture-button or an implant 60-90 min; total wrist arthrodesis 90-150 min; total wrist arthroplasty 120-180 min
Length of stay
Day case for the thumb; day case or one night for wrist fusion and arthroplasty, decided by the patient's home and the other hand rather than by the operation. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV before the cuff goes up (3 g over 120 kg) for anything that leaves an implant: suture button, K-wire, plate or prosthesis; many surgeons give it for a simple trapeziectomy as well
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
Mechanical only; upper limb day surgery carries negligible baseline risk, and the rheumatoid patient's risk is the disease's, not the operation's
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV with the block, for its duration as much as for nausea; ondansetron 4 mg IV when a general anaesthetic is given
Tell the patient
Your hand will be numb and useless for most of the day and into the night; when the feeling comes back the thumb will be sore for two or three days, worst on the first night, and the tablets started before the numbness wears off are what control it, then it settles while the cast does the work.
The trap
The block that made a small operation painless wears off at 2 am in a woman in her seventies who is alone at home with a cast on her dominant hand: hand resection arthroplasty sits in the top dozen of 179 procedures for day 1 pain, so the dexamethasone, the first oral doses in recovery and the written night plan are not optional extras

What the surgeon is doing and why

The trapeziometacarpal joint is a saddle with almost no bony constraint. Its stability is ligamentous, mainly the anterior oblique (beak) ligament and the dorsoradial ligament, and the loads across it are large: a pinch at the fingertip is multiplied many times by the time it reaches the thumb base. When the ligaments stretch the metacarpal base subluxes dorsally and radially, the volar cartilage wears, the joint grinds, the metacarpal drifts into adduction so the first web closes, and the metacarpophalangeal joint hyperextends to make up the lost span (the Z-thumb). The patient is usually a woman in her sixties or seventies, often with the same disease in the other hand, and she presents with pain at the base of the thumb on pinch, a positive grind test and a hand that drops cups. The surgical options share a single idea: take the joint out.

Trapeziectomy removes the trapezium, whole or in pieces, through a dorsal or a volar incision over the thumb base. That leaves a gap the height of the bone between the scaphoid and the metacarpal base, and the metacarpal would settle into it and impinge on the scaphoid, so the second half of the operation is about holding the metacarpal up. The variants differ only in how:

  1. Simple trapeziectomy holds it with nothing but the haematoma that fills the space and fibroses, a K-wire across the gap in some hands, and a thumb spica cast.
  2. Ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition (LRTI) harvests half of flexor carpi radialis (or a slip of abductor pollicis longus) through forearm incisions, passes it through a drill hole in the metacarpal base to suspend the metacarpal, and rolls the remainder into the space as a spacer.
  3. Suture-button suspensionplasty drills across the bases of the first and second metacarpals and tensions a suture between two buttons so the thumb metacarpal hangs from the index; no tendon is harvested.
  4. Implant arthroplasty keeps the trapezium, reams it for a cup, broaches the metacarpal for a stem and fits a ball-and-socket joint; motion and pinch return faster, at the price of a revision rate trapeziectomy does not have.
  5. Arthrodesis, for the young manual worker who needs pinch more than motion, cuts both surfaces and plates them.

The meta-analysis of seven randomised trials and one controlled trial (656 thumbs) found that adding ligament reconstruction to trapeziectomy improved grip and tip pinch at a year, changed neither pain nor the DASH score, and doubled the complications at three months; the authors recommend the simple operation unless strength is specifically needed. Surgeons vary, and all five variants are in routine use. If the metacarpophalangeal joint hyperextends beyond about 30 degrees the surgeon adds a capsulodesis or a fusion of that joint, a second bone operation inside the first.

The wrist operations on this card are the end of a different road: a scapholunate or scaphoid non-union collapse (SLAC or SNAC) that has worn through the radiocarpal and midcarpal joints, a rheumatoid wrist that has subluxed and destroyed itself, Kienböck’s disease, or a failed partial fusion. Total wrist arthrodesis takes the pain away by removing every moving joint between the radius and the third metacarpal: a dorsal approach, decortication of the radiocarpal and midcarpal surfaces, bone graft packed into every gap, and a precontoured plate from the distal radius over the capitate to the third metacarpal in about 10-15 degrees of extension. The result is a strong, painless wrist that does not move. Total wrist arthroplasty resurfaces the same joints with a radial component on a stem and a carpal component screwed into a fused distal carpal row, for the low-demand (usually rheumatoid) patient who wants to keep some motion; the carpal component loosens over years. In the systematic review of rheumatoid wrists, 343 arthrodeses and 618 arthroplasties had complication rates of 17% and 19%, both relieved pain, and the long-term survival data for the arthroplasty are still missing. The partial fusions (four-corner fusion, proximal row carpectomy) are the midcarpal alternatives for an earlier stage of collapse and share the anaesthetic of the total fusion.

The pain logic is bone in a small, richly innervated hand that is then immobilised. The trapeziectomy leaves bleeding cancellous surfaces on three bones, a drilled tunnel, a harvested tendon with its forearm incisions, and an incised capsule under lifted thenar muscle; the wrist fusion decorticates three or four joints, strips dorsal periosteum under a plate, and takes graft from the distal radius or the excised carpal bones. None of it is loaded afterwards, because the cast does the loading, so the pain peaks on day 1-2 and falls fast. The size of the incision misleads. In the 179-procedure cohort hand resection arthroplasty ranked 11th and metacarpophalangeal arthrodesis 8th for day 1 pain, above most major operations, and in the one randomised trial that measured it, 92% of trapeziectomy patients given a short-acting block and systemic analgesia alone reported moderate-to-severe maximum pain on day 1 and 81% on day 2. With a long-acting block, dexamethasone and an oral regimen that starts before the block recedes, it is a 3: an expected block, opioid for two or three nights, and a fast fall. Wrist fusion sits at the upper end of the same band, with a day 1 peak that can reach 6; a distal radius plate sits a band below, because there a fracture that hurt before surgery is fixed rather than a joint newly cut out.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The patient, the anaesthetic choice and the day-case decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a still hand, a dry field under a tourniquet for 45-150 minutes, and a patient who can go home the same day with a cast on; for a wrist fusion they also want fluoroscopy and sometimes a bone graft from a second site.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The patient decides the anaesthetic more than the operation does. She is in her seventies, often on an anticoagulant, sometimes diabetic, sometimes rheumatoid with the airway and cervical spine that implies, and the other hand is arthritic too. A brachial plexus block with sedation avoids the general anaesthetic, covers the operation and the first evening, and is the author’s default. A supraclavicular or infraclavicular block covers the whole hand and the radial forearm in one injection; an axillary block does the same only if the musculocutaneous nerve is included, because the thumb base incision and the forearm incisions for the tendon harvest sit in the lateral antebrachial cutaneous and superficial radial territories as well as the median one. In the anticoagulated patient the axillary approach has the compressible vessels. Dexamethasone 8 mg IV goes in with the block. The day-case decision rests on who is at home and whether the patient can manage a cast on her dominant hand, a block that has not yet worn off and tablets on a timetable; nearly 40% of the WALANT trapeziectomy cohort said afterwards that they had not understood their post-operative medication, which is the gap to close now.

  2. 2 Arm table, tourniquet and antibiotic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The arm is laid out on a radiolucent table with the shoulder abducted no more than 90 degrees and the tourniquet high on the arm; the thumb base is approached in mid-pronation with the hand on its ulnar border, and the wrist fusion in full pronation. The surgeon wants the cuff up before the skin incision and down before the dressing goes on so that the bed can be checked for bleeding.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV must be in before the cuff inflates, because nothing given afterwards reaches the hand; suture buttons, K-wires, plates and prostheses are implants. The cuff is the one thing the block does not cover. At 45-60 minutes of upper-arm tourniquet a sedated patient becomes restless with a dull ache under the cuff and the blood pressure drifts up; the treatment is more sedation and a word about time, not more local anaesthetic in the arm. Under a general anaesthetic the same rise reads as light anaesthesia. Some surgeons use a forearm cuff for a trapeziectomy, which is better tolerated and sits within a distal block’s territory; a wrist fusion needs the upper arm. Pad the ulnar nerve of the other arm and watch for an assistant leaning on the arm table and levering the shoulder into abduction.

  3. 3 Approach to the thumb base: radial artery and superficial radial nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A dorsal incision over the first metacarpal base passes between the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus tendons on one side and extensor pollicis longus on the other; a volar (Wagner) incision follows the glabrous border and lifts the thenar muscles off the trapezium. Branches of the superficial radial nerve cross the dorsal incision, and the radial artery runs across the floor of the snuffbox directly over the scaphotrapezial joint, the deep margin of the dissection.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing here needs your hand, but two things need your attention later. A superficial radial nerve branch cut or caught in scar produces a neuroma or dysaesthesia over the dorsum of the thumb, which presents as pain that outlasts the trajectory on this card and is not treated with more opioid. The radial artery, if nicked, bleeds only when the cuff comes down, and the surgeon will want the cuff deflated before closure to see it.

  4. 4 Capsulotomy and trapeziectomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The capsule is opened longitudinally and the trapezium freed from the metacarpal, the trapezoid and the scaphoid, and from the flexor carpi radialis tendon that runs in a groove on its volar surface. It comes out whole with a towel clip or in pieces with an osteotome and rongeur; the surgeon checks that no fragment is left against the tendon and that the scaphotrapezial surface is clean.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the bone step and the mechanism of the card: three raw cancellous surfaces in a space that will fill with haematoma. Under a block it is silent; under a general anaesthetic without a block the heart rate climbs here and again at the drill hole. Osteotome work against a held hand transmits through the arm table, and a sedated patient notices the hammering through the ears more than the hand. The trapeziectomy for an implant arthroplasty is instead a reaming of the trapezium for a cup and a broaching of the metacarpal canal for a stem, the same mechanism on a smaller scale with a press-fit at the end.

  5. 5 Suspension: tendon harvest and bone tunnel, suture button, or implant

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For LRTI, half of flexor carpi radialis is harvested through one or two transverse forearm incisions and delivered into the wound, a drill hole is made through the base of the first metacarpal, the tendon is passed through it and sutured to itself under enough tension to hold the metacarpal level with the index, and the rest is rolled and parked in the space. The suture-button technique drills obliquely across both metacarpal bases and tensions a suture between buttons until the thumb metacarpal sits level with the index without pinching the two together. The implant is impacted and the joint reduced and tested through its range.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The tendon harvest adds the second site of pain, in the forearm: a muscle that has lost half its tendon aches for a week in a way the patient attributes to the cast, and the forearm incisions are the ones an axillary block without the musculocutaneous component leaves uncovered. The drill hole through the metacarpal base is the second bone injury. The suspension is the one point where the thumb is held under tension and the surgeon wants the hand absolutely still for the tying; under a block that is automatic, and under a general anaesthetic a request for relaxation here is a request for depth, not for a neuromuscular blocker. An over-tightened suture-button pulls the metacarpals together and impinges, and the surgeon checks for it now by moving the thumb through opposition.

  6. 6 The metacarpophalangeal joint and the K-wire

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A hyperextended metacarpophalangeal joint will collapse the reconstruction, so a joint that hyperextends past about 30 degrees gets a volar capsulodesis, an extensor pollicis brevis transfer, or a fusion with a plate or compression screw. Some surgeons drive a K-wire across the trapezial space or into the second metacarpal to hold the thumb distracted for four to six weeks; others rely on the suspension and a cast.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A metacarpophalangeal fusion turns a 3 into the operation the 179-procedure cohort ranked eighth of all procedures for day 1 pain, because it adds a second set of cut cancellous surfaces compressed under a plate; the trajectory on this card then peaks a point higher and the night plan matters more. The K-wire adds a pin tract that aches at its skin exit and a second visit for removal under local anaesthetic in clinic. Neither changes the block.

  7. 7 Closure, tourniquet release, splint and the night plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The capsule is repaired over the space, the thenar muscles laid back, the skin closed, and the thumb put into a bulky dressing and a spica splint or cast with the thumb abducted and the interphalangeal joint free. The surgeon wants the cuff down before the dressing so that the bed and the radial artery can be inspected.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cuff deflation after 60-90 minutes produces the usual brief fall in pressure and the flush of the arm; a small patient under sedation notices the tingling, the warmth and the reperfusion ache for a few minutes. The splint goes on before the patient is awake enough to move the hand, and the arm is slung before transfer, because a patient with a dense block will let the hand hang or lie on it. The first paracetamol and NSAID dose is timed from here, and the night plan is written in words the patient can read with one hand: the block lasts 12-20 hours with dexamethasone, the tablets start before the numbness wears off, the opioid is for the first two nights, and the hand is kept above the heart.

  8. 8 Wrist fusion: dorsal approach, neurectomy, decortication and graft

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A straight dorsal incision over the third metacarpal and the distal radius, the extensor retinaculum opened over the third compartment with extensor pollicis longus transposed out of the way, a posterior interosseous neurectomy on the floor of the fourth compartment to denervate the dorsal capsule, and a dorsal capsulotomy. The radiocarpal and midcarpal surfaces (radius, lunate, capitate, and the capitate to third metacarpal joint) are decorticated with a burr or rongeur to bleeding bone and the gaps packed with cancellous graft taken from the distal radius through the same wound, from the excised bones, or from the iliac crest when the defect is large or the bone rheumatoid.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is a 90-150 minute tourniquet case with the bone mechanism multiplied across three or four joints and a strip of stripped dorsal periosteum, which is why the wrist fusion runs at the top of the card’s band. The iliac crest, if used, is the second operative site and the one no upper-limb block reaches: it needs the surgeon’s infiltration and is the harvest that keeps patients in overnight with a sore hip rather than a sore wrist. The neurectomy is deliberate denervation of the dorsal capsule and does not change the block. Tourniquet time is the thing to watch and announce at 90 minutes, because the surgeon still has a plate to fit.

  9. 9 Wrist fusion plate and cast; the total wrist arthroplasty variant

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A precontoured dorsal fusion plate is laid from the distal radius across the carpus to the third metacarpal shaft, the wrist held in 10-15 degrees of extension and slight ulnar deviation, and fixed with locking screws at both ends and a compression screw across the capitate; fluoroscopy checks the position before the retinaculum is closed over the plate and the wrist is casted for six weeks. For an arthroplasty the distal radius is cut and broached for a stem, the proximal carpal row is partly resected, the distal row is fused around a carpal plate with screws into the capitate, hamate and metacarpals, and the components are seated press-fit or cemented according to the design.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The plate lies along bone whose periosteum has been stripped the length of the wound: the periosteal mechanism, raw and incisional, on top of the bone. The fusion is rigid from the moment the screws are locked, so nothing moves afterwards and the pain falls after day 2. The arthroplasty’s cement, where it is used, is a few millilitres in a distal radius with no canal pressure behind it and carries no cement implantation syndrome risk worth a precaution; its broaching and impaction are the bone work. The rheumatoid patient having either operation has thin skin that tears under tape, a wrist that bleeds more than the operation suggests, and a contralateral hand that cannot take over, which is the real reason for the overnight stay.

  10. 10 Recovery, discharge and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The thumb reconstruction is protected by the cast for four to six weeks and then mobilised; the surgeon wants the fingers moving from day one, the hand elevated, and the patient back for a wound check and K-wire removal. The wrist fusion is in a cast for six weeks with the fingers free.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block recedes at home, overnight, and the pain that follows is the whole problem of this operation. In the ambulatory cohort rebound pain occurred in half of all block patients, more often after bone surgery, in women, and when intravenous dexamethasone had been omitted. In the observational comparison of axillary block against general anaesthesia for hand surgery, pain scores with the block rose to meet the general anaesthesia group at about three hours on the ward and never overshot it: the block defers pain rather than creating it, and a regimen started before it recedes meets the pain at the level a general anaesthetic patient would have had all along. Discharge needs a sling, a demonstrated ability to take the tablets, written instructions and a telephone number; a dense block is not a reason to keep the patient, and a cast with fingers that cannot be moved for pain is a reason to call the surgeon.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone, small and well innervated, in a cast: a high early peak that falls by day 3 and needs no cover beyond that. No PROSPECT guideline exists for hand surgery, so the plan is built from the mechanism, the day-case rebound literature and one procedure-specific trial. The defensible default is a brachial plexus block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (supraclavicular or infraclavicular for complete cover of the radial forearm and thumb base; axillary with a deliberate musculocutaneous component in the anticoagulated patient) placed before the tourniquet, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, sedation for the cuff, regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started in recovery rather than at the first complaint, and an oral opioid for the first two nights. The block lasts 12-20 hours with dexamethasone; the patient is told it will wear off at night and what to do when the fingers start to tingle.

The alternative with the strongest trial behind it is the Barcelona design: a short-acting block for the operation and levobupivacaine 0.125% on the radial and median nerves at the elbow for about ten hours of analgesia without motor block, which cut moderate-to-severe day 1 pain from 92% to 33% and day 2 pain from 81% to 21%, with less rescue analgesia and less nausea. It gives the patient a hand she can use that evening, which matters when the other hand is arthritic, and the author’s reading is that it is the better plan for the patient who has had a bad night after a dense block before.

WALANT is a third plan rather than a compromise. Tumescent lidocaine 1% with adrenaline 1:100,000, buffered, infiltrated at the thumb base and along the tendon harvest 25-30 minutes before incision, no tourniquet, no sedation and no fasting in an established unit; in the two series on this card the patients were satisfied, all those followed to two years would choose it again, complex thumb reconstructions ran around 73 minutes, and one patient in 16 was converted for anxiety. The authors of the second series advise an anaesthetist present and a fasted patient for a unit’s first cases. The night plan under WALANT is the same as after a block; the local anaesthetic lasts hours, not a day.

A catheter is rarely right. The pain falls by day 3, a cast covers most of the territory, and an infraclavicular catheter at home in a woman in her seventies is a management problem of its own; it earns its place for the bilateral or revision case, the opioid-tolerant patient and the one whose last block ended in an unmanageable night. Escalation triggers: pain above 7 after the block has receded, with warm pink fingers that move, is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were taken; pain out of proportion inside a cast with tight swollen fingers is a cast problem and the cast is split; burning pain with colour change and hypersensitivity in the second or third week is complex regional pain syndrome, which the wrist and hand produce more often than any other region, and it needs the surgeon and the pain service early rather than a larger opioid dose.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Simple trapeziectomy versus reconstruction. The randomised evidence favours the simple operation on pain and function at a year, with fewer early complications; the tendon harvest adds a forearm site and a block that must cover it. Ask which the surgeon is doing before the block is chosen.
  • Suture-button suspension. No tendon harvest, a second metacarpal drilled, and a fracture of the index metacarpal base as the characteristic complication; the K-wire is usually omitted.
  • Implant arthroplasty. Reaming and broaching rather than excision, a faster return of pinch, and a revision population a decade on who come back for a trapeziectomy with a loose cup in a sclerotic bed: a longer, bloodier case.
  • The Z-thumb. A metacarpophalangeal fusion or capsulodesis added to the trapeziectomy moves the day 1 peak up a point and is the item the 179-procedure cohort ranked eighth of all operations.
  • Bilateral disease. One hand at a time; the second operation is scheduled when the first can hold a cup. A patient who turns up for the second side with a vivid memory of the first night is the one for whom the distal-block or catheter plan is chosen.
  • The anticoagulated patient. The axillary approach is compressible; the supraclavicular is not. Neither operation bleeds enough to need the anticoagulant stopped for the surgery itself, which makes the block choice the only decision.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis. Cervical spine instability and a difficult airway argue for the block; steroid cover; thin skin; anaemia; biologics held by the surgeon’s timetable; and a contralateral hand that cannot take over, which is the overnight stay.
  • Diabetes. Dexamethasone 8 mg raises glucose for a day and is still worth giving; the ward or the patient needs to know.
  • Iliac crest graft. A second site that no upper-limb block reaches, with its own week of pain, a lateral femoral cutaneous nerve at risk and a haematoma; infiltrate it, and expect it to be the complaint on day 1.
  • Total wrist arthroplasty. The carpal component loosens over years; the revision is a fusion with a large defect and an iliac crest graft, and belongs on this card at its longest and bloodiest.

Key sources

One randomised trial measured day 1 and day 2 pain after trapeziectomy directly and showed what a long-acting distal block does to it, and the 179-procedure cohort ranks hand resection arthroplasty and metacarpophalangeal arthrodesis in its top dozen. The surgical variant evidence is a meta-analysis of randomised trials that favours the simple operation. The WALANT series are small and uncontrolled and are cited for feasibility and patient preference, not for pain. The wrist evidence is a systematic review of rheumatoid cohorts with complication rates and no pain trajectory, so the wrist half of the trajectory is the author’s extrapolation from the mechanism, and the block, catheter and night-plan advice is author’s judgement built on the ambulatory rebound cohort and the observational comparison of axillary block with general anaesthesia.

  1. Liu Q, Xu B, Lyu H, Lee JH. Differences between simple trapeziectomy and trapeziectomy with ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition for the treatment of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2022;142:987-996
    Seven randomised trials and one controlled trial, 656 thumbs: ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition gave better grip and tip pinch at a year, the same pain, DASH and key pinch, and twice the complications at three months; the authors recommend simple trapeziectomy unless strength is specifically needed
  2. Rodríguez Prieto M, González FJ, Sabaté S, et al. Low-concentration distal nerve blocks with 0.125% levobupivacaine versus systemic analgesia for ambulatory trapeziectomy performed under axillary block: a randomized controlled trial. Minerva Anestesiol 2018;84:1261-1269
    50 day-case trapeziectomies under a mepivacaine axillary block, randomised to radial and median nerve blocks at the elbow with 5 mL levobupivacaine 0.125% each or to systemic analgesia alone: moderate-to-severe maximum pain in 33% versus 92% on day 1 and 21% versus 81% on day 2; the distal blocks lasted about 10 h with no motor block and reduced rescue analgesia and nausea. The authors describe trapeziectomy as one of the most painful procedures in ambulatory surgery
  3. Schubert AK, Wiesmann T, Volberg C, et al. Rebound pain and postoperative pain profile following brachial plexus block compared to general anaesthesia: an observational study. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2023;67:1414-1422
    132 elective hand and forearm operations, 66 under an axillary block (prilocaine 1% 30 mL plus ropivacaine 0.2% 10 mL) and 66 under general anaesthesia: pain scores lower with the block until about 3 h on the ward, then equal; no overshoot above the general anaesthesia group at any point and no excess opioid, although the usual definitions of rebound pain were met as the block faded
  4. Reiser D, Brandt V, Sagerfors M. Patient experience of trapeziectomy for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis in wide-awake local anaesthesia no tourniquet, 2-year follow-up. Acta Chir Orthop Traumatol Cech 2024;91:175-181
    23 patients, mean age 64, trapeziectomy under WALANT: all 21 followed to two years would choose the same anaesthetic again, pain and function improved as after trapeziectomy under general anaesthesia, and nearly 40% said they had been given inadequate information about their post-operative medication
  5. Castelo F, Santos C, Costa B, et al. Wide-awake local anesthesia no tourniquet for rhizarthrosis surgery: technique and experience for 16 consecutive cases. Cureus 2023;15:e45705
    16 thumb base operations under WALANT including six prosthetic replacements and two revisions: tumescent anaesthesia 20-25 min before surgery, mean operating time 73 min, one conversion for anxiety, satisfaction 9 out of 10; the authors advise an anaesthetist present and a fasted patient for a unit's first cases
  6. Zhu XM, Perera E, Gohal C, Dennis B, Khan M, Alolabi B. A systematic review of outcomes of wrist arthrodesis and wrist arthroplasty in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. J Hand Surg Eur Vol 2021;46:297-303
    23 studies, 343 arthrodeses and 618 arthroplasties in rheumatoid wrists: complication rates 17% and 19%, both relieve pain and improve grip, arthroplasty improves DASH and PRWE by clinically meaningful margins, and long-term arthroplasty survival data are still missing
  7. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain (NRS 3 or less rising to 7 or more within 24 h) in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of intravenous dexamethasone OR 1.78
  8. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: small hand and foot operations rank among the most painful on day 1, with arthrodesis of the metacarpophalangeal joints at rank 8 and hand resection arthroplasty at rank 11, and patients after minor surgery received little opioid and reported high scores

Upper limb › Wrist and hand

20 Hand trauma: metacarpal and phalangeal fixation, tendon and nerve repair

K-wires, screws and plates; flexor and extensor tendon repair; digital nerve repair; replantation and revascularisation principles

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Small bones drilled, wired or plated through a thin soft tissue envelope, with periosteum stripped for a plate; a repaired tendon that is small, splinted and deliberately unloaded; a throbbing, dependent, swollen hand as the secondary driver. Replantation is a different problem: the pain is modest, and the block is there for vasodilatation rather than analgesia

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Axillary, infraclavicular or supraclavicular brachial plexus block as the sole anaesthetic, with intravenous dexamethasone; a continuous infraclavicular or axillary catheter for replantation and revascularisation
Catheter: selective No catheter for fixation, tendon or nerve repair: a single shot with dexamethasone and a written night plan is the defensible default. A catheter for replantation and revascularisation, where its job is a sustained sympathetic block and a pain-free patient for the days in which the anastomosis is at risk; the randomised evidence shows better perfusion and less vascular insufficiency, not better survival
Alternatives: WALANT (lidocaine 1% with adrenaline 1:100,000, no tourniquet, no sedation), which lets the surgeon test a tendon repair under active movement; Digital or wrist block for a single-digit procedure distal to the palm; General anaesthesia with a block or surgeon infiltration for the long case, the child, or the patient who cannot lie still; Intravenous regional anaesthesia for a short closed procedure, which leaves no analgesia afterwards
Position
Supine with the arm abducted on a hand table, surgeon and assistant seated either side, image intensifier coming in from the end of the table; the operating microscope replaces it for nerve and vessel work
Tourniquet
Yes. Upper arm tourniquet at 250 mmHg for most cases, forearm tourniquet in some hands, none under WALANT; in replantation it is used for dissection and released before the anastomosis
Cement
No
Blood loss
Negligible under tourniquet; a replant or a mangled hand oozes for hours once the cuff is down, and a replanted digit treated with leeches or deliberate bleeding can drop the haemoglobin over days
Duration
20-40 min for closed reduction and K-wires; 45-90 min for a plate or screws; 45-120 min for a flexor tendon repair, longer with a digital nerve or several digits; 4-12 h for replantation, by the number of digits
Length of stay
Day case for almost everything; 5-7 nights of warm-room monitoring after replantation or revascularisation. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV before tourniquet inflation for implants and open injuries; bites and heavily contaminated wounds get the unit's broader regimen, and closed K-wiring is covered by a single dose or none by surgeon preference
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
None for day-case hand surgery; chemoprophylaxis for the replant patient on bed rest, alongside whatever antithrombotic the surgeon runs for the anastomosis (aspirin, heparin or dextran, and surgeons vary)
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV, which also prolongs the block; ondansetron 4 mg IV if a general anaesthetic or opioid is used
Tell the patient
Your arm will be numb and heavy for most of the day; the hand throbs when the feeling comes back, usually in the evening or overnight, so keep it raised above your heart and take the tablets before bed rather than waiting for the pain.
The trap
The emergency hand list is a day of small operations in young patients who have been starved since midnight and sent home with a dense block: the fasting, the dead arm in a sling and the 2 am rebound are where the harm is, not the anaesthetic

What the surgeon is doing and why

The hand is a set of small bones moved by long tendons that glide through tight tunnels, fed by two arteries per digit and supplied by nerves a millimetre or two across. Every structure sits within a few millimetres of every other, so an injury rarely damages one thing and a repair of one thing scars to its neighbours. That is the surgical problem in one sentence: the hand tolerates fracture and laceration well and tolerates stiffness badly. Everything the hand surgeon does is aimed at fixation or repair strong enough to let the fingers move within days, because a finger that is held still for four weeks heals solidly and never bends again.

Four operations make up the emergency hand list, and they are often combined in one patient.

  1. Fixation of metacarpals and phalanges. Most hand fractures are treated in a splint. The ones that come to theatre are rotated (the finger crosses its neighbour when the patient makes a fist), shortened, intra-articular, open or multiple. The options run from closed reduction and percutaneous K-wires (quick, no dissection, wires out at four weeks, joints stiff in the meantime) through lag screws to a plate, which gives the stability for immediate movement at the price of stripping periosteum and putting metal under the extensor tendon.
  2. Flexor tendon repair. A divided flexor retracts into the palm and will not heal unless its ends are brought together inside the fibrous sheath. The surgeon retrieves the proximal end, passes it under the pulleys and joins the ends with a multi-strand core suture and a running epitendinous stitch. The repair has to be strong enough for early active movement and slim enough to glide under the pulleys; too bulky and it triggers or sticks, too weak and it ruptures in the second week. Zone 2, between the distal palmar crease and the middle of the middle phalanx where two tendons share one sheath, is the unforgiving one.
  3. Extensor tendon repair. Extensors are flat, superficial and easy to reach, so the repair is technically simpler; the difficulty is that they are thin, hold a suture poorly, and stick to the bone and skin on either side.
  4. Nerve and vessel repair. A digital nerve is repaired under the microscope with 9-0 or 10-0 sutures and no tension; the patient gets protective sensation back over months. A digital artery is repaired the same way when the finger is pale or when both arteries are cut.

Replantation and revascularisation sit at the far end of the same spectrum. A replant is every one of the above in a fixed order: the bone is shortened and fixed so that everything else can be repaired without tension, then extensor, flexor, arteries, nerves and veins, with at least two veins for each artery where they can be found. Revascularisation is the same operation in a digit that is still attached by something. Survival depends on warm ischaemia time, the mechanism (a clean cut does well, a crush or avulsion does not) and the patency of anastomoses less than a millimetre across in the days afterwards. In one series of 157 digits, ischaemia time and length of surgery were the significant predictors.

The pain logic splits in two. For fixation, the mechanism is bone and periosteum in a hand with almost no soft tissue cover, plus the swelling of a dependent limb, and the 179-procedure cohort is a warning against dismissing it: small bony hand operations, with metacarpophalangeal arthrodesis among the worst of all, scored far higher on day 1 than their size suggested, largely because nobody planned for them. With a block and a regimen that is actually taken, a plated metacarpal behaves like a distal radius fixation: a 2, with a sharp first night. A tendon repair is a tendon under tension only in name; the tendon is small, the splint holds it slack, and the pain is the incision and the swelling. Replantation hurts less than its length suggests, because the replanted part is denervated. There the block is doing a different job, described in step 9.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The emergency list: fasting, urgency and the choice of technique

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Most hand trauma is urgent rather than emergent. A closed fracture can wait a week, a tendon or nerve several days, and a clean open injury is washed out and closed in the emergency department on the day and repaired on a planned list. The true emergencies are the devascularised digit, the replant, the high-pressure injection injury and the infected flexor sheath or bite. The surgeon wants the short cases done in the day and the list is ordered by theatre availability, not by the clock on anyone’s stomach.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Two fasting problems arrive on the same list and they are opposites. The first is the replant or the devascularised finger that came in an hour after lunch: a block as the sole anaesthetic, with no sedation, is the technique that makes the stomach nearly irrelevant, and it is the author’s default; if a general anaesthetic is needed (a child, an eight-hour case, a patient who cannot lie still), it is a rapid sequence induction with a tube, not a wait of six hours while the ischaemia clock runs. A block does not abolish the fasting question, because a failed or outlasted block converts to general anaesthesia mid-case, and deep sedation on top of a full stomach is the worst of both options. The second problem is far more common: the fit 25-year-old with a metacarpal fracture who was told nil by mouth from midnight and reaches theatre at 5 pm, dehydrated, hypoglycaemic and angry. Clear fluids until called for is the fix, and it is an anaesthetic instruction, not a ward one. In a randomised comparison of a short-acting infraclavicular block against general anaesthesia for day-case hand and wrist surgery, 79% of the block patients bypassed the recovery unit against 25%, with less pain on arrival: on a list of eight short cases that difference is the list finishing.

  2. 2 Examination, documentation and the block

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has documented which tendons work and which digital nerves feel before any local anaesthetic went in, because after the block nobody can tell. For a tendon repair some surgeons want the patient awake and able to move the finger on request.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Confirm that the nerve examination is written down before you place the block, and that nobody infiltrated a digit in the emergency department without recording sensation first. Choose the block by where the tourniquet goes and how long the case is. An axillary or infraclavicular block covers the hand and forearm reliably; the upper arm tourniquet pain that appears at 45-60 min is ischaemic and only partly a matter of the intercostobrachial nerve, so plan sedation or a forearm cuff for a long awake case. For a single digit distal to the palm a wrist or digital block is enough and leaves a working arm. If the surgeon wants active movement to test a repair, that is a WALANT case or a distal block with a forearm tourniquet deflated for the test, not a plexus block, which paralyses the muscles that move the tendon. Dexamethasone 8 mg IV goes in now.

  3. 3 Tourniquet, washout and exploration

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Hand surgery needs a bloodless field because the structures are small and blood stains everything the same colour. Open wounds are extended in zigzag (Bruner) incisions so that scars do not cross flexion creases and contract; contaminated wounds, bites and injection injuries are debrided widely first, and the definitive repair may be deferred.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Antibiotic in before the cuff goes up. Note the inflation time and say it aloud at 60 and 90 min. A fight bite over a metacarpophalangeal joint is a septic arthritis until washed out, and the patient may be febrile, intoxicated or both. High-pressure injection injuries look trivial at the fingertip and need a long decompression up the forearm: the booking understates the case. Under WALANT there is no tourniquet; the adrenaline needs about 25 min to give its best field, so the infiltration is done before the patient reaches theatre, and the ceiling is lidocaine 7 mg/kg with adrenaline.

  4. 4 Skeletal fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Bone first, because every soft tissue repair is set to length against a stable skeleton. Closed reduction and K-wires for the fracture that reduces and holds; lag screws for a long spiral; a dorsal or lateral plate for a transverse or comminuted shaft, which means incising periosteum and placing metal under the extensor mechanism; shortening of the bone by several millimetres in a replant so that vessels and nerves meet without tension.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    K-wiring is fast and repeatedly image-guided: lead on, hands out of the beam, and expect the case to finish before the block has fully set if you placed it late. Plating adds 30-45 min and is the bony, periosteal step that drives the first night’s pain; this is the patient who needs the night plan most. Rotation is checked by flexing the fingers passively into the palm, which under a general anaesthetic needs a relaxed forearm, and under a block already has one.

  5. 5 Flexor tendon repair

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The proximal stump is retrieved from the palm, threaded beneath the pulleys and held with a needle while a four- or six-strand core suture and an epitendinous stitch are placed. The A2 and A4 pulleys are preserved or vented just enough to let the repair glide. The surgeon then pulls on the tendon or asks for active flexion to see that the repair passes the pulleys without gapping or catching.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A still hand for 45-90 min of fine work under loupes: a twitch as the block recedes or a cough under a light general anaesthetic matters here more than anywhere else on the list. If the case is under WALANT, the patient flexes and extends the finger on request and the surgeon revises the repair on the spot; the pooled comparative studies (five studies, 624 fingers) show no difference in rupture, tenolysis or reoperation against conventional anaesthesia and a modest advantage in range of motion, on weak data. The argument for it is the test, not the outcome figures. For the anaesthetist a WALANT flexor repair means no sedation at all, since a drowsy patient cannot cooperate, and a long time lying still on a narrow table.

  6. 6 Extensor tendon repair

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The flat extensor is repaired with mattress or running sutures, the joint may be pinned in extension for a mallet or central slip injury, and the wound is closed over it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Short, superficial and well suited to a distal block or WALANT. The only trap is the dorsal laceration over a knuckle that turns out to be a tooth wound into the joint, which converts a 20-minute repair into a washout and an admission for intravenous antibiotics.

  7. 7 Digital nerve and artery repair

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The microscope comes in. Nerve ends are trimmed back to healthy fascicles and coapted without tension; a gap is bridged with a conduit or a graft. An artery is repaired if the digit is poorly perfused. The tourniquet is released to confirm flow.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The microscope shows the surgeon every movement magnified 10 to 20 times, including the patient’s breathing transmitted down the arm and the table being bumped. Tell the room before you adjust anything. From the moment an artery is repaired the anaesthetic changes aim from analgesia to perfusion: warm patient, full circulation, no pain, no shivering, and blood pressure at the patient’s normal.

  8. 8 Replantation: two teams, a long case and the set-up

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    One team prepares the amputated part on a side table (tagging arteries, veins and nerves, debriding, shortening bone) while the other prepares the stump. The order of repair is fixed and each digit takes hours. The surgeon’s priorities are the thumb, multiple digits, any level in a child, and a clean mechanism; a single crushed finger in a heavy smoker is usually not replanted.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Plan for 4-12 h from the start: a block with a catheter placed before the first incision, a general anaesthetic with a tube for most adults once the case is expected to exceed what anyone can lie still for, a urinary catheter, forced-air warming and warmed fluids from induction, a second cannula in a foot or the other arm, and pressure areas padded as for any all-day case. The theatre is warmed. The author’s practice is an infraclavicular catheter, because it stays in place under a bulky dressing and an elevated arm better than an axillary one. The tourniquet is used for the dissection and comes down before the anastomosis; from then on blood loss is a slow, continuous ooze that is easy to underestimate over eight hours.

  9. 9 Microvascular anastomosis and reperfusion

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Arteries are sutured with eight or so stitches of 10-0 or 11-0 nylon, with a reversed vein graft if there is a gap; the clamps come off, the digit pinks up, and then two veins are repaired for each artery if they exist. Spasm is treated with warm saline, topical papaverine or lidocaine, and patience.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The folklore is that vasopressors kill replants. The evidence is thinner than the rule. No trial has tested vasopressors in digital replantation; in head and neck free flaps the pooled studies show no increase in flap failure with perioperative vasopressors. A digital artery is a smaller, spasm-prone vessel in a cold extremity, so the extrapolation is uncertain in both directions. The defensible position is to make the question rare rather than to answer it: keep the patient warm and full, run the block so that the limb is vasodilated and the anaesthetic can be light, treat hypotension first with volume and by lightening the anaesthetic, and when a vasopressor is still needed give the smallest effective dose by infusion and tell the surgeon. Hypotension is no kinder to a 1 mm anastomosis than phenylephrine. The surgeon may ask for heparin (commonly 2,500-5,000 units IV) before the clamps come off. The block is the one intervention with trial data: in a randomised trial of 71 replanted digits, a continuous ropivacaine 0.2% infusion at 5 mL/h gave warmer digits and higher arterial flow at every time point to 48 h, lower pain scores (0.5 against 1.9) and less vascular insufficiency at 48 h (8.3% against 29%) than systemic analgesia. Seven-day survival was 97% against 91%, which was not different, and an older retrospective series of 146 patients found no survival effect either. The catheter improves the conditions for survival; nobody has shown that it improves survival.

  10. 10 Closure, dressing and splint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Skin is closed loosely, or left partly open or grafted over a replant because a tight closure strangles the veins. A bulky, non-constricting dressing and a splint hold the wrist and fingers in the position that protects the repair: flexed for a flexor tendon, extended for an extensor, with the fingertips visible.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The splint goes on before the patient is moving. For a replant, emergence is part of the operation: no coughing against the tube, no shivering, no pain and no retching, each of which is a sympathetic surge delivered straight to the anastomosis. Extubate deep or on a remifentanil tail if the airway allows, treat nausea in advance, and have the catheter bolused and running before the volatile is off.

  11. 11 Recovery, the first night and replant monitoring

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Day-case patients go home in a high arm sling with the hand above the heart. Tendon patients see the hand therapist within days for a thermoplastic splint and an early active movement protocol. A replant goes to a warm room for five to seven days of hourly colour, capillary refill, turgor and temperature checks; a pale digit is arterial and goes back to theatre; a blue, congested one is venous and gets leeches or goes back to theatre.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For the day-case patient the risks are the insensate arm and the night. The hand goes home in a sling the patient cannot take off in their sleep, with a warning about hot drinks, heaters and car doors. First doses of paracetamol and an NSAID are given before discharge and the written plan says to take the next ones at bedtime whether or not the hand is still numb. Half of ambulatory block patients describe rebound pain, with bone surgery, younger age and female sex raising the odds and intravenous dexamethasone lowering them; the young patient with a plated metacarpal has most of the risk factors. For the replant, the catheter runs for the monitoring period, the room stays warm, and the surgeon’s bans on nicotine and caffeine are theirs to enforce. A catheter that is giving good analgesia also masks nothing important here, since the monitoring is by colour and temperature and not by pain.

Pain plan

The mechanism for fixation is bone and periosteum under thin cover, short-lived and NSAID-responsive, with a rebound first night; for tendon and nerve repair it is the incision and the swelling. The plan is therefore a single-shot plexus block that doubles as the anaesthetic, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID started before the block recedes and taken regularly for three to five days, strict elevation, and a small supply of oral opioid for the first two nights after a plate or a multi-digit injury. Closed K-wiring and soft tissue repairs often need no opioid at all. An NSAID is not withheld on bone-healing grounds for a course this short; where a surgeon objects, the objection is usually about a replant and bleeding rather than union.

Choice of local anaesthetic is a real decision on this list. A long-acting agent (ropivacaine 0.5%) with dexamethasone gives 12 to 18 hours and carries the patient through the evening, at the cost of a flail, insensate arm at home and a rebound in the small hours. A short-acting agent (lidocaine or mepivacaine with adrenaline) gives a working hand by the time the patient is home and puts the onset of pain in daylight, where the oral regimen can meet it, and it is what made the randomised day-case comparison work. The author’s practice is short-acting for K-wires and soft tissue, long-acting with dexamethasone for plates and multiple digits, and to say which was used on the discharge sheet.

No catheter for any of the day-case operations: the pain does not last long enough to justify it, and this is author’s judgement extrapolated from the distal radius evidence rather than a hand-specific trial. The catheter belongs to replantation and revascularisation, where the indication is perfusion. Ropivacaine 0.2% at 5 mL/h for the monitoring period is the regimen with trial support. Systemic opioid for a replant is kept low to avoid nausea and retching.

Escalation: pain that rises steadily in a splinted hand, with tight swollen fingers, is the dressing until proven otherwise, and splitting it to skin is the first treatment. Severe pain on passive extension of the fingers after a crush, an injection injury or a revascularisation is compartment syndrome of the hand or forearm; a dense block delays the complaint, which is one more reason to use short-acting agents after crush injuries and to say so to the surgeon. Throbbing pain with fever at day 2 to 4 after a bite or a contaminated wound is infection.

Pitfalls and variants

  • WALANT. Surgeon-delivered, no tourniquet, no sedation, and often no anaesthetist. When you are asked to stand by, the job is monitoring and reassurance, and the lidocaine dose is the surgeon’s infiltration plus anything you add. Adrenaline in the finger is safe in the doses used; phentolamine is the reversal agent if a digit stays white.
  • The intoxicated or uncooperative patient. Hand trauma keeps company with alcohol, fights and self-harm. A block as the sole technique needs a patient who will lie still for an hour; if that is in doubt, the case waits for sobriety when it can and gets a general anaesthetic when it cannot.
  • Tourniquet time in the multi-structure case. Bone, two tendons and a nerve in one finger runs past two hours. Agree a release at 120 min in advance (see the tourniquet).
  • Crush, injection and compartment risk. Short-acting block or general anaesthesia with infiltration, and a surgeon who knows what was used.
  • Replant failure modes. Arterial spasm in the first hours (cold, pain, hypovolaemia, hypotension), venous congestion in the first days. The return to theatre is an emergency with the catheter already in place: bolus it and the patient may not need a general anaesthetic.
  • Anticoagulation after replantation. Aspirin, heparin, dextran and leeches are all used and surgeons vary. A patient on heparin with an indwelling catheter needs the catheter removal timed against the dose.
  • Infection cases. A flexor sheath infection or a septic joint is a washout under tourniquet in a patient who may be bacteraemic; block or general anaesthesia both work, and an infected axilla or cellulitis tracking up the arm moves the block proximal or off the menu.

Key sources

The hand trauma literature is surgical; the anaesthetic evidence is borrowed. The day-case case for a block rests on one small randomised trial from 2004 and two decades of practice. WALANT for flexor tendons has a meta-analysis of five mostly non-randomised studies. The replantation catheter has one recent randomised trial showing better perfusion and less vascular insufficiency without a survival difference, and an older retrospective series showing no survival effect. The vasopressor rule has no direct evidence in digits at all; the head and neck free flap data are cited to show how weak the dogma’s foundations are, not to licence phenylephrine in a replant. The catheter and local anaesthetic choices for the day-case operations are the author’s judgement.
