    126 patients: no difference in Oxford or Harris hip score at 12 months; thromboembolic events more frequent after resurfacing (p=0.049), wound complications more frequent after total hip
  5. Vendittoli PA, Riviere C, Roy AG, Barry J, Lusignan D, Lavigne M. Metal-on-metal hip resurfacing compared with 28-mm diameter metal-on-metal total hip replacement: a randomised study with six to nine years follow-up. Bone Joint J 2013;95-B:1464-1473
    192 patients: revision 6% after resurfacing (five femoral head collapses) against 4% after total hip, not different; higher UCLA activity after resurfacing; groin pain needing investigation in six resurfacings and no total hips; osteolysis 37% after total hip and 2.4% after resurfacing
  6. Goulding K, Beaulé PE, Kim PR, Fazekas A. Incidence of lateral femoral cutaneous nerve neuropraxia after anterior approach hip arthroplasty. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2010;468:2397-2404
    Through an anterior approach, lateral femoral cutaneous nerve neuropraxia in 91% of resurfacings against 67% of total hips, reflecting the larger exposure
  7. Regulatory Affairs Professionals Society. MHRA updates alert on metal-on-metal hip implants, 29 June 2017 (summarising MHRA MDA/2017/018)
    Annual blood metal ion and imaging surveillance recommended for all women with a resurfacing, men with a femoral component of 48 mm or less, and all large-head stemmed metal-on-metal hips
  8. Carella M, Bugada D, Van de Velde M, et al. PROSPECT guideline for total hip arthroplasty: updated systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Anaesthesia 2026 (online ahead of print)
    The nearest procedure-specific analgesic guidance; paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor and single-dose IV dexamethasone for all, single-shot supra-inguinal fascia iliaca or PENG block recommended, local infiltration where a block is not feasible

Hip and knee › Hip

24 Revision total hip arthroplasty

Aseptic loosening, instability, periprosthetic fracture and the reimplantation stage of infection: extended trochanteric osteotomy, cement removal, acetabular reconstruction with augments and cages, long stems

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Periosteum. A long femoral osteotomy (or a canal reamed and stripped to its full length for a long stem) and a pelvis cut, grafted and screwed into: periosteal and endosteal stripping along the length of the femur is the dominant driver, with bone from the acetabular and femoral preparation, muscle from a re-opened and extended exposure, and a trochanter that is cabled and loaded by every abductor contraction

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Spinal with an epidural catheter (combined spinal-epidural), or a general anaesthetic with a lumbar plexus or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca catheter; infiltration is a supplement, not the plan
Catheter: routine This is the hip operation where a continuous technique has its strongest claim: the osteotomy and the stripped femur hurt for days, the patient is often frail and opioid-intolerant, and movement-evoked pain limits the physiotherapy that the surgeon needs; the choice between epidural and perineural catheter is the unit's, and the author's default is a low-dose epidural for the cup-and-stem revision and a perineural catheter where anticoagulation or the fracture pathway forbids one
Alternatives: Continuous supra-inguinal fascia iliaca catheter (author's judgement; the catheter trial in hip arthroplasty compared femoral with lumbar plexus); Continuous posterior lumbar plexus catheter; Single-shot PENG or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block with a written rescue plan for the liner-only revision; Intrathecal morphine up to 0.1 mg with the spinal where no catheter is placed
Position
Lateral decubitus with pelvic clamps for the posterior approach, for 2-5 hours; the leg is draped free and brought through large arcs with a loosened pelvis, and the dependent side is at risk for the whole of that time
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Sometimes. Most modern femoral revisions are uncemented modular tapered stems into a long canal; cement is used in cement-in-cement revision, impaction grafting with a cemented stem, and in the very old or irradiated femur. A long cemented stem in a long, freshly reamed canal is the highest-risk BCIS step in elective orthopaedics
Blood loss
800-2,000 mL and beyond; in a six-centre prospective cohort on tranexamic acid, one in six revisions was transfused, with each 1 g/dL of lower pre-operative haemoglobin raising the odds by 79% and each extra hour of surgery by 74%
Duration
2-5 h skin to skin; a liner exchange at the short end, a both-component revision with osteotomy and acetabular reconstruction at the long end, and the pre-operative plan is the only reliable predictor
Length of stay
4-10 nights; longer for the frail, the infected and the fractured. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), re-dosed at 4 h and after each 1.5 L of blood loss; given before incision when the organism is already known and never held in a septic patient; held until deep samples are taken only when infection is suspected and the aspirate was negative or not done, by agreement with the surgeon, and then given
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision with a second dose at 3 h or by infusion; in the revision meta-analysis TXA cut transfusion odds to about a quarter and the haemoglobin fall by more than 1 g/dL with no excess thromboembolism
VTE
Chemoprophylaxis by unit protocol, started once the epidural catheter timing allows; the risk is high (long operation, frail patient, immobility) and the bleeding risk is also high, which is the one argument for mechanical prophylaxis first and the drug the next morning
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (omitted or discussed in a reimplantation for infection by some surgeons) and ondansetron 4 mg IV
Tell the patient
This is a much bigger operation than your first hip: expect to be in hospital most of a week, to need a blood transfusion possibly, to have a pain catheter for a few days, and to be on crutches with restricted weight bearing for six weeks or more while the bone heals around the new implant.
The trap
The long cemented stem in a long reamed canal of a frail patient: the canal has been stripped of marrow by reamers for its full length, the cement column is longer and the pressurisation greater than in any primary, the patient has already lost a litre of blood, and the grade 2 and 3 cement events that are rare in primaries happen here; an arterial line, a vasopressor infusion already running and the surgeon's warning before the gun is loaded are the minimum

What the surgeon is doing and why

A primary hip replacement fails in one of five ways and the way it failed is the operation. A loose cup or stem (aseptic loosening, the commonest) has to be dug out of bone eaten away by wear debris and replaced by something that will hold in what is left. An unstable hip has a malpositioned component, a worn liner, a weak abductor mechanism or all three, and the surgeon changes the orientation, the head size, the liner constraint or the whole construct. A periprosthetic fracture around a loose stem needs the stem out and a long stem past the fracture, which is this card with a trauma pathway attached (see periprosthetic fracture). An infected hip has its own card (periprosthetic joint infection), but the second-stage reimplantation of a two-stage exchange is a revision in every physical sense and belongs here. And a metal-on-metal bearing with a pseudotumour needs a soft-tissue debridement and a bearing exchange, with the abductors sometimes destroyed by the reaction.

The common problem is that the surgeon is working in scar, through an old approach, against implants that are either loose in bone that has gone or fixed in bone that must be cut to release them, with less bone to build on than the primary surgeon had. The sequence:

  1. In through the old scar by the posterior approach, the most extensile; scar dissected off the trochanter, the sciatic nerve (now in scar and possibly displaced) and the thickened capsule; dislocate and assess what is loose and what is fixed.
  2. Remove the femoral component. A loose stem comes out with a tap. A fixed uncemented stem or a long cement mantle does not, and the surgeon makes an extended trochanteric osteotomy, a 12-20 cm longitudinal cut hinging a third of the femoral circumference open on its vastus lateralis attachment, so the stem and the cement can be removed under vision; it unites in 98% once cabled back.
  3. Remove the acetabular component, classify what is left (Paprosky: contained defects with an intact rim at one end, pelvic discontinuity at the other) and rebuild it with a larger cup and screws, porous metal augments, a cup-cage or antiprotrusio cage, impaction grafting with mesh, or a custom triflange. Each option up that list adds an hour, several hundred millilitres, and screws placed blind into a pelvis with the external iliac and obturator vessels on the far side.
  4. Ream the femur for its length to bleeding bone and fix a new stem in the diaphysis below the damage: a modular tapered uncemented stem, a long cemented stem, or impaction grafting with a cemented stem.
  5. Trial, reduce, test stability (a constrained liner or a dual-mobility bearing if the abductors are gone), cable the osteotomy, repair what soft tissue there is, close over drains.

The anaesthetic reading: everything the primary card says about reaming, cement and the pelvic clamps is still true, and three things are new. The dissection is long, bloody and unpredictable: 800 mL is a quiet revision and 2 L is not unusual, and in a six-centre cohort on tranexamic acid one revision in six was transfused, predicted by pre-operative haemoglobin, INR and operative hours rather than by the type of revision. The patient is older and frailer than the primary patient was, and may be anaemic, anticoagulated and opioid-tolerant before you meet them. And a long cemented stem in a canal just reamed to bleeding bone for its full length is the highest-risk bone cement implantation syndrome step in elective orthopaedics: hypotension in 38% and desaturation in 25% of one long-stem series, against 2% and 17% in elective primaries.

The pain logic is different in kind. The dominant mechanism is periosteum: a long femoral osteotomy or a stripped canal, cabled back and loaded by every contraction of the abductors hanging off the trochanteric fragment, and a pelvis cut and screwed into. Beneath it are bone (two reamed surfaces), muscle (a re-opened and extended dissection) and, where the abductors have been detached, a repair under tension. The operation has created a fracture-like injury along the femur that the patient feels for a week and that is re-provoked by the partial weight bearing the surgeon prescribes. A 4 on the Part B scale, the only hip arthroplasty card to earn one, and the only one where a catheter is routine rather than selective.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The plan: what is coming out, what is going in, how long, and which anaesthetic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has planned this from radiographs, a CT and the old operation notes, and knows whether the stem needs an osteotomy, whether the cup needs augments or a cage, whether cement is going in, and roughly how long it will take. None of that is on the theatre list, and the surgeon needs 2-5 hours of a still, relaxed patient on their side and a patient who will tolerate partial weight bearing on a cabled osteotomy from day 1.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Ask, and plan from the answer. A liner exchange is 90 minutes and 300 mL; a both-component revision with an osteotomy and a cup-cage is four hours and two litres. The pre-operative haemoglobin is the strongest predictor of transfusion and the one thing correctable in advance, the INR the second; a crossmatch of two to four units, cell salvage from the start, a large-bore cannula and an arterial line are the author’s defaults for anything beyond a liner exchange. The neuraxial-versus-general evidence for primary hips is extrapolated here, reasonably, because these patients are older and sicker than the primary cohort, but a single-shot spinal does not cover a four-hour revision. The options are a combined spinal-epidural with the epidural run during the case and for two or three days after, or a general anaesthetic with a tracheal tube and a perineural catheter (lumbar plexus or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca) placed before induction. The author’s default is the combined spinal-epidural for a planned cup-and-stem revision where anticoagulation and platelets allow, with the arterial line placed awake, and the general anaesthetic with a catheter where an epidural is impossible or the case is on the fracture pathway. Under general anaesthesia the end-tidal carbon dioxide is the right heart monitor for the cement step, an argument for the tube in the frail patient having a long cemented stem.

  2. 2 Lateral decubitus for a long case

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The posterior approach is the most extensile and the one that can be carried down the femur for an osteotomy; a few surgeons use a direct lateral or anterolateral approach for a cup-only revision.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Everything on the posterior primary card, multiplied by the duration. The dependent arm, axilla, ear, eye and peroneal nerve are at risk for four hours rather than one; the clamps compress the abdomen and the dependent lung for the same period, so the ventilated patient needs a ventilator set for lower compliance and the sedated spinal patient needs their saturation watched. Pressure areas on the dependent hip, knee, ankle and breast need padding that would be excessive in a primary. Warming is a problem from the first hour: a long wound, cell salvage, a cold theatre and litres of irrigation during cement removal all cool the patient, and the forced-air blanket goes on from the start. The pelvis shifts in the clamps as the patient relaxes and the surgeon levers; the surgeon notices it on the cup orientation, you notice it on the airway and the arm.

  3. 3 Antibiotic, tranexamic acid, cell salvage and the baseline

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A re-operated joint, a long operation and large implants: infection is the complication that converts a revision into a two-stage exchange. In a suspected infection, deep tissue samples are the diagnosis and the antibiotic must not reach them first.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g over 120 kg) before the knife in an aseptic revision, re-dosed at 4 hours and after each 1.5 L of blood loss; when infection is suspected and no organism has been identified the antibiotic is held until the surgeon has taken samples; with a known organism, a septic patient or a second-stage reimplantation it is given before incision, by explicit agreement, and then given. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision with a second dose at 3 hours or an infusion: in the revision meta-analysis it cut the transfusion odds to about a quarter and the haemoglobin fall by more than 1 g/dL with no excess thromboembolism, and the one in six transfused in the prospective cohort were all on it. Cell salvage runs skin to skin in anything beyond a liner exchange; in a suspected infection the salvaged blood is not returned. Record the pre-induction pressure for the cement target later.

  4. 4 Exposure through scar, the sciatic nerve and dislocation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The old scar is extended, gluteus maximus split again through adhesions, and scar dissected off the posterior trochanter and whatever remains of the rotators to reach the capsule. The sciatic nerve is tethered in scar and may be closer to the field than it was; many surgeons find and protect it first. The hip is then dislocated, which in a stiff revision may need the head taken off the trunnion or the neck of a loose stem cut, and the surgeon assesses which components are loose, which are fixed, and whether the plan survives contact with the hip.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Dissection through scar bleeds continuously and diffusely in a way a primary approach does not: a few hundred millilitres before the joint is open. The sciatic nerve is at risk from retraction now and from lengthening later, and a pre-operative examination of foot dorsiflexion and sensation, written down, is the only way to separate a new injury from an old one; under a combined spinal-epidural it is done before the block. Forcible dislocation of a scarred hip in an osteoporotic patient is where the intra-operative periprosthetic fracture happens, converting a cup revision into a both-component revision with an osteotomy; the surgeon’s language changes and so does your estimate of the next three hours. The femoral vein is kinked from here until reduction, which may be hours away.

  5. 5 Femoral component removal: the extended trochanteric osteotomy and cement removal

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A loose stem comes out easily. A well-fixed uncemented stem (removed for infection, instability or a damaged trunnion) or a long cement mantle does not, and attempts to remove it from above perforate the femur. The extended trochanteric osteotomy cuts the lateral femur longitudinally for 12-20 cm and hinges the lateral third of the shaft open on its vastus lateralis attachment, exposing the whole stem and the cement for removal under vision with osteotomes, burrs and ultrasonic tools. The osteotomy’s length is set by the implant and the cement to be removed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The step that gives the operation its pain score and most of its blood loss. The femur is opened along a third or more of its length, and periosteal and endosteal bleeding from the osteotomy, the cancellous bed the cement is chipped from and the perforations cement removal produces runs continuously inside the canal where it cannot be seen. Cell salvage earns its place here. Ultrasonic cement removal heats the bone and the irrigation that goes with it cools the patient. The fragment can fracture (the commonest complication, with the trochanter fracturing in about 9%), which adds cables and time. Nothing pharmacological changes except the vigilance: a haemoglobin on a gas every hour, the pressure supported, and a second unit checked before the cup is started.

  6. 6 Acetabular component removal and reconstruction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A loose cup is levered out; a fixed cup is cut out with curved osteotomes around its rim to preserve bone. What is left is classified and rebuilt: a larger hemispherical cup with screws for a contained defect, porous metal augments for a missing rim, a cup-cage or antiprotrusio cage for a discontinuity, impaction grafting with mesh and a cemented cup, or a custom triflange. Each is more surgery than the last, and all put screws into the ilium and ischium with the external iliac vessels, the obturator vessels and the sciatic nerve on the far side.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming a damaged acetabulum to bleeding bone and placing screws blind into a pelvis is the second bleeding focus and the one with catastrophic potential: a screw or reamer through the medial wall into the external iliac vein presents as a pressure that falls and keeps falling with nothing to see in the wound, and the response is to say so, to have blood in the room, and to expect a vascular surgeon rather than more vasopressor. A cage or a triflange adds an hour, and antibiotic re-dosing falls due about now. The pelvis’s contribution to the pain is bone and periosteum where the ilium has been stripped for a cage, which is why the revision patient hurts in the buttock as well as the thigh.

  7. 7 Femoral reconstruction: the long stem and the cement decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The new stem has to bypass the damaged proximal femur and the osteotomy and fix in the diaphysis below. Most surgeons use a modular tapered uncemented stem reamed to a tight fit in the isthmus; some use a long cemented stem, cement-in-cement revision into a sound existing mantle, or impaction grafting (morselised allograft hammered into the canal) with a cemented polished stem. The canal is reamed for its full length to bleeding bone before any of these.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming a long canal vents fat and marrow into the circulation for longer and from a larger surface than any primary; transient desaturation and hypotension are the rule and the right ventricle is the organ under load. If a cemented stem follows, this is the highest-risk cement step in elective orthopaedics: a long column of cement pressurised into a long, freshly reamed, bleeding canal in a patient who has been on their side for three hours, has lost a litre or more, and is older and frailer than any primary patient. The hip fracture cement precautions apply in full, with an arterial line: the surgeon’s warning before mixing, a washed and dried canal, a retrograde gun on a plug and no heavy pressurisation; the pressure within 20% of baseline before the cement goes in, a vasopressor infusion running rather than boluses, fluid up to date, metaraminol and adrenaline drawn up, and the end-tidal carbon dioxide watched for the fall that means the right heart has met an embolised pulmonary bed. Grade 2 and 3 events are rare in primaries and are not rare here; the treatment is right heart failure’s: oxygen, vasopressor, adrenaline early, fluid with judgement, resuscitation if it comes to that. An uncemented tapered stem avoids the cement column but not the reaming, and its impaction down a long canal is the hardest hammering of the case.

  8. 8 Trial, reduction, stability and the constrained or dual-mobility bearing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The hip is reduced and tested through a range of positions; with a long stem, a rebuilt cup and often a weak or absent abductor mechanism, stability is the surgeon’s main worry and the reason the revision dislocation rate is several times the primary’s. A larger head, a lipped or constrained liner, or a dual-mobility bearing is chosen accordingly. Leg length is harder to judge because the landmarks are gone.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Each trial reduction is a hard pull on a long construct in a frail patient, the pressure dips with it, and after a cemented stem each reduction is a further embolic moment. The leg is commonly lengthened in a revision, because the surgeon is tensioning soft tissue that has lost the structures that held the primary, and the sciatic nerve pays for it: this is the hip operation with the highest nerve injury rate and lengthening is the mechanism. Nothing to add pharmacologically; the examination in recovery is what matters.

  9. 9 Osteotomy repair, soft-tissue repair and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The osteotomy fragment is cabled back around the new stem with two or three cables; what remains of the capsule and rotators is repaired; detached abductors are reattached; and the wound is closed over drains, which most revision surgeons still use.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the antiemetic and the second tranexamic acid dose if due. The cabled osteotomy is what the patient will feel for a week: a long bone, cut and cabled, that moves a little with every step and every abductor contraction. Start the epidural infusion or confirm the perineural catheter is running now, so the patient wakes with it working. Drains and the thigh are the first night’s blood loss; the haemoglobin at six hours and the next morning decide the transfusion.

  10. 10 Recovery, the first days and the frail patient's week

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants partial or toe-touch weight bearing on the osteotomy and the ingrowth stem for six weeks or more, hip precautions where the abductors are compromised, and a patient out of bed on day 1 regardless.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The revision patient is the one the primary pathway was not written for. The epidural or catheter runs for two to three days with a low-dose local anaesthetic that leaves the quadriceps working enough to transfer; the oral regimen starts before it stops; the opioid-tolerant patient keeps their baseline and has the pain service involved from day 0; and the haemoglobin, renal function and delirium screen are checked daily, because the frail elderly revision patient becomes delirious, hypotensive and anaemic in the first 48 hours more often than any other elective orthopaedic patient. A foot drop is the sciatic nerve and the surgeon sees it in recovery; a thigh that swells with a falling haemoglobin is bleeding at the osteotomy; new severe pain on standing with a short leg is a dislocation of a construct already known to be unstable. Chemoprophylaxis starts when the epidural timing allows and the bleeding has settled, usually the next morning.

Pain plan

The mechanism is a long femoral osteotomy or a stripped canal, cabled back and loaded by every step, plus a pelvis cut into, in a patient who is frail, often opioid-tolerant, and expected to mobilise on a construct that hurts when it moves. That is a periosteal, movement-evoked, several-day injury, and it is the hip operation where a continuous technique has its strongest claim.

PROSPECT’s basic regimen carries over: paracetamol with an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the kidneys and the age allow (in this population often not, so the NSAID is a daily decision rather than a standing order), a single intravenous dexamethasone dose, and opioids as rescue. The single-shot blocks PROSPECT recommends for primary hips do not address revision, and a single shot does not cover a four-hour operation or three days of osteotomy pain; the guideline’s silence is the honest position and the catheter advice here is the author’s judgement from the mechanism and the comparative trials in hip arthroplasty generally. The author’s default is a combined spinal-epidural for the planned cup-and-stem revision, the epidural run as a low-dose local anaesthetic infusion for two to three days and stopped when the patient is transferring and the oral regimen has been in for a day. Where an epidural is impossible (anticoagulation that cannot be paused, an instrumented spine, the fracture pathway’s timing) the alternative is a perineural catheter placed before a general anaesthetic: a posterior lumbar plexus catheter, or a supra-inguinal fascia iliaca catheter as the motor-sparing compromise. The randomised comparison of continuous femoral against lumbar plexus techniques after hip arthroplasty gave the same pain scores, with the lumbar plexus patients walking five times as far on the first morning, which is the argument against a femoral catheter in any hip. Surgeon-delivered infiltration is a supplement to any of these and never the plan. Intrathecal morphine up to 0.1 mg with the spinal is reasonable where no catheter is placed and the patient will be an inpatient for a week anyway.

For the liner-only or head-only exchange the mechanism is the primary’s and so is the plan: a spinal, infiltration, and a single-shot PENG or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block if infiltration is not offered.

Rebound risk is high: when a single-shot block wears off at 2 am on a cabled osteotomy the patient goes from comfortable to immobile, and a revision patient sent to the ward on a single shot without a written rescue plan is the commonest pain service referral of the week. Escalation triggers: rising thigh pain with a tense swollen thigh and a falling haemoglobin is bleeding at the osteotomy; buttock and leg pain with a foot drop is the sciatic nerve; new pain on movement with a short externally rotated leg is a dislocation; pain with a fever on day 3 after a reimplantation is the infection that was not cleared. The opioid-tolerant patient’s baseline is never stopped on the day of surgery and the rescue doses are scaled to it; a ketamine infusion for the first 48 hours is the author’s practice in that patient, with the usual low-grade evidence behind it.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Scope. The liner exchange, the head and liner exchange for wear or trunnion corrosion, the cup-only revision, the stem-only revision, the both-component revision with osteotomy and the pelvic discontinuity are different operations under one name; the pre-operative plan, not the list, tells you which.
  • The frail elderly patient. Anaemic, on a diuretic, cardiopulmonary disease, the BCIS risk group, delirium-prone, and the one in whom the extrapolated mortality benefit of neuraxial anaesthesia is most likely to be real. An arterial line, a catheter technique, a monitored bed overnight and an orthogeriatrician are the standard.
  • Anticoagulation. Warfarin for atrial fibrillation or a mechanical valve is common here, the INR predicts transfusion, and the epidural timing rules decide whether the catheter is neuraxial or perineural; plan it a week ahead.
  • The opioid-tolerant patient. Years of a painful loose hip produce a patient on long-term opioids; the baseline continues, the catheter is routine, and the pain service is involved from the start. See opioid-tolerant and chronic pain patients.
  • Vascular injury. Acetabular screws, reamers and cages near the medial wall, and a pelvic discontinuity: the external iliac and obturator vessels are the hidden bleed, and the sign is a pressure that falls with nothing in the wound.
  • Impaction grafting. Morselised allograft hammered into the canal with a cemented stem to follow: prolonged hard impaction, a large embolic load, and a full cement step at the end of a long case.
  • Reimplantation for infection. The antibiotic is held until samples are taken, dexamethasone is discussed with the surgeon, salvaged blood is not returned, and the patient has had a spacer and weeks of immobility and intravenous antibiotics: anaemia, renal impairment and deconditioning are the baseline. See periprosthetic joint infection.
  • Metal-on-metal revision for a pseudotumour. The implant exchange is the easy part; the soft-tissue debridement, the destroyed abductors and the dual-mobility or constrained bearing that follow are the operation, and the dislocation rate afterwards is high.
  • Periprosthetic fracture around a loose stem. This card’s femoral reconstruction on the fracture pathway’s timing, with the fracture patient’s physiology: see periprosthetic fracture.

Key sources

The evidence for revision hip arthroplasty is weakest in the areas that matter to the anaesthetist. The blood loss and transfusion data are good (a six-centre prospective cohort and a tranexamic acid meta-analysis); the cement data are extrapolated from hemiarthroplasty and the long-stem series in the Donaldson review; the neuraxial-versus-general evidence is extrapolated from primaries; and there is no procedure-specific analgesic guideline and no randomised comparison of epidural against perineural catheter in revision hips. The catheter recommendation is the author’s judgement from the mechanism, the one hip arthroplasty catheter trial, and the demands of mobilising a frail patient on an osteotomy, and it is labelled as such.

  1. Sershon RA, Fillingham YA, Malkani AL, et al. Independent risk factors for transfusion in contemporary revision total hip arthroplasty. J Arthroplasty 2021;36(8)
    175 revisions at six centres, all on tranexamic acid: 16.6% transfused; each 1 g/dL lower pre-operative haemoglobin raised transfusion odds by 79%, each 0.1 higher INR by 158%, each extra hour of surgery by 74%; revision type did not predict transfusion
  2. Xin X, et al. Intravenous tranexamic acid reduces blood transfusions in revision total hip arthroplasty: a meta-analysis. J Comp Eff Res 2019;8:917-928
    8 studies, 3,533 TXA and 11,007 control patients, mostly non-randomised: transfusion OR 0.23, about one unit fewer transfused, haemoglobin fall reduced by over 1 g/dL, no difference in thromboembolic events (OR 0.85)
  3. Ilfeld BM, Mariano ER, Madison SJ, et al. Continuous femoral versus posterior lumbar plexus nerve blocks for analgesia after hip arthroplasty: a randomized, controlled study. Anesth Analg 2011;113:897-903
    47 hip arthroplasty patients, ropivacaine 0.2% infusions for two days: average daily pain 3.6 against 3.5, equivalent; patients with the lumbar plexus catheter walked 11 m on the first morning against 2 m with the femoral catheter
  4. Mancino F, Cacciola G, Di Matteo V, et al. Reconstruction options and outcomes for acetabular bone loss in revision hip arthroplasty. Orthop Rev 2020;12(Suppl 1):8655
    The Paprosky classification guides acetabular reconstruction; the options run from hemispherical and jumbo cups through porous metal augments, cup-cage constructs, antiprotrusio cages, impaction grafting with mesh and structural allograft to custom triflange components, with no long-term comparative data between modern systems
  5. Orthobullets evidence summary: extended trochanteric osteotomy in revision total hip arthroplasty
    Union in 98%; fragment fracture the commonest complication with greater trochanter fracture in 9%; fragment migration over 1 cm in 7%; the osteotomy is used to remove well-fixed stems and cement and its length is set by the implant and the cement to be removed
  6. Association of Anaesthetists of Great Britain and Ireland, Griffiths R, White SM, Moppett IK, et al. Safety guideline: reducing the risk from cemented hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture 2015. Anaesthesia 2015;70:623-626
    The cement precautions: surgeon's warning, washed and dried canal, retrograde gun on a plug, no heavy pressurisation in the high-risk patient; anaesthetist with systolic within 20% of baseline, vasopressor ready, arterial line in the higher-risk patient, end-tidal carbon dioxide as the right heart monitor
  7. Donaldson AJ, Thomson HE, Harper NJ, Kenny NW. Bone cement implantation syndrome. Br J Anaesth 2009;102:12-22
    Grades 1-3 by saturation, systolic fall and collapse; in a series of 55 cemented long-stem arthroplasties, hypotension in 38% and desaturation in 25%, against 2% and 17% in 48 elective primary cemented hips
  8. Memtsoudis SG, Cozowicz C, Bekeris J, et al. Anaesthetic care of patients undergoing primary hip and knee arthroplasty: consensus recommendations from the ICAROS group based on a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Anaesth 2019
    Strong recommendation for neuraxial anaesthesia in hip arthroplasty on mortality, pulmonary, renal, thromboembolic, infective and transfusion outcomes; derived from primary arthroplasty and extrapolated here
  9. Carella M, Bugada D, Van de Velde M, et al. PROSPECT guideline for total hip arthroplasty: updated systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Anaesthesia 2026 (online ahead of print)
    The primary THA guideline; its basic regimen (paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, single-dose IV dexamethasone) carries over, its single-shot block recommendations do not address revision, and continuous techniques were not reviewed for primary surgery

Hip and knee › Hip

25 Hip arthroscopy: FAI and labral repair

Femoroacetabular impingement: cam and pincer resection, labral repair or debridement, capsulotomy and repair, with the hip in traction over a perineal post

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Capsule. An interportal or T-shaped capsulotomy through the iliofemoral ligament, a labrum sutured back to a decorticated acetabular rim, and a femoral neck burred to reshape the cam; plus the joint distracted for an hour against a perineal post and the soft tissues filled with irrigation fluid. Capsule and labrum dominate; the bone work is a burr on a neck, not a reaming

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
General anaesthesia with surgeon-delivered intra-articular and portal infiltration; no routine peripheral nerve block
Catheter: no No continuous technique for a day-case operation whose pain is a 2; a catheter would answer a question nobody asked
Alternatives: PENG block, single shot, for the patient who predicts a bad course or the larger case (capsular plication, gluteal repair), accepting that quadriceps weakness after PENG occurs in a quarter of patients in some series; Spinal anaesthesia where the patient prefers it, sized to a two-hour case, with the traction and the position in mind; Fascia iliaca block is not recommended: in the randomised sham-controlled trial it did not improve pain and increased quadriceps weakness and falls
Position
Supine on a traction table (lateral decubitus in some hands) with both feet in padded boots, a large well-padded perineal post lateralised against the medial thigh of the operative side, the operative leg in slight flexion, abduction and internal rotation, and traction applied until the joint space opens 8-10 mm on the fluoroscope; traction released for the peripheral compartment
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal; what you see is irrigation. The haemoglobin does not move
Duration
60-150 min; a simple cam resection and labral debridement at the short end, a labral reconstruction or a capsular plication with gluteal work at the long end; traction time, usually 45-90 min of that, is the figure that predicts the complications
Length of stay
Day case. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); anchors are implants
Tranexamic acid
Not needed for blood loss; some surgeons ask for TXA 1 g IV for arthroscopic visibility, which is a reasonable request
VTE
Mechanical only in most units; chemoprophylaxis for the patient's own risk factors, and the oral contraceptive pill in a young woman having a long traction case is one of them
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; the day-case population is young, female and opioid-naive, which is the high-risk nausea phenotype
Tell the patient
You will go home the same day on crutches; the hip aches and feels stiff for a week or two, the groin and the front of the thigh may be numb from the traction post for a few days, and the numbness and the swelling of the thigh both settle.
The trap
The abdomen: irrigation fluid pumped at high flow through a capsulotomy tracks along the psoas into the retroperitoneum and the peritoneal cavity, and the reported abdominal compartment syndromes presented at the end of long cases as a distended abdomen with hypotension, rising airway pressures and a falling temperature; feel the abdomen every 30 minutes and at the end of every case with a capsulotomy or a psoas release, before the drapes come off

What the surgeon is doing and why

Femoroacetabular impingement is a hip whose ball and socket are the wrong shape for each other. A cam lesion is a bump on the femoral head-neck junction that is driven into the acetabular rim in flexion and internal rotation, shearing the cartilage off the rim from the inside; a pincer lesion is an over-covering acetabular rim that the neck strikes, crushing the labrum between them. Either way the labrum, the fibrocartilaginous ring that seals the joint and holds the fluid film, is torn, and the patient (a young adult, often an athlete, often a woman) has groin pain in flexion and a positive impingement test. The surgeon’s aim is to reshape the bone so that the two no longer collide and to repair the labrum so that it seals again. If the cartilage is already gone the operation does not work, which is why the surgeon is selective and why some of these patients come back years later for a total hip.

The whole operation is done through two or three portals with the joint pulled apart. The sequence:

  1. Traction. The hip is a deep ball-and-socket under negative pressure, and the surgeon cannot get a scope between the head and the acetabulum unless the joint is distracted 8-10 mm. That is done on a traction table against a perineal post, with the foot in a boot, and checked on the fluoroscope: the seal of the joint has to be broken (the vacuum sign) before the space opens, which takes a considerable force. The central compartment work (labrum, rim, cartilage) is all done under traction.
  2. Portals and capsulotomy. The anterolateral portal is placed under fluoroscopy, then an anterior or mid-anterior portal, and the two are joined by an interportal capsulotomy through the iliofemoral ligament, 2-4 cm long, to give the instruments room. Some surgeons extend it into a T down the neck. The capsulotomy is what makes the operation possible and what the patient feels afterwards; most surgeons now close or plicate it at the end because an unrepaired capsulotomy in a loose-jointed young woman produces instability.
  3. Rim and labrum. The pincer rim is burred back; the labrum is detached or elevated, the rim decorticated to bleeding bone, and the labrum sutured back with two to four anchors so that it seals against the head again. An irreparable labrum is debrided or, in a few hands, reconstructed with a graft.
  4. Traction off, cam resection. The hip is flexed, which exposes the head-neck junction in the peripheral compartment without traction, and the cam is burred away with a motorised burr until the head is round on the fluoroscope through a range of positions. Too much resection and the neck fractures; too little and the impingement persists, which is the commonest reason for a revision scope.
  5. Add-ons. A psoas tenotomy for a snapping or impinging iliopsoas, a trochanteric bursectomy or gluteal tendon repair through the peritrochanteric space, a ligamentum teres debridement. Each adds time and fluid.
  6. Capsular closure, portal closure, and home.

The anaesthetic reading. This is an operation whose pain is a 2 and whose hazards are all mechanical, and they come in three groups. The traction, applied against a perineal post, loads the pudendal nerve, the perineal skin and the genitals, and stretches the sciatic and peroneal nerves; in the large prospective series pudendal numbness occurred in 1.4%, foot sensory loss in 0.8%, and traction beyond 60 minutes raised the whole complication rate. The irrigation pump, run at high flow through a capsulotomy into the soft tissues of the hip, puts litres into the thigh and, in the reported cases, along the psoas into the retroperitoneum and the peritoneal cavity; abdominal compartment syndrome has been reported perhaps a dozen times, with a cardiac arrest, laparotomies and one paracentesis that drained 3 L, and the common features were a long case, a capsulotomy and a psoas release. And the surgeon’s requests for a low pressure and a relaxed patient are requests made of you for the surgeon’s view and the surgeon’s traction, and they are reasonable in a young patient lying flat and unreasonable at the extremes.

The pain logic: capsule is the dominant mechanism (a cut through the thickest ligament in the body, a labrum sutured to a raw rim), then the bone of the cam resection, which is a burr on a neck and not a reaming, and under both the traction and the fluid. It is sharp with movement and settles in days; it is not re-provoked by loading, because the patient is on crutches and the labrum is not weight-bearing. A 2 on the Part B scale, and in the 179-procedure cohort hip arthroscopy does not appear in the 40 highest-scoring operations. The young, female, opioid-naive population is the one with the highest nausea risk and, in the ambulatory block data, the highest rebound risk, which is an argument for an antiemetic plan and an oral regimen started before discharge rather than for a block.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 General anaesthesia, the airway, and the block question decided in advance

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs 60-150 minutes of a motionless, relaxed patient on a traction table with a C-arm over the pelvis, and a patient who can go home on crutches that afternoon.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    General anaesthesia with a tracheal tube and neuromuscular block is the author’s default: the surgeon’s request for relaxation at the traction step is a request for muscle relaxation (a tense hip needs more force to distract, and more force is more pudendal and sciatic injury), a tube protects the airway for a long case with the head away from you and a C-arm swinging over the chest, and the end of the case needs an abdominal examination before extubation. A spinal is a reasonable option for the patient who wants one, sized to two hours, with the understanding that a sedated spontaneously breathing patient under a traction and a pump is harder to assess at the end than a ventilated one; the one reported abdominal compartment syndrome under a spinal declared itself as dyspnoea and abdominal pain in the final minutes. The block decision belongs here and is covered in the pain plan; the short version is no fascia iliaca block, a PENG only for the selected patient, and surgeon-delivered infiltration for everyone.

  2. 2 Positioning on the traction table: the post, the boots and the leg

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Distraction needs a counter-force, which is the perineal post against the medial thigh; a large, well-padded post, lateralised against the operative thigh rather than centred on the perineum, spreads the load away from the pudendal nerve. The operative foot goes into a boot with the leg in slight flexion, abduction and internal rotation; the other leg goes into the contralateral boot in abduction to make room for the C-arm, or is left free.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The post is the pudendal nerve: in the pooled series pudendal injury occurred in 4.3% of patients where a post was used and 0.5% where it was not, all resolving within three months. Check that the post is padded, that it sits on the thigh and not the perineum, and that the genitals are clear of it and not trapped; in a man the scrotum and penis go away from the post and are looked at again after the traction is on. The boots are the feet: a loose boot allows the foot to slip and the traction to be applied through the ankle, a tight boot is a skin and a nerve problem; the contralateral foot in a boot under counter-traction is at the same risk. Arms across the chest on a rest, out of the C-arm’s path. Then the thing nobody else will do: look at the whole patient from the end of the table once the traction is on, because the pelvis will have shifted against the post and the head and the arms will have moved with it.

  3. 3 Traction applied and the vacuum broken

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Traction is increased until the joint seal breaks (seen as a crescent of air on the fluoroscope) and the joint space opens 8-10 mm. A stiff, muscular or guarded hip needs more force, and the surgeon cannot work in the central compartment with less than full distraction.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the moment the surgeon asks for relaxation, and under general anaesthesia the answer is neuromuscular block, because a relaxed hip distracts with less force and the force is the injury. Start the traction clock. The series are consistent that traction time predicts complications: over 60 minutes the rate rose significantly, and hips with pudendal neurapraxia had an hour of traction against 45 minutes in those without. The surgeon’s practice is to release traction when moving to the peripheral compartment and to re-apply it only if needed; your practice is to say the time out loud at 45 minutes and every 15 minutes after that, which is a request that every experienced hip arthroscopist will understand. The pressure often rises as the traction goes on and the pelvis loads the post; a young patient tolerates it and it is not a reason to deepen.

  4. 4 Portals, capsulotomy and the irrigation pump

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals under fluoroscopy, then the interportal capsulotomy to create working space. The irrigation pump is set at 40-60 mmHg and flows continuously; the capsulotomy means the fluid is no longer contained in the joint.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve runs across the anterior portal site and is disturbed in 16.5% of patients in the prospective series, persisting at six months in 1.6%; it is a portal injury, not a traction one, and the patient will report numbness over the anterolateral thigh. The capsulotomy opens the hip to the thigh and the pump fills it: from this point the thigh swells, the fluid tracks where the anatomy lets it, and the two reported routes to the abdomen are along the psoas into the retroperitoneum and from there into the peritoneum. Warm the irrigation or the patient, because 20 L of room-temperature fluid through the hip over two hours is the cooling system that the hypothermia in two of the reported compartment syndrome cases reflects. The surgeon’s request for a systolic of 90-100 for a clear view is reasonable in a flat, young, well patient, which is who is on the table; it is not reasonable in the older patient with hypertension having a scope for a different indication.

  5. 5 Rim trimming, labral takedown and repair under traction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The pincer rim is burred back, the labrum elevated, the rim decorticated to bleeding bone, and the labrum sutured back with anchors so that it seals against the femoral head. This is the longest part of the central compartment work and all of it is under traction.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The capsule and labrum mechanism is created here: a labrum sutured onto raw bone and a capsule held open by instruments, which the patient will feel on every flexion for a week. The anchors are implants, which is the reason for the antibiotic. Bone dust and bleeding from the decorticated rim fog the view, and this is the step that produces the request for a lower pressure and a higher pump; the pump is the surgeon’s lever. The traction clock is running; this step is where it is most often forgotten.

  6. 6 Traction released, cam resection in the peripheral compartment

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The joint is reduced, the hip flexed to 30-45 degrees to relax the anterior capsule and expose the head-neck junction, and the cam burred away under fluoroscopic and arthroscopic control until the head is spherical through flexion and rotation. The neck must not be over-resected (a femoral neck fracture after a scope is a resection of more than about 30% of the neck diameter, and the patient is told to protect it on crutches for that reason) and the retinacular vessels that supply the head run along the posterosuperior neck and are kept out of the field.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Traction off is the moment the perineum and the feet get their blood back; note the total traction time. The cam resection is the bone mechanism, a burr on a neck rather than a reaming, and in a young patient it is well tolerated. The flexed leg in a boot is a different loading of the sciatic nerve and the peroneal nerve at the fibular neck; the knee is checked. This is where the case runs long if the surgeon is thorough, and the fluid keeps running.

  7. 7 Add-ons: psoas release, peritrochanteric work and the fluid problem

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A psoas tenotomy at the lesser trochanter or through the capsule treats a snapping or impinging iliopsoas; trochanteric bursectomy, iliotibial band release and gluteus medius repair are done in the peritrochanteric space with the leg abducted and the traction off; ligamentum teres debridement in the central compartment.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The psoas release is the step most consistently present in the abdominal compartment syndrome reports, because it opens the fluid’s path along the psoas into the retroperitoneum; four of the seven cases reviewed had one. The peritrochanteric space is a large potential space that holds litres. From this point the examination is the abdomen: distension, a tense wall, rising airway pressures on the ventilator, a pressure that falls without a reason in the field, a core temperature that drops. The treatment of the established syndrome is drainage (a paracentesis drained 3 L in one case) or a laparotomy; the prevention is a surgeon who knows the clock and a pump that is not run at pressures and flows that the anatomy cannot drain. Say the fluid volume out loud when the bags are changed, and say the deficit if the pump displays one.

  8. 8 Capsular closure, portal closure and the abdomen before the drapes come off

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The capsulotomy is closed or plicated with two or three sutures (more in the patient with laxity), the portals closed, and a dressing applied; the leg comes out of the boot and the post is removed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Before the drapes come off and before any plan to extubate, examine the abdomen: a soft, flat abdomen with normal airway pressures and a normal temperature is the common finding, and anything else is not extubated until it is explained. Look at the perineum and the genitals for the pressure marks and the oedema the post leaves; look at both feet. Give the antiemetic. A patient under a spinal who complains of abdominal pain or breathlessness at this point has declared the diagnosis and the ultrasound probe is the next step, not reassurance.

  9. 9 Recovery, the oral regimen and home

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the patient home on crutches with partial weight bearing for two to six weeks depending on what was done, with hip flexion limited for a repaired labrum and a closed capsule, and a physiotherapy programme that starts within days.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The pain in recovery is capsular and sharp with movement, and settles with the first doses of paracetamol and an NSAID given before the patient leaves, plus a few oral opioid doses for the first two nights. Nausea in this population is the thing that stops discharge; the dexamethasone and ondansetron at induction and emergence are not optional. The anterolateral thigh numbness and the perineal numbness are expected and are explained before they are reported, because a young woman who wakes with a numb perineum and was not told has had a bad day. A quadriceps that will not hold the patient’s weight on the first standing attempt is a block, if one was given, and is the reason the fascia iliaca block was abandoned for this operation. The thigh will be swollen with fluid for a day or two; a thigh that is tense, with pain out of proportion and a numb foot, is a compartment syndrome of the thigh, reported after this operation, and is the surgeon’s problem now.

Pain plan

The mechanism is a capsulotomy, a labrum sutured to a raw rim and a burred femoral neck, in a joint distracted for an hour and filled with fluid: sharp with movement, settling in days, not re-provoked by loading. That is a 2, and the plan is built for a day case: paracetamol and an NSAID started before discharge and continued for a week, a few oral opioid doses for the first two nights, dexamethasone and ondansetron for the nausea that this population produces, and surgeon-delivered local anaesthetic into the joint and the portals at the end of the case.

The block question has a clear negative and an open positive. The negative is the fascia iliaca block: in the randomised sham-controlled trial of 80 patients having arthroscopy for impingement, a pre-operative fascia iliaca block changed neither the pain scores nor the opioid use over 24 hours, and produced more quadriceps weakness and more falls, and the authors could not recommend it; a femoral nerve block carries the same motor cost for the same absent benefit. The open positive is the PENG block: in the pooled trials across hip surgery it gave the same pain scores as fascia iliaca with less opioid at 24 hours, and in the one hip arthroscopy trial that combined it with a lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block it gave lower pain scores and less quadriceps weakness than fascia iliaca, but it is being compared with a block that does not work, and the trials that report motor function after PENG find quadriceps weakness in over a quarter of patients in some series. The author’s practice is no routine block: infiltration for everyone, and a single-shot PENG for the patient who predicts a bad course (chronic pain, a previous bad day-case night, opioid tolerance) or the larger operation (capsular plication, gluteal tendon repair, labral reconstruction), with the patient told that the leg may not hold them for the first evening. That is a judgement, not an evidence statement; there is no PROSPECT guideline for hip arthroscopy and the nearest one, for total hip arthroplasty, addresses a different mechanism.

No catheter. Rebound is moderate because the population is young, female and opioid-naive, which are the ambulatory block predictors, but the thing that wears off is infiltration rather than a dense block, and the first oral doses go in before discharge. Escalation triggers: a thigh that is tense and swollen with pain out of proportion is a thigh compartment syndrome; perineal or anterolateral thigh numbness is expected and settles; abdominal pain or distension at home on the evening of surgery is the compartment syndrome that was missed in theatre and needs an emergency department, not a phone call.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Traction time is the complication rate. Over 60 minutes the rate rises; the surgeon’s practice of releasing traction for the peripheral compartment and your practice of calling the time are the two controls.
  • The perineal post. Padded, large, lateralised onto the thigh; the genitals checked before and after traction. Post-free traction systems exist and the pooled pudendal injury rate without a post is a tenth of the rate with one.
  • Lateral decubitus. Some surgeons scope the hip on its side with traction applied through a boot on a lateral distractor; the airway access, the dependent arm and the post are the lateral-position issues, and the fluid tracks differently.
  • The obese patient. Harder to distract, longer traction, more force, a deeper wound for the fluid to fill; many surgeons will not scope above a BMI of about 35.
  • Fluid extravasation and the abdomen. The capsulotomy, the psoas release, the long case and the high-flow pump are the reported associations; the signs are distension, airway pressure, hypotension and hypothermia; the examination before extubation is the prevention of the catastrophe, and the hernia in the history is a reason to examine twice.
  • Thigh compartment syndrome. Reported after fluid extravasation into the thigh; a tense thigh with disproportionate pain in recovery.
  • The request for hypotension. Reasonable in a flat young patient; the pump pressure is the surgeon’s lever before yours.
  • Hypothermia. Litres of room-temperature irrigation over two hours; forced-air warming from the start and the fluid warmed where the pump allows.
  • The female athlete on the pill. Long traction, immobility on crutches and oestrogen: the one day-case arthroscopy population where chemoprophylaxis is discussed rather than dismissed.
  • Revision arthroscopy and conversion. Scar makes the capsule harder to open and the distraction harder; a scope that fails for adhesions or cartilage loss ends up as a periacetabular osteotomy or a total hip in the following years, and the surgeon will often say so at the time.
  • The dysplastic hip. A labral tear in a shallow socket is the symptom, not the disease; a scope that repairs the labrum without addressing the dysplasia makes it worse, and the right operation is the periacetabular osteotomy.

Key sources

The complication data are good: a 1,615-hip prospective multicentre series with a validated grading scheme and a pooled analysis of pudendal injury. The abdominal compartment syndrome literature is case reports, perhaps a dozen, and the card’s advice to examine the abdomen before extubation is drawn from their common features rather than from any trial. The block evidence is one well-designed negative randomised trial for fascia iliaca and a small, heterogeneous and early literature for PENG; the card’s no-routine-block default is the author’s reading of that and is labelled as such. There is no procedure-specific analgesic guideline.

  1. Larson CM, Clohisy JC, Beaulé PE, et al. Intraoperative and early postoperative complications after hip arthroscopic surgery: a prospective multicenter trial utilizing a validated grading scheme. Am J Sports Med 2016;44(9)
    1,615 hips, mean age 30: overall complication rate 8.3%, almost all minor; lateral femoral cutaneous nerve disturbance 16.5% (persisting beyond 6 months in 1.6%), pudendal perineal numbness 1.4%, foot sensory deficits 0.8%, chondral injury 1.2%, labral puncture 0.9%, no fluid extravasation; traction over 60 min raised the complication rate (p<0.001) and pudendal neurapraxia hips had 61.5 min of traction against 43.8 min; complications more frequent in women
  2. Habib A, Haldane CE, Ekhtiari S, de Sa D, Simunovic N, Belzile EL, Ayeni OR. Pudendal nerve injury is a relatively common but transient complication of hip arthroscopy. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc 2018;26:969-975
    24 studies, 3,405 patients: pudendal nerve injury in 1.8%, all resolving within 6 weeks to 3 months; 4.3% in studies using a perineal post against 0.5% in those without; longer traction times associated
  3. Ciemniewska-Gorzela K, Piontek T, Szulc A. Abdominal compartment syndrome: the prevention and treatment of possible lethal complications following hip arthroscopy: a case report. J Med Case Rep 2014;8:368
    A 53 kg woman under spinal with propofol sedation: at the end of a 2 h case with psoas release, acute dyspnoea, tachycardia, a distended abdomen and a systolic in the 60s-90s; paracentesis drained 3 L of clear fluid with immediate recovery. Reviews seven earlier reports (95-165 min cases, five with capsulotomy, four with psoas release): distension the consistent sign, with hypotension, raised airway pressure, hypothermia, one cardiac arrest and three laparotomies
  4. Behrends M, Yap EN, Zhang AL, Kolodzie K, Kinjo S, Harbell MW, Aleshi P. Preoperative fascia iliaca block does not improve analgesia after arthroscopic hip surgery, but causes quadriceps muscle weakness: a randomized, double-blind trial. Anesthesiology 2018;129:536-543
    80 patients, fascia iliaca block against sham before hip arthroscopy for impingement: pain scores and opioid use over 24 h the same, quadriceps strength deficit greater and falls more frequent in the block group; the authors could not recommend the block
  5. Ying H, Chen L, Yin D, Ye Y, Chen J. Efficacy of pericapsular nerve group block vs. fascia iliaca compartment block for hip surgeries: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Surg 2023;10:1054403
    6 randomised trials, 258 patients across hip surgery: pain scores the same at 6, 12 and 24 h; 24 h opioid consumption lower with PENG by about 9 mg morphine equivalent with high heterogeneity; quadriceps weakness after PENG reported in over a quarter of patients in some trials; moderate certainty, described as preliminary
  6. Liu M, Gao M, Hu Y, et al. Pericapsular nerve group block combined with lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block versus fascia iliaca block for hip arthroscopy. J Pain Res 2024 (OrthoEvidence summary)
    78 patients: PENG with lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block gave lower static and dynamic pain scores and less quadriceps weakness than fascia iliaca block over 48 h
  7. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    Hip arthroscopy does not appear in the 40 highest-scoring procedures; the cohort's top of the table is open calcaneal reduction, spinal fusion and foot arthrodesis

Hip and knee › Hip

26 Periacetabular osteotomy

Bernese (Ganz) periacetabular osteotomy for acetabular dysplasia and retroversion in the adolescent and young adult hip

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Four osteotomies through the pelvis leaving a free acetabular fragment on three screws, loaded through the hip by every protected step for six to eight weeks before it unites; beneath that, iliacus and the abductors stripped off both tables of the ilium, the direct head of rectus femoris taken down or retracted, a capsule re-tensioned by the reorientation, and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve in the wound

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
General anaesthesia with a continuous regional technique for the first 48 h: a low-concentration lumbar epidural where the pathway tolerates its side effects, or a suprainguinal fascia iliaca or erector spinae catheter with surgeon periarticular infiltration where early walking and simple chemoprophylaxis are the priority; IV dexamethasone and two doses of tranexamic acid in all
Catheter: routine A continuous technique is the author's default for an operation with a score of 5; which one is a pathway decision rather than an evidence verdict. The epidural has the best analgesia on record for the first 48 h and the longest stay; a fascia iliaca or erector spinae catheter, or a single-shot suprainguinal fascia iliaca block with dexamethasone and infiltration, trades about a point of pain on day 0-1 for a day less in hospital and a leg that walks
Alternatives: Single-shot suprainguinal fascia iliaca block with IV dexamethasone plus surgeon periarticular infiltration (the enhanced-recovery pathway in the recent cohorts); Lumbar erector spinae plane catheter (less weakness, numbness and hypotension than an epidural in the one comparison, slightly more pain on day 0); Combined spinal-epidural where the surgeon's first hour can be covered by the spinal and the epidural run from the pubic cut onwards; Surgeon periarticular injection alone on a two-night pathway, accepting day 0-1 pain near 5
Position
Supine on a radiolucent table with the image intensifier on the operative side; the leg is draped free so the hip can be flexed and adducted for the ischial cut and ranged for the impingement check; some surgeons add a small bump under the ipsilateral buttock
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Calculated loss 900-1,500 mL, rising about 11% for every hour of surgery; before tranexamic acid a third to a half of patients were transfused, with it 10-30%; cell salvage is routine
Duration
120-180 min for the osteotomy alone in experienced hands; 180-240 min with a concomitant hip arthroscopy or an open femoral osteochondroplasty, and well beyond that early in a surgeon's experience
Length of stay
2-4 nights: two on a block-and-infiltration pathway, three to four with an epidural. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision, 3 g over 120 kg; repeat at 4 h or after 1.5 L of loss, both of which this operation can reach
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision and 1 g IV at closure, the two-dose regimen used in the randomised trial
VTE
Chemoprophylaxis (LMWH or aspirin by unit protocol) plus mechanical prophylaxis and early mobilisation; a long pelvic operation in a young patient is not low risk, three of 205 patients in the multicentre cohort had a thromboembolic event, and an epidural catheter sets the timing of every dose
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; a young woman, a long case and an opioid-based rescue plan is the highest-risk phenotype in the book
Tell the patient
This is a big operation on the pelvis: expect a few nights in hospital, crutches with limited weight through the leg for six to eight weeks, and a hip that is sore for weeks rather than days before the benefit arrives.
The trap
The size of the operation is hidden by the age of the patient: calculated blood loss is about a litre and rises with every hour, a third of patients were transfused before tranexamic acid, and the haematocrit in a 20-year-old woman settles a third below her baseline; group and crossmatch, cell salvage, two doses of tranexamic acid and a written plan for the day the catheter comes out are the minimum, not the maximum

What the surgeon is doing and why

Acetabular dysplasia is a socket that is too shallow and faces the wrong way. The femoral head is covered laterally and anteriorly by labrum instead of bone, the load that should spread over a hemisphere is carried on the edge, and the labrum hypertrophies, tears and the cartilage beside it delaminates. Left alone, the hip arrives at arthroplasty in its forties. The periacetabular osteotomy cuts the acetabulum free from the pelvis as a single fragment, rotates it so that bone sits over the head, pushes it medially so that the joint reaction force falls, and fixes it with screws until it unites. It is a reconstruction of the pelvis in a patient who is usually a woman in her late teens or twenties: the multicentre complication cohort had a mean age of 25 and was 70% female. The same osteotomy rotated the other way treats acetabular retroversion.

The Bernese design keeps the posterior column intact, and that one decision explains the operation. Because the ischial and retroacetabular cuts stop short of the posterior column, the pelvic ring stays in one piece, the fragment is held by screws rather than an external fixator, the patient can sit and bear partial weight from the first day, and the birth canal is unchanged. It also explains the two cuts the surgeon cannot see: the ischial cut is made under the capsule by feel and fluoroscopy, and the retroacetabular cut runs down the quadrilateral plate with the sciatic notch a centimetre behind it.

The sequence is fixed. Get onto the pelvis through a modified Smith-Petersen approach, taking the anterior superior iliac spine or the sartorius origin, lifting iliacus off the inner table and working under rectus femoris and iliocapsularis to the capsule. Make four cuts: ischium below the socket, superior pubic ramus medial to the iliopectineal eminence, the supra-acetabular ilium towards the pelvic brim, and the retroacetabular cut down the quadrilateral surface to meet the ischial cut. Mobilise the fragment on a Schanz screw, reorient it under the image intensifier, fix it with three or four screws from the iliac crest, graft the gap, open the joint if the labrum or the head-neck junction needs attention, repair and close. A hip arthroscopy may precede the osteotomy under the same anaesthetic; it adds its own time, not to the osteotomy’s.

The pain logic follows from a free piece of pelvis held by screws. The dominant mechanism is bone, but not the bone of a single cut that is then rested: four cancellous surfaces across the ilium, pubis and ischium, with the fragment loaded through the hip by every protected step for six to eight weeks until it unites, and a pubic ramus that unites slowly or not at all. Beneath that is muscle, from iliacus and the abductors stripped from both tables of the ilium and the rectus origin taken down, so every hip flexion and every transfer hurts; a capsule re-tensioned by the reorientation (in cadaveric testing the osteotomy reduced abduction and internal rotation and increased adduction and external rotation); and nerve, because the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve runs through the wound. The early peak with a working continuous technique is a 3 or 4; the 5 is earned afterwards. In the largest analgesic cohort, patients on a periarticular injection pathway left hospital with a pain score of 4.8, and when patients describe dissatisfaction with this operation, half of it is pain. Compare hip arthroscopy, which treats the labral consequences of the same dysplasia through portals and sits at 2.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative plan: blood, the continuous technique, and chemoprophylaxis timing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon’s requirements are a still patient on a radiolucent table for two to three hours, a field dry enough to see osteotomes going into bone they cannot see, and a patient who can get out of bed with crutches the next morning.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Three decisions are made in clinic, not on the day. Blood: the calculated loss is 900-1,500 mL in the series that measured it, 11% more for every hour of surgery, and the haematocrit nadir settles at about 0.69 of the pre-operative value, so a 20-year-old woman with a borderline haemoglobin needs iron and a crossmatch, not a group and hold. The analgesic technique: a continuous technique for the first 48 h is the author’s default for a score of 5, and the choice between a lumbar epidural and a peripheral catheter or single-shot block with infiltration is set by the unit’s pathway (see the pain plan), because the epidural changes the length of stay, the bladder catheter and the timing of every anticoagulant dose. Chemoprophylaxis: three of 205 patients in the multicentre cohort had a thromboembolic event, so youth does not exempt this operation from LMWH or aspirin.

  2. 2 Induction, lines, position and the regional technique

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The patient is supine on a radiolucent table with the image intensifier on the operative side, and the leg is draped free so that the hip can be flexed and adducted for the ischial cut and ranged at the end for impingement. Fluoroscopy is used for every cut and for the correction.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A tracheal tube for a two to three hour supine case with a litre of loss and a C-arm over the abdomen; two large cannulae; an arterial line is the author’s practice because the losses come in pulses at the cuts and the pressure needs to be readable while the surgeon is asking for it to be low. Cefazolin 2 g IV and tranexamic acid 1 g IV before the knife, dexamethasone 8 mg IV for the block as much as for nausea. If an epidural is the plan it goes in before induction at L2-3 or L3-4 and is tested; a combined spinal-epidural lets the spinal carry the exposure and the epidural start from the first cut. A suprainguinal fascia iliaca block takes 30-40 mL of ropivacaine 0.375% in an adult (the total with any surgeon infiltration kept under 3 mg/kg, which matters in the adolescent) and six minutes. Warm the patient from the start and pad the contralateral leg with care: one of the nine reoperations in the multicentre cohort was a decompression of the other leg’s peroneal nerve.

  3. 3 Approach: the spine, the iliacus and the rectus origin

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The incision runs along the anterior iliac crest and down towards the thigh. The anterior superior iliac spine is osteotomised with the sartorius and inguinal ligament attached, or the sartorius is released; iliacus is lifted subperiosteally off the inner table down to the pelvic brim; the direct head of rectus femoris is taken down or, in the rectus-sparing modification, retracted; iliocapsularis is elevated off the capsule to expose the front of the joint and the infracotyloid groove. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve crosses the field under the inguinal ligament, is protected, and still produces dysaesthesia in a proportion of patients.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first bleeding is from the inner table and the nutrient vessels of the ilium as iliacus comes off, steady rather than dramatic, and the cell salvage should be collecting from now. Retractors on iliacus lie on the femoral nerve. Muscle relaxation makes the inner table reachable; a light patient with a tense iliopsoas is an unworkable field. The muscle mechanism of the pain is created here, and it is the part a fascia iliaca block covers well.

  4. 4 The ischial cut

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The first and blindest cut. A curved osteotome is passed under the capsule along the infracotyloid groove to the ischium below the acetabulum and driven through the medial two-thirds of the ischium, stopping short of the posterior cortex so that the posterior column survives. The surgeon works by feel and by the lateral and anteroposterior images; the sciatic nerve lies posterolateral to the osteotome’s tip, and the hip is flexed and adducted to relax the capsule and the nerve.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The surgeon will ask for the leg in flexion and adduction and for stillness; neuromuscular block is the right answer rather than depth. Nothing bleeds much here. A sciatic palsy after this operation originates at this osteotome or from a posterior column fracture, and the reviews find it more often with the ilioinguinal and two-incision approaches than with this one; it declares itself when the block recedes, so the foot is examined the morning after, not only in recovery.

  5. 5 The pubic cut

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The superior pubic ramus is divided medial to the iliopectineal eminence. Retractors are placed around the ramus to protect the obturator neurovascular bundle beneath it and the femoral vessels in front of it; a corona mortis, the anastomosis between obturator and external iliac systems that crosses the ramus in a proportion of pelves, is the vessel that bleeds here.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Brisk venous bleeding from behind the ramus is the obturator plexus or a corona mortis and is controlled with packing and patience; the arterial bleed that needed embolisation in the adolescent series and an external iliac vein injury are the rare versions. A sudden pressure fall here is surgical, not anaesthetic, and the cell salvage, the second cannula and the crossmatched blood are what you brought for it. The retractor on the front of the ramus compresses the femoral vessels: a leg that is pale and pulseless at the end of the case was clamped here.

  6. 6 The supra-acetabular and retroacetabular cuts

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The iliac cut runs from the outer table below the anterior inferior iliac spine towards the pelvic brim and stops a centimetre short of the iliopectineal line. From its end the retroacetabular cut turns down the quadrilateral surface at roughly 120 degrees, behind the socket and in front of the posterior column, to meet the ischial cut from above. The surgeon has the inner table exposed and the outer table only felt; the greater sciatic notch, the superior gluteal vessels and the sciatic nerve are behind the osteotome.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The largest bleed of the operation: cancellous bone on both surfaces of a thick iliac cut, the venous plexus on the quadrilateral plate and the nutrient vessels of the ilium, with the superior gluteal artery as the thing that must not be hit. The request for a lower pressure arrives here. Hold a mean of 60-65 mmHg in a healthy 25-year-old for the minutes it takes, and not lower, because the dysplastic hip is the only abnormal organ in this patient. A cut that strays into the posterior column converts the operation: the pelvic ring is broken, the fragment is unstable, plate fixation and a longer, bloodier case follow, and three of 715 patients in the large single-surgeon series were reoperated for exactly that.
