    618 patients aged 14-25 at high risk of failure: adding an iliotibial band tenodesis cut clinical failure from 40% to 25% and graft rupture from 11% to 4%; the tenodesis group had more pain at three months, persisting on the KOOS to six months
  14. Samei M, Daliri M, Sadeghi M, Ganji R, Parsa A, Ebrahimzadeh MH. Arthroscopic anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with and without tourniquet use: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis on clinical outcomes. BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2024;25:994
    Seven trials: with a tourniquet, drain output 100 mL higher, pain 0.42 points higher at 24 h and 0.40 at 48 h, thigh girth 1.8 cm less, and no difference in operating time
  15. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJ, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: open knee ligament reconstruction ranked among the most painful of all 179 procedures on day 1, alongside spinal fusion, calcaneal reduction and foot arthrodesis; the arthroscopic reconstruction on this card is a different operation from the open one in that cohort
  16. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients: rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78. The ACL patient carries every risk factor

Hip and knee › Knee

33 Multiligament knee reconstruction

Reconstruction after knee dislocation: cruciates, posterolateral corner and medial side, single-stage or staged

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Tendon under tension. Three or four grafts pulled through bone tunnels and fixed under tension at different knee angles, then loaded by every degree of the early motion the surgeon needs to prevent arthrofibrosis; underneath that, six to ten tunnels drilled through femur, tibia and fibula, wide medial and lateral dissections, one or two graft harvest sites, a long tourniquet and a knee that was already traumatised

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
General anaesthesia with a continuous adductor canal (femoral triangle) catheter, surgeon infiltration of the lateral and posterior dissection, and IV dexamethasone; sciatic block withheld until the peroneal nerve and the compartments have been examined after surgery
Catheter: routine A continuous technique is the author's default for a score of 5: the tension-and-motion mechanism outlasts any single shot by days. The adductor canal is chosen because it leaves the sciatic territory examinable, which is where the peroneal nerve and all four leg compartments live; this is judgement, since no trial has compared block strategies in multiligament reconstruction
Alternatives: Single-shot popliteal sciatic block with dilute local anaesthetic as a rescue on day 0 or 1, after a documented peroneal examination and with the surgeon's agreement; IPACK block for posterior capsular pain where the surgeon cannot infiltrate it; Femoral nerve catheter: stronger analgesia, a quadriceps that will not fire in a brace-dependent knee; Lumbar epidural for the opioid-tolerant patient, accepting that it masks both the nerve examination and compartment pain; Single-shot adductor canal block on the donor leg when a contralateral graft is harvested
Position
Supine with a lateral thigh post and a foot bolster so the knee rests at 90 degrees and can be moved from full extension to deep flexion; both legs prepared when a contralateral graft is planned; some surgeons turn prone or lateral for an open tibial inlay PCL
Tourniquet
Yes. High thigh cuff, used in instalments: the operation outlasts any single safe inflation, so it is inflated for the open parts and deflated for the arthroscopic ones, or released for a reperfusion interval at 120 min. Usually omitted altogether after a popliteal artery repair
Cement
No
Blood loss
200-500 mL across the case, most of it into the knee and thigh after the cuff comes down; transfusion is unusual unless a vascular repair or other injuries are in the picture
Duration
3-6 h for a single-stage cruciate, posterolateral and medial reconstruction; 2-3 h for each stage of a staged plan
Length of stay
1-3 nights. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV before the tourniquet (3 g over 120 kg), repeated at 4 h; allograft does not change the regimen
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision is reasonable for the haemarthrosis; no multiligament-specific trial. Discuss it first when there is a fresh arterial repair
VTE
Chemoprophylaxis is the default (LMWH or a direct oral anticoagulant by unit protocol) through the period of restricted weight-bearing: a long operation, a tourniquet, a brace and a traumatised limb in one patient. The catheter and any anticoagulation for a vascular repair set the timing
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV; a long case in a young patient on opioids is high risk for nausea
Tell the patient
This is a much bigger operation than an ordinary ligament reconstruction: the knee hurts for the first week, the bending exercises are the painful part and also the important part, and the numbing tube in your thigh is there to make those first days manageable.
The trap
The popliteal artery and the leg compartments: know the vascular status before you start, have someone feel the calf throughout the arthroscopy because a torn capsule lets irrigation fluid into the leg, and do not place a block that hides the peroneal nerve or the compartments before they have been examined

What the surgeon is doing and why

A knee that has dislocated has torn at least two of its four main ligament groups and usually three: both cruciates plus the medial side, the posterolateral corner, or both. The Schenck classification counts them (KD I one cruciate plus a collateral, KD II both cruciates, KD III both cruciates and one side, medial or lateral, KD IV everything, KD V with a fracture). Many dislocations reduce themselves before anyone sees them, so the patient arrives with a swollen, grossly unstable knee and a normal-looking radiograph, and the injury is under-called. The tibia has moved a full bone’s width relative to the femur with the popliteal artery tethered above at the adductor hiatus and below at the soleus arch, and the common peroneal nerve wrapped round the fibular neck. In the pooled literature 18% of dislocations have a vascular injury and 25% a nerve injury, almost always the peroneal, and the pattern most at risk is the one with the lateral side torn.

The surgeon’s problem is that a knee with no cruciates and no collateral cannot be made stable by repairing what is left. Primary repair of the posterolateral corner fails two to three times as often as reconstruction, and cruciate stumps do not hold sutures. So the operation rebuilds each ligament with a tendon graft passed through bone tunnels placed at the anatomical attachments:

  1. Posterior cruciate: a tunnel from the front of the tibia to the back, exiting a few millimetres in front of the popliteal artery, and one or two femoral tunnels. This is the central pillar and is done first.
  2. Anterior cruciate: tibial and femoral tunnels as in an ordinary ACL reconstruction, positioned so that they do not collide with the others.
  3. Posterolateral corner: through a lateral incision the peroneal nerve is found and freed, then one or two grafts rebuild the fibular collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament through a fibular head tunnel, a tibial tunnel and two femoral tunnels.
  4. Medial side: the medial collateral and posterior oblique ligaments are repaired if acute and of good tissue, or reconstructed with a graft through femoral and tibial tunnels.

That is six to ten tunnels in one knee and three or four grafts. A patient has only so many spare tendons, so the grafts come from both hamstrings, the quadriceps tendon, the other leg, or a tissue bank; allograft is used far more here than in isolated ACL surgery. Each graft is tensioned and fixed at a specific angle (the posterior cruciate at 90 degrees with the tibia pulled forward, the lateral structures at about 30 degrees, the anterior cruciate near extension), in a fixed order, because the first graft sets the position of the joint for the rest.

Timing is a trade-off the surgeon makes before you meet the patient. Operating in the first three weeks gives better tissue planes, repairable collateral structures and better scores in the pooled comparisons; operating in the first few days means a swollen limb, a torn capsule that leaks arthroscopy fluid into the leg, and more arthrofibrosis. Most surgeons wait one to three weeks for the capsule to seal and the swelling to settle, with the knee in a brace or, if it will not stay reduced or the artery has been repaired, a spanning external fixator. Some stage the reconstruction (collaterals and posterior cruciate first, anterior cruciate months later) to shorten each operation and reduce stiffness.

The pain logic explains the score. In the 179-procedure cohort, open knee ligament reconstruction was among the most painful operations of all on day 1, and that was for lesser procedures than this one. The dominant mechanism is tendon-tension: several grafts fixed under tension and then deliberately moved, because the commonest complication is arthrofibrosis (a manipulation under anaesthesia in about 9% in the acute posterolateral series) and the only prevention is early range of motion. Underneath it is bone (every tunnel is a drilled osteotomy), muscle (wide medial and lateral dissections and a harvest site or two), and a long tourniquet. The early peak is no higher than a total knee replacement; what earns the 5 is that the movement-evoked pain is renewed at every physiotherapy session for weeks.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Before the day: artery, nerve, timing and the plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs to know that the limb is perfused, what the peroneal nerve was doing before surgery, which ligaments are being rebuilt, with which grafts, and in how many stages.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Read the vascular work-up yourself. An ankle-brachial index below 0.90 after a dislocation predicted an arterial injury needing surgery in every case in the prospective series, and 0.90 or above excluded one; a CT angiogram is the usual next step and intimal injuries can declare late. A patient with a popliteal repair or bypass arrives with a vein graft behind the knee, fasciotomy wounds, an antiplatelet or anticoagulant, and a surgeon who will not want a tourniquet: that changes the block timing, the blood loss and the duration. Record the peroneal nerve function (ankle and great toe dorsiflexion, first web space sensation) in your own notes; one in four of these patients has a deficit before anyone operates, and a foot drop found after your block will otherwise be yours. Ask which leg the grafts are coming from. Screen for the things that travel with high-energy trauma, and for the low-velocity dislocation in the patient with a BMI over 40, who has a higher neurovascular injury rate and a harder airway.

  2. 2 Anaesthesia, the catheter and the examination under anaesthesia

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With the patient asleep and relaxed the surgeon examines both knees: drawer, Lachman, varus and valgus at 0 and 30 degrees, the dial test for the posterolateral corner. This is the definitive map of what is torn and decides the final plan.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    General anaesthesia with a secured airway is the default because of the duration; a spinal does not last and an epidural hides the leg afterwards. Place the adductor canal catheter before induction or immediately after it, at the mid-thigh level and well clear of the tourniquet and the medial incision; the cuff sits high on the thigh, so tunnel the catheter proximally and anteriorly or accept that it goes in at the end of the case under a sterile drape change. Dexamethasone 8 mg IV now. Urinary catheter for anything planned beyond four hours, arterial line only for the patient’s own comorbidity or a fresh vascular repair, forced-air warming on the upper body. Full relaxation for the examination is helpful and brief.

  3. 3 Position, tourniquet strategy and graft harvest

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The knee must move freely from extension to 120 degrees and hold at 90 degrees hands-free. Autografts are harvested first (hamstrings through an anteromedial incision, quadriceps tendon through a short suprapatellar one, sometimes from the other leg) and prepared on a side table while the arthroscopy starts; allografts are thawed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Agree the tourniquet plan aloud: when it goes up, the 120 min limit, and which part of the operation will run without it (see the tourniquet). Antibiotic in before inflation and again at four hours. A contralateral harvest means a second painful leg that nobody blocked: a single-shot adductor canal block on that side is the fix, and the combined local anaesthetic dose across catheter bolus, second block and surgeon infiltration needs adding up for a case this size. Pad the other leg, the heels and the ulnar nerves for a five-hour case, not a one-hour one.

  4. 4 Arthroscopy and the fluid that goes where the capsule lets it

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The joint is inspected, torn menisci are repaired or resected, the cruciate stumps are cleared and the tunnel sites prepared. The surgeon needs fluid distension to see.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the step with the limb-threatening complication. A dislocation tears the capsule, most often posteriorly, and the tear is under-recognised on MRI; arthroscopic fluid follows it into the calf or the thigh. Surgeons counter it by waiting for the capsule to seal, using gravity inflow or low pump pressure, making an outflow incision and working quickly. Your part is surveillance: a nominated person feels the calf and thigh every 15 min through the drapes during the arthroscopic phase and says the result aloud. A calf that becomes tense means stop, convert to dry or open technique and reassess; it does not mean finish the tunnel first. The same fluid can track proximally in a long case, and litres of room-temperature irrigation cool the patient.

  5. 5 Posterior cruciate reconstruction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tibial tunnel is drilled from the front of the tibia to the posterior cruciate footprint on the back, under arthroscopic and fluoroscopic control, with a guard on the guide wire because the popliteal artery lies immediately behind the posterior capsule. The femoral tunnel or tunnels are drilled inside-out or outside-in. The graft is pulled up through the tibia, round the “killer turn” at the back, and into the femur.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The guide wire and reamer breaking through the posterior tibial cortex is the moment the popliteal vessels are at risk. Under tourniquet a vascular injury is silent until the cuff comes down, so the first sign may be a wound that fills, a pale foot or a pressure that sags at deflation; without a tourniquet it is a field that suddenly cannot be cleared. Blood is grouped and screened for every multiligament case, and you should know how to reach a vascular surgeon from that theatre before the case starts. Some surgeons use an open tibial inlay through a posteromedial approach instead, which may mean a position change in mid-operation.

  6. 6 Anterior cruciate tunnels and graft passage

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Tibial and femoral tunnels are placed anatomically while avoiding convergence with the posterior cruciate and collateral tunnels; the graft is passed but not yet fixed on the tibial side.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing new physiologically; note the tourniquet clock. If the plan is to deflate for a reperfusion interval, this is the usual place, and the deflation brings the usual fall in pressure, rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide and a warm acidotic bolus from a large limb. Re-dose muscle relaxant only if the surgeon needs it for flexion; tensioning later is easier to judge without it.

  7. 7 Posterolateral corner and the peroneal nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A lateral hockey-stick incision. The common peroneal nerve is identified behind biceps femoris and released around the fibular neck, both to protect it and because it is often tethered in scar and haematoma. A tunnel is drilled through the fibular head, another through the proximal tibia from front to back, and two in the lateral femoral condyle; one or two grafts are routed to rebuild the fibular collateral, popliteus and popliteofibular ligament.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The nerve is handled, retracted and sometimes found already stretched or ruptured; what the surgeon sees here is the best prognostic information anyone will have, so ask and write it down. This step is the reason the sciatic block waits. A dense popliteal block placed before surgery makes a new foot drop uninterpretable for 12 to 24 hours in the one operation where the surgeon has just dissected the nerve, and it also removes the pain that announces a calf compartment syndrome. The lateral and posterior dissection is infiltrated by the surgeon before closure instead.

  8. 8 Medial side

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A medial incision; the superficial medial collateral and the posterior oblique ligament are repaired to bone with anchors if the tissue is good, or reconstructed with grafts through femoral and tibial tunnels. The saphenous nerve and its infrapatellar branch cross the field.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The medial incision sits close to an adductor canal catheter entry point: this is why the catheter is placed proximally or at the end. Numbness lateral to the incision afterwards is the infrapatellar branch, a surgical consequence and not a block complication, and worth saying to the patient in advance.

  9. 9 Tensioning and fixation in sequence

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With every graft passed, the knee is reduced and the grafts are fixed one at a time: posterior cruciate at 90 degrees with an anterior drawer to restore the tibial step-off, then the posterolateral grafts at about 30 degrees with a valgus and internal rotation force, then the anterior cruciate near extension, then the medial side at 20-30 degrees with varus. The position at each fixation is held by an assistant and checked on the image intensifier.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The surgeon needs a motionless patient and a leg that is not fighting the assistant; a stable depth is the contribution, not a late dose of relaxant that will still be there at closure. Every interference screw is one more point of graft fixed under tension. From here the mechanism on this card exists, and the catheter should be bolused before the end rather than after emergence.

  10. 10 Tourniquet down, haemostasis, closure and brace

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The cuff is released, bleeding from tunnels and dissections is controlled, drains are placed by some surgeons, the wounds are closed in layers and a hinged brace is locked in extension, with a posterior calf support to stop the tibia sagging on the new posterior cruciate.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    At deflation, look at the foot and feel the pulses with the surgeon before the dressings go on: capillary refill, a palpable or Doppler dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial, and a calf that is soft. A pulse that was present before surgery and is absent now is a popliteal injury or a tunnel-related problem until proven otherwise and is dealt with on the table. Give the antiemetic, check the temperature after a long irrigated case, and start the catheter infusion.

  11. 11 Recovery and the first 48 hours

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the knee protected in the brace, the quadriceps firing, the patella mobile, and passive flexion started within days on a set protocol, with touch or partial weight-bearing for six weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Three things are examined in recovery and written down with a time: foot perfusion, peroneal function (dorsiflexion of the ankle and great toe), and the compartments. The adductor canal infusion blocks the saphenous territory and the anterior capsule; it does not block the deep peroneal or tibial nerves, so ischaemic calf pain and pain on passive toe movement still get through, which is the reason it was chosen. Pain that escalates on a running catheter with a tense calf is a surgical review, not a bolus. Once the peroneal examination is documented, posterior and lateral pain that the oral regimen cannot hold is a fair indication for a single-shot popliteal sciatic block with dilute local anaesthetic, agreed with the surgeon and with compartment checks continuing. The catheter runs for 48-72 h, through the first physiotherapy sessions. Chemoprophylaxis starts by unit protocol, timed against the catheter.

Pain plan

The mechanism is grafts under tension in a knee that has to be moved, on top of a great deal of drilled bone, so this is one of the few knee operations where a continuous technique is the author’s default rather than the exception. The plan: general anaesthesia; an adductor canal catheter with a bolus of ropivacaine 0.5% 15-20 mL and an infusion of ropivacaine 0.2% for 48-72 h; surgeon infiltration of the lateral, posterior and harvest-site dissection with a weight-checked dose; intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg; regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor from the first evening unless the surgeon has a specific objection; and an oral opioid, modified-release for the first two or three days in most patients with immediate-release rescue, tapered over the first fortnight. Ketamine by low-dose infusion is reasonable intra-operatively and for the first night in the opioid-tolerant patient.

The block choice follows from two competing facts. The pain is circumferential: anterior and medial from the tunnels and the medial dissection (femoral and saphenous territory), posterior and lateral from the posterior cruciate tunnel, the capsule and the posterolateral corner (sciatic territory). A femoral plus sciatic combination would cover all of it. But the sciatic territory is also where the surveillance is: the peroneal nerve the surgeon has just dissected, and the four compartments of a leg that has had trauma, fluid and a tourniquet. The defensible default is to block the half that can be blocked safely and continuously, cover the other half with infiltration and systemic analgesia, and add a sciatic block later only as a deliberate, documented decision. The adductor canal is preferred over the femoral nerve because the patient is brace-dependent and needs a quadriceps; in ACL reconstruction the randomised comparison found the adductor canal block noninferior for analgesia with better quadriceps strength. None of this has been tested in multiligament surgery, where the literature on analgesia is close to empty.

The rebound problem is larger than after an ACL. The patient is young, the surgery is bone, and a single shot ends at 2 am on the first night with the worst of the pain still to come: the three risk factors from the rebound cohort and a curve that peaks on day 1 and 2. A unit that cannot run a catheter should keep the patient in for at least two nights and plan a repeat single-shot block on the morning of day 1.

Escalation: pain above 7 with a soft calf, a warm foot and a firing extensor hallucis is treated with the rescue opioid, a catheter bolus and a check that the regular drugs were given. Pain out of proportion with a tense calf, or pain on passive toe movement, is compartment syndrome until pressures or a surgeon say otherwise (see compartment syndrome). A tense, hot knee in the first day is a haemarthrosis. A cool or pale foot at any time is the popliteal artery.

Pitfalls and variants

  • After a popliteal artery repair. A vein graft or stent behind the knee, healed or healing fasciotomies, antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, usually no tourniquet (so a wetter, longer case with real blood loss), and a surgeon who will limit flexion. Deep blocks and catheters are timed against the anticoagulant, and foot perfusion checks continue hourly overnight.
  • Staged reconstruction. Each stage is shorter and less painful than the single-stage operation; the first stage (collaterals and posterior cruciate) carries most of the neurovascular risk and the catheter indication, the second is close to an ordinary ACL.
  • Spanning external fixator in place. The first operation may be fixator removal, examination under anaesthesia and reconstruction in one sitting, through pin sites that are colonised.
  • Pre-existing foot drop. A quarter of dislocations have a nerve injury before surgery. Document it, tell the patient that the block did not cause it, and still keep the sciatic territory examinable, because a partial lesion can worsen.
  • The low-velocity dislocation in severe obesity. A fall from standing height dislocates the knee in a patient with a very high BMI; neurovascular injury is more common, the tourniquet fits badly, the ultrasound views are poor and the airway and ventilation over five hours are their own problem.
  • Allograft versus autograft. Allograft shortens the operation and removes the harvest-site pain; bilateral autograft harvest adds a second painful leg and a second block.
  • Open tibial inlay posterior cruciate. A posteromedial approach beside the popliteal vessels, sometimes with a turn to prone or lateral in mid-case: the airway, eyes and pressure areas are re-checked as for a new position.
  • Arthrofibrosis. The commonest complication and the reason analgesia matters beyond comfort: the patient who cannot tolerate flexion in the first weeks returns for a manipulation under anaesthesia.
  • Thromboembolism. Trauma, a long tourniquet, a brace and restricted weight-bearing in one limb. A swollen calf at two weeks is a thrombosis, and a tense calf at two hours is a compartment.
  • Opioid-tolerant and chronic pain patients. Common in a trauma population that has waited weeks for surgery on opioids. The catheter is not optional for them, and the pain service should know before the day.

Key sources

The neurovascular figures rest on a systematic review of 862 dislocations and a small, clean prospective study of the ankle-brachial index. Timing and repair-versus-reconstruction rest on systematic reviews of low-level series. The fluid extravasation risk is described in case reports and narrative review, with no reliable incidence. There is no trial of any analgesic or regional technique in multiligament reconstruction: the block strategy on this card is the author’s reasoning from the innervation, the surveillance needs and the ACL literature, and should be read as that.

  1. Medina O, Arom GA, Yeranosian MG, Petrigliano FA, McAllister DR. Vascular and nerve injury after knee dislocation: a systematic review. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2014;472:2621-2629
    862 dislocations: vascular injury in 18%, of which 80% were repaired and 12% of repaired limbs came to amputation; nerve injury in 25%; highest vascular injury rates in KD IIIL (32%) and posterior dislocations (25%)
  2. Mills WJ, Barei DP, McNair P. The value of the ankle-brachial index for diagnosing arterial injury after knee dislocation: a prospective study. J Trauma 2004;56:1261-1265
    38 dislocations: all 11 patients with an ankle-brachial index below 0.90 had an arterial injury needing surgery; none of the 27 at 0.90 or above had one on serial examination and duplex
  3. Vicenti G, Solarino G, Carrozzo M, et al. Major concern in the multiligament-injured knee treatment: a systematic review. Injury 2019;50 Suppl 2:S89-S94
    Surgery beats non-operative care (Lysholm 85 v 67); six studies of timing favour surgery within three weeks (Lysholm 89 v 82, more range of motion); posterolateral corner repair fails more often than reconstruction (39% v 8%)
  4. Fortier LM, Knapik DM, Condon JJ, et al. Higher success rate observed in reconstruction techniques of acute posterolateral corner knee injuries as compared to repair: an updated systematic review. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc 2023;31:5565-5578
    12 studies, 288 patients operated within four weeks: failure 21.9% after repair and 7.1% after reconstruction; arthrofibrosis needing manipulation under anaesthesia in 8.7%, the commonest complication
  5. Harris G, Kermanshah A, Patel N, et al. Characterization of posterior capsular injury for preoperative planning in closed knee injuries: a narrative review. J Orthop 2025;68:323-330
    Posterior capsular tears, common in multiligament injuries and under-recognised on MRI, allow arthroscopic irrigation fluid to extravasate into the leg, with compartment syndrome as the rare consequence; argues for looking for the tear before planning arthroscopy
  6. Abdallah FW, Whelan DB, Chan VW, et al. Adductor canal block provides noninferior analgesia and superior quadriceps strength compared with femoral nerve block in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Anesthesiology 2016;124:1053-1064
    100 outpatient ACL reconstructions, ropivacaine 0.5% 20 mL: adductor canal block noninferior to femoral block for opioid use and pain over 24 h, with better preserved quadriceps strength; the nearest randomised evidence, and it is from a smaller operation
  7. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    Open knee ligament reconstruction ranked among the most painful of 179 procedures on day 1
  8. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients: rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, and absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78

Hip and knee › Knee

34 High tibial and distal femoral osteotomy

Medial opening wedge and lateral closing wedge tibial osteotomy; distal femoral osteotomy for valgus; plate fixation with or without bone graft

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A near-complete cut through the widest cancellous bone of the tibia or femur, levered open or closed on an intact hinge and then loaded with every step until it unites; the periosteum is elevated around the whole circumference at the cut, the superficial medial collateral ligament is released and then stretched by the opening, and a tourniquet and a possible iliac crest harvest sit on top

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Spinal or general anaesthesia with a single-shot adductor canal block, posterior cover by surgeon infiltration or an IPACK block, and IV dexamethasone; an overnight stay as the default
Catheter: selective An adductor canal catheter for 48 h earns its place for the opioid-tolerant patient, a double-level or bilateral osteotomy, and a large correction with graft harvest; single shot plus posterior cover for the standard opening wedge. Sciatic blocks and catheters are avoided because the anterior compartment and the peroneal nerve are the structures under surveillance. Author's judgement on three small trials and one retrospective series
Alternatives: Femoral triangle or femoral nerve block for a distal femoral osteotomy, where the cut is above the adductor canal block's reach; IPACK block, which outperformed the adductor canal block alone over the first 10 h in one trial; Surgeon periarticular and periosteal infiltration as the only regional component; Fascia iliaca infiltration or a field block at the iliac crest when autograft is harvested
Position
Supine on a radiolucent table with the whole leg from hip to ankle draped free and visible to the image intensifier, a lateral post and foot bolster, and the knee able to go from full extension (alignment check) to 90 degrees (posterior cut)
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Common for the tibial osteotomy, 60-90 min at the thigh; some surgeons operate without one so that bleeding is seen and controlled before closure. A distal femoral osteotomy is too proximal for a standard cuff: a sterile high-thigh tourniquet or none
Cement
No
Blood loss
Little in the field under tourniquet; the cut cancellous surfaces bleed into the leg afterwards, so the calculated loss is several hundred mL and the haemoglobin falls over 48 h. Transfusion is rare
Duration
60-120 min for a single osteotomy, including a preliminary arthroscopy; 150-210 min for a double-level correction or one combined with ligament or cartilage surgery
Length of stay
1-2 nights; day case in selected patients on an established pathway. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV before the tourniquet (3 g over 120 kg)
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision; in the pooled HTO trials it reduced total blood loss by about 220 mL and the haemoglobin fall, with no excess thrombosis
VTE
Chemoprophylaxis by unit protocol for the period of restricted weight-bearing, plus mechanical prophylaxis: a cut long bone, a tourniquet and a patient on crutches
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV
Tell the patient
The bone has been cut and held with a plate, so it behaves like a controlled fracture: expect two or three hard days, pain when you put weight through the leg for several weeks, and a steady improvement as the bone heals.
The trap
This is not a small knee operation: it is a deliberate fracture in a young, working patient who was booked as a day case, with a first night that needs a plan and an anterior compartment that needs to be examinable

What the surgeon is doing and why

A knee that is bowed carries its load through one compartment. In a varus knee the line from the centre of the hip to the centre of the ankle passes medial to the knee, the medial cartilage takes most of the body weight, wears, and the wear increases the bow. The patient is typically 40 to 60, active, often a manual worker, with medial joint pain and a lateral compartment that is still healthy. A knee replacement would work and would wear out; a unicompartmental replacement restricts heavy use. An osteotomy keeps the patient’s own joint and moves the load: the bone is cut just outside the joint and re-angled so that the weight-bearing line passes through the healthy compartment instead.

Where the cut goes depends on where the deformity is. Varus usually lives in the proximal tibia, so the standard operation is a high tibial osteotomy. Valgus usually lives in the distal femur, so the mirror-image operation is a distal femoral osteotomy. Large deformities get both.

There are two ways to change the angle of a bone:

 Opening wedge (medial tibia)        Closing wedge (lateral tibia)

    |        |                           |        |
    |  cut   |  lateral hinge            | wedge  |
  ==>--------o  stays intact             o--------<==  bone removed,
    | gap    |                           |        |    gap closed
    | opens  |                           |        |
   plate medial, gap may be grafted     plate or staples lateral,
                                        fibula must be released

The medial opening wedge is the dominant technique. Through an anteromedial incision the surgeon releases the distal superficial medial collateral ligament, passes two guide wires obliquely from the medial metaphysis towards the tip of the fibular head, and saws along them through the medial, anterior and posterior cortices, stopping about a centimetre short of the lateral cortex. That bridge of intact lateral bone is the hinge. A second, ascending cut behind the tibial tubercle leaves the patellar tendon attached to the distal fragment. The cut is then levered open slowly, over minutes, until a long rod or cable from the hip centre to the ankle centre crosses the knee at the planned point (classically 62% of the way across the plateau from the medial side), and an angle-stable plate is fixed across the gap. Gaps beyond about 10-12 mm are often filled with iliac crest autograft, allograft wedges or a synthetic substitute; smaller gaps are left to fill themselves.

The lateral closing wedge removes a measured wedge from the lateral tibia and closes the gap. It unites faster because bone meets bone, but it needs the anterior compartment muscles lifted off the tibia and the fibula released (an osteotomy of the fibula or a disruption of the proximal tibiofibular joint), which puts the common peroneal nerve and the anterior compartment at risk.

A distal femoral osteotomy is the same idea above the joint: a lateral opening wedge or a medial closing wedge of the supracondylar femur, through a subvastus approach with the vastus elevated off the septum, the femoral vessels a few centimetres away at the adductor hiatus, and a long plate.

The pain logic is the logic of a fracture that somebody then walks on. The cut crosses the full width of well-innervated metaphyseal bone; the periosteum is elevated front, medial and back to make room for the saw and the retractors; the opened gap stretches the medial soft tissues; and the hinge sometimes cracks. In 244 opening wedge osteotomies under a standard multimodal protocol, a lateral hinge fracture occurred in 95 and independently raised day 1 pain, by about half a point. Unlike the bone work of an arthroplasty, the pain generator has not been removed and the cut bone is loaded from the first days: modern locking plates allow partial weight-bearing early, and each step compresses and shears the osteotomy until it unites at 6 to 12 weeks. That is why this sits at a 4 with total knee arthroplasty rather than at a 3 with ACL reconstruction: a moderate bone peak, a rebound first night, and movement- and load-evoked pain for weeks. It does not reach a 5 because nothing is under tension and the trajectory falls steadily.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Planning, the booking and the anaesthetic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has measured the correction on long-leg standing films and knows the opening in millimetres, whether a graft is planned and from where, and whether an arthroscopy, cartilage procedure or ligament reconstruction is being added.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The correction size is your pain predictor: a 6 mm opening without graft is at the bottom of this card’s range, a 14 mm opening with iliac crest autograft or a double-level osteotomy at the top. Spinal anaesthesia suits a single osteotomy of 60-90 min and is what most of the trial populations had; general anaesthesia suits the combined or double-level case. Place the adductor canal block before either, at mid-thigh and clear of the cuff, and give dexamethasone 8 mg IV. Decide the posterior cover now: either the surgeon infiltrates the posterior periosteum and capsule under direct vision, or an IPACK block goes in with the adductor canal block. Document ankle and great toe dorsiflexion before any block, because the peroneal nerve is one of the structures this operation can injure. The patient is often booked as a day case on the strength of a small incision; the default should be one night.

  2. 2 Position, tourniquet and arthroscopy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The whole limb must be visible on the image intensifier from the femoral head to the ankle so that alignment can be checked with a rod. Most surgeons begin with an arthroscopy to confirm that the lateral compartment is healthy enough to take the load and to deal with meniscal tears or loose bodies.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Lead for everyone, since the intensifier is used repeatedly from hip to ankle. Antibiotic before the cuff, tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision. If the arthroscopy finds lateral compartment damage the operation may stop there, which is rare and worth knowing is possible. A tourniquet is used by most for the tibial osteotomy; a surgeon who works without one will want normotension and will lose a few hundred mL in the field.

  3. 3 Approach and medial release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    An oblique anteromedial incision over the pes anserinus. The hamstring tendons are retracted or released, and the distal fibres of the superficial medial collateral ligament are elevated off the tibia so that the medial side can open; without that release the opening wedge would compress the medial compartment it is meant to unload. A blunt retractor is passed behind the tibia, directly on bone, to protect the popliteal vessels.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve crosses this incision and is often cut: a patch of numbness lateral to the scar is expected and is not a block injury. The subperiosteal elevation here and around the back of the tibia is the periosteal component of the pain and the target for the surgeon’s infiltration.

  4. 4 Guide wires and the hinge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Two parallel wires are driven from the medial cortex towards the tip of the fibular head under fluoroscopy. They define the plane of the cut and its end point, which must sit in the safe zone at the level of the proximal tibiofibular joint, where the surrounding soft tissue supports the lateral cortex.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Dead time with repeated screening. A hinge point that is too low or too medial is what later cracks into the lateral cortex or the plateau, lengthening the case and worsening the first day.

  5. 5 The cuts

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    An oscillating saw and then osteotomes complete the transverse cut through the posterior and medial cortices up to the hinge, with the knee flexed to 90 degrees so that the popliteal artery falls back from the posterior cortex, and the ascending anterior cut frees the tubercle fragment.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The posterior cortex is cut within a centimetre of the popliteal artery and the tibial nerve, with only a retractor between. Arterial injury is rare, is silent under tourniquet, and declares itself at deflation as a wound that fills, a pale foot, or days later as a pulsatile swelling behind the knee. Under spinal the patient feels vibration and hears the saw: sedation or headphones. This is the peak of intra-operative nociception under general anaesthesia if the block has not set.

  6. 6 Opening the wedge and checking alignment

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Stacked osteotomes or a spreader open the cut gradually, over several minutes, so that the lateral hinge deforms plastically and does not snap. The knee is brought into full extension, the alignment rod is laid from hip centre to ankle centre and screened at the knee, and the opening is adjusted until the line crosses the target point. The posterior gap is kept larger than the anterior so that the tibial slope is not increased.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The surgeon needs the leg fully extended and still for the alignment check, with an assistant applying axial load at the heel; a patient moving under light sedation at this point costs accuracy. A crack that the room hears is the hinge. The surgeon will add a lateral screw or staple, or accept it and slow the weight-bearing, and you should move the patient up one notch on the pain plan, since a hinge fracture is an independent predictor of a worse first day.

  7. 7 Plate fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A long medial angle-stable plate bridges the gap, with locking screws in the proximal fragment under the plateau and in the shaft. The construct is a splint that has to carry body weight across an open gap for two to three months.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Drilling and screw insertion; nothing physiological. The plate sits subcutaneously on the medial tibia and is a common source of late local pain, which is why many are removed after union (see removal of metalwork).

  8. 8 Filling the gap

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Small openings are left empty. Larger ones are packed with cancellous or tricortical autograft from the iliac crest, allograft wedges, or a ceramic substitute, to speed union and support the plate.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    An iliac crest harvest is a second operation with its own periosteal pain, often the worse of the two sites on day 1 and outside any knee block. Ask the surgeon to infiltrate the crest and the periosteum generously before closing it, and count that volume against the total local anaesthetic dose with the adductor canal block, the IPACK and the knee infiltration.

  9. 9 Tourniquet down, haemostasis and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The cuff is released before closure by surgeons who want to see the bleeding from the cut surfaces and the vessels behind the tibia; others close under tourniquet with a drain. The hamstring layer is closed over the plate and the leg goes into a hinged brace or a simple dressing by surgeon preference.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    At deflation look at the foot with the surgeon: colour, capillary refill and a pulse. Blood from the osteotomy now tracks into the calf, which is the mechanism of the swelling, the bruising to the ankle and the occasional compartment problem. Give the antiemetic. If an adductor canal catheter is planned and the entry point was too close to the field to place earlier, it goes in now.

  10. 10 Recovery, the first night and weight-bearing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants early knee movement, an active quadriceps, and protected weight-bearing on crutches that progresses to full weight over two to six weeks depending on the plate, the gap and the hinge.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Three checks before the spinal or block obscures them further and again as it recedes: foot perfusion, ankle and great toe dorsiflexion, and a soft anterior compartment. An adductor canal block leaves the deep peroneal and tibial territories intact, so pain on passive toe flexion and a tense shin still mean what they should. The first oral paracetamol and NSAID go in before the spinal recedes, the rescue opioid is charted with a dose that reflects a 4 and not a knee arthroscopy, and the patient is told that the first steps on crutches will hurt at the cut and that this is the bone being loaded, not the plate failing. Rebound pain is the expected course after a single-shot block for bone surgery in a young patient, so the night plan is written down.

Pain plan

The mechanism is a loaded bone cut with a circumferential periosteal elevation, so the block has to cover the front and the back of the proximal tibia for the first night and the oral regimen has to carry the patient for weeks. The innervation is split: the anteromedial tibia, the incision and the medial periosteum are saphenous and femoral territory; the posterior cortex and capsule are tibial and sciatic territory. The three small trials line up with that anatomy. An adductor canal block against placebo cut early opioid use sharply (17% against 70% needing opioid in the first 12 h) without weakening the quadriceps. A femoral block and a sciatic block, compared head to head under general anaesthesia with full multimodal analgesia, gave identical morphine use at 24 h (24 mg in each group), which reads as each covering half the operation. And an IPACK block gave lower pain for the first 10 h and longer analgesia than an adductor canal block alone, which says the posterior half matters.

The defensible default follows: spinal or general anaesthesia; a single-shot adductor canal block with ropivacaine 0.5% 15-20 mL; posterior cover by surgeon infiltration of the posterior periosteum and capsule or by an IPACK block; intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg; regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor; and an oral opioid for the first three to five days, with a modified-release component for the first two nights in most patients. On NSAIDs and bone healing, surgeons vary: the worry is non-union of an opening wedge, the human evidence for harm from a short course is weak, and the author’s practice is a course limited to the first one to two weeks unless the surgeon objects.

Why not the sciatic block, which would cover the posterior tibia better than either alternative. Because the structures at risk in this operation are in its territory: the anterior compartment, which takes the bleeding from the osteotomy and is directly dissected in a closing wedge, and the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck. A dense sciatic block makes a foot drop uninterpretable and removes the pain that announces a compartment syndrome. The adductor canal and IPACK combination covers most of the pain and leaves both examinable. This is the author’s judgement; the one trial that used a sciatic block reported no harm in 25 patients, which is not a safety signal either way.

The catheter decision: an adductor canal catheter for 48 h is reasonable where the patient or the operation predicts a hard course (opioid tolerance, double-level or bilateral surgery, a large opening with crest harvest, a hinge fracture in a patient who is already struggling), and unnecessary for a standard opening wedge with good posterior cover. There is no trial of continuous techniques in osteotomy.

Escalation: pain above 7 on day 1 with a soft shin and normal toe movement is treated with the rescue opioid and a check that the regular drugs were given; a rescue adductor canal block the next morning largely spares the quadriceps. Pain out of proportion with a tense anterior compartment, or pain on passive plantarflexion of the toes, is compartment syndrome until proven otherwise (see compartment syndrome). A sudden increase in pain on weight-bearing in the first weeks, with a new deformity or a click, is loss of fixation through a hinge fracture.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Lateral closing wedge tibial osteotomy. Anterior compartment muscles elevated, the fibula released, the peroneal nerve close to both: more compartment and nerve risk, more muscle pain, faster union. Keep the sciatic territory examinable and say so in the notes.
  • Distal femoral osteotomy. The cut is in the supracondylar femur, above the reach of a distal adductor canal block: use a femoral triangle or femoral nerve block and accept some quadriceps weakness for the first day. The vastus is elevated and aches. The femoral vessels lie posteromedial to the cut. Blood loss is higher than for the tibia and a standard tourniquet does not fit.
  • Double-level osteotomy. Femur and tibia in one sitting for a large deformity: two to three hours, both pain territories, more bleeding, and the clearest catheter indication on this card.
  • Combined procedures. Osteotomy with ACL reconstruction, cartilage repair or meniscal transplant is common in the younger patient; the pain course is set by the osteotomy and the duration by the rest.
  • Iliac crest autograft. A second pain site that no knee block reaches; infiltration at the crest is the only cover.
  • Hinge fracture. Common in opening wedges, usually stable, sometimes extending into the plateau. It lengthens the case, restricts weight-bearing and raises day 1 pain modestly.
  • The smoker and the patient with a high BMI. Both delay union of an opening wedge, and both are over-represented in the population offered this operation. The NSAID conversation with the surgeon matters more for them.
  • Day-case pathways. Feasible in established units with a spinal, blocks, infiltration and a written night plan. The failure mode is the rebound at 2 am in a young patient with a cut tibia, and a pathway without a reliable overnight contact is not ready.
  • Popliteal artery injury. Rare, and silent under tourniquet. A foot that is pale at deflation is treated as an arterial injury on the table, and a pulsatile popliteal swelling in the first weeks is a pseudoaneurysm.
  • Thromboembolism. A long bone cut and reduced weight-bearing: calf swelling is common from the haematoma alone, which makes a thrombosis easy to miss.

Key sources

There is no PROSPECT guideline for osteotomy and the analgesic evidence is four small single-centre trials: one of adductor canal block against placebo, one of femoral against sciatic block, one of IPACK against adductor canal block, and a retrospective series on hinge fractures and pain. They agree with each other and with the anatomy, which is the main reason to trust them. The tranexamic acid meta-analysis is small but consistent with the arthroplasty evidence. The compartment and peroneal nerve cautions are consensus from the surgical literature, without reliable incidence figures, and the advice against sciatic block is the author’s judgement.

  1. Kull C, Martin R, Rossel JB, Nguyen A, Albrecht E. Femoral vs sciatic nerve block to provide analgesia after medial open wedge high tibial osteotomy in the setting of multimodal analgesia: a randomized, controlled, single-blinded trial. J Clin Anesth 2024;93:111355
    50 patients under general anaesthesia, ropivacaine 100 mg to either nerve: IV morphine at 24 h was 24 mg in both groups, with no difference in rest or dynamic pain to 48 h or function at six months; neither single nerve covers the operation
  2. Sim JA, Lee MG, Jung WS, Lee BK, Lee BH. Clinical efficacy of adductor canal block in medial open wedge high tibial osteotomy. Knee 2021;29:9-14
    35 patients, single-shot adductor canal block against saline: lower pain in the first 12 h, opioid needed in 12 h by 17% against 70%, heavy opioid use over 72 h in 8% against 50%, no quadriceps weakness
  3. Aboelfadl GM, Elawamy AM, Ahmed SH, Askar FJ, Aboelfadl AM. Infiltration of local anesthetic in the interspace between the popliteal artery and capsule of the posterior knee (IPACK block) versus adductor canal block for pain relief after open wedge high tibial osteotomy: a randomized clinical trial. Minerva Anestesiol 2024;90:618-625
    60 patients under spinal, bupivacaine 0.25% 20 mL with dexamethasone: IPACK gave lower pain scores for the first 10 h, longer analgesia (about 490 against 300 min), less rescue analgesia and a shorter stay than adductor canal block
  4. Jung WH, Agiwal Y, Goyal S, Kim DH, Takeuchi R. Intraoperative lateral hinge fractures and early postoperative pain burden after medial opening wedge high tibial osteotomy. Cureus 2026;18:e115457
    244 opening wedge osteotomies under spinal with a standard multimodal protocol: day 1 mean pain 3.8 with a hinge fracture (95 patients) and 3.3 without; a hinge fracture independently predicted more pain, by about half a point
  5. Fang Q, Zhang Z, Wang D, et al. Effect of tranexamic acid on blood management during a high tibial osteotomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Orthop Surg 2022;14:1940-1950
    Six studies: tranexamic acid lowered total blood loss by a weighted mean of 219 mL and the day 1 haemoglobin fall by about 10 g/L, with no difference in thrombotic events
  6. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
