  • The ipsilateral femoral neck fracture. Present in a minority of high-energy shaft fractures and missed on the trauma series; it changes the operation to a retrograde nail with screws into the neck, or a cephalomedullary device, and adds an hour.
  • Bilateral femoral fractures. Two litres in the thighs before the operation, two reamings, a higher fat embolism rate (4.6% against 2.9% in the systematic review), a free-leg technique, and a patient who is borderline by definition. One or both fixators first is a reasonable call.
  • The floating knee. Ipsilateral femoral and tibial fractures, usually nailed through one knee incision (retrograde femur, antegrade tibia); a long case with two reamings and a sore knee for months.
  • The obese patient. The trochanter cannot be reached antegrade, so retrograde nailing; a traction table that may not take the weight; a difficult airway and a difficult arterial line.
  • The older patient after a fall. The same nail with a hip fracture physiology: anticoagulants to reverse, a dry patient, a long reaming of an osteoporotic canal that bleeds, and delirium on the ward. The hip fracture card applies.
  • The pathological fracture. A metastasis in the shaft means a long nail reamed through tumour, with embolisation of tumour and fat together, often a larger blood loss, and a conversation about the rest of the skeleton and the prognosis before the operation.
  • The open femoral fracture. Antibiotics within an hour of injury, debridement, and either a primary nail (most Gustilo I-IIIA fractures) or an external fixator for the contaminated or vascular injury; see the open fracture card.
  • The head-injured patient. Early fixation does not cause secondary brain injury; hypoxia, hypotension and raised intracranial pressure do, and a reaming-induced desaturation is a brain insult in this patient.
  • The perineal post complaint. Numbness of the genitalia or erectile dysfunction after the traction table is a pudendal neuropraxia; it resolves over weeks to months, needs documentation, and is prevented by padding and short traction times.
  • Nail removal. Elective removal of a femoral nail after union is harder than it looks and bleeds more than expected; see removal of metalwork.

Key sources

The evidence on timing is the strongest part of this card and the weakest part of most anaesthetists’ knowledge of it: Bone’s randomised trial for early fixation, Scalea’s series for damage control, and Pape’s randomised trial for the borderline patient between them define who is nailed on the day. The reamed versus unreamed question is settled by the Canadian trial. The fat embolism literature is observational and the incidence has fallen with early fixation. The perineal post review is recent and sobering. There is no procedure-specific analgesia guideline; the block and catheter advice here is extrapolated from the hip fracture recommendations and is the author’s judgement where the card says so.

  1. Bone LB, Johnson KD, Weigelt J, Scheinberg R. Early versus delayed stabilization of femoral fractures: a prospective randomized study. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1989;71:336-340
    178 patients randomised to early or delayed femoral stabilisation: in the multiply injured group, delayed fixation carried more ARDS, fat embolism and pneumonia, a longer stay and more ICU days; the trial that made early fixation the standard
  2. Pape HC, Rixen D, Morley J, et al. Impact of the method of initial stabilization for femoral shaft fractures in patients with multiple injuries at risk for complications (borderline patients). Ann Surg 2007;246:491-499
    165 multiply injured patients randomised to primary nailing within 24 h or external fixation with later conversion: in the 44 borderline patients, primary nailing carried an adjusted odds ratio of 6.69 for acute lung injury; in stable patients primary nailing shortened ventilation
  3. Scalea TM, Boswell SA, Scott JD, et al. External fixation as a bridge to intramedullary nailing for patients with multiple injuries and with femur fractures: damage control orthopedics. J Trauma 2000;48:613-621
    43 patients with initial external fixation compared with 284 primary nailings: temporary external fixation was safe in multiply injured patients, the paper that named damage control orthopaedics
  4. Lempert M, Halvachizadeh S, Ellanti P, et al. Incidence of fat embolism syndrome in femur fractures and its associated risk factors over time: a systematic review. J Clin Med 2021;10:2733
    15 studies, 3,095 patients: fat embolism syndrome fell from 7.9% (1960-1979) to 1.7% (2000-2019); bilateral fractures 4.6% versus unilateral 2.9%; TOE detects embolic material during reaming in 88% of patients; mortality 1-10%; treatment supportive
  5. Attenasio A, Kraeutler MJ, Hong IS, et al. Are complications related to the perineal post on orthopaedic traction tables for surgical fracture fixation more common than we think? A systematic review. Patient Saf Surg 2023;17:5
    10 studies, 351 patients, 83.5% femoral shaft fractures: erectile dysfunction in 10.0%, genital sensory disturbance in 6.3%, perineal skin necrosis in 3.1%; pudendal palsy correlated with summed perineal pressure; risk factors are traction force and time; posts under 9 cm diameter may contribute
  6. CRASH-2 trial collaborators. Effects of tranexamic acid on death, vascular occlusive events, and blood transfusion in trauma patients with significant haemorrhage (CRASH-2): a randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet 2010;376:23-32
    20,211 bleeding trauma patients: tranexamic acid 1 g then 1 g over 8 h reduced all-cause mortality (14.5% vs 16.0%) with no excess of vascular occlusive events; the benefit is confined to treatment within 3 h of injury
  7. Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society. Nonunion following intramedullary nailing of the femur with and without reaming: results of a multicenter randomized clinical trial. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2003;85:2093-2096
    224 patients randomised to reamed or unreamed femoral nailing: nonunion 1.7% reamed versus 7.5% unreamed, with no difference in pulmonary complications
  8. Giannoudis PV, MacDonald DA, Matthews SJ, et al. Nonunion of the femoral diaphysis: the influence of reaming and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. J Bone Joint Surg Br 2000;82:655-658
    Case-control study associating NSAID use with femoral diaphyseal nonunion and delayed healing; the paper behind many surgeons' request to withhold NSAIDs after nailing

Trauma › Trauma

41 Tibial shaft nailing and tibial plateau fixation

Infrapatellar and suprapatellar intramedullary nailing of the tibial shaft; open reduction and internal fixation of tibial plateau fractures, staged with a spanning external fixator for high-energy patterns

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A reamed tibial canal with an entry through the patellar tendon or the knee (nail), or a crushed articular surface elevated, grafted and plated under periosteal stripping on one or both sides of the proximal tibia (plateau), in a limb whose soft-tissue envelope is thin, bruised and swollen; plus the tourniquet and the raw bone defect that a bone graft fills. The compartment syndrome risk shapes the block, not the pain

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Single-shot popliteal sciatic and adductor canal (or femoral) blocks with dilute local anaesthetic and no adjuncts, placed after a documented compartment examination and with a surveillance plan the surgeon has agreed; dense long-acting blocks and catheters avoided in the fresh high-energy fracture
Catheter: selective Avoided in the fresh high-energy shaft fracture and the fracture-dislocation plateau in the first 48 h, where the compartment syndrome risk is highest; reasonable for the delayed definitive plateau fixation at 7-14 days with a fixator already on, when the swelling has settled and the window for compartment syndrome has closed
Alternatives: Spinal anaesthesia for the isolated shaft nail in a stable fasted patient, with a short-acting agent so the leg can be examined by the evening; General anaesthesia with multimodal analgesia and ketamine, no block, for the fracture-dislocation plateau in the first 48 h; Surgeon's local infiltration at the entry point and plate incisions
Position
Supine on a radiolucent table; knee flexed over a triangle or bolster for infrapatellar nailing, semi-extended over a small bump for suprapatellar nailing; supine with a bump under the hip and the knee flexed for lateral plateau plating; the leg often brought over the side or a posteromedial approach done with the hip externally rotated
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Not used for nailing (reaming needs the bleeding bone to be seen and a thigh tourniquet obstructs the entry point); commonly used for plateau ORIF at 250-300 mmHg for up to 120 min, deflated before closure in a limb whose circulation is already in question
Cement
No
Blood loss
Shaft nailing 200-400 mL; plateau ORIF 300-600 mL under tourniquet and more once it is released, with a bicondylar dual-incision case bleeding across a long operation. The fracture itself has lost 500 mL or more into the leg
Duration
Shaft nailing 60-120 min; lateral plateau ORIF 90-150 min; bicondylar plateau with dual incisions and bone graft 180-300 min
Length of stay
2-5 nights for a shaft nail; the staged plateau has two admissions or one long one, with the definitive fixation at 7-14 days and a stay of 3-7 nights after it. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); open fractures were due their antibiotic within an hour of injury and follow the open fracture plan
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction for plateau ORIF; reasonable for nailing
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin from the night of surgery, continued through the non-weight-bearing period for a plateau fracture (6-12 weeks); mechanical prophylaxis on the other leg
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (it also prolongs whatever block is used, so it is withheld when a short, examinable block is the aim) and ondansetron 4 mg IV
Tell the patient
The first two days after a tibial operation are the hard ones, because the leg swells inside a tight skin; the pain then settles over a week, and the knee stays sore at the front for a long time after a nail, which is normal and not a sign of anything wrong.
The trap
Compartment syndrome is the complication of this bone, it declares itself in the first 48 h, and the thing that hides it is a dense long-acting block that nobody planned a surveillance for: the current UK guidance is that dilute single-shot blocks without adjuncts do not delay the diagnosis when the observation is competent, and that a block placed without that observation does

What the surgeon is doing and why

The tibia is the bone with the worst soft-tissue envelope in the body: a subcutaneous anteromedial border, a thin skin over it with a poor blood supply, and four muscle compartments bound by unyielding fascia behind and lateral to it. Everything that is difficult about tibial fracture surgery follows from that. A shaft fracture bleeds into compartments that cannot expand, so compartment syndrome is the complication of this bone and not of the femur. A plateau fracture crushes the articular surface of the knee and swells the skin over it until the surgeon cannot close an incision, so high-energy plateau fractures are fixed in two stages a fortnight apart. The anaesthetic decisions on this card (the block, the tourniquet, the timing) are all soft-tissue and compartment decisions before they are pain decisions.

    tibial injury
         |
   +-----+------------------------+
 shaft fracture               plateau fracture
   |                               |
 reamed locked nail        low energy (Schatzker I-III,
   |                       lateral split or depression):
 infrapatellar               single-stage ORIF, lateral plate
 (knee flexed, through           |
  patellar tendon)        high energy (IV-VI, medial, bicondylar,
    or                    fracture-dislocation):
 suprapatellar              day 0  spanning external fixator
 (semi-extended,             +/- fasciotomy
  through the joint)        day 7-14  ORIF when the wrinkle
                                      sign returns

Shaft nailing. The nail is a reamed, locked intramedullary splint, as for the femur, inserted from the top of the tibia. The infrapatellar approach flexes the knee to 90 degrees over a bolster and splits or retracts the patellar tendon to reach the entry point; the fracture is reduced by hand against the flexed knee, which is awkward for proximal fractures. The suprapatellar approach nails the tibia semi-extended through a small incision above the patella and a cannula through the patellofemoral joint, which holds the fracture reduced by gravity and gives better alignment (4% against 26% malalignment in the systematic review) at the cost of instruments through the articular cartilage. Anterior knee pain is the signature complaint after tibial nailing whichever route is used, 29% after suprapatellar and 39% after infrapatellar in the pooled studies, not significantly different; it is attributed to the tendon split, the fat pad, the nail tip and the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve, and it lasts for months.

Plateau fixation. The Schatzker classification sorts plateau fractures by energy and side: I-III are lateral split, split-depression and pure depression fractures from a valgus force; IV is the medial plateau, a high-energy injury that is really a fracture-dislocation of the knee with a popliteal artery and a peroneal nerve at risk; V and VI are bicondylar, with VI dissociating the metaphysis from the shaft. The low-energy lateral fracture is fixed in one sitting through a lateral incision: the depressed joint surface is elevated through a cortical window, the void beneath it filled with bone graft or substitute, and a lateral plate buttresses the split. The high-energy fracture arrives with a leg too swollen to open: the surgeon spans the knee with an external fixator on day 0, does a fasciotomy if the compartments are tight, and returns at 7-14 days when the skin wrinkles again to plate both columns through lateral and posteromedial incisions. In the series of 67 high-energy plateaus spanned within 48 h, compartment syndrome occurred in 27%, and in 53% of medial fracture-dislocations; ten cases declared after the frame was on, and three were diagnosed late. Wound breakdown and infection after extensive stripping run at around 20% in the older series, which is the reason for the staging.

The pain logic is bone with two amplifiers. The reamed canal and the entry point (nail), or the elevated, grafted and plated metaphysis (plateau), hurt as bone does for two or three days, then fall. The amplifiers are the tourniquet for a long plateau fixation and the soft-tissue envelope: the leg swells inside skin that cannot stretch, and movement-evoked pain limits the early knee range a plateau fixation needs. The score is 4: the first 48 h need a robust plan, rebound after a single-shot block is high because the bone and the swelling are both at their worst when it wears off, and the plateau patient has a knee that must bend while non-weight-bearing for six to twelve weeks. A catheter would be the obvious answer and is exactly what the compartment syndrome risk argues against in the first two days, which is the tension this card is about.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Emergency department: splint, compartments, block decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the fracture splinted, the skin and compartments examined and documented, a CT for any plateau fracture, an ankle-brachial index or CT angiogram for a medial plateau or a knee that looks dislocated, and the staging decision made.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The compartment examination before any block is the baseline against which the next 48 h are read: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch of the toes, a tense compartment, and later paraesthesia; the pressure measurement (a differential of diastolic minus compartment pressure below 30 mmHg is McQueen’s threshold for fasciotomy) belongs to the surgeon. The block decision follows the Association of Anaesthetists’ 2021 guideline: a single-shot peripheral block with a lower concentration of local anaesthetic and no adjuncts is not associated with delayed diagnosis provided surveillance is competent; a dense, long-acting block or a neuraxial technique that lasts well beyond the operation is to be avoided; the patient is told and consents; and neither surgeon nor anaesthetist can veto the other. The retrospective series of 791 tibial fixations found compartment syndrome diagnosed in hospital in 2.2% overall and no excess of missed cases with blocks, with the caveat that all four missed cases in the blocked group had catheters.

  2. 2 Induction and the unfasted, swollen leg

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A closed shaft fracture is nailed within 24 h in a stable patient; a high-energy plateau is spanned the same day and fixed a fortnight later; a low-energy plateau waits for the swelling to settle if the skin is in doubt.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The acute case is a rapid sequence induction counted from the time of injury. A spinal is reasonable for the isolated shaft nail in a stable, fasted patient if a short-acting agent is used so the leg can be examined that evening; it is the wrong technique for a fracture-dislocation plateau in the first 48 h. The delayed definitive plateau fixation with a frame on is an elective anaesthetic with a block or a catheter that the compartment window no longer argues against. Cefazolin 2 g IV; dexamethasone withheld when the aim is a short, examinable block.

  3. 3 Positioning and the tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Nailing: supine, knee flexed over a triangle (infrapatellar) or semi-extended over a bump (suprapatellar), the C-arm from the opposite side, no tourniquet because the reamed bone must bleed and a thigh cuff obstructs the entry. Plateau: supine with a bump under the ipsilateral hip and the knee flexed for the lateral approach; the posteromedial approach needs the hip externally rotated and the leg figure-of-four; a thigh tourniquet at 250-300 mmHg is common.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The tourniquet on a plateau fixation runs long, often to its 120-min limit before the surgeon asks for a deflate-and-reinflate, and it is applied to a limb whose circulation is already in doubt; see the tourniquet. A plateau fracture-dislocation with a vascular injury does not get a tourniquet. The peroneal nerve at the fibular neck is the nerve at risk from positioning and from the lateral plate, and a foot drop after surgery is attributed to the block until someone checks the timeline; document the foot before the block.

  4. 4 Nailing: entry point and reaming

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Infrapatellar: a 3-cm incision over the patellar tendon, the tendon split or retracted, an awl or guidewire into the anterior plateau just medial to the lateral tibial spine, and the canal opened. Suprapatellar: a 3-cm incision above the patella, a protective cannula through the patellofemoral joint, and the same entry point reached with the knee at 20 degrees. Flexible reamers are passed over a guidewire across the reduced fracture to 1-1.5 mm over the nail diameter.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming the tibia embolises marrow as the femur does, with a smaller load. The thing that matters at this step is the compartment pressure: reaming raises it, the fracture has already bled into the deep posterior compartment, and a leg that is tense at the end of a nailing is one the surgeon should feel before the drapes come off. The tendon split and the entry through the fat pad are the anterior knee pain that follows.

  5. 5 Nailing: nail insertion, locking and the compartment check

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The nail is driven over the guidewire, locked proximally through a jig and distally freehand under imaging, the fracture compressed by backslapping, and alignment and rotation checked against the other leg.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Freehand distal locking is 10-15 min of fluoroscopy with a still leg. At the end of the case, before the patient wakes, the surgeon examines the compartments, and some will measure pressures in a high-energy fracture; this is the moment the first 48 h of surveillance starts from. A patient waking with a working dilute block will not report pain out of proportion that evening, so the ward observations have to be the palpation, the passive stretch of the toes and the pressure, on a chart, by someone trained to read it.

  6. 6 Plateau: the spanning external fixator

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For the high-energy fracture, two pins in the femur and two in the tibial shaft, connected by bars across the knee, restore length and alignment by ligamentotaxis and hold the leg still while the swelling settles. A fasciotomy is done at the same sitting if the compartments are tight, and in the medial fracture-dislocation many surgeons release them prophylactically.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A short general anaesthetic, 30-45 min, often at night, in a patient who may have other injuries. No block that lasts beyond the operation: compartment syndrome in this group declares itself in the next 48 h in up to half of medial fracture-dislocations and a fifth of bicondylar fractures, and the frame holding the foot in neutral makes the examination harder, which is how the late diagnoses in the series happened. Analgesia for the first two days is opioid-based and multimodal, with ketamine, and the pain score that matters is the one that rises despite it.

  7. 7 Plateau: the wait and the wrinkle sign

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon waits 7-14 days until the skin over the proximal tibia wrinkles when pinched, the fracture blisters have epithelialised and the swelling has gone; opening earlier costs a wound breakdown and a deep infection in a joint with a plate in it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The patient is on the ward in a frame, immobile, on opioids; this is the window for VTE, for pin-site infection and for the delirium of an older patient. The definitive operation is then elective in all but name, and the compartment window has closed: a catheter is reasonable for the definitive fixation and the author’s preference for a bicondylar case.

  8. 8 Plateau: approach, elevation of the joint surface and bone graft

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through an anterolateral incision the surgeon lifts the anterior compartment off the lateral plateau, opens the submeniscal joint, elevates the depressed articular fragments from below through a cortical window with a bone tamp under fluoroscopy, and packs the void with autograft from the iliac crest, allograft or a calcium phosphate substitute. A bicondylar fracture adds a posteromedial incision between the pes anserinus and the medial gastrocnemius to buttress the medial column.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the long step under tourniquet. An iliac crest graft adds a second painful wound that outlasts the knee, and the surgeon should say in advance whether one is planned, because it changes the block (a fascia iliaca block or infiltration for the crest) and the first week’s pain. The periosteal stripping on two sides of the tibia is the periosteum mechanism, raw and incisional, and the reason the dual-incision plateau sits at the top of this card’s range.

  9. 9 Plateau: plating and tourniquet release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A lateral locking plate buttresses the lateral column with rafting screws under the elevated joint surface; a medial or posteromedial plate holds the medial column; the construct is checked under imaging and the knee taken through a range to confirm stability.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tourniquet release after 90-120 min is the reperfusion moment: the fall in pressure, the rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide and potassium, the fall in temperature, and bleeding from bone that was dry a minute ago; the haemoglobin after a bicondylar fixation is lower than the field suggested. Reinflation for closure is a request to refuse in a leg with a compromised envelope.

  10. 10 Closure, splint and the first 48 h

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Layered closure over the plate without tension, sometimes a drain, a bulky dressing and a hinged brace or a splint; the surgeon wants early passive knee range from day 1 and no weight-bearing for 6-12 weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For the nail, the compartment surveillance runs for 48 h on a chart; the regular regimen starts in recovery and the opioid is given regularly rather than on request. For the plateau, the first two nights are the worst of this card: the leg is swollen in a dressing, the bone defect under the graft aches, and the brace has to move. Rebound after a dilute single-shot block is high and arrives in the small hours; the plan for it is the opioid already charted and a nurse who knows the difference between rebound pain and pain out of proportion. Low molecular weight heparin from the night of surgery.

  11. 11 Day 1 onwards

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Physiotherapy starts the knee moving on day 1 for a plateau (the joint surface is held by the rafting screws and stiffness is the enemy) and the patient walking non-weight-bearing on crutches; the nail patient weight-bears as tolerated from day 1.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Movement-evoked pain limits the physiotherapy on a plateau and is the argument for a catheter once the compartment window has closed; a rescue block on day 2 is reasonable in a patient whose compartments have been examined and recorded as soft. Anterior knee pain after a nail is a weeks-to-months complaint and not an acute problem. The leg that is more painful on day 2 than day 1, with a tense calf, has a compartment syndrome until someone measures the pressure.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone with a swollen, inelastic envelope and a tourniquet, so the plan is multimodal from the trauma bay with a regional technique chosen for the compartment risk rather than for the pain alone. There is no PROSPECT guideline for tibial fracture surgery; the structure is the author’s, built on the Association of Anaesthetists’ 2021 guideline for lower leg trauma and the regional anaesthesia literature for knee and ankle surgery.

The block: for the shaft nail and the low-energy plateau, a single-shot popliteal sciatic block and an adductor canal block (or a femoral block for the plateau, where the anterolateral incision crosses the femoral territory) with a dilute local anaesthetic and no perineural or intravenous adjunct, placed after a documented compartment examination and with a surveillance chart the surgeon has agreed. The retrospective evidence is that blocks placed this way do not hide compartment syndrome and reduce opioid use; the case reports that frightened a generation of surgeons involved dense blocks and no surveillance. For the high-energy shaft fracture with a tense leg at presentation and the medial plateau fracture-dislocation in the first 48 h, no block that outlasts the operation, and a multimodal general anaesthetic with ketamine as the analgesic backbone; this is the author’s judgement and the surgeon’s, agreed before the case, because the guideline says neither can veto the other and the only way to honour that is to decide together.

The catheter: no, in the first 48 h of a fresh high-energy fracture, because every one of the missed compartment syndromes in the blocked group of the large series had a catheter. Yes, selectively, for the delayed definitive plateau fixation at 7-14 days when the window has closed and the operation is long and movement-evoked pain will limit the knee; a popliteal sciatic catheter with a dilute infusion and the compartments still examined daily.

The oral regimen shape: regular paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor for the first week unless the surgeon withholds it for union, a regular opioid for the first 48-72 h and then as needed, ketamine at low dose for the unblocked patient, and the night plan written for the rebound. Rebound is high: when a dilute block recedes on the first night the bone and the swelling are both at their peak, and the pain is severe for an hour or two until the regular regimen catches up. Escalation: pain that is out of proportion to the operation, pain on passive stretch of the toes, a tense compartment or rising opioid requirement in the first 48 h is a compartment syndrome until the pressure says otherwise; the response is the surgeon and a pressure measurement, not more opioid and not a rescue block.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The medial plateau fracture-dislocation. A knee dislocation that reduced itself: a popliteal artery at risk, a peroneal nerve palsy, compartment syndrome in half, and a surgeon who spans and fasciotomises on day 0. No block, an arterial line, and a vascular surgeon’s number.
  • The open tibial fracture. The commonest open long bone fracture, because the bone is subcutaneous; antibiotics within an hour, debridement, a nail for most Gustilo I-IIIA fractures or a fixator for IIIB and vascular injuries, and the open fracture card.
  • Suprapatellar nailing. Semi-extended, better alignment, instruments through the patellofemoral joint; the same anterior knee pain in the pooled data. A bump under the knee rather than a triangle, and the C-arm comes in lower.
  • The proximal third shaft fracture. Hard to align with an infrapatellar nail (the fragment flexes); many surgeons plate it or use the suprapatellar route. A plated proximal tibia is a bigger soft-tissue dissection and a tourniquet.
  • The distal third and the pilon. A fracture that extends into the ankle joint is a pilon and belongs on the ankle and pilon card: staged, soft-tissue driven, and worse.
  • The fasciotomised leg. If the compartments were released on day 0, the leg comes back for debridement and closure every 48-72 h and a block is now reasonable; see compartment syndrome and fasciotomy.
  • Iliac crest bone graft. A second wound that hurts for longer than the knee and is often forgotten in the plan; infiltration or a fascia iliaca block for the crest, and the patient warned.
  • Intravenous dexamethasone. It prolongs the block by several hours and reduces rebound, which is the wrong trade when the aim is a block that has worn off by the evening examination; withhold it in the fresh fracture and use it for the delayed fixation.
  • The spinal that will not wear off. A plain bupivacaine spinal lasts into the evening and a leg that cannot be examined for 4 h after a high-energy nailing is the neuraxial version of the dense block the guideline warns against; a short-acting agent or a general anaesthetic instead.

Key sources

The regional anaesthesia and compartment syndrome evidence is the point of this card and it has changed: the 2021 Association of Anaesthetists guideline moved the profession from “no blocks in tibial fractures” to “dilute single-shot blocks with surveillance”, and the 2025 series of 791 patients is the largest cohort to find no excess of missed compartment syndrome with blocks, with the catheter caveat. McQueen’s differential pressure threshold is the diagnostic standard. The surgical evidence is observational. There is no procedure-specific analgesia guideline, and the catheter timing advice is the author’s reading of the compartment window rather than a trial result.

  1. Association of Anaesthetists. Regional analgesia for lower leg trauma and the risk of acute compartment syndrome: guideline from the Association of Anaesthetists. Anaesthesia 2021
    Literature of case reports and series: lower-concentration peripheral blocks without adjuncts are not linked to delayed diagnosis when post-injury and post-operative surveillance is effective; dense, long-lasting neuraxial or peripheral blocks are to be avoided; observations by trained staff at set intervals with objective scoring charts; patient consent documented; neither surgeon nor anaesthetist can veto the other's recommendation
  2. Kakalecik J, et al. Relationship between perioperative regional anesthesia and the risk of missing acute compartment syndrome following tibia fractures. Anesth Analg 2025
    791 tibial shaft and plateau fixations at one level 1 centre, 610 with regional anaesthesia: compartment syndrome diagnosed in hospital in 2.2% overall; missed compartment syndrome (persistent motor deficit at 3 months) 0.7% versus 1.7%, not different; all four missed cases in the regional group had catheters; opioid use lower with blocks
  3. McQueen MM, Court-Brown CM. Compartment monitoring in tibial fractures: the pressure threshold for decompression. J Bone Joint Surg Br 1996;78:99-104
    116 tibial fractures, 2.6% acute compartment syndrome: a differential pressure (diastolic minus compartment pressure) of 30 mmHg predicted the need for fasciotomy more reliably than absolute compartment pressures of 30 or 40 mmHg
  4. Schatzker J, McBroom R, Bruce D. The tibial plateau fracture: the Toronto experience 1968-1975. Clin Orthop Relat Res 1979;138:94-104
    94 plateau fractures; the six-type classification with type-specific treatment that every plateau card still uses
  5. Compartment syndrome in Schatzker type VI plateau fractures and medial condylar fracture-dislocations treated with temporary external fixation. J Orthop Trauma 2009 (PubMed 19633459)
    67 patients spanned within 48 h: compartment syndrome in 27% overall, 18% of Schatzker VI fractures and 53% of medial fracture-dislocations; ten cases declared after frame placement, including three diagnosed late
  6. Leliveld MS, Verhofstad MHJ, Van Bodegraven E, Van Haaren J, Van Lieshout EMM. Anterior knee pain and functional outcome following different surgical techniques for tibial nailing: a systematic review. Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg 2021;47:763-772
    14 studies, 1,447 patients: anterior knee pain 29% after suprapatellar and 39% after infrapatellar nailing, not significantly different; malalignment 4% versus 26%; no difference in chondropathy, infection, function or quality of life

Trauma › Trauma

42 Ankle and pilon fracture fixation

Malleolar ankle ORIF (lateral, medial, posterior malleolus and syndesmosis) and tibial pilon fractures, staged with a spanning external fixator and fixed when the skin wrinkles

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Malleolar fragments reduced and plated or screwed through small incisions over subcutaneous bone, with a tourniquet; the pilon adds an impacted articular surface elevated and grafted through an envelope that has already been injured once. The mechanism is bone and periosteum under thin skin, and the block that covers it so well is the reason the rebound is the problem

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Popliteal sciatic block plus a saphenous (adductor canal) block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone, under general anaesthesia or sedation; the ankle is the operation where the block is the anaesthetic as well as the analgesic
Catheter: selective A single shot with dexamethasone and a written night plan is the day-case default for malleolar ORIF; a popliteal catheter earns its place for the pilon, the calcaneus-like high-energy foot, the opioid-tolerant patient and anyone whose previous block ended in a 3 am rebound
Alternatives: Spinal anaesthesia (inferior to blocks for the first 27 h in the AnAnkle trial, with more opioid); General anaesthesia with surgeon's infiltration where a block is refused or contraindicated; Ankle block for isolated distal fibular work in a patient who needs motor function preserved
Position
Supine with a bump under the ipsilateral buttock to internally rotate the leg for the lateral malleolus; the bump removed or the leg externally rotated for the medial side; prone or lateral for a direct posterior malleolar approach, which changes the airway plan; the pilon often needs an anteromedial or anterolateral approach with the leg on a radiolucent platform
Tourniquet
Yes. Thigh tourniquet set from the limb occlusion pressure (Part A, the tourniquet) for most malleolar fixations, 45-90 min; a pilon fixation runs longer and the tourniquet is often released before the articular reduction is checked; the swollen or vascular leg may get none
Cement
No
Blood loss
Under 200 mL for malleolar ORIF; 200-400 mL for a pilon, mostly after tourniquet release
Duration
Isolated lateral malleolus 45-60 min; bimalleolar or trimalleolar with syndesmosis 60-120 min; pilon ORIF 120-240 min, after a 30-min spanning fixator on day 0
Length of stay
Day case or one night for malleolar ORIF; the pilon has a day-0 fixator admission and a 2-5 night definitive admission at 7-14 days. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV before the tourniquet is inflated (3 g over 120 kg); open fractures were due their antibiotic within an hour of injury and follow the open fracture plan
Tranexamic acid
Not routinely needed for malleolar ORIF; tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction is reasonable for a pilon
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin through the immobilised period for a patient with their own risk factors or a pilon; mechanical prophylaxis on the other leg; practice varies for the day-case malleolar patient in a boot, and the decision is made rather than defaulted
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (prolongs the block, reduces rebound) and ondansetron 4 mg IV
Tell the patient
The foot will be completely numb and floppy for most of the first day; the pain then arrives over an hour or two, usually in the night, and the tablets taken before bed and again when the tingling starts are what get you through it. It settles quickly after the second day.
The trap
The block wears off at 3 am in a day-case patient at home with no analgesia taken and a leg that was pain-free when they left: rebound pain after a popliteal block for ankle fracture surgery affected 44% of patients in the trial that tested it and 15% with intravenous dexamethasone, so the dexamethasone and the written night plan are the operation's analgesia, not the block

What the surgeon is doing and why

An ankle fracture and a pilon fracture both break the distal tibia and fibula at the joint, and they are different operations because of the direction of the force. The malleolar fracture is a rotational injury: the talus twists in the mortise, the fibula breaks at or above the joint line, the medial malleolus or the deltoid ligament fails, and sometimes the posterior malleolus and the syndesmosis go too. The joint surface of the tibia is intact; the mortise is simply unstable, and the surgeon’s job is to put the talus back under the tibia and hold it there with a fibular plate, a medial screw or two, a posterior malleolar screw if the fragment is large, and a syndesmosis screw or suture-button if the fibula will not stay reduced. The soft tissues are bruised but the envelope is usually intact, and the operation is a day case in a fit patient.

The pilon is an axial injury: a fall from a height or a foot on a brake pedal drives the talus up into the tibial plafond and shatters it. The articular surface is impacted and comminuted (Ruedi-Allgower III), the metaphysis is crushed, the fibula is usually broken, and the skin over the front of the ankle, with the thinnest envelope in the lower limb, has taken the same energy. Early open reduction through that skin produced wound breakdown, deep infection and amputation at rates the surgeons of the 1990s called unacceptable, and the answer was staging: a spanning external fixator and a fibular plate on day 0 to restore length and let the swelling go, a CT once the fracture is out to length, and definitive fixation at 7-14 days when the skin wrinkles when pinched and the fracture blisters have healed. The definitive operation is then an anteromedial or anterolateral approach chosen from the CT exit of the fracture line, elevation of the impacted articular fragments, bone graft into the metaphyseal void, and a plate; the worst fractures get a circular frame instead and a year of rehabilitation.

   rotational injury                    axial injury
   (talus twists in mortise)            (talus driven into plafond)
          |                                     |
   malleolar fracture                    pilon fracture
   joint surface intact                  joint surface impacted
   envelope bruised                      envelope injured
          |                                     |
   ORIF when swelling allows             day 0: spanning fixator
   (same day to 7 days),                        +/- fibular plate
   day case, block as anaesthetic        day 7-14: CT, wrinkle sign,
                                                 ORIF or frame

The pain logic is bone and periosteum under a thin skin, and the block question dominates. The fibular plate sits on subcutaneous bone with a strip of periosteum lifted; the medial malleolar screws cross a fracture that is now compressed; the pilon adds an elevated, grafted articular surface and a metaphysis full of bone substitute. All of this is well covered by a popliteal sciatic block with a saphenous block for the medial skin, which is why ankle surgery is the lower-limb operation where the block is the whole anaesthetic. The cost is the rebound: in the AnAnkle trial, blocks beat spinal anaesthesia for pain and opioid use over 27 h and 99% of block patients would choose them again, but the authors noted intense pain as the blocks wore off; in the trial that tested dexamethasone for exactly this, rebound pain affected 44% of ankle ORIF patients with a plain block and 15% with intravenous dexamethasone, lasting about 3 h either way. The Gerbershagen cohort, in which blocks were rarely used, ranked open reduction of the calcaneus the single most painful procedure of 179 and foot arthrodesis seventh; the malleolar ankle is not in that company, but the pilon and the high-energy hindfoot are its neighbours. The score is 3 for the malleolar ankle: a block is expected, opioids are needed on the first two days, and the pain falls quickly because the mechanism is bone. The pilon sits a point higher on duration and the second operation, and the card says so where it matters.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Presentation: reduce, splint, and decide the day

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A dislocated ankle is reduced in the emergency department before the radiograph, because the skin over the medial malleolus tents and dies within hours; a swollen ankle is elevated in a backslab and fixed within a day if the skin allows or at 5-10 days if it does not. A pilon gets a CT after the spanning fixator, not before, because the fracture is only readable at length.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The reduction in the department is a sedation or a block; a popliteal block for a fracture-dislocation is the kindest reduction and does not hide a compartment syndrome in a malleolar injury, which is not the at-risk pattern the 2021 guideline describes. The fasting state is counted from the injury for the same-day case. The decision between day-of-injury surgery and a delay belongs to the surgeon’s reading of the skin; for the anaesthetist the delayed case is the easier one, fasted and on a planned list, and the day-case plan applies to it.

  2. 2 Block, airway and the night plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a still foot, a bloodless field under tourniquet, and a patient who will go home that evening with the leg elevated.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A popliteal sciatic block (20-30 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% or 0.75%) and a saphenous block in the adductor canal (10 mL) with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, under sedation or a light general anaesthetic with a supraglottic airway; the block is the anaesthetic, and a general anaesthetic that is only there to stop the patient feeling the tourniquet after 45 min is a small one. The saphenous block is not optional: the medial malleolar incision and the skin over the medial ankle are saphenous territory, and a block that misses it hurts on the medial side the moment the surgeon starts there. Spinal anaesthesia is a legitimate alternative, inferior in the trial for the first 27 h and the wrong choice for a day case. Cefazolin 2 g IV before the tourniquet goes up. The written night plan (what to take at bedtime, what to take when the tingling starts, what the opioid is for) is written now and handed over in recovery; the trial data say the rebound comes in the small hours in a third to a half of patients without dexamethasone.

  3. 3 Positioning and the tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with a bump under the ipsilateral buttock internally rotates the leg so the lateral malleolus faces up; the bump comes out for the medial side; a large posterior malleolar fragment needs a posterolateral approach with the patient prone or lateral, or a figure-of-four position. A thigh tourniquet at 250-300 mmHg.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The prone posterior malleolus is a different anaesthetic: a tracheal tube, a turn, pressure areas, and a case that cannot be a day case in an older patient. Tourniquet time for a trimalleolar fixation with a syndesmosis runs to 90 min, and the tourniquet pain that a popliteal block does not cover (the thigh cuff is above it) is what the sedation or general anaesthetic is for; see the tourniquet. The swollen leg with fracture blisters, the diabetic foot and the leg with peripheral vascular disease are the ones the surgeon may not tourniquet, and the field bleeds instead.

  4. 4 Lateral malleolus: fibular plate

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through a lateral incision the surgeon reduces the fibular fracture to length and rotation, because the fibula is the key to the mortise, and fixes it with a lag screw and a neutralisation plate, or a locking plate in osteoporotic bone, or a posterolateral antiglide plate. The superficial peroneal nerve crosses the field above the joint line and the sural nerve lies behind it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The plate on subcutaneous bone with a strip of periosteum lifted is the periosteal mechanism and the pain the patient feels on day 1-2; there is no deep muscle to dissect. Nothing to do at this step but note the tourniquet time.

  5. 5 Medial malleolus and deltoid

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The medial malleolus is reduced through a small medial incision and fixed with two partially threaded screws or a tension band; a deltoid ligament rupture with an intact medial malleolus is usually left to heal once the fibula is out to length. The saphenous vein and nerve run across the incision.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the saphenous territory, and the step that tells you whether the adductor canal block worked: a patient under sedation who flinches as the medial incision is made has a popliteal block and no saphenous block.

  6. 6 Posterior malleolus and syndesmosis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A posterior malleolar fragment over a quarter of the joint surface, or one that leaves the talus subluxed, is fixed from the front with screws or from behind through a posterolateral approach with a buttress plate. The syndesmosis is then stress-tested under the image intensifier (a hook test or external rotation); if the fibula moves, it is reduced by hand with the foot in neutral and held with one or two screws across both bones or a suture-button.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The syndesmosis reduction needs the foot held still and in neutral while the surgeon images and places the screw; a patient who moves under light sedation here costs a malreduction. The stress test and the imaging add 15-30 min to a case that felt finished.

  7. 7 Closure, splint and emergence

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Layered closure without tension over the fibular plate, a well-padded backslab or boot with the ankle at neutral, and elevation; the surgeon wants the foot above the heart for 48 h and non-weight-bearing for 6 weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tourniquet release before closure is the surgeon’s call and the moment the field starts to bleed; the reperfusion changes are modest at 60-90 min. Emergence is unremarkable; the foot is numb. The splint goes on before the patient lightens, because a patient with a dense sciatic block will otherwise let the foot drop off the trolley without noticing.

  8. 8 Recovery, discharge and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The fixation is stable from the moment the screws are in; the surgeon wants elevation, the splint untouched and a clinic review at two weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first paracetamol and NSAID dose goes in before discharge. The patient goes home with a numb, insensate foot, crutches, a written night plan and someone at home; the discharge criteria are the same as for any day case, and a working block is not a reason to keep the bed. The rebound comes at about 26 h after the block with intravenous dexamethasone and 17 h without, in the one trial that timed it, usually at night, rises over an hour to its peak, lasts about 3 h and responds to the opioid that the patient should already have taken; the trial data make the dexamethasone and the plan the two interventions that decide whether the patient telephones. Day 1-2 is the peak; by day 3 the regular regimen is enough and the opioid is stopped.

  9. 9 The pilon on day 0: spanning fixator and fibular plate

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Two pins in the tibial shaft and one or two in the calcaneus or the talus, connected by bars across the ankle, pull the fracture out to length by ligamentotaxis; many surgeons plate the fibula at the same sitting through the lateral skin, which is usually the least injured side, to set the length. A CT follows.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A 30-60 min general anaesthetic, often at night, in a patient who may have fallen from a height and has a spine and a calcaneus to think about. A popliteal block is reasonable here (the pilon is not the compartment syndrome pattern that the tibial shaft is), but a short one, because the leg will be examined for the next 48 h. Analgesia for the fortnight in the frame is oral and the leg is elevated.

  10. 10 The pilon at 7-14 days: definitive fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    When the skin wrinkles and the blisters have epithelialised, the surgeon opens the ankle through the approach the CT dictates (anteromedial for a medially exiting fracture line, anterolateral for a lateral exit), reconstructs the joint surface from the key fragment outwards, elevates the impacted segments, fills the metaphyseal void with autograft, allograft or substitute, and applies a medial or anterolateral plate. The most comminuted fractures get a circular frame with fine wires instead, and a long rehabilitation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the long, elective operation on this card and the one where the catheter has the strongest claim: 2-4 h, a tourniquet to its limit and released, a bone graft (an iliac crest donor site if autograft is used, which needs its own analgesia), and a patient who will be in more pain for longer than the malleolar patient and is not going home that night. A popliteal catheter with a dilute infusion, a saphenous single shot and the usual regimen is the author’s preference; the compartment window of the first 48 h has passed. The haemoglobin after tourniquet release in a long case is worth checking in an older patient.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone and periosteum under thin skin, fully covered by a popliteal sciatic plus saphenous block, so the plan is built around the block and its rebound. There is no PROSPECT guideline for ankle fracture surgery; the trial evidence is good. AnAnkle randomised 150 ankle fracture patients to popliteal sciatic plus saphenous blocks or spinal anaesthesia, all with paracetamol, ibuprofen and PCA morphine, and found the blocks superior for pain and opioid use over 27 h, with the caveat that the pain as the block wore off was substantial and sometimes intense. The dexamethasone trial randomised 130 bimalleolar and trimalleolar ORIFs with the same blocks to intravenous dexamethasone or saline: rebound pain 15% against 44%, the block 8 h longer, the first analgesic request at 26 h rather than 17 h. The ambulatory rebound cohort of 972 patients adds the risk factors: bone surgery, younger age, female sex, and no intravenous dexamethasone.

The defensible default for malleolar ORIF is therefore a single-shot popliteal sciatic block and a saphenous block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, under sedation or a light general anaesthetic, regular paracetamol and an NSAID started before discharge, oral opioid for the first two nights, and a written night plan that tells the patient to take the bedtime dose whether or not the foot hurts and the next dose when the tingling starts. The catheter is the right call for the pilon’s definitive fixation, for the opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, for the patient with a previous catastrophic rebound night, and for the unit that admits its ankle fractures and can run an infusion; it is not needed for the malleolar day case and adds a dislodgement and a leaking dressing to a patient going home on crutches.

Escalation triggers: pain above 7 when the block has worn off, with the splint intact and the toes pink and moving, is rebound and is treated with the opioid already charted; pain that is severe inside the splint with a foot that is cold, pale or paraesthetic is a tight cast or a vascular problem and the splint is split; pain that persists beyond day 3 with a hot ankle is an infection. The malleolar ankle is not a compartment syndrome injury in the way the tibial shaft is, and the 2021 guideline’s caution about dense blocks is aimed at the shaft and the high-energy proximal tibia, not at this card.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The elderly, osteoporotic, diabetic ankle. The fibular plate does not hold, the skin does not heal, and the surgeon may choose a fibular nail, a hindfoot nail through the calcaneus and talus, or a cast. A diabetic neuropathic foot (Charcot) is a different disease with a different operation and a long cast. Blocks are still the right anaesthetic.
  • The open ankle fracture. Common because the medial skin is thin: antibiotics within an hour, debridement, often primary fixation if the wound is clean, and the open fracture card.
  • The fracture-dislocation with skin at risk. Reduced in the department before anything else; a block in the department is the kindest way to do it.
  • The posterior malleolus done prone. A tracheal tube, a prone turn with a fractured ankle, and no day case.
  • The syndesmosis screw that will not hold the foot in neutral. A malreduced syndesmosis is the commonest technical error in ankle fixation and the surgeon’s concern; for you it means a still foot during the imaging and a case that runs 20 min longer than the booking.
  • The calcaneus in the same patient. A fall from a height that produces a pilon often produces a calcaneal fracture or a spine fracture; the calcaneus is the most painful operation in the Gerbershagen cohort and has its own staging and its own catheter decision.
  • Day case criteria. A dense popliteal block is not a reason to delay discharge, but the patient needs crutches they can use, elevation at home, the night plan, the dexamethasone already given, and a telephone number; a patient who lives alone and cannot manage stairs stays the night.
  • Rebound in the opioid-tolerant patient. The worst phenotype for this operation: a catheter or an admission with a planned regimen, not a single shot and a prescription.
  • The patient who refuses the block. A general anaesthetic with surgeon’s infiltration and a spinal both work; the first night is worse and the opioid requirement doubles, which the trial data make explicit.

Key sources

The analgesia evidence for ankle fracture surgery is better than for most trauma operations because the operation is common, short and standardised. AnAnkle is the randomised comparison of blocks against spinal anaesthesia; the dexamethasone trial is the randomised answer to the rebound problem the AnAnkle authors flagged; the ambulatory rebound cohort gives the risk factors. The pilon evidence is surgical and observational, and the staging protocol rests on the wound complication history rather than a trial. The Gerbershagen cohort places the hindfoot and foot arthrodesis among the most painful operations in surgery, with the caveat that few of those patients had a block; it is cited here as context for the high-energy foot rather than as a ranking of the malleolar ankle, which it did not list. The catheter advice is the author’s judgement.

  1. Sort R, Brorson S, Gogenur I, et al. Peripheral nerve block anaesthesia and postoperative pain in acute ankle fracture surgery: the AnAnkle randomised trial. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:881-888
    150 patients randomised to popliteal sciatic plus saphenous blocks with ropivacaine or spinal anaesthesia, all with paracetamol, ibuprofen and PCA morphine: 27-h pain and opioid score median minus 26.5% with blocks versus plus 54.3% with spinal; rebound pain as the blocks wore off was substantial and sometimes intense; 99% of block patients would choose the same again
  2. Gao M, Li Y, Yu J, et al. The effects of intravenous dexamethasone on rebound pain after nerve block in patients with ankle fracture: a randomized controlled trial. J Pain Res 2023;16:1127-1136
    130 bimalleolar and trimalleolar ORIFs with popliteal and adductor canal ropivacaine blocks: rebound pain 44% with saline versus 15% with intravenous dexamethasone; block about 8 h longer, first analgesic request 26 h versus 17 h; rebound lasted about 3 h in both groups
  3. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain in 49.6%: bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, and absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78
  4. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: open reduction of the calcaneus was the single most painful procedure in the cohort, with foot arthrodesis seventh and open ankle ligament reconstruction 54th; 22 of the 40 most painful operations were orthopaedic or trauma procedures on the extremities, in a cohort where regional techniques were rarely used
  5. Jacob N, Amin A, Giotakis N, Narayan B, Nayagam S, Trompeter AJ. Management of high-energy tibial pilon fractures. Strategies Trauma Limb Reconstr 2015;10:137-147
    Ruedi-Allgower classification; early ORIF of type C fractures had unacceptable soft-tissue complication rates; the staged protocol (spanning fixator, definitive fixation at 7-14 days when swelling settles, after a planning CT) from Patterson and Cole and Sirkin; approach chosen from the CT fracture exit; fibular plating optional; long-term outcomes often deteriorate
  6. Association of Anaesthetists. Regional analgesia for lower leg trauma and the risk of acute compartment syndrome. Anaesthesia 2021
    Dilute single-shot blocks without adjuncts are not associated with delayed diagnosis when surveillance is effective; dense long-lasting blocks are to be avoided in the at-risk leg; the at-risk injuries are tibial shaft and high-energy proximal tibia rather than the malleolar ankle

Trauma › Trauma

43 Pelvic and acetabular fracture fixation

Pelvic ring: binder, external fixation, iliosacral screws, symphyseal plating. Acetabulum: Kocher-Langenbeck, ilioinguinal and anterior intrapelvic approaches

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. Large muscle envelopes split or lifted off the pelvis (gluteus maximus and the short rotators posteriorly; the abdominal wall and iliacus anteriorly), subperiosteal exposure and plating of the innominate bone, nerves retracted for hours (sciatic, lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator), on top of a high-energy fracture with its own haematoma and often other injuries; then eight to twelve weeks in which sitting, turning and transferring all load the pelvis

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
General anaesthesia with a systemic multimodal plan (ketamine, paracetamol, opioid PCA) as the base; for anterior approaches a fascia iliaca catheter placed by the surgeon under the iliac fascia or by ultrasound at the end; for the posterior approach nothing that blocks the sciatic nerve until it has been examined
Catheter: selective A fascia iliaca or quadratus lumborum catheter is reasonable after an anterior approach and an epidural after an isolated injury in a patient whose anticoagulation can wait; none is routine, because the comparative studies show no clear opioid or pain benefit from regional techniques here and every option competes with nerve surveillance or thromboprophylaxis. The pain earns a catheter; the evidence and the logistics do not yet deliver one
Alternatives: Lumbar epidural: the most complete analgesia, no advantage in the one case-control study, and in conflict with early chemoprophylaxis and the sciatic examination; Quadratus lumborum block, equivalent to fascia iliaca block on pain scores in one small trial of anterior acetabular surgery; Lumbar or sacral erector spinae plane block for posterior approaches, on case-report evidence; Surgeon infiltration of the wound and the iliac crest; No block for percutaneous screws
Position
Supine on a radiolucent table for the pelvic ring (iliosacral screws, symphyseal plate, external fixation) and the anterior acetabular approaches; prone or lateral for the Kocher-Langenbeck approach, with the hip extended and the knee flexed to slacken the sciatic nerve; some surgeons use a traction table
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Under 100 mL for percutaneous screws; 300-500 mL for a symphyseal plate; 500-1,500 mL for an acetabular approach and beyond 2 L for a combined or extended one. In the randomised acetabular trial the mean loss was 635 mL and 41% were transfused
Duration
30-60 min for iliosacral screws; 60-90 min for a symphyseal plate; 2-3 h for a posterior wall through a Kocher-Langenbeck approach; 3-6 h for an ilioinguinal, anterior intrapelvic or combined approach
Length of stay
5-10 nights for an isolated injury; set by the other injuries in polytrauma. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), repeated every 4 h and after 1.5 L of loss; broader cover by unit protocol for open fractures and bladder or bowel injury
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction is common and defensible, but two randomised trials and a meta-analysis in acetabular fixation show no reduction in blood loss or transfusion; the early dose given to the bleeding trauma patient within 3 h of injury is a separate indication
VTE
The highest-risk injury in orthopaedic trauma: LMWH as soon as the bleeding risk allows, usually within 24-48 h of injury, withheld around surgery and restarted that night or the next morning, continued for weeks; mechanical prophylaxis throughout; a pre-operative duplex or a filter for the patient whose surgery was delayed without prophylaxis, by unit protocol
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV and ondansetron 4 mg IV; a PCA and a long abdominal-wall operation make nausea likely
Tell the patient
This is a big operation to hold a broken pelvis or hip socket in place; the first week is hard, the pain is managed with several medicines together and a button you control, and you will be on crutches or in a chair for two to three months while the bone heals.
The trap
There are two different patients on this card: the one bleeding to death from the pelvis on day 0, who needs a binder, blood and an interventional radiologist rather than an operation, and the stable one a week later having a long reconstruction, whose blood loss, sciatic nerve and clots are yours to look after

What the surgeon is doing and why

The pelvis is a ring: two innominate bones joined at the front by the symphysis and at the back to the sacrum by the strongest ligaments in the body. A ring cannot break in one place and displace, so a displaced pelvic injury is always at least two lesions, front and back. The posterior lesion decides everything. If the posterior ligaments hold, the pelvis is stable or only rotationally unstable (the “open book”). If they are torn, one half of the pelvis can move up and back relative to the spine, and the venous plexus on the front of the sacrum, the internal iliac branches and the lumbosacral nerve roots are torn with it. That is the injury that kills on day 0 by bleeding into a retroperitoneal space that an open pelvis has enlarged.

The acetabulum is a different problem in the same bone. It is a joint surface, the socket of the hip, formed where an anterior and a posterior column of bone meet. The femoral head is driven into it, in a car crash or increasingly in an elderly fall, and breaks off a wall, a column or both. An isolated acetabular fracture rarely kills, but a socket that heals with a step of more than a couple of millimetres wears out within years. So the surgery is a joint reconstruction: anatomical reduction and rigid plates, done within about two weeks before the fragments stick.

The operations therefore fall into three groups, usually on different days.

  1. Emergency control of the pelvic ring: a binder at the level of the greater trochanters, then an anterior external fixator or a posterior clamp, with angioembolisation or preperitoneal packing for the bleeding. The aim is volume reduction and tamponade, not reduction of the fracture.
  2. Definitive fixation of the ring: percutaneous iliosacral screws across the sacroiliac joint or sacral fracture under fluoroscopy, and a plate across the symphysis through a Pfannenstiel incision, or an internal or external anterior fixator.
  3. Acetabular reconstruction, by an approach chosen for the fracture. Posterior wall and posterior column fractures: Kocher-Langenbeck, through gluteus maximus with the short external rotators divided and the sciatic nerve in the field throughout. Anterior column and most both-column fractures: the ilioinguinal approach, which lifts the abdominal wall off the iliac crest and inguinal ligament and works through three windows around the iliopsoas and the external iliac vessels, or the anterior intrapelvic (modified Stoppa) approach, which goes through the midline behind the rectus and along the pelvic brim from the inside.

The pain logic follows from the size of what is lifted. These are the largest muscle dissections in orthopaedic trauma: the whole of the iliacus off the inner pelvis, or the gluteus maximus split and the rotators cut, with subperiosteal exposure of the bone and long plates. Nerves are retracted for hours. The fracture itself bled into the same tissue planes days earlier. Afterwards nothing is rested: the patient is touch weight-bearing for 8 to 12 weeks, and every transfer, every turn in bed and every hour sitting loads the pelvis. Muscle is the dominant tag, with periosteum, bone and nerve behind it, and the curve is the reason for the 5: a peak on days 1 and 2 no higher than other major operations, then a slow decline over weeks in a trauma population with a high rate of persistent pain.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Day 0: the unstable pelvis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Most pelvic fracture bleeding is venous and from the cancellous fracture surfaces, and it tamponades once the ring is closed and the retroperitoneum intact. The minority that keeps bleeding has an arterial source. The team’s sequence is a binder, exclusion of chest and abdominal sources, then embolisation, packing or both, depending on what the hospital can deliver in minutes.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is resuscitation, not orthopaedic anaesthesia. Check that the binder is over the greater trochanters and not the iliac crests, and leave it on. Activate the massive transfusion protocol early, give tranexamic acid if within 3 h of injury, keep the calcium and temperature up, and do not chase a normal pressure before haemorrhage control. Where the patient goes is not settled by evidence: in the pooled series, packing and embolisation could not be separated on mortality once like was compared with like, and more than a quarter of packed patients still needed embolisation. You may be giving this anaesthetic in an angiography suite, away from help, with a patient who is not yet intubated: take the rapid infuser, the blood and a second pair of hands. Induction in a hypovolaemic patient with a tamponading haematoma is the moment of arrest; reduced doses, blood running and the surgeon or radiologist ready. See polytrauma sequencing.

  2. 2 Emergency skeletal stabilisation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    An anterior external fixator (pins in the iliac crests or above the acetabula) or a posterior clamp holds the volume reduction the binder achieved and allows access to the abdomen and groins. It is a 20-30 min procedure, often combined with packing through a low midline incision or a laparotomy.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The binder is cut or shifted for access and the pelvis can re-open as it comes off: have the blood ahead. Packing opens the preperitoneal space and releases tamponade before it restores it. A urethral catheter may have been deferred for blood at the meatus; a suprapubic one placed by the urologist sits exactly where the symphyseal plate will later go, which the pelvic surgeon will want to know. This is damage control: stop when the physiology says so.

  3. 3 Before definitive surgery

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Definitive fixation waits until the patient is resuscitated and the surgeon has CT reconstructions and a plan, usually day 2 to 10. Earlier, the pelvis bleeds heavily when opened; later than two to three weeks, reduction is fought against callus.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    See the patient as a trauma patient a week on: lungs after rib fractures and transfusion, a haemoglobin that has drifted down, a week of bed rest. Three specific questions. What prophylaxis has been given and when was the last dose: a patient who has had none for a week has a real chance of an existing deep vein thrombosis, and units vary between duplex screening and a filter. What do the sciatic and femoral nerves do now: document ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion and quadriceps function, because about 5% of acetabular fractures arrive with a sciatic palsy and the operation adds to that. And is there a urological injury, a Morel-Lavallee lesion over the flank or a closed head injury that changes the position or the plan.

  4. 4 Anaesthesia, lines and blood

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs complete muscle relaxation for hours, since reduction is done against the largest muscles in the body, and a table that takes fluoroscopy in several oblique planes.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    General anaesthesia with a tracheal tube and continuous neuromuscular block monitored with a nerve stimulator; a request for “more relaxation” during reduction is literal. Arterial line and two large cannulae for any open acetabular approach, urinary catheter, temperature probe, forced-air warming and a fluid warmer. Cross-match four units for an anterior or combined approach. On cell salvage and tranexamic acid the evidence is less supportive than habit: two retrospective series returned a mean of 345 and 484 mL of salvaged blood, with no reduction in allogeneic transfusion in the larger one and more benefit in complex fracture types in the other; and two randomised trials and a meta-analysis of tranexamic acid in acetabular fixation found no reduction in loss or transfusion. The author’s practice is to set up salvage in collect-only mode for anterior, combined and complex cases and process if the reservoir fills, and to give tranexamic acid 1 g IV on the argument of low cost, while planning as though neither will change the transfusion. Pre-operative anaemia and operating time were the predictors of transfusion in the trial.

  5. 5 Positioning

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine for the ring and for anterior acetabular approaches, with the leg draped free so the hip can be flexed to relax iliopsoas and the femoral vessels. Prone or lateral for Kocher-Langenbeck, with the knee flexed to at least 60-90 degrees and the hip extended throughout to take tension off the sciatic nerve.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Prone positioning of a trauma patient with a pelvic fracture, rib fractures and perhaps a cleared-but-sore cervical spine needs enough people and a moment of real blood loss as the pelvis is moved. The abdomen must hang free, the eyes and face are checked after every table movement, and arms are positioned around any upper limb injuries. In a series of 644 posterior approaches the rate of iatrogenic sciatic palsy was the same prone and lateral (about 3%), so the position is the surgeon’s preference and the knee flexion is the thing to protect: if the leg holder slips and the knee extends, say so.

  6. 6 Percutaneous iliosacral screws

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A cannulated screw is passed from the outer ilium across the sacroiliac joint into the body of S1 or S2 over a guide wire, steered on inlet, outlet and lateral fluoroscopy through a corridor a few millimetres wide between the sacral foramina, the L5 root in front and the spinal canal behind.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A short, nearly bloodless procedure with a great deal of radiation and a surgeon whose view depends on the image. Bowel gas and contrast in the bladder or bowel obscure the sacrum, so mention any recent contrast study. Some surgeons run neuromonitoring of the L5 and S1 roots, which means no relaxant after intubation and a total intravenous anaesthetic; ask before induction. Pain afterwards is modest and no block is needed.

  7. 7 Symphyseal plating

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through a Pfannenstiel incision the recti are split in the midline or partly released, the bladder is held back with a malleable retractor, the symphysis is closed with a clamp and a plate is laid across the top of the pubic bodies.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Deep relaxation so the recti can be retracted. The bladder is directly under the surgeon’s hand; a catheter that stops draining or drains blood is reported at once. The retropubic venous plexus bleeds briskly and briefly. Loss is 300-500 mL.

  8. 8 Kocher-Langenbeck approach

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A curved incision over the greater trochanter, gluteus maximus split in line with its fibres, piriformis and the obturator internus tendon divided and reflected, the obturator internus cushioning the sciatic nerve from the retractors, and the posterior wall and column exposed. The hip may be distracted or dislocated to clear fragments from the joint. The wall fragments are reduced and held with a contoured plate and screws that must not enter the joint.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The sciatic nerve is in the field for the whole operation, under a retractor, in a patient whose nerve may already be bruised by the dislocation. Pooled incidence of iatrogenic palsy is about 1-3%, with roughly three in four recovering fully; the peroneal division is the vulnerable part. Your contributions are the knee flexion, a mean pressure that perfuses the nerve, and no long-acting sciatic or sacral plexus block that would hide a deficit in recovery. The superior gluteal vessels at the sciatic notch are the source of sudden bleeding in this approach, and they retract into the pelvis when cut. Loss is typically 500-800 mL.

  9. 9 Ilioinguinal and anterior intrapelvic approaches

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Ilioinguinal: an incision from the iliac crest to the midline above the symphysis, the abdominal muscles and iliacus lifted off the crest and the inner pelvis, and the inguinal canal opened so that the iliopsoas with the femoral nerve, and the external iliac vessels, can each be slung and moved aside to work through three windows. Anterior intrapelvic: a midline or Pfannenstiel entry behind the rectus, then along the pelvic brim from inside, with the surgeon standing on the opposite side. Both give access to the anterior column and the quadrilateral plate without opening the hip.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    These are the long cases and the wet ones. The external iliac vein is retracted for hours and can tear or thrombose. On the back of the superior pubic ramus an anastomosis between the obturator and the external iliac or inferior epigastric vessels (the corona mortis) crosses the field in a substantial minority of patients and must be found and tied before it is torn, because the cut end retracts into the obturator canal. A sudden, large venous bleed in the middle of an otherwise steady case is one of these. The femoral nerve and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve are stretched by the retractors, and thigh numbness afterwards is the rule. Keep the hip flexed on a bolster as the surgeon asks, keep the relaxant on, and keep a running tally of the suction, the swabs and the salvage reservoir against an hourly blood gas.

  10. 10 Reduction and fixation: the long middle

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Reduction of an acetabulum is done with clamps, ball spikes and traction through small windows, checked by feel and fluoroscopy, and may take longer than everything else together. Long plates are contoured along the pelvic brim or the posterior column, with screws aimed down narrow safe corridors.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The pattern is steady loss rather than a single event: 100-300 mL an hour from bone and muscle for three or four hours. Transfuse to the trend, not to a number reached after the fact; correct the calcium and the temperature; repeat the antibiotic at four hours. The frequent table tilts for oblique views move your lines and your pressure transducer. A fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide with hypotension during work near the iliac veins is air or thrombus until shown otherwise.

  11. 11 Closure, imaging and what goes home with the patient

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Final fluoroscopic views confirm that no screw is in the joint. The muscle is reattached to the crest or the trochanter, drains are common, and the abdominal wall is repaired in layers after an anterior approach to prevent a hernia.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The abdominal wall closure needs relaxation to the end, so plan the reversal accordingly.
