If a regional technique is being used, this is when it is placed: the surgeon can lay a catheter under the iliac fascia against the femoral nerve before closing an anterior approach, with no extra procedure, or you can place a fascia iliaca or quadratus lumborum catheter under ultrasound once the dressings are on. Start the ketamine and the PCA before emergence. Extubate the isolated injury; keep the polytrauma patient with a 2 L loss and a long prone time intubated without apology.

  12. 12 Recovery and the first week

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a documented nerve examination, a check radiograph or CT, the patient sitting out within a day or two and touch weight-bearing on the injured side for 8 to 12 weeks. After a posterior approach many give indomethacin or a single dose of radiotherapy to prevent heterotopic bone in the abductors.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Examine and record sciatic function (ankle and toes, up and down) and femoral function as soon as the patient can cooperate; a new foot drop is the surgeon’s business that evening. High dependency care for a combined approach, a large transfusion or other injuries. Thromboprophylaxis restarts that night or the next morning by agreement with the surgeon and is the single most important drug chart entry of the week; any neuraxial or deep catheter has to fit around it. If indomethacin is prescribed for heterotopic ossification it is also the patient’s NSAID, and a second one is not added.

Pain plan

The mechanism is muscle and periosteum over a large area, loaded for weeks, so by the logic of this book a continuous technique has a strong claim. The evidence does not yet support one. A case-control study of posterior wall fixation found no difference in pain scores, time to mobilisation or length of stay when an epidural was added to general anaesthesia. A retrospective cohort of 205 pelvic and acetabular fixations found that regional anaesthesia was associated with no less, and at some time points more, opioid use, which probably says more about who was selected for a block than about blocks. For anterior approaches, a surgeon-placed catheter under the iliac fascia gave three-day morphine use similar to an epidural (5.0 and 6.0 mg) and less than half that of no regional technique (12.7 mg), a difference that did not reach significance in 85 patients; and a small randomised trial found no difference in pain scores between a quadratus lumborum block and a fascia iliaca block. That is the whole comparative literature.

The defensible default is therefore systemic and multimodal, with regional analgesia added where the approach makes it easy and safe. For every patient: regular paracetamol; an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor once bleeding and renal function allow, or the surgeon’s indomethacin doing that job; ketamine at induction and by low-dose infusion for 24-48 h; an opioid PCA converted to oral modified-release and immediate-release opioid by day 2 or 3, with a written taper, because this is a population in which a discharge prescription easily becomes a habit. Gabapentinoids are reserved for established neuropathic symptoms from a nerve that was injured or stretched.

Regional additions, as author’s judgement. After an ilioinguinal or anterior intrapelvic approach: a fascia iliaca catheter (surgeon-placed or ultrasound-guided) or a quadratus lumborum catheter for 48-72 h, covering the iliac fossa, the groin and the anterior hip; the femoral nerve has already been stretched, so its function is documented first and a dilute infusion is used. After a Kocher-Langenbeck approach: nothing in the sciatic distribution on the day; a lumbar or sacral erector spinae plane block is a low-risk option supported only by case reports; surgeon infiltration of the gluteal wound is simple and reasonable. An epidural gives the most complete analgesia for any approach and is the right choice for the occasional isolated injury in an opioid-tolerant patient, but it masks the sciatic examination, drops the pressure in a patient who has bled, and has to be placed and removed around the anticoagulant that matters most this week. For percutaneous screws alone, no block.

Escalation: buttock and posterior thigh pain with a new foot drop is the sciatic nerve or a gluteal haematoma compressing it; a swollen leg is a thrombosis; burning anterolateral thigh pain is the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and is usually temporary; groin pain on any hip movement with a clunk is a screw in the joint or a lost reduction. Pain still severe at two weeks, with allodynia, is the start of a chronic pain trajectory and merits referral before discharge.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The elderly acetabular fracture. A low-energy fall onto the hip in an osteoporotic patient is now a common presentation: the same approaches, a frailer patient, sometimes an acute total hip replacement at the same sitting, which adds arthroplasty blood loss and a possible cement step to a fracture operation.
  • Combined and extended approaches. A both-column fracture needing front and back exposure is two operations, sometimes with a turn in the middle; six hours and 2 L are realistic, and staging over two days is a reasonable request to make of the surgeon when the physiology is drifting.
  • Fracture-dislocation of the hip. The dislocated head is reduced as an emergency, under a brief deep anaesthetic with full relaxation, to protect the head’s blood supply and the sciatic nerve; definitive fixation follows days later.
  • Urological and bowel injury. A bladder or urethral injury changes the catheter, the antibiotic and the infection risk of anterior plates; an open pelvic fracture with a rectal or perineal wound needs a diverting colostomy and has a far higher mortality.
  • Morel-Lavallee lesion. A closed degloving over the flank or trochanter, full of haematoma and fat necrosis, lies under the planned incision or under a block site and is colonised more often than it looks.
  • Anterior subcutaneous internal fixator. Pedicle screws above the acetabula joined by a subcutaneous rod: quick and well tolerated, with compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve as the common complaint and of the femoral nerve as the rare serious one.
  • Sacral fractures with root injury. Neurological deficits in the L5 and S1 roots and the bladder are part of the injury; document them before any neuraxial technique is considered.
  • Thromboembolism. Proximal thrombosis in the pelvic veins is not seen by a leg duplex. A fall in saturation in the first fortnight is a pulmonary embolus until imaged.
  • Obesity. Every approach is deeper, the fluoroscopy is poorer, wound complications are much more frequent, and prone positioning for hours becomes the main anaesthetic risk.
  • The anticoagulated older patient. A minor-looking pubic ramus fracture can bleed slowly to shock over hours; reverse early and image with contrast.

Key sources

The evidence here is better for what does not work than for what does. Tranexamic acid has two randomised trials and a meta-analysis in acetabular fixation, all negative. Cell salvage has retrospective series that disagree on whether it saves allogeneic blood. Packing against embolisation for the unstable pelvis has a meta-analysis that concludes the cohorts cannot be compared. The sciatic nerve figures come from a meta-analysis and a large single-centre series. Analgesia has a negative case-control study of epidurals, a confounded cohort, a small retrospective comparison of surgeon-placed catheters and one small randomised trial comparing two blocks with each other. The pain score of 5 and the regional recommendations are the author’s judgement from the anatomy and should be revised when a proper trial exists.

  1. McDonogh JM, Lewis DP, Tarrant SM, Balogh ZJ. Preperitoneal packing versus angioembolization for the initial management of hemodynamically unstable pelvic fracture: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2022;92:931-939
    18 studies, 579 patients: crude mortality 23% after packing and 32% after embolisation in non-comparable cohorts, no difference in the studies with both arms; 27% of packed patients still needed embolisation for control
  2. Lack WD, Crist BD, Seymour RB, Harvin W, Karunakar MA; TXA Study Group. Effect of tranexamic acid on transfusion: a randomized clinical trial in acetabular fracture surgery. J Orthop Trauma 2017;31:526-530
    88 patients: overall transfusion rate 40.9% and mean estimated loss 635 mL; no difference in transfusion, blood loss or thromboembolism between tranexamic acid and placebo; low pre-operative haemoglobin and long operations predicted transfusion

    Six studies, 764 patients: no difference in estimated blood loss, transfusion rate, thromboembolism or infection with tranexamic acid

  6. Bigsby E, Acharya MR, Ward AJ, Chesser TJ. The use of blood cell salvage in acetabular fracture internal fixation surgery. J Orthop Trauma 2013;27:e230-e233

    Median three-day morphine use 5.0 mg with a surgeon-placed catheter, 6.0 mg with an epidural and 12.7 mg with neither, not statistically different; the catheter matched the epidural and added no procedure

    46 patients under spinal anaesthesia for anterior intrapelvic fixation, randomised to fascia iliaca or quadratus lumborum block: no difference in pain scores at any time; less morphine in the first 24 h after the quadratus lumborum block

Trauma › Trauma

44 Humeral shaft fixation

Open plating by posterior or anterolateral approach, minimally invasive plating and antegrade nailing; the radial nerve before and after

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Periosteum. A long plate laid on a bone exposed over 15-20 cm, with triceps or brachialis split to reach it and periosteum stripped at the fracture; for a nail, reaming of the canal and an entry hole through the rotator cuff that makes the shoulder the sore part. The fracture is rigid afterwards, which removes the pre-operative pain of moving bone ends, and the arm is not weight-bearing

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
General anaesthesia with surgeon wound infiltration and IV dexamethasone; a single-shot supraclavicular or infraclavicular block offered in recovery once radial nerve function has been examined and written down
Catheter: rarely The pain is periosteal and settles within three days, so a single shot given after the nerve check covers the worst of it; a catheter is for the non-union with iliac crest graft in an opioid-tolerant patient, and then only after the nerve examination
Alternatives: Pre-operative supraclavicular block by explicit agreement with the surgeon, when a complete radial palsy is already documented or when the surgeon will see the nerve and would not re-explore on the day whatever the examination showed; Supraclavicular block with sedation as the sole anaesthetic for the patient who should not have a general anaesthetic, accepting the delayed nerve examination; Interscalene or superior trunk block for the shoulder pain of an antegrade nail, on the same nerve-check terms; Surgeon infiltration alone with systemic multimodal analgesia
Position
Lateral decubitus with the arm over a padded bolster for the posterior approach (prone in some hands); supine with an arm table for the anterolateral approach and minimally invasive plating; beach chair for antegrade nailing
Tourniquet
No. The incision runs too far proximally for a cuff; a sterile tourniquet is used by a few surgeons for distal-third fractures only
Cement
No
Blood loss
200-500 mL for open plating, more for a non-union taken down through callus; under 150 mL for a nail or a minimally invasive plate
Duration
90-150 min for open plating; 60-90 min for a nail or minimally invasive plate; 150-240 min for a non-union with bone graft
Length of stay
One night for most isolated fractures; day case in selected patients; set by the other injuries in polytrauma. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg)
Tranexamic acid
Not routine; tranexamic acid 1 g IV is reasonable for a non-union or a pathological fracture
VTE
Mechanical and early mobilisation for an isolated arm; chemoprophylaxis is decided by the other injuries and the patient's own risk
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV
Tell the patient
The plate or rod holds the bone still, which takes away the grinding pain you have now; the arm aches for a few days, and the first thing we will ask when you wake is to lift your wrist and thumb so we know the nerve beside the bone is working.
The trap
A block placed before surgery turns the most important finding in recovery, a new wrist drop, into something nobody can interpret for 18 hours: examine and record the radial nerve before the anaesthetic and after it, and block in between only with the surgeon's agreement

What the surgeon is doing and why

The humeral shaft is a forgiving bone. It is wrapped in muscle with a good blood supply, it does not bear weight, and the shoulder and elbow compensate for 20 degrees of angulation or a few centimetres of shortening without the patient noticing. For that reason most shaft fractures have been treated in a functional brace, and the one randomised trial of plating against bracing found no meaningful difference in arm function at a year. What it also found is that 30% of the braced patients needed an operation within the year because the fracture had not healed, and an operation through an established non-union is longer and bloodier than the primary one.

So the patients who reach theatre are selected. Some have an absolute reason: an open fracture, a vascular injury, a floating elbow, a pathological fracture, bilateral fractures, or polytrauma in which a fixed arm lets the patient use crutches and be nursed. Some have a fracture that will not stay acceptably aligned in a brace, which is commoner with transverse fractures, obesity and large breasts. And some have chosen early fixation for a faster return to work over six to twelve weeks of a mobile fracture. A fourth group arrives months later with a non-union.

One structure dominates the operation. The radial nerve leaves the axilla, winds around the back of the humerus in direct contact with bone in the spiral groove, and pierces the lateral intermuscular septum about a hand’s breadth above the elbow to reach the front of the arm. It is tethered at the septum, so a fracture of the middle or distal third can stretch it, bruise it or trap it between the fragments. In the pooled literature 11.8% of shaft fractures have a radial nerve palsy at presentation; 88% of those recover, most of them spontaneously, and early exploration does not improve the result. The surgeon then has to operate next to the same nerve, and each technique meets it differently:

  Technique                 Nerve seen    Where the nerve is at risk
  Posterior plate           yes, always   dissected off bone, plate
                                          slid beneath it
  Anterolateral plate       distally      under retractors; brachialis
                                          split protects it
  Minimally invasive plate  no            distal incision, and blind
                                          under the anterior plate
  Antegrade nail            no            closed reduction, reaming,
                                          lateral distal locking screw

Plating means exposing the bone. The posterior approach splits or lifts triceps, finds the radial nerve and its companion artery in the groove, mobilises them, and lays a plate on the flat posterior surface with the nerve crossing over it; it suits middle and distal-third fractures. The anterolateral approach goes between biceps and brachialis proximally and splits brachialis distally, leaving its lateral half as a cushion over the nerve; it suits proximal and middle-third fractures and a supine patient. Minimally invasive plating slides an anterior plate under brachialis through two small incisions without opening the fracture. Nailing passes a rod down the canal from the top of the humerus through a hole in the rotator cuff, or the interval beside it, and locks it with screws at each end.

The comparisons are consistent in direction and weak in quality. The posterior approach carries more iatrogenic palsy than the anterolateral (69 of 497 against 35 of 678 in the pooled studies, OR 2.72), with similar recovery. Nailing has less iatrogenic palsy, less infection, less blood loss and a shorter operating time than open plating, at the cost of fracture comminution during insertion and the shoulder complaints of a cuff entry point. Minimally invasive plating had the lowest odds of radial nerve injury in the network meta-analysis of randomised trials, on wide intervals.

The pain logic: the dominant mechanism for a plate is periosteum, a raw, incisional and deep ache along the arm from a bone exposed over most of its length through a split muscle, peaking on day 1 and settling over three days. For a nail the arm is nearly painless and the shoulder is not, because of the cuff. Two things keep this at a 3. The fracture, which hurt with every movement in a sling, is now rigid, and many patients have less pain on day 2 than they had the week before. And the bone is not loaded.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Before the anaesthetic: the radial nerve and the reason for surgery

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has recorded whether the patient can extend the wrist, the fingers at the knuckles and the thumb, and whether the back of the first web space feels normal. A palsy present from the injury is usually observed; a palsy that appears after a manipulation or an operation raises the question of a trapped nerve.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Examine the nerve yourself and write it down with the time: wrist extension, thumb extension, sensation over the first dorsal web space. It takes 20 seconds and it is the baseline against which the recovery-room examination will be read. Then find out which patient this is. The isolated fracture in a fit adult is routine. The polytrauma patient has a chest, a head and other fractures that set the priorities (see polytrauma sequencing). The pathological fracture has a cancer, often myeloma, renal cell or breast, with anaemia, hypercalcaemia and a tumour that may bleed heavily. The non-union has had months of disuse and often months of opioids.

  2. 2 The anaesthetic and the block decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants to see the wrist and thumb lift in recovery. After a closed nailing or a minimally invasive plate the nerve was never seen, so a new palsy may mean it is caught in the fracture or under the plate, and many surgeons would re-explore that day. After an open plating the nerve was seen and protected, and a new palsy is more often watched.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    General anaesthesia is the default: the positions are awkward for an awake patient and the block that would make it comfortable is the block in question. Have the conversation before induction and record its outcome. If the surgeon would act on an immediate post-operative examination, no long-acting block goes in beforehand, the surgeon infiltrates the wound, and you offer a block in recovery once the examination is documented. If a complete palsy is already present, or the surgeon says the plan would be observation whatever the examination shows, a pre-operative supraclavicular block is reasonable and gives a smoother case. A dense plexus block does not injure the radial nerve; what it does is delay a diagnosis and leave the block as a possible explanation in the notes. Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction either way.

  3. 3 Positioning by approach

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Lateral with the arm draped over a padded bolster and the forearm hanging gives the posterior approach a vertical humerus and lets the elbow flex; some surgeons prefer prone. Supine with an arm table suits anterolateral and minimally invasive plating. Beach chair, with the shoulder off the edge of the table and extended, gives the nail its entry point.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Lateral and prone: a tracheal tube, the dependent arm and eye protected, the neck neutral, and the fractured arm lifted onto the bolster by the surgeon with traction, because the bone ends move and bleed. Beach chair: the blood pressure that matters is at the head and not at the cuff, with the cuff on the other arm or the leg, and the same vasopressor-supported, no-deliberate-hypotension approach as for shoulder arthroplasty. A patient with rib fractures on the dependent side, or a pelvis, may not tolerate the lateral position and that changes the surgeon’s approach.

  4. 4 Posterior approach and the radial nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A midline posterior incision, triceps split between its long and lateral heads or lifted from the lateral side, and the radial nerve found with the profunda brachii artery where they cross the bone. The nerve is freed proximally and distally and held in a loop so the plate can pass under it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The surgeon may ask for no muscle relaxant so that a nerve stimulator, or simply a twitch on touching the nerve, helps to identify it; settle that before you give a second dose. The profunda brachii is the bleeder in this approach. Handling the nerve is what produces the transient palsies, and how the nerve looked (in continuity, bruised, trapped or divided) is worth asking about and writing down, because it decides what a wrist drop in recovery means.

  5. 5 Anterolateral approach and minimally invasive plating

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Open: biceps is retracted medially and brachialis split along its length, which is possible because its medial half is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve and its lateral half by the radial; the radial nerve is found distally between brachialis and brachioradialis. Minimally invasive: a proximal incision between deltoid and biceps and a distal one over the front of the lower humerus, with a long plate tunnelled between them under brachialis and the fracture reduced by traction under fluoroscopy.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The musculocutaneous nerve and its terminal sensory branch, the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, are the structures at the distal incision: numbness along the radial border of the forearm afterwards is theirs. Minimally invasive plating trades dissection for radiation and for an indirect reduction that needs a relaxed arm and an assistant holding traction. It is the gentlest version of this operation for pain.

  6. 6 Reduction and plating

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The fracture is cleaned, reduced and held with clamps, then compressed with a lag screw and a neutralisation plate or bridged with a long locking plate, with at least three or four screws each side. In a non-union the fibrous tissue and sclerotic bone ends are resected back to bleeding bone and the gap is packed with graft, often from the iliac crest.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Clamps around the humerus are placed on bone, with the nerve in view on one side and the brachial artery and median nerve across the medial septum on the other. Bleeding is steady from the bone ends and the split muscle and is 200-500 mL in a fresh fracture. A non-union doubles the time and the loss and adds a second, often more painful, wound at the iliac crest that no arm block covers: have the surgeon infiltrate it. A pathological fracture through a vascular metastasis can bleed far beyond this range; such tumours are embolised beforehand when the diagnosis is known.

  7. 7 Antegrade nailing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With the shoulder extended, a short incision at the edge of the acromion, a split in the deltoid and a small incision in the supraspinatus tendon or the rotator interval give access to the top of the humeral head. A guide wire is passed across the fracture, the canal is reamed by most surgeons, and the nail is inserted and locked proximally through a jig and distally freehand.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming and nail passage in a humerus produce far less marrow embolisation than in a femur, and oxygenation changes are unusual in an isolated injury; in bilateral or pathological fractures with a compromised chest it is no longer negligible (see fat embolism). The proximal locking screws pass near the axillary nerve, and a lateral-to-medial distal locking screw passes near the radial nerve, which is why most surgeons lock from front to back through a small open incision. The fracture is reduced closed: if the nerve lies between the fragments nobody sees it. Blood loss is small. This is the technique with the most to gain from an immediate nerve examination.

  8. 8 Closure and the nerve check on waking

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Muscle falls back over the plate, the fascia is closed, the wound is infiltrated, and the arm goes into a sling. The surgeon records in the operation note where the nerve lies in relation to the plate, for whoever takes the plate out.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Plan the emergence around an examination: a patient who is awake, comfortable and able to follow a command within a few minutes of leaving theatre. That means short-acting agents, the wound infiltrated, paracetamol and an opioid on board, and no residual neuromuscular block. As soon as the patient can cooperate, ask for the wrist to be lifted and the thumb raised, and write the result and the time in the anaesthetic record as well as telling the surgeon.

  9. 9 Recovery, the block and going home

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With rigid fixation the surgeon wants the elbow and shoulder moving within days and the hand used for light tasks at once. A patient with a radial palsy gets a wrist splint and hand therapy while it recovers.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    With the examination documented, a single-shot supraclavicular block (or infraclavicular for a mid or distal exposure) is now simply good analgesia: 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%, on top of the dexamethasone already given. Offer it to the open plating patient with pain above 4 in recovery, to the non-union, and to anyone opioid-tolerant; the minimally invasive plate and the nail often do not need it. A block given at 4 pm wears off in the small hours, so the oral regimen starts before discharge from recovery and the patient who goes home the same day has a written night plan and a sling that stays on while the arm is numb. If a new palsy is found, no block is placed until the surgeon has decided between re-exploration and observation.

Pain plan

The mechanism is periosteal and muscular, short-lived, in a limb that is rested, so the plan is a general anaesthetic with surgeon infiltration, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, regular paracetamol and an NSAID from the first evening, an oral opioid for two to four days, and a single-shot plexus block timed after the nerve examination for those who need it. Surgeons vary on NSAIDs after fracture fixation; the concern is non-union, the evidence for harm from a short course is weak, and the author’s practice is a course of a week or less unless the surgeon objects, and none for a non-union operation.

The block decision is the distinctive part of this card and it is a decision about information, not about nerve safety. There is no trial of regional anaesthesia in humeral shaft fixation and no evidence that a plexus block worsens a traumatic or iatrogenic radial neuropathy. The argument for waiting is the surgical one: one in nine fractures has a palsy before surgery, a further few per cent acquire one during it (most often with the posterior approach and open plating), and the immediate examination separates the two and, after a closed technique, may send the patient back to theatre. A pre-operative block removes that examination for 12 to 24 hours with dexamethasone on board. The cost of waiting is small, because the operation is done under general anaesthesia regardless and the block works as well at the end as at the beginning. The defensible default is therefore to block afterwards. Blocking beforehand is reasonable when the examination cannot change anything: a complete palsy already documented, or a surgeon who has stated that the nerve will be visualised and a new deficit observed.

Which block follows from the incision. The shaft and its periosteum are supplied by the radial, musculocutaneous and axillary nerves, with skin over the lateral and posterior arm from the axillary and radial nerves and the medial arm from the intercostobrachial; a supraclavicular block covers nearly all of it and an infraclavicular block covers the middle and distal shaft. An axillary block does not reach high enough. The shoulder pain of an antegrade nail is suprascapular and axillary territory, which a supraclavicular block reaches incompletely and an interscalene or superior trunk block reaches well.

A catheter is rarely justified: the curve falls within three days. Rebound after a single shot is moderate here, lower than after wrist or ankle surgery in the author’s experience, because the fixed fracture hurts less than the unfixed one did; the rebound cohort’s risk factors (bone surgery, younger age, no dexamethasone) still apply. Escalation: severe pain with a tense arm and pain on passive finger extension is a compartment syndrome of the arm or forearm, which is rare and associated with vascular injury and crush; increasing pain with a swollen, bruised arm in a patient on an anticoagulant is a haematoma, and one that presses on the radial nerve produces a palsy hours after a normal examination, which is the reason to repeat the examination before the patient leaves.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Pre-existing radial nerve palsy. Common, usually a neurapraxia, and usually observed. It removes the argument against a pre-operative block only if it is complete; a partial palsy can still worsen and still needs a post-operative examination.
  • Palsy that appears after a closed manipulation or between examinations. Treated by many surgeons as a nerve in the fracture and explored; this may be the indication for the operation.
  • Holstein-Lewis pattern. A spiral fracture of the distal third with the nerve tethered at the septum beside the spike: the highest-risk configuration for both injury-related and surgical palsy.
  • Non-union surgery. Longer, bloodier, an iliac crest wound, a nerve stuck in scar, and a patient who may be opioid-tolerant: the one catheter indication, and a tranexamic acid case.
  • Pathological fracture. A nail is the usual implant because it protects the whole bone; the anaesthetic is governed by the cancer (haemoglobin, calcium, renal function, other lesions in the cervical spine and femur) and by bleeding from vascular metastases.
  • Polytrauma. A humeral shaft is fixed early to allow crutches and nursing, often at the same sitting as a femur or tibia; position and timing are set by the chest and the head, and the arm takes whichever technique fits the position the other operations need.
  • Vascular injury. A brachial artery repair comes with a fasciotomy of the forearm, an anticoagulant and no plexus block until the compartments are no longer in question.
  • Beach chair hypotension during nailing. The same cerebral perfusion problem as any sitting shoulder operation, in a trauma patient who may be hypovolaemic.
  • The patient who must avoid general anaesthesia. A supraclavicular block with an intercostobrachial supplement and light sedation is workable for an anterolateral or minimally invasive plate in the supine position, and the delayed nerve examination is an accepted cost that the surgeon agrees to in advance.
  • Removal of the plate. Rarely needed, and the hazardous part of it is the radial nerve lying over the metal: see removal of metalwork.

Key sources

The radial nerve figures rest on a large systematic review of injury-related palsy and several meta-analyses of iatrogenic palsy by approach and implant, which agree in direction (posterior and open plating worst, nailing and minimally invasive plating best) and are built on small, heterogeneous studies. The decision to operate at all is informed by one good randomised trial. There is no trial of any regional technique in humeral shaft fixation: the advice to block after the nerve examination is the author’s judgement about the value of that examination, consistent with the approach on the elbow fracture card.

  1. Shao YC, Harwood P, Grotz MR, Limb D, Giannoudis PV. Radial nerve palsy associated with fractures of the shaft of the humerus: a systematic review. J Bone Joint Surg Br 2005;87:1647-1652
    4,517 fractures in 21 papers: radial nerve palsy in 11.8%, most often with middle and middle-distal third fractures and transverse or spiral patterns; overall recovery 88.1%, spontaneous recovery 70.7% in those managed expectantly; early exploration did not improve the final result
  2. Shon HC, Yang JY, Lee Y, Cho JW, Oh JK, Lim EJ. Iatrogenic radial nerve palsy in the surgical treatment of humerus shaft fracture, anterolateral versus posterior approach: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Orthop Sci 2023;28:244-250
    Nine studies, 1,303 patients: iatrogenic palsy in 35 of 678 after the anterolateral approach and 69 of 497 after the posterior approach (OR 2.72 for posterior); recovery rates did not differ
  3. Protasio Netto J, Giordano V, Elias N, Belangero WD, Cavalcante B. Minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis, open reduction and plate fixation, and intramedullary nailing for humeral shaft fractures: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Injury 2026;57:113551
    12 trials, 647 patients: minimally invasive plating had lower odds of iatrogenic radial nerve injury (OR 0.21) and of reoperation (OR 0.18) than open plating; nailing ranked between them; the result depended on two trials and the intervals are wide
  4. Nadeem A, Abbasi H. Outcomes of intramedullary nailing versus plate fixation in the management of humeral shaft fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Cureus 2024;16:e72473
    26 studies, 1,674 patients: nailing had less iatrogenic radial nerve palsy (RR 0.48) and infection (RR 0.44), similar non-union, and more intra-operative comminution (RR 3.04); heterogeneous
  5. Hu Y, Wu T, Li B, Huang Y, Huang C, Luo Y. Efficacy and safety evaluation of intramedullary nail and locking compression plate in the treatment of humeral shaft fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Comput Math Methods Med 2022;2022:5759233
    14 studies, 903 patients: shorter operating time and less blood loss with a nail than with a locking plate
  6. Ramo L, Sumrein BO, Lepola V, et al. Effect of surgery vs functional bracing on functional outcome among patients with closed displaced humeral shaft fractures: the FISH randomized clinical trial. JAMA 2020;323:1792-1801
    82 patients: DASH score at 12 months 8.9 after plating and 12.0 after bracing, a difference of 3.1 points that was neither significant nor clinically important; 30% of the bracing group needed surgery within the year for failure to heal
  7. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients: rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, and absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78

Trauma › Trauma

45 Open fractures, external fixation and damage control orthopaedics

Gustilo grading, the antibiotic clock, debridement and irrigation, spanning and temporary external fixation, the second hit and the conversion decision in the polytrauma patient

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A high-energy fracture with its periosteum stripped by the injury, splinted by pins drilled through skin, muscle and both cortices; a wound extended and debrided to bleeding muscle and left open or under a negative pressure dressing; then reopened every 48-72 h until it is covered. The frame removes most of the fracture pain; the debrided wound and the pin sites are what remain

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
General anaesthesia with a rapid sequence induction and multimodal analgesia including ketamine; a dilute single-shot peripheral block for the limb (popliteal sciatic and adductor canal for the leg, brachial plexus for the arm) only after a documented compartment examination and with a surveillance plan the surgeon has agreed
Catheter: rarely Not in the first 48 h of a fresh high-energy fracture, because compartment syndrome occurs in open fractures as often as in closed ones and the catheter is the device that has hidden it; reasonable later for the flap day or the staged definitive fixation, once the window has closed and the limb is examined daily
Alternatives: Brachial plexus block for the open forearm or humerus, dilute and single shot, with the same surveillance logic; No block at all for the night-time damage control fixator in a polytrauma patient who needs serial examination of the limb or the head; Surgeon's infiltration of pin sites and wound edges with long-acting local anaesthetic
Position
Supine on a radiolucent table with the whole limb in the field and the C-arm from the opposite side; the leg on a bolster or brought over the side for a posterior wound; lateral or prone only for a posterior pelvic or scapular wound, which is rare
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Applied and left down in most hands: the surgeon judges muscle viability by colour, consistency, contractility and bleeding, and an inflated cuff removes two of the four; some surgeons inflate briefly for a bloodless look at a vessel or nerve, and never for a limb with a vascular injury
Cement
No
Blood loss
The fracture and the wound have bled before you meet them: 500 mL for a tibia, 1-1.5 L for a femur, more for a pelvis. Debridement and a fixator add 200-500 mL; a fasciotomy or a vascular repair at the same sitting adds much more. Group and hold for an isolated limb; crossmatch for a Gustilo IIIC, a femur or a polytrauma patient
Duration
60-120 min for debridement, irrigation and a fixator on one limb; 30-45 min for a damage control fixator alone; several hours when a vascular repair, a fasciotomy or a flap is done at the same sitting
Length of stay
Set by the soft tissue, not the bone: a few nights for a Gustilo I or II fracture nailed and closed at the first operation; weeks for a IIIB with a frame and a flap, with returns to theatre every 48-72 h in between. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g over 120 kg) as soon as possible after injury and within the hour, almost always already given in the emergency department and redosed for the operation; Gram-negative cover (gentamicin) added for Gustilo III and heavily contaminated wounds in most protocols; duration set by the wound and the protocol rather than by a day count, and stopped soon after soft tissue cover
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 h of injury for the bleeding patient, then 1 g over 8 h (CRASH-2); 1 g IV at induction for the debridement is reasonable
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin from the night of injury or surgery when the bleeding risk allows; mechanical prophylaxis on the uninjured leg; a frame and a flap mean weeks of immobility and the prophylaxis runs for all of them
Antiemetic
Ondansetron 4 mg IV; dexamethasone 8 mg IV is reasonable (a single dose did not raise the surgical site infection rate in the 8,880-patient PADDI trial, which was elective surgery and not open fractures) but it prolongs any block, so it is withheld when a short examinable block is the aim
Tell the patient
The first operation cleans the wound and holds the bone with a frame on the outside; most people need two or three more trips to theatre over the next week to check the wound and cover it, and the leg hurts most in the first two days and each time it is reopened.
The trap
The antibiotic is the intervention that matters most and it is not yours to delay: in type III open tibias an antibiotic more than 66 min after injury carried nearly four times the odds of deep infection and wound cover beyond five days seven times, so the question in the anaesthetic room is when the first dose went in, not whether the patient is fasted

What the surgeon is doing and why

An open fracture is a soft tissue injury with a bone in it. The energy that broke the bone has also torn the muscle, stripped the periosteum, devascularised the skin and pushed road, soil or water into the wound; the bacteria that matter arrive at the moment of injury, not on the ward. Everything the surgeon does in the first week follows from that: the wound is treated before the fracture, the fracture is held in a way that adds no soft tissue damage, and the aim is a clean, covered, vascularised wound within 72 h so that a fracture-related infection, the complication that turns a six-week injury into a two-year one, never starts.

The Gustilo grade is the shared language and it grades the soft tissue, not the bone. Type I is a clean wound under 1 cm; type II is 1-10 cm without extensive soft tissue damage; type III is extensive soft tissue damage, heavy contamination, a segmental fracture, a farm injury or a high-velocity gunshot, split into IIIA (enough periosteum and muscle left to cover the bone), IIIB (periosteal stripping and exposed bone that needs a flap) and IIIC (an arterial injury that needs repair). The grade is assigned in theatre after debridement, because the skin wound on the trolley says little about the dead muscle beneath it. The grade predicts infection: in the original 1,025-fracture series the type III infection rate was 44% before the authors’ protocol and 9% under it, and in a 642-patient series from 2020 deep infection ran at 2.1% in type I, 7.6% in type II and 14.6% in type III.

The surgeon’s aims are in a fixed order, and the first is not surgical. Antibiotics within an hour of injury: in 137 type III open tibias, an antibiotic more than 66 min after injury carried an odds ratio of 3.78 for deep infection and wound cover beyond five days an odds ratio of 7.39; with both done early the infection rate was 2.8%, with both delayed 40.5%, and time to debridement did not predict infection at all. Then photograph, seal and splint the wound. Then debride in theatre: the six-hour rule is dead (16 cohorts, 3,539 fractures, no association between debridement timing and infection at any threshold or grade) and the BOAST standard replaced it with a stratified clock: immediately for agricultural, aquatic or sewage contamination and for vascular compromise or compartment syndrome, within 12 h for other high-energy open fractures, within 24 h for low-energy ones. Then irrigate with saline at low pressure, because the 2,447-patient FLOW trial found pressure made no difference and soap was worse than saline. Then stabilise, because a stable fracture lets the soft tissues heal and is the second antibiotic: most Gustilo I to IIIA fractures whose wound can be covered at once are fixed definitively at the first operation (the BOAST standard permits internal fixation only when cover can follow immediately), and the rest get an external fixator, pins through skin and both cortices away from the wound and joined by bars, which holds length and alignment without adding stripping, goes on in 30 min at night, can span a joint, and is converted to a nail or plate once the wound is covered. Then cover within 72 h, by delayed primary closure or a flap, as a combined orthoplastic decision, with a second look every 48-72 h until then.

The same fixator does a second job in the polytrauma patient, and that is where damage control enters. The injured patient has had a first hit: tissue destruction, shock, hypoxia and the inflammatory response they provoke. A long operation with its own blood loss, hypothermia and marrow embolisation is a second hit, and in the patient whose lungs and endothelium are already primed it is what tips them into acute lung injury and organ failure. The EPOFF trial measured it: in 35 stable polytrauma patients randomised to primary femoral nailing or a fixator, interleukin-6 rose over the 24 h after the nail and did not rise after the fixator, nor after the later conversion. Pape’s randomised trial of 165 polytrauma patients turned the marker into an outcome: in the 44 borderline patients, primary nailing carried an adjusted odds ratio of 6.69 for acute lung injury against a fixator with a nail later. Damage control orthopaedics is a fixator in minutes for the unstable or borderline patient, resuscitation in intensive care, and definitive fixation once the physiology says so; the Early Appropriate Care protocol puts numbers on “says so” (a lactate below 4.0 mmol/L, a pH of 7.25 or above, or a base excess of -5.5 mmol/L or better, with fixation within 36 h once met). The whole decision is on the polytrauma card; this card covers the fixator and the wound.

The pain logic. The mechanism is bone: a fractured, mobile long bone with its periosteum stripped by the injury, which the frame splints, so most of the fracture pain is gone when the pins are tight. What remains is the debrided wound (muscle and skin cut back to bleeding tissue and left open), the pin sites (drill holes through cortex with skin and muscle moving over them) and the swelling of a limb that bled into itself. The score is 3, with a tail that does not fall as cleanly as a closed fracture’s because the wound is reopened every two or three days and the flap day is a second operation. The compartment caveat that shapes the tibial card applies in full: an open fracture does not decompress its compartments, and the 198-fracture series found compartment syndrome in 9.1% of open tibial shafts, rising with the severity of the injury.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The emergency department: the antibiotic, the photograph and the splint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the antibiotic in, the wound photographed and sealed under saline gauze and film, the limb realigned and splinted with pulses and nerves documented before and after, and the vascular and compartment status settled.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    You will rarely be there, but you inherit the consequences. Find out the time of injury and of the first antibiotic and write both on the chart, because the dose is due again for the operation and the hour-long window is the one number in this card that changes outcome. Sedation or a block for the reduction is reasonable; a dense long-acting block before anyone has examined the compartments is not, and a femoral or fascia iliaca block for a femoral fracture is the exception because the thigh is not the compartment site the leg is. Tetanus (a booster for a tetanus-prone wound, immunoglobulin as well if the course is incomplete or unknown) is the department’s job and worth a question.

  2. 2 Classifying the patient, not the fracture

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Before the surgeon chooses between a fixator and a nail, the trauma team has to say whether the patient is stable, borderline or unstable: lactate and base deficit, temperature, coagulation, the chest and head injuries, the transfusion count. A borderline patient gets a fixator and a second operation in days; a stable one gets the whole operation tonight.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Have this conversation in the trauma bay with the numbers in front of both of you, because once the patient is asleep the surgeon’s default is to finish. A patient under the Early Appropriate Care lines who is warm, not coagulopathic and off vasopressors can have definitive fixation; in the 335-patient series the complication rate was 19.7% against 22.1% historically, and highest in patients who met only one of the three. A patient who meets none of them is a damage control patient whatever the wound looks like. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 h of injury if there is bleeding, then 1 g over 8 h: in the 20,211-patient CRASH-2 trial it reduced all-cause mortality from 16.0% to 14.5% and death from bleeding from 5.7% to 4.9% with no excess of thrombosis. Crossmatch for a femur, a IIIC or any patient with another injury.

  3. 3 Induction: the full stomach, the lines and the block decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a still patient and a relaxed limb for the reduction; for a fixator, nothing more; for a definitive nail, the femoral or tibial card follows.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Rapid sequence induction, with the fasting clock counted from the injury rather than the last meal, because pain, opioids and shock stopped gastric emptying at the roadside. Two large cannulae; an arterial line for the polytrauma patient, the IIIC and any case that may become a vascular repair. The block decision is the one the Association of Anaesthetists wrote its 2021 guideline for: a dilute single-shot peripheral block without adjuncts, placed after a documented compartment examination and with a surveillance plan the surgeon has agreed, is not linked to delayed diagnosis when the observation is competent; a dense, long-acting block or a neuraxial technique is to be avoided; and neither of you can veto the other, which means deciding together before the drapes go on. For the night-time damage control fixator in a patient who will be examined hourly for a head injury and a leg, the default is no block and a multimodal general anaesthetic with ketamine. Redose the cefazolin if more than 4 h have passed since the emergency department dose, and add the Gram-negative cover the protocol asks for in a type III wound.

  4. 4 Positioning, the tourniquet that stays down and the preparation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The whole limb is in the field, joint above to joint below, because the pins go in well away from the wound and the extensions run along fasciotomy lines; the C-arm comes from the opposite side. The skin is prepared with the splint off and the fracture held by an assistant.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Taking the splint off is the most painful moment of the day and the first time the fragments have moved freely since the reduction; it needs depth before it happens, and the fracture bleeds again. A tourniquet is usually applied and left uninflated, because muscle viability is judged by colour, consistency, contractility and bleeding and an inflated cuff hides two of the four; a limb with a vascular injury gets no cuff at all. Warm the patient from the start: cold on arrival, exposed from hip to toe, and about to have litres of room-temperature saline poured over the limb.

  5. 5 Wound extension, debridement and irrigation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The wound is extended so that the whole zone of injury can be seen and the extension does not compromise a later flap. Dead and contaminated skin, fat, fascia and muscle are excised back to tissue that bleeds and contracts, the bone ends are delivered into the wound and cleaned, and cortical fragments with no soft tissue attachment are discarded, because dead bone is a sequestrum and a culture plate. The Gustilo grade is assigned now. Then litres of saline at low pressure wash out what the knife has loosened; high pressure drives bacteria into tissue planes and soap damages the cells trying to heal, which is why FLOW moved practice away from both.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Bleeding muscle by design: a debridement that does not bleed has not been done, and the loss from a type III leg is steady rather than dramatic over 30-60 min. The moment the periosteum turns out to be stripped over several centimetres is the moment a IIIA becomes a IIIB, the plastic surgeon is telephoned and the plan for the frame and the cover changes. Muscle contractility under cautery is part of the assessment, and a request to hold off relaxant until the muscle has been tested is reasonable. The irrigation is heat loss and nothing else.

  6. 6 Stabilisation: the fixator

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Half-pins are drilled through small incisions into the bone away from the zone of injury, two above and two below the fracture, and connected with clamps and bars; across a joint for a periarticular fracture, the frame holds the limb out to length by ligamentotaxis.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Drilling through cortical bone under imaging: quick, bloody at each pin and painful afterwards in the way a drill hole through periosteum is. A frame across a knee or ankle fixes the foot and makes the compartments harder to examine, which is how the late diagnoses in the spanning fixator series happened. A damage control fixator is 30-45 min from skin to bars and is the point at which, in the borderline patient, the operation stops; a surgeon who proposes to ream a femur in a patient with a lactate of 6 mmol/L and a chest injury is proposing the second hit the randomised trial put an odds ratio of 6.69 on, and that conversation is better had now than in intensive care.

  7. 7 The compartments

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon examines the compartments at the end of the debridement and measures pressures in a high-energy tibia or forearm; an open wound does not decompress a compartment, and a fasciotomy at this sitting beats one tomorrow.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The examination at the end of the case is the baseline for the next 48 h and the moment the surveillance starts, so write the time and the findings. A dilute single-shot block will have receded by the evening; dexamethasone and perineural adjuncts are withheld for that reason. If a fasciotomy is done, the limb moves to the compartment syndrome card, with its blood loss, its open wounds and its own pain score.

  8. 8 The vascular injury: the IIIC limb

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A pulseless limb with a fracture is revascularised within 6 h of injury or the muscle dies: a temporary intraluminal shunt by the vascular surgeon, the fixator so a mobile fracture cannot disrupt the repair, then the definitive vein graft, and a prophylactic fasciotomy in most hands because the reperfused compartments will swell.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A long case booked as a short one, with two teams, no tourniquet, a reperfusion event when the shunt opens (potassium, acid, myoglobin, a fall in pressure) and a blood loss measured in units. Heparin at the surgeon’s request with the head and the pelvis considered first; an arterial line, warmed products and a plan for the compartments. The unstable patient here is the one in whom the amputation conversation is had early; the BOAST standard puts delayed primary amputation within 72 h after a multidisciplinary assessment, and the amputation card covers what follows.

  9. 9 Dressing, the open wound and the plan for cover

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A type I or II wound is often closed at the first operation; a type III is left open or loosely closed over the bone, with the extensions closed, under a negative pressure dressing that is not disturbed on the ward. The orthoplastic plan is written: second look at 48 h, definitive cover by 72 h.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The negative pressure canister collects blood nobody counts; check it in recovery. Awake extubation after a rapid sequence induction. The first night’s analgesia is opioid-based and multimodal with ketamine, and the pain score the ward acts on is the one that rises despite it; the compartment surveillance chart is the document that matters tonight.

  10. 10 The second look, the flap and the conversion

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The patient returns at 48-72 h for a repeat debridement; doubtful muscle has declared itself, and the wound is closed, covered with a local or free flap, or dressed again. The fixator is converted to a nail or plate once the wound is covered and before the pin tracts colonise, in most hands within two weeks, and in the polytrauma patient after the inflammatory peak of the first days has passed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Each return is a short general anaesthetic in a patient who is now fasted, on opioids and often anaemic; a block is reasonable at the second look once the compartments have been examined and recorded, and a catheter for the flap day. The flap day is a different anaesthetic: 4-8 h of microsurgery, a warm, well-filled, vasodilated patient with a mean pressure the plastic surgeon has named, vasopressors avoided where possible, a haemoglobin not allowed to fall far, and a urinary catheter. The conversion to a nail in a polytrauma patient is the second-hit question asked again; in EPOFF the delayed conversion did not raise the markers the primary nail did.

Pain plan

The mechanism is a fractured, periosteum-stripped bone splinted by a frame under a debrided wound that is reopened every two or three days, so the plan is a multimodal general anaesthetic with a regional component chosen for the compartment risk rather than for the pain, and a catheter held back until the window has closed. There is no PROSPECT guideline for open fractures; the structure is the author’s, built on the Association of Anaesthetists’ 2021 guideline for lower leg trauma.

The block. For the leg, a single-shot popliteal sciatic block with an adductor canal or femoral block, dilute (ropivacaine 0.2% or equivalent), no perineural adjunct and no intravenous dexamethasone, placed after the compartment examination has been written down and with a surveillance chart the surgeon has agreed; the aim is a block that has receded by the evening examination. For the arm, a brachial plexus block on the same terms, because the forearm has compartments too. For the night-time damage control fixator in a polytrauma patient, no block: the patient needs serial examination of the limb and often the head, the operation is 40 min, and the first 48 h belong to the surveillance. This is the author’s judgement, agreed with the surgeon before the case.

The catheter. Rarely, and never in the first 48 h of a fresh high-energy fracture: the large tibial series found every missed compartment syndrome in its blocked group had a catheter, and the open fracture carries the same compartment risk as the closed one. It earns its place later, for the flap day, when the limb has been examined daily for a week, the case is long and a sympathectomised warm limb is what the plastic surgeon wants, and for the staged definitive fixation once the window has closed.

The oral regimen shape: regular paracetamol; an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the surgeon accepts it (many withhold NSAIDs after a high-energy tibial or femoral fracture for fear of non-union, an observational association and their call); a regular opioid for the first 48-72 h with a patient-controlled analgesia pump for the young high-energy patient; and low-dose ketamine for the unblocked and the opioid-tolerant patient. Rebound is moderate: when the dilute block recedes the frame is holding the bone and the pain is a sore wound and sore pins, severe for an hour or two until the regular regimen catches up. Each return to theatre resets the clock by a day.

Escalation: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch of the toes or fingers, a tense compartment or a rising opioid requirement in the first 48 h is a compartment syndrome until the pressure says otherwise, and the response is the surgeon and a measurement, not a rescue block and not more morphine. Pain that rises at day 3-5 with a wound that smells, a fever and a rising C-reactive protein is a fracture-related infection and the surgeon sees it before the dressing is changed.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The isolated low-energy open fracture. Debrided, fixed and closed in one sitting; the closed fracture’s anaesthetic with an antibiotic clock, and a dilute block is reasonable.
  • The open femur. A reamed nail for most IIIA wounds in a stable patient; a fixator for the borderline patient and the contaminated or vascular wound; the femoral card for the reaming decision.
  • The open forearm. Plated at the first operation in most clean wounds, with a brachial plexus block on the same compartment terms as the leg; forearm compartment syndrome is real and under-recognised.
  • The farm, river and sewage wound. Immediate debridement whatever the hour, broader antibiotic cover per the protocol, and a return at 24 h rather than 48 h.
  • Pin site infection and the long frame. Pin infection is common and usually superficial, and is the reason a late conversion to a nail carries a higher infection rate than an early one; a circular frame for a bone defect stays on for months, with pin pain, sleep loss and opioid escalation as the course, and a pain service referral at the second week beats one at the second month.
  • The head-injured patient. Hypoxia, hypotension and raised intracranial pressure cause the secondary injury, not early fixation; the fixator over the nail in the first days.
  • Fat embolism and the fixator. A fixator reams no canal and embolises no marrow, one of its two advantages over a nail in a borderline patient; the other is time.

Key sources

The infection evidence is good and consistent: the Gustilo series, the antibiotic timing study that put an hour on the clock, the systematic review that killed the six-hour rule, FLOW for irrigation and the BOAST standard that turns them into a pathway. The damage control evidence is smaller but randomised: EPOFF for the measured second hit and Pape’s borderline trial for the clinical one, with the Early Appropriate Care series supplying the resuscitation thresholds from a prospective, non-randomised cohort. The regional anaesthesia advice is the Association of Anaesthetists’ guideline applied to open wounds, with the 1986 series as the reason an open fracture earns no exemption. There is no procedure-specific analgesia guideline; the block and catheter timing is the author’s reading of the compartment window.

  1. Gustilo RB, Anderson JT. Prevention of infection in the treatment of one thousand and twenty-five open fractures of long bones: retrospective and prospective analyses. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1976;58:453-458
    The classification paper: 673 retrospective and 352 prospective open long bone fractures; debridement, irrigation, primary closure for types I and II, delayed closure for type III, no primary internal fixation except with a vascular injury, and antibiotics before surgery; type III infection fell from 44% to 9% under the protocol; cephalosporin identified as the prophylactic of choice
  2. Lack WD, Karunakar MA, Angerame MR, et al. Type III open tibia fractures: immediate antibiotic prophylaxis minimizes infection. J Orthop Trauma 2015;29:1-6
    137 type III open tibias: antibiotics beyond 66 min after injury (OR 3.78) and wound cover beyond 5 days (OR 7.39) independently predicted deep infection; 2.8% with both done early, 40.5% with both delayed; time to debridement was not a predictor
  3. Schenker ML, Yannascoli S, Baldwin KD, Ahn J, Mehta S. Does timing to operative debridement affect infectious complications in open long-bone fractures? A systematic review. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2012;94:1057-1064
    16 cohort studies, 3,539 open fractures: no difference in infection between early and late debridement at any threshold, in any Gustilo grade or for deep infection alone; the six-hour rule has little support
  4. FLOW Investigators. A trial of wound irrigation in the initial management of open fracture wounds. N Engl J Med 2015;373:2629-2641
    2,447 open fractures randomised in a 2-by-3 design: reoperation for wound or bone healing or infection was the same at high, low and very low irrigation pressure (13.2%, 12.7%, 13.7%), and higher with castile soap than saline (14.8% versus 11.6%, HR 1.32)
  5. Mener A, Staley CA, Lunati MP, Pflederer J, Reisman WM, Schenker ML. Is operative debridement greater than 24 hours post-admission associated with increased likelihood of post-operative infection? J Surg Res 2020
    642 open fractures: infection 8.7% overall, 2.1% in type I, 7.6% in type II and 14.6% in type III; debridement beyond 24 h was not associated with infection, while the number of operations and time to definitive wound closure were
  6. British Orthopaedic Association. BOAST: Open Fractures. December 2017
    Antibiotics within an hour of injury; debridement immediately for agricultural, aquatic or sewage contamination or vascular compromise, within 12 h for other high-energy open fractures and within 24 h for low-energy ones; a combined orthoplastic plan; definitive internal fixation only if cover can follow immediately; definitive cover within 72 h; delayed primary amputation within 72 h where indicated
  7. Blick SS, Brumback RJ, Poka A, Burgess AR, Ebraheim NA. Compartment syndrome in open tibial fractures. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1986;68:1348-1353
    198 open tibial shaft fractures: compartment syndrome in 9.1%, rising with the severity of soft tissue and bone injury and commonest in comminuted grade III injuries; an open wound does not decompress the compartments
  8. Pape HC, Grimme K, Van Griensven M, et al. Impact of intramedullary instrumentation versus damage control for femoral fractures on immunoinflammatory parameters: prospective randomized analysis by the EPOFF Study Group. J Trauma 2003;55:7-13
    35 stable polytrauma patients randomised to primary nailing or external fixation: IL-6 rose over the 24 h after primary nailing and did not rise after external fixation or after the later conversion to a nail; the measured second hit
  9. Pape HC, Rixen D, Morley J, et al. Impact of the method of initial stabilization for femoral shaft fractures in patients with multiple injuries at risk for complications (borderline patients). Ann Surg 2007;246:491-499
    165 multiply injured patients randomised to primary nailing within 24 h or external fixation with later conversion: in the 44 borderline patients, primary nailing carried an adjusted odds ratio of 6.69 for acute lung injury; in stable patients primary nailing shortened ventilation
  10. Scalea TM, Boswell SA, Scott JD, et al. External fixation as a bridge to intramedullary nailing for patients with multiple injuries and with femur fractures: damage control orthopedics. J Trauma 2000;48:613-621
    43 patients with initial external fixation compared with 284 primary nailings: temporary external fixation was safe in multiply injured patients, the paper that named damage control orthopaedics
  11. Weinberg DS, Narayanan AS, Moore TA, Vallier HA. Assessment of resuscitation as measured by markers of metabolic acidosis and features of injury. Bone Joint J 2017;99-B:122-127
    335 patients with pelvic, acetabular, femoral or spinal fractures under the Early Appropriate Care protocol: definitive fixation within 36 h once lactate was below 4.0 mmol/L, pH 7.25 or above, or base excess -5.5 mmol/L or better; complications 19.7% against 22.1% in the historical cohort, and highest (34.3%) when only one parameter was met
  12. Association of Anaesthetists. Regional analgesia for lower leg trauma and the risk of acute compartment syndrome: guideline from the Association of Anaesthetists. Anaesthesia 2021
    Lower-concentration peripheral blocks without adjuncts are not linked to delayed diagnosis when surveillance is effective; dense, long-lasting neuraxial or peripheral blocks are to be avoided; observations by trained staff at set intervals; neither surgeon nor anaesthetist can veto the other's recommendation
  13. Corcoran TB, Myles PS, Forbes AB, et al. Dexamethasone and surgical-site infection. N Engl J Med 2021;384:1731-1741
    PADDI: 8,880 patients having non-urgent surgery of 2 h or more randomised to dexamethasone 8 mg IV or placebo; surgical site infection 8.1% versus 9.1%, noninferior, with nausea and vomiting reduced from 53.9% to 42.2%
  14. CRASH-2 trial collaborators. Effects of tranexamic acid on death, vascular occlusive events, and blood transfusion in trauma patients with significant haemorrhage (CRASH-2): a randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet 2010;376:23-32
    20,211 bleeding trauma patients randomised within 8 h of injury to tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h, or placebo: all-cause mortality 14.5% versus 16.0% (RR 0.91), death from bleeding 4.9% versus 5.7%, no excess of vascular occlusive events

Trauma › Trauma

46 Compartment syndrome and fasciotomy

Diagnosis by examination and pressure, the regional anaesthesia argument and its evidence, two-incision four-compartment leg fasciotomy, forearm and thigh release, and the open wounds, second looks and closure that follow

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. Two full-length incisions through skin and fascia over swollen, ischaemic and then reperfused muscle that bulges out and is left open; dead muscle cut back to bleeding tissue; the wounds reopened every 48-72 h and finally pulled shut under tension or skin grafted, usually on top of the fracture that started it. The ischaemic pain goes with the release; a large raw muscle surface and a neuropathic element from the ischaemic nerves replace it

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
No block at the index fasciotomy: general anaesthesia with opioid, low-dose ketamine and paracetamol, so that the limb's nerves can be examined afterwards; a popliteal sciatic and saphenous block or catheter from the first second look onward, once every compartment is open and the neurological baseline is written down
Catheter: selective Never before decompression in a limb at risk; reasonable after it, from the second look, for the patient facing three or four returns to theatre and a skin graft, provided all compartments were released, the post-release neurology is documented and the other limbs are not themselves at risk
Alternatives: Brachial plexus block or catheter (infraclavicular or axillary) for the forearm fasciotomy, on the same terms; Opioid patient-controlled analgesia with a low-dose ketamine infusion and no block at any stage; Femoral or fascia iliaca block for the skin graft donor site on the thigh
Position
Supine with the whole limb prepared from groin to toes (or axilla to fingertips on an arm table), a bolster under the calf so both the medial and lateral sides can be reached, and nothing circumferential left on the limb
Tourniquet
No. Not inflated: the limb is already ischaemic and the surgeon judges the muscle by its bleeding and contraction
Cement
No
Blood loss
200-500 mL at the index operation from skin edges and swollen muscle, then a continuous ooze into dressings and the negative pressure canister that nobody counts; much more with a reperfused limb, a coagulopathy or a muscle debridement. The haemoglobin falls across the series of operations rather than in any one of them
Duration
30-60 min for a leg or forearm fasciotomy; 20-45 min for each second look; 45-90 min for delayed closure or split skin grafting
Length of stay
One to three weeks, set by the wound: two to four returns to theatre at 48-72 h intervals before closure or grafting, on top of whatever the fracture needs. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g over 120 kg) before incision and at each return to theatre; the open fracture protocol applies if there is one
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction is reasonable for a raw muscle surface that will ooze for days; not trial evidence for this operation
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin once the wound ooze allows, usually from the day after the index operation; mechanical prophylaxis on the other limb; the immobility lasts weeks
Antiemetic
Ondansetron 4 mg IV and dexamethasone 8 mg IV; the block-prolonging effect of dexamethasone no longer matters once the compartments are open
Tell the patient
The cuts were made to save the muscle and they are left open on purpose; you will come back to theatre every two or three days until the swelling has gone down enough to close them, and the leg is sore and tight for the whole of that time.
The trap
Before the release, a rising opioid requirement or breakthrough pain through a working block or epidural is the diagnosis announcing itself, and the response is the surgeon and a pressure measurement within the hour, not a bolus; after the release, the block is no longer the enemy

What the surgeon is doing and why

A muscle compartment is a closed box: bone on one side, inelastic fascia on the others, with muscle, nerves and the vessels that feed them inside. After a fracture, a crush, a reperfusion or a tight cast the contents swell or bleed, and because the box cannot expand the pressure rises. The arterial pulse is not the casualty. Capillary flow depends on the gradient between arteriolar pressure and tissue pressure, and once tissue pressure comes within about 30 mmHg of the diastolic pressure the capillaries empty, the muscle becomes ischaemic, ischaemic muscle swells further, and the loop closes on itself. Nerve conduction fails within an hour or two; muscle is dead after six to eight hours at body temperature. The foot stays pink and the pulse stays palpable throughout, which is why waiting for pallor and pulselessness is waiting for an amputation.

The surgeon’s only treatment is to open the box. A fasciotomy divides the skin and the fascia along the full length of every involved compartment, lets the muscle bulge out, and leaves the wound open because the muscle will keep swelling for 24 to 48 hours and a closed skin is as tight an envelope as the fascia was. Timing is the whole outcome: in the classic series normal function followed 68% of releases done within 12 h of onset and 8% of those done later, with complications in 4.5% and 54%. The British standard is that decompression follows the diagnosis immediately, and that the wound is re-explored within 72 h.

The diagnosis is the difficult part, and it is the part you share. The textbook signs are pain out of proportion to the injury, pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the compartment (the toes dorsiflexed for the deep posterior and flexed for the anterior), a tense compartment, and paraesthesia in the nerve that runs through it. Their test characteristics are poor in one direction: across four prospective studies each sign had a sensitivity of 13-19% and a specificity of 97%, so their absence is reassuring and any one of them alone gives a probability of only about 25%, rising to 93% with three. Pressure measurement fills the gap. The threshold that survived is the differential pressure, diastolic minus compartment pressure, below 30 mmHg; it outperformed absolute pressures in the original 116-fracture study, and with continuous monitoring in 850 tibial fractures it had a sensitivity of 94% and a specificity of 98%. Note what the threshold contains: the diastolic pressure is yours. A hypotensive patient under anaesthesia has a lower differential pressure for the same compartment, and a single reading taken at a diastolic of 45 mmHg on the table overcalls the diagnosis, which is why surgeons who measure in theatre ask for the pre-induction diastolic.

Who gets it: the young man with a tibial shaft fracture above all, then high-energy tibial plateau fracture-dislocations, forearm fractures, crush injuries, the revascularised limb, the limb that lay under an unconscious body, and occasionally the well leg after hours in lithotomy. An open fracture is not exempt (see open fractures), and the tibial risk shapes the block on the tibial card.

The regional anaesthesia controversy needs stating exactly, because it is argued louder than the evidence allows. The surgical fear is that a block removes the one symptom that prompts the examination. The evidence for and against is almost entirely case reports. The 2009 systematic review found 28 reports and series, 23 of them about epidurals: in 32 of 35 patients the classic signs were present despite the epidural, 18 with documented breakthrough pain, and the authors found no convincing evidence that patient-controlled opioid or regional analgesia delays diagnosis when the patient is properly watched. A 2016 review of 34 articles reached the same reading. A 2020 surgical review of peripheral blocks in long bone fractures found six single-patient reports, two with a delayed diagnosis and four without, and concluded the opposite way: that no conclusion is possible and blocks belong in research settings. Both readings are honest descriptions of the same thin literature. The newer comparative data are larger and reassuring without being decisive: among 791 operative tibial fractures the rate of missed compartment syndrome was 0.7% with a nerve block and 1.7% without, not different, but all four missed cases in the block group had a catheter; and a 2026 systematic review of five comparative studies and 105,139 trauma patients found no study in which regional anaesthesia raised the incidence or delayed the diagnosis. The Association of Anaesthetists turned this into a workable rule in 2021: avoid dense blocks that far outlast the surgery, accept dilute blocks without adjuncts when the surveillance is real, chart the observations, document the patient’s consent, and neither specialty holds a veto. The British orthopaedic standard says the same from the other side: a joint decision and an agreed monitoring policy. The Part A chapter on nerve injury and compartment syndrome carries the full argument; this card is about the limb in which the diagnosis has been made.

The pain logic changes at the moment of release. Before it, the pain is ischaemic muscle, unresponsive to opioid, and it is the diagnostic signal. After it, the mechanism is muscle in the Part B sense: a large soft tissue wound with swollen muscle exposed over 20-30 cm on each side of the limb, re-traumatised at every dressing change and second look, then closed under tension or grafted. Add a neuropathic element in any patient whose nerves were ischaemic for hours, and usually a fresh fracture and its fixation. The score is 5: no single day is as bad as a knee replacement’s first, but the plateau runs for a fortnight because the operation is repeated, and the shape of the curve earns the 5.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The call: surveillance, examination and the pressure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon is trying to make a diagnosis from soft signs in the first 48 h after an injury or operation. The standard is an hourly documented assessment of every at-risk limb, release of all circumferential dressings and re-evaluation within 30 min when symptoms appear, and a pressure measurement when the picture is unclear or the patient cannot report.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    You are often the person who generates the first signal. A patient whose opioid requirement climbs through the night, who has breakthrough pain through a working epidural or block, or whose pain is not touched by a bolus that worked 4 h earlier has the pattern that 18 of the 35 reported epidural cases showed before anyone acted.
