  1. Rupp M, Walter N, Biehl C, Heiss C. Chronic osteomyelitis: pathophysiology and treatment. Z Orthop Unfall 2026
    Review: biofilm as the reason chronic infection resists antibiotics; the Cierny-Mader classification of anatomical type and host; stage-appropriate radical debridement, dead space management with local antibiotic carriers, soft tissue cover and later bone reconstruction; single-stage protocols and shorter systemic courses
  2. McNally MA, Ferguson JY, Lau ACK, et al. Single-stage treatment of chronic osteomyelitis with a new absorbable, gentamicin-loaded, calcium sulphate/hydroxyapatite biocomposite: a prospective series of 100 cases. Bone Joint J 2016;98-B:1289-1296
    100 patients, 80 of them compromised hosts, treated by debridement, multiple sampling, culture-specific antibiotics, stabilisation, dead space filling with the biocomposite and primary closure: infection eradicated in 96 with one operation, with three fractures and six wound leaks; outcome independent of host class and organism
  3. Ferguson J, Diefenbeck M, McNally M. Ceramic biocomposites as biodegradable antibiotic carriers in the treatment of bone infections. J Bone Jt Infect 2017;2:38-51
    Review of calcium sulphate, calcium phosphate and polyphasic carriers: adequacy of debridement remains the key to cure, local carriers deliver far higher antibiotic concentrations than systemic dosing, fill the dead space, dissolve without a removal operation and allow single-stage surgery with closure; carrier choice keyed to the Cierny-Mader stage
  4. Tetreault MW, Wetters NG, Aggarwal V, Mont M, Parvizi J, Della Valle CJ. The Chitranjan Ranawat Award: should prophylactic antibiotics be withheld before revision surgery to obtain appropriate cultures? Clin Orthop Relat Res 2014;472:52-56
    65 patients with culture-positive prosthetic joint infection randomised to prophylactic antibiotics before the incision or after three sets of operative cultures: operative cultures matched the pre-operative organism in 82% and 81%, statistically equivalent; the authors conclude prophylaxis should not be withheld for fear of the cultures
  5. Acosta-Olivo C, Vilchez-Cavazos F, Blazquez-Saldana J, et al. Comparison of open arthrotomy versus arthroscopic surgery for the treatment of septic arthritis in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Int Orthop 2021;45:1947-1959
    20 studies, 10,249 patients: arthrotomy carried higher odds of re-infection (OR 1.35) and complications (OR 1.32) and a stay 0.57 days longer than arthroscopy; the knee (OR 1.50) and shoulder (OR 1.24) drove the re-infection difference; the authors rate the evidence insufficient for firm conclusions
  6. Ramirez-Acosta K, Sanchez-Enriquez S, Madrigal-Rodriguez M, et al. Comparative effectiveness of repeated joint aspiration, arthroscopic lavage, and open arthrotomy in adult native knee septic arthritis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. J Orthop 2025;70:183-195
    25 studies, 21,917 patients, one randomised: arthroscopic lavage had higher clinical success than arthrotomy (OR 2.52) and fewer complications (OR 0.69); repeated aspiration carried more re-intervention (OR 3.35) than arthroscopy; no difference in stay or mortality; the authors propose arthroscopy as the reference standard in the immunocompetent adult
  7. Bovonratwet P, Nelson SJ, Bellamkonda K, et al. Similar 30-day complications for septic knee arthritis treated with arthrotomy or arthroscopy: an American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program analysis. Arthroscopy 2018;34:213-219
    168 arthrotomies and 216 arthroscopies for the septic knee: no difference in adverse events, return to theatre or readmission at 30 days after adjustment; serious adverse events occurred in a quarter to a third of both groups, a measure of how sick the population is
  8. Jaffe D, Costales T, Greenwell P, Christian M, Henn RF. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection is a risk factor for unplanned return to the operating room in the surgical treatment of a septic knee. J Knee Surg 2017;30:872-878
    80 adult septic knees: a single washout succeeded in 75.8% of arthroscopic and 80.9% of open cases, not different; MRSA was the only independent predictor of an unplanned second washout, with a higher synovial white cell count also associated after arthroscopy
  9. Couderc M, Gomez S, Mathieu S, et al. Longitudinal incidence of native septic arthritis in France: a 13-year analysis of the National Health Data System database. Rheumatology (Oxford) 2026;65(5)
    109,160 adult native joint episodes 2009-2022: incidence rose from 13 to 16.2 per 100,000 adults per year; mean age 62, 65% men, staphylococci in 48%; all-cause mortality 3.2% at one month, 8.4% at six and 11.4% at twelve; risk factors rheumatoid arthritis (OR 4.7), drug addiction (4.5), complicated diabetes (4.4) and dialysis (4.0)

Trauma › Trauma

49 Removal of metalwork

Elective removal of plates, screws, wires and intramedullary nails after fracture healing: the short case that overruns, stripped and cold-welded screws, broken hardware, and what the antibiotic trial showed

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Periosteum. An old scar reopened and the implant dug out of the bone and scar that have grown over it, with subperiosteal dissection along a plate or a re-entry through the patellar tendon or the gluteal muscles for a nail; empty screw holes and no fracture. A single screw or wire through a stab incision is a 1; a long locking plate or a nail is a 2, and a 3 on the day the screws strip and the surgeon is burring metal for an hour

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
Surgeon's infiltration of the wound with long-acting local anaesthetic under general anaesthesia; a regional block as the sole anaesthetic where it suits the site (axillary or supraclavicular for forearm and hand, popliteal and saphenous for ankle and foot) or a short-acting spinal for the lower limb
Catheter: no No indication: there is no fracture, no osteotomy and nothing under tension; the pain is incisional and falls within two or three days
Alternatives: Single-shot peripheral nerve block as the anaesthetic for forearm, hand, ankle and foot metalwork, chosen to outlast a tourniquet and a doubled operating time; Short-acting spinal (prilocaine or chloroprocaine) for lower limb metalwork in a day-case patient, accepting that it may not outlast a difficult extraction; General anaesthesia with a supraglottic airway and infiltration alone
Position
Supine for most; whatever position put the metal in is the position that takes it out: lateral for a posterior distal humeral or lateral femoral plate, a traction table or a flexed knee over a triangle for a nail, prone for a posterior malleolar plate or spinal instrumentation
Tourniquet
Yes. Routine for limb metalwork distal to the mid-thigh or mid-arm; the cuff clock keeps running through a difficult extraction, and a stripped screw at 90 min means deflation before the metal is out; not possible for clavicle, proximal humerus, proximal femur or pelvis
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal under tourniquet; 100-300 mL for a femoral or tibial nail or a plate above the cuff; more when bone has to be removed to free the implant
Duration
15-30 min for a syndesmotic screw or wires; 30-60 min for a plate or nail as booked; allow double, because in one locking plate series the mean was 71 min, the range 28-180 min and five of 36 cases passed two hours
Length of stay
Day case. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
The one randomised trial (cefazolin 1 g IV against saline before removal of metalwork below the knee) showed no reduction in surgical site infection; many units still give cefazolin 2 g IV, and it is clearly indicated when metal is being replaced, the case is long, or infection is suspected (in which case it is withheld until samples are taken)
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
Early mobilisation; chemoprophylaxis only for the patient's own risk factors or a period of protected weight-bearing in a cast
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 4-8 mg IV and ondansetron 4 mg IV, as for any day case
Tell the patient
This is usually a small operation and you go home the same day; it is sore for a few days rather than weeks, and the bone needs protecting from heavy loads for about six weeks while the screw holes fill in.
The trap
The booking says 30 minutes and the metal has not been told: a locking screw that has cold-welded to its plate or a hexagonal head that strips turns a day-case removal into a two-hour operation with a burr, a tourniquet at its limit and a block or spinal that is running out

What the surgeon is doing and why

Fracture implants are scaffolding: once the bone has united they carry no load that the bone cannot, and most stay in for life. A minority come out, and the reason matters to you because it sets the operation. Symptomatic metal is the commonest: a plate under thin skin (clavicle, olecranon, distal fibula, medial malleolus, the subcutaneous tibia), a nail whose entry point hurts the knee, a screw tip that catches a tendon. Planned removal is the second: a syndesmotic screw, wires through a growth plate, elastic nails in a child, a bridging plate across a joint. Then come the removals that are steps in another operation (metal out so an arthroplasty can go in), the patient’s own wish, and the suspected infection or non-union, which is a different operation that happens to start the same way and belongs on the osteomyelitis or revision cards.

The indication is softer than the theatre list suggests, and the surgical literature has been walking it back. The syndesmotic screw is the clearest example: in the RODEO trial of 152 patients, leaving the screw in unless it caused trouble was noninferior to routine removal for ankle function at a year and at four years, and the routine-removal arm had 12 complications in 73 patients against one in 79. Removal has a cost, and the cost is mostly wound.

What the surgeon has to do sounds trivial and is not always. The old scar is reopened, and the plane beneath it is no longer anatomy: nerves that were found and protected at the first operation are now embedded in scar on top of the plate (the superficial radial nerve over a radial plate, the radial nerve over a posterior humeral plate, the superficial peroneal nerve over a fibular plate). Bone has grown over the plate edges and into the empty holes and has to be cleared with an osteotome before a screwdriver will seat. Then each screw has to turn. Two things stop it. The first is a stripped head: the hexagonal or star recess is soft, especially in titanium, it has usually been torqued once already, and if the driver is not fully seated in a recess full of fibrous tissue it rounds off on the first attempt. The second is cold welding: a locking screw threads into the plate as well as the bone, and titanium on titanium under load fuses at the thread, so the screw and plate become one piece. Titanium also osseointegrates, so the screw shank is held by bone along its length. In a series of 36 locking plate removals from the femur and tibia, 10.6% of 349 screws and 38.9% of cases were difficult, the mean operating time was 71 min with a range of 28-180 min, and nothing about the patient, the plate or the time since surgery predicted which case it would be.

When a screw will not turn, the surgeon climbs a ladder: a new driver and an impact to seat it; a conical reverse-threaded extraction screw; a hollow trephine drilled over the shank; cutting the plate between the holes so each fragment can be rotated out with its screw; a carbide or diamond burr to grind the screw head off, after which the plate lifts away and the headless shank is either unscrewed with a chuck, over-drilled, or left in the bone. Nails have their own version: the end cap is overgrown and has to be found under imaging, the extraction bolt has to thread into a nail whose top is full of bone, the nail may have been bent by a later injury, and a broken nail needs hooks, stacked guidewires or a window cut in the cortex. Each rung adds time, heat, metal debris and bone loss, and the surgeon will not know which rung is needed until the first screw is tried.

The pain logic is simple and favourable. There is no fracture, no osteotomy and nothing repaired under tension. The dominant mechanism is periosteum: a scar and a strip of bone surface re-dissected, with screw holes that behave like small drill holes. That is a score of 1 for a single screw or wire through a stab incision and 2 for a long plate or a nail, a day or two of incisional pain that responds to paracetamol and an NSAID. The only thing that moves it is the difficult extraction, which adds an hour of bone removal and tourniquet and gives the patient a 3 for the first two days.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The booking: what is in there and what will get it out

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Implants are manufacturer-specific. The surgeon needs the original operation note or the implant record to know the make, the screw head (hexagonal, star, cruciate, proprietary), whether the screws are locking, and whether the metal is titanium or steel, and then needs the matching driver and a broken-screw set on the table. A radiograph shows broken screws, bone overgrowth and whether the fracture has united.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Read the same radiograph. A short steel plate with non-locking screws on a fibula is the 30 min case the list promises. A long titanium locking plate on a distal femur or proximal tibia, metal that has been in for years, a broken screw visible on the film, or a nail with no visible end cap are each a reason to plan for 2 h: a technique that can be extended, a second patient who is not fasting against a fixed clock, and a conversation with the surgeon about where they will stop. Metal put in at another hospital with no record is the highest-risk booking of all.

  2. 2 Choosing the anaesthetic for a case of unknown length

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a still limb and, for most sites, a tourniquet. Nothing about the operation needs muscle relaxation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The choice is driven by how the technique fails if the case doubles. General anaesthesia with a supraglottic airway and wound infiltration fails gracefully and is the author’s default for anything with locking screws. A peripheral block as the sole anaesthetic suits the forearm, hand, ankle and foot and tolerates a long case, but must cover the tourniquet; an axillary or supraclavicular block does for an arm cuff, and a popliteal and saphenous block with a calf cuff avoids the thigh tourniquet that an awake patient will not tolerate beyond 45-60 min. A short-acting day-case spinal (prilocaine or chloroprocaine) is elegant for the 30 min ankle and is the technique most exposed by a stripped screw at 70 min; if the radiograph suggests difficulty, choose something else. Children’s metalwork is general anaesthesia with infiltration or a block placed asleep.

  3. 3 The antibiotic decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Removal of metalwork is classed as clean surgery, yet its infection rate is not that of clean surgery: old scar, a poorly vascular subcutaneous site, dead space where the plate was, and often a biofilm on the implant that was never clinically apparent.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The WIFI trial is the evidence and it is negative. In 477 patients having metalwork removed from below the knee, cefazolin 1 g IV gave an infection rate of 13.2% against 14.9% with saline, a difference of 1.7% with a confidence interval from 8.0% fewer to 4.6% more. The striking number is the baseline: 14% of these wounds became infected with or without the antibiotic. A second trial of cefazolin 2 g IV was designed because the first may have under-dosed; its protocol is published and no result has been reported. Practice therefore varies and both positions are defensible: no prophylaxis for a simple removal below the knee on the trial evidence, or cefazolin 2 g IV on the grounds that the dose tested was low, the drug is cheap and the wound is high-risk. Give it without debate when new metal is going in, when the case becomes long, or for an immunosuppressed patient, all of whom the trial excluded. Withhold it until deep samples are taken when the reason for removal is suspected infection or non-union.

  4. 4 Position, tourniquet and the clock

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A bloodless field lets the surgeon see nerves in scar and seat the driver cleanly in the screw head. The position is that of the original operation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Note the inflation time and say it aloud at 60 and 90 min. A difficult extraction is the commonest reason for a tourniquet to reach 120 min in a minor case, and the surgeon who is one screw from finishing will not volunteer to deflate. Deflation with the wound open means bleeding from every screw hole and a worse view for the hardest part of the operation, so the earlier warning is the useful one. For a prone or lateral case the airway decision is the position’s, not the operation’s: a tracheal tube for a prone posterior malleolar plate even though the removal takes 20 min.

  5. 5 Reopening the scar and finding the metal

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The incision follows the old one. The surgeon dissects through scar to the implant, identifies any nerve at risk before it is cut, and clears fibrous tissue and bone from the plate surface and from every screw recess, because a driver seated in a recess full of tissue is how a head strips.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The stimulating part of a simple removal is here and at closure; the rest is turning screws. If you are relying on a block, this is where a missed cutaneous territory shows (the intercostobrachial and medial cutaneous nerves for a medial elbow incision, the saphenous for a medial malleolus). Avoid relaxant where a motor nerve lies in the scar: a radial nerve over a humeral plate is found partly by its twitch.

  6. 6 Turning the screws

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Each screw is backed out by hand. Non-locking steel screws usually come easily. Titanium locking screws are the problem: cold-welded into the plate at the head, osseointegrated along the shank, with a soft recess.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Count with the surgeon. If the first three screws turn, the case will run to time. The words to listen for are “it’s stripped” and a request for the extraction set, and the moment you hear them is the moment to revise everything downstream: tell the recovery unit, re-time the next patient, check how much of the tourniquet, the spinal or the block is left, and convert early rather than late. Converting an awake patient to general anaesthesia at 90 min with the cuff up and a burr running is harder than doing it at 60 min.

  7. 7 The extraction ladder: extractors, trephines and the burr

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A stripped screw is tried with a reverse-threaded conical extractor; if that fails, the head is ground off with a carbide or diamond burr so the plate can be lifted, or the plate is cut between holes; the remaining shank is gripped and unscrewed, over-drilled with a hollow trephine that removes a cylinder of bone with it, or left in place. Burring metal produces heat and a slurry of metal particles that the surgeon irrigates continuously to protect the skin and the wound.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is slow, noisy and unpleasant for an awake patient, who can feel vibration through bone outside a block and can smell it. Trephining removes real bone, turns a screw hole into a 6-8 mm defect, and is where the post-operative pain steps up from a 2 to a 3; give the intravenous NSAID and a longer-acting opioid now rather than in recovery. The decision to leave a headless shank in the bone is a good surgical decision, not a failure, and the patient needs to be told it was deliberate.

  8. 8 Lifting the plate or pulling the nail

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The plate is levered off the bone, sometimes with bone that has grown over its edges and sometimes, as in six of the 36 cases in the locking plate series, with screws still attached. For a nail the locking screws come out first, the proximal end is found (through the patellar tendon or a suprapatellar portal for a tibia, through the gluteal muscles for a femur), bone is cleared from its top, an extraction bolt is threaded in and the nail is driven out backwards with a slotted hammer.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nail extraction is the only part of this operation with real blood loss, from the re-opened entry point and the empty canal, and the only part done without a tourniquet in the femur; 100-300 mL is usual. It is also impact loading on a supraglottic airway and a head that moves with every blow, so check the airway and the pressure areas afterwards. Fat embolism from an empty, unreamed canal is not a practical concern. A nail that will not move after the bolt is seated usually means a locking screw has been missed or a broken tip is retained; expect imaging and a pause.

  9. 9 Closure, tourniquet down and the empty holes

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The wound is irrigated of metal debris and closed over the dead space the implant leaves. Screw holes are stress risers: the cortex is weaker until they fill in over six to eight weeks, and the forearm, where both bones were plated, is the classic site of refracture.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Infiltration of the wound and the periosteal bed with long-acting local anaesthetic is the whole regional plan for most patients and worth asking for by name. Tourniquet deflation after a long inflation in a day-case patient brings the usual transient fall in pressure and a wound that oozes from every hole; a compression dressing follows. Paracetamol 1 g IV and an NSAID before the end.

  10. 10 Recovery and discharge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the patient home, mobile and protected from heavy loading: no contact sport, heavy lifting or impact for about six weeks, with weight-bearing as comfort allows.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Standard day-case discharge. The patient who had a block as the anaesthetic goes home with a numb limb and written instructions; rebound is mild here because there is no fresh bone injury, unless the case was a difficult one with trephined bone, in which case the bone-surgery odds ratio from the rebound pain study applies and the oral opioid is worth supplying. Tell the patient if any metal was left behind and that it was a decision.

Pain plan

The mechanism is a re-dissected scar and periosteum with empty screw holes, so the plan is the simplest in the trauma section: wound infiltration, paracetamol and an NSAID, with an oral opioid offered for the first two nights after a plate or nail and not at all after a single screw. There is no procedure-specific guideline and no need for one.

Block choice follows the anaesthetic, not the pain. Where a block is the anaesthetic (forearm, hand, ankle, foot) it will also cover the first evening; where the case is done under general anaesthesia, the surgeon’s infiltration does the same job and a block adds a numb limb to a day-case discharge for little gain. The catheter decision is no, without qualification. The exceptions that deserve a single-shot block under general anaesthesia are the author’s judgement: the tibial or femoral nail in a young patient (adductor canal or femoral, for the knee entry), the clavicle plate (superficial cervical plexus or surgeon’s infiltration), and the patient with chronic pain or opioid tolerance in whom a minor operation is not minor.

Oral regimen shape: regular paracetamol and an NSAID for three to five days (there is no healing fracture to argue about, so the NSAID objection that surgeons raise in acute trauma does not apply); a small supply of immediate-release opioid for a plate or nail; nothing else.

Escalation: pain at day 3-7 that is rising, with a red, discharging wound, is the surgical site infection that one in seven of the trial’s below-knee patients developed, and it needs the surgeon. Sudden pain with a deformity after a trivial load in the first six weeks is a refracture through a screw hole.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The syndesmotic screw. A 15 min operation through a stab incision, often under local anaesthesia with sedation; a 1 on the scale. The randomised evidence now favours leaving it unless it causes symptoms, so the routine removal list is shrinking.
  • Wires and tension bands. Olecranon and patellar wires back out and prominent ends are the reason for removal; short, superficial, a 1, and suited to infiltration with or without sedation.
  • Elastic nails and plates in children. Planned removal at 6-12 months; general anaesthesia; the nail end may be buried in bone and a 15 min case becomes 45 min.
  • Tibial and femoral nails. The largest elective removals: a re-entry through the knee or the hip abductors, 100-300 mL of blood loss, anterior knee pain that does not reliably improve after the nail comes out, and a patient who may stay overnight.
  • Removal as the first stage of an arthroplasty. Old hip screws or a plate out before a hip or knee replacement at the same sitting: the case is the arthroplasty with an hour added and an unpredictable start, and the antibiotic is given.
  • Suspected infection or non-union. Not this card: antibiotics are held for samples, the bone is debrided, the wound may be left open, and the pain score and length of stay belong to the osteomyelitis card.
  • Broken implants. A broken plate or nail means the fracture did not unite; the removal is the first step of a revision fixation with bone graft, blood loss and a pain score two points higher.
  • Nerves in scar. Transient palsy after removal is the complication the surgeon fears most (the radial nerve at the humerus, the superficial radial and posterior interosseous nerves at the forearm, the peroneal nerve at the proximal fibula). A block makes the post-operative examination uninformative for hours; where the nerve was at risk, say so on the chart, or use infiltration instead.
  • The awake patient and the burr. Sedation depth that was right for turning screws is not right for 40 min of metal cutting; convert to general anaesthesia early.
  • Spinal instrumentation. Removal of pedicle screws and rods is a prone spinal operation with a muscle-stripping exposure and belongs with the fusion card for position and pain, at about a 3.

Key sources

The antibiotic question has one good randomised trial, negative at a 1 g dose, with a 2 g successor that has not reported. The difficulty of locking plate removal rests on a single 36-case series and a technique review, which match every trauma surgeon’s experience. The syndesmotic screw evidence is randomised with four-year follow-up. Nothing has been published on analgesia for this operation specifically, and the plan above is a deduction from the mechanism.

  1. Backes M, Dingemans SA, Dijkgraaf MGW, et al. Effect of antibiotic prophylaxis on surgical site infections following removal of orthopedic implants used for treatment of foot, ankle, and lower leg fractures: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA 2017;318:2438-2445
    WIFI trial: 477 patients in 19 Dutch hospitals randomised to cefazolin 1 g IV or saline before removal of metalwork below the knee; surgical site infection within 30 days in 13.2% versus 14.9% (difference -1.7%, 95% CI -8.0 to 4.6, p=0.60); overall infection rate 14.0%, far above the 2% expected of clean surgery
  2. Sanders FRK, Penning D, Backes M, et al. Wound infection following implant removal of foot, ankle, lower leg or patella; a protocol for a multicenter randomized controlled trial investigating the (cost-)effectiveness of 2 g of prophylactic cefazolin compared to placebo (WIFI-2 trial). BMC Surg 2021;21:69
    Protocol only: a double-blind superiority trial of cefazolin 2 g IV against placebo with infection at 90 days as the outcome, designed because the first trial may have under-dosed; no result reported
  3. Suzuki T, Smith WR, Stahel PF, Morgan SJ, Baron AJ, Hak DJ. Technical problems and complications in the removal of the less invasive stabilization system. J Orthop Trauma 2010;24:369-373
    36 locking plate removals (15 tibias, 21 femurs, 349 screws) at a mean of 13 months: difficulty with 37 screws (10.6%) in 14 cases (38.9%); mean operating time 71 min (28-180), five cases over 120 min; burrs, bolt cutters, extraction taps and levering the plate off with screws attached; one transient peroneal palsy, two superficial infections; no predictor of difficulty
  4. Hak DJ, McElvany M. Removal of broken hardware. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2008;16:113-120
    Technique review: extractors, trephines and extraction bolts for stripped and broken screws; carbide drills and high-speed metal-cutting tools for cold-welded locking screws; hooks, guidewires and commercial extractors for broken nails; a bone window for a broken solid nail; no single technique is uniformly successful
  5. Sanders FRK, Birnie MF, Dingemans SA, et al. Functional outcome of routine versus on-demand removal of the syndesmotic screw: a multicentre randomized controlled trial. Bone Joint J 2021;103-B:1709-1716
    RODEO: 152 patients analysed; on-demand removal noninferior to routine removal at 8-12 weeks for ankle function at one year (median OMAS 80 versus 85); complications in 12 of 73 after routine removal and 1 of 79 with on-demand removal
  6. van den Heuvel S, Penning D, Sanders F, et al. Functional outcome of routine versus on-demand removal of the syndesmotic screw. Bone Jt Open 2023;4:957-963
    Four-year follow-up of RODEO in 109 patients: no functional difference (median OMAS 85 routine, 90 on demand); the authors recommend on-demand removal as standard
  7. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, and absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78

Trauma › Trauma

50 Polytrauma: sequencing, the second hit and when to operate

Early total care, damage control orthopaedics and early appropriate care; lactate and base deficit as the gate; trauma coagulopathy, tranexamic acid and massive transfusion; fat embolism; the order of operations; and the conversation before the surgeon starts

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Several fractured, periosteum-stripped bones at once, usually with rib fractures that hurt with every breath and soft tissue wounds that are reopened; staged operations reset the curve every few days, so the pain is the sum of the injuries and has no single peak. The score is for the patient, not for any one operation

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Systemic multimodal analgesia built on opioid and low-dose ketamine in the first 24-48 h, while coagulation, compartments, the head and the spine are still open questions; femoral or fascia iliaca block for a femoral fracture from the emergency department; regional techniques for the chest wall and the limbs added as each of those questions closes
Catheter: selective Chest wall catheters (thoracic epidural, paravertebral, erector spinae or serratus plane) for three or more rib fractures once coagulation is normal and the spine is cleared; limb catheters for the staged reconstructions after the compartment window has closed; none on the night of injury in a coagulopathic patient
Alternatives: Thoracic epidural or paravertebral catheter for multiple rib fractures or flail chest in a patient with normal coagulation and a cleared spine; Erector spinae or serratus anterior plane catheter where neuraxial techniques are barred by coagulopathy, anticoagulation or spinal injury; Opioid patient-controlled analgesia with a ketamine infusion and no regional technique
Position
Supine on a radiolucent table with spinal precautions until the spine is cleared, both groins and the abdomen and chest prepared so that any cavity can be opened without repositioning; lateral and prone positions belong to the reconstruction phase, not the first night
Tourniquet
Sometimes. For life-threatening limb haemorrhage before theatre and for distal limb work in a stable patient; released as early as possible in a shocked patient, whose reperfusion load arrives on top of an existing acidosis
Cement
No
Blood loss
Already large and still running: 1-1.5 L for each closed femoral fracture, 500 mL for a tibia, 2-3 L or more for an unstable pelvic ring, before any incision. Damage control surgery adds little; early total care with a reamed nail or pelvic fixation adds 500-1500 mL
Duration
Damage control: fixators on each long bone in 30-45 min apiece and out of theatre within about 90 min of orthopaedic time. Early total care: 2-6 h, by agreement, with stopping points
Length of stay
Weeks; intensive care first, then two to five further operations over 5-14 days. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g over 120 kg), redosed at 4 h and after every 1.5 L of blood loss; open fractures follow their own clock, with the first dose due within an hour of injury
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min as early as possible and within 3 h of injury, then 1 g IV over 8 h; not started beyond 3 h, when CRASH-2 found more deaths from bleeding
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis from arrival; low molecular weight heparin as soon as bleeding is controlled and any head or spinal cord injury permits, usually within 24-72 h; the polytrauma patient is among the highest-risk patients in the hospital
Antiemetic
Ondansetron 4 mg IV; not a priority in a patient going to intensive care ventilated
Tell the patient
The broken bones will be fixed in stages: a quick, safe hold on the first night, then the proper repairs over the following week once the body has recovered from the injury itself.
The trap
The decision that matters is made before induction, not at hour three: agree with the surgeon which class the patient is in, what the short version of the operation is, and which numbers will make you both stop, because once a nail is half way down a femur nobody volunteers to convert to a fixator

What the surgeon is doing and why

A patient with several injuries is not several patients with one injury each. The fractures bleed, the bleeding produces shock, the shock and the tissue damage switch on an inflammatory and coagulation response, and that response, not the fractures, is what kills in the first week. The orthopaedic surgeon’s problem is that fixing the bones helps this patient (a stabilised femur stops bleeding, stops shedding marrow fat, stops hurting, and lets the patient be sat up and nursed) and that the operation to fix them is itself an injury. Everything on this card is about choosing the size of that second injury.

The history of the idea runs in three steps, and each is still partly right.

Early total care. Through the 1970s long bone fractures in the multiply injured were put in traction until the patient was “well enough”, and the patients died of pneumonia, fat embolism and sepsis on their backs. Bone’s 1989 randomised trial of 178 femoral fractures settled it: in the multiply injured, delayed stabilisation brought more ARDS, fat embolism and pneumonia and longer intensive care. Fix everything within 24 h became the rule.

Damage control. The rule was then applied to patients it harmed: the shocked patient with a lung contusion who had a reamed femoral nail at 3 am and was on a ventilator for three weeks. The explanation is the second hit. The injury primes neutrophils and endothelium; a long operation with blood loss, hypothermia and marrow embolised to the lungs lands on a primed system and tips it into lung injury and organ failure. The EPOFF trial measured the signal (interleukin-6 rose after a primary nail and did not rise after a fixator or after delayed conversion), and Pape’s randomised trial of 165 patients gave it a clinical size: in the 44 “borderline” patients, primary nailing carried an adjusted odds ratio of 6.69 for acute lung injury, while in stable patients the primary nail meant less time on the ventilator. Damage control orthopaedics is the response: an external fixator in 30 minutes, intensive care, and the definitive operation days later.

Early appropriate care. Damage control was in turn over-applied, and stable patients were given two operations and a pin-site infection for no benefit. The current position asks one question: has this patient been resuscitated. In 1,443 patients with operated femoral, pelvic, acetabular or spinal fractures, chest injury was the strongest predictor of pulmonary complications, lactate was the most specific laboratory predictor, and correction of acidosis with fixation inside 24-48 h went with an uncomplicated course. The protocol built on it permits definitive fixation of those injuries within 36 h once the lactate is below 4.0 mmol/L, the pH is 7.25 or above, or the base excess is -5.5 mmol/L or better; in its 335-patient validation complications were 19.7% against 22.1% historically, and highest, at 34.3%, in patients operated on having met only one of the three.

So the surgeon sorts the patient into one of four classes, and the class, not the radiograph, chooses the operation:

                     injured patient, resuscitation running
                                    |
        +---------------+-----------+-----------+----------------+
        |               |                       |                |
     STABLE        BORDERLINE               UNSTABLE        IN EXTREMIS
  lactate falling  responds, but:        still shocked,     bleeding to
  warm, clotting   chest injury,         acidotic, cold,    death
  no pressor       ISS high, pelvis,     coagulopathic
        |          or numbers stall             |                |
        |               |                       |                |
  early total     re-measure after       damage control:    haemorrhage
  care: nail,     resuscitation;         fixators, stop,    control only;
  fix, close      improving = nail,      intensive care     splints, no
                  not = fixator                              orthopaedics

The borderline patient is the one the argument is about and the one in whom your numbers decide: the patient with a femoral fracture and a chest injury, with bilateral contusions, with a pelvic ring injury and shock at the scene, with a lactate that fell from 6 to 3.5 mmol/L and then stopped.

The pain logic is cumulative rather than procedural. The mechanism is bone, several times over, plus the chest wall. Stabilisation is itself the most effective analgesic for a long bone fracture. What is left after it is the pain of rib fractures with every breath, of wounds reopened every two or three days, and of staged definitive operations that each reset the curve. The score of 5 describes a patient whose pain is severe for a week or more and whose regional options open one at a time as coagulation, the spine and the compartments are cleared.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The trauma bay: measuring the first hit

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Before any orthopaedic decision the team needs to know how big the injury was and whether the patient is still bleeding: primary survey, pelvic binder, splints and traction, whole-body CT if the patient is stable enough to reach it, and a blood gas.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Four things are yours from the first minute. The time of injury, because the tranexamic acid clock runs from it: 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h, given within 3 h. In CRASH-2 the benefit was largest within the first hour (death from bleeding RR 0.68), smaller at 1-3 h (RR 0.79), and reversed after 3 h (RR 1.44); in the Australasian PATCH trial prehospital dosing lowered 28-day mortality from 21.8% to 17.3% without changing functional survival at six months. The first lactate and base deficit, because every later decision is a comparison with them. Temperature, because a patient at 34 C on arrival will be at 33 C after CT unless someone acts. And a coagulation sample before the fluids go in: about a quarter of severely injured patients are coagulopathic on arrival, before any dilution, and those patients had four times the mortality.

  2. 2 Classify the patient

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs the patient named as stable, borderline, unstable or in extremis, because the class selects between a nail and a fixator. The classification rests on shock (pressure, lactate, base deficit, transfusion so far), coagulation, temperature and the soft tissue load (chest, abdomen, pelvis, head).

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Supply the trend, not the snapshot. A lactate of 3.5 mmol/L that was 6 an hour ago in a warm patient off vasopressors is a stable patient. The same figure, static for 2 h, in a patient on noradrenaline who has had six units is borderline at best. A normal blood pressure means little in a 25-year-old; the base deficit and the lactate are the honest measures of how much oxygen debt is outstanding. Say the class aloud and have the surgeon agree to it.

  3. 3 The conversation before the surgeon starts

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon is choosing an operation for a patient whose physiology may change during it, and needs to commit to a short version in advance.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Settle these before induction, in the room, with the general or trauma surgeon present if a cavity is involved. One: the class, and the numbers behind it. Two: the plan and the bail-out, stated as operations (“nail the femur if the lactate is under 4 after the laparotomy; otherwise a fixator and out”). Three: the stopping rules, as numbers both of you will act on: a lactate that rises on two samples, a temperature below 35 C, a pH below 7.25, a vasopressor dose that is climbing, visible non-surgical ooze, or a transfusion count passing an agreed figure. Four: the head. If there is a brain injury, whether intracranial pressure is being monitored and what mean pressure it needs; without a monitor in a patient with an abnormal scan, a long elective-style reconstruction is unsafe to judge. Five: the spine, cleared or not, and therefore how the patient may be positioned. Six: the compartments and who will watch them in a patient who cannot report. Seven: blood, meaning whether the massive transfusion pack is in the room rather than available. Eight: the bed afterwards.

  4. 4 Induction with resuscitation already running

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs the patient on the table quickly, still, and with the cervical spine protected.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Rapid sequence induction with manual in-line stabilisation and a videolaryngoscope; ketamine or a reduced dose of whatever you use best, with the vasopressor in the hand rather than in the drawer, because induction removes the sympathetic drive that was holding the pressure. Ventilation with positive pressure cuts venous return in an empty patient and converts a simple pneumothorax into a tension one; know where the chest drains are. Large-bore access above the diaphragm for abdominal and pelvic bleeding, an arterial line early, and warmed fluid from the first bag. Balanced transfusion from the start: the PROPPR trial of 680 patients found no mortality difference between 1:1:1 and 1:1:2 plasma, platelets and red cells, but fewer deaths from exsanguination in the first 24 h (9.2% against 14.6%) and more patients achieving haemostasis (86% against 78%). Give calcium chloride 10 mL of 10% IV with every few units, guided by the ionised calcium, because citrate arrives faster than a shocked liver clears it. Fibrinogen is replaced when it is low; empirical early cryoprecipitate for everyone did not change mortality in the 1,604-patient CRYOSTAT-2 trial. Permissive hypotension until bleeding is controlled is reasonable for the torso and wrong for the patient with a head or spinal cord injury.

  5. 5 Life before limb: haemorrhage control and the head

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The order of operations is fixed by what kills first. Cavity bleeding comes first: laparotomy or thoracotomy, and for the pelvis a binder, then preperitoneal packing or angioembolisation with an anterior fixator. An expanding intracranial haematoma is evacuated at the same time or next.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This phase belongs to the trauma and neurosurgical cards of other books; what matters here is its effect on the orthopaedic decision. The patient who needed a damage control laparotomy is by definition not a candidate for early total care tonight. Re-measure lactate, base deficit, temperature and coagulation at the end of the cavity surgery: those numbers, not the ones from the trauma bay, are the gate for what the orthopaedic surgeon may now do.

  6. 6 Limb-saving surgery

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Next come the injuries that cost the limb within hours: an arterial injury (a temporary shunt, then stabilisation, then the definitive repair), a compartment syndrome, a dislocation that is not reduced, and the contaminated open fracture.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    These are done whatever the class, in their shortest form. A shunt and a fixator take 45 min; a vein graft takes 3 h and belongs to a resuscitated patient. Fasciotomy and reperfusion add potassium and acid to a patient who already has both; see the compartment syndrome card. The debridement and the fixator are on the open fracture card.

  7. 7 The long bones: nail or fixator

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The femur is the fracture that matters most, because an unstabilised femur keeps bleeding, keeps embolising fat and keeps the patient flat. In a stable patient the surgeon nails it now (femoral shaft nailing); in an unstable one a fixator goes on in 30 min; in a borderline one the choice follows the post-resuscitation numbers. The tibia, the pelvis and the spine follow the same logic in that order; the upper limb, the foot and periarticular fractures are splinted and wait.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming is the measurable second hit: marrow fat and debris reach the lungs with every pass, the pulmonary artery pressure rises, and in a patient with contused lungs the oxygenation that was adequate at the start is not adequate at the end. Watch the end-tidal carbon dioxide and the airway pressures during reaming and nail insertion and tell the surgeon what you see; the mechanism and the differential for a collapse at this moment are in the fat embolism chapter. In the borderline patient this is the step the stopping rules were written for. Bilateral femoral fractures are a marker of a much larger injury and nearly always a damage control case on the first night.

  8. 8 Re-measuring during the operation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has agreed to stop if the patient deteriorates, and needs to be told in time to stop cleanly, between bones rather than in the middle of one.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Sample every 30-60 min and at every natural break: gas, lactate, ionised calcium, haemoglobin, and a viscoelastic test or coagulation screen where available. Announce the result against the agreed rule, not as a number in isolation. The natural breaks are the points at which the operation can end: after the fixator, after the first bone, before the second limb. A lactate rising across two samples, a temperature that will not come above 35 C, or diffuse ooze from wound edges and cannula sites means the next procedure on the list does not start. This is the part of the card that is the author’s practice rather than trial evidence; the trials set the thresholds for starting, not for stopping.

  9. 9 Intensive care and the days that follow

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon hands the patient to intensive care to be warmed, transfused, ventilated protectively and re-examined, with the conversion to definitive fixation planned for when the physiology allows.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Three things are easy to lose at handover. The compartments, in a sedated patient with a fixator on a tibia: pressure monitoring or a named examiner. Fat embolism syndrome, which declares itself at 12-72 h with hypoxia, confusion and petechiae in the patient with long bone fractures, and is more likely in the femur left in traction than in the one stabilised. And the timing of the return: the early appropriate care thresholds apply again at 24-36 h, and a patient who meets them goes back for definitive fixation then. The traditional teaching is that days 2-4, the peak of the inflammatory response, are the worst days for a long reconstruction and that the non-urgent definitive surgery sits better from about day 5; the resuscitation-based protocols have narrowed that advice to the patient who has not normalised, and for that patient it still holds.

  10. 10 Definitive reconstruction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Conversion of fixators to nails or plates (within about two weeks, before pin tracts colonise), fixation of the pelvis and acetabulum, then periarticular fractures once the soft tissues allow, then the upper limb and the face. Several teams often want the same anaesthetic.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    These are long elective-style operations in a patient who is anaemic, catabolic, on opioids, has a tracheostomy or a recently extubated airway and healing lungs. Limit the day: the author’s rule is that combined procedures are agreed by duration (about 6 h) and by blood loss, not by how many surgeons are waiting. This is the phase in which regional anaesthesia earns its place, because the coagulation is normal, the spine is cleared or fixed, and the compartment window has closed: catheters for the limb being reconstructed, and a chest wall technique if the ribs are still limiting ventilation.

Pain plan

No procedure-specific guideline covers a patient with five injuries. The plan follows the mechanism (several fractured bones and a chest wall, with staged surgery) and is constrained by four questions that are open on the first night and close over the first days: is the patient coagulopathic, are the compartments at risk, can the patient report (head injury, intubation), and is the spine cleared. Regional techniques are added as each question closes. This structure is the author’s.

First 24-48 h. Intravenous opioid by infusion or patient-controlled pump, paracetamol, and low-dose ketamine (0.1-0.2 mg/kg/h), which preserves pressure and airway reflexes and blunts the escalation of opioid requirement. A femoral or fascia iliaca block for a femoral fracture is reasonable from the emergency department, because the thigh is not the compartment risk the leg is and the block reduces the opioid given to a patient with a head or chest injury. No neuraxial technique, no deep block and no catheter while the coagulation is abnormal. NSAIDs wait for the kidneys and the bleeding to declare themselves, usually 48-72 h.

The chest. Three or more rib fractures, a flail segment, age over 65 or a falling vital capacity is where regional analgesia changes outcome rather than comfort, because the alternative is opioid, hypoventilation and pneumonia. A thoracic epidural or paravertebral catheter is the classical answer once coagulation is normal and the spine is cleared; an erector spinae or serratus anterior plane catheter is the answer when either condition is not met, which in polytrauma is often. Catheter decision: selective, and this is the commonest indication.

The limbs. For the staged reconstructions after day 5, the block and catheter follow the procedure card for that operation. Before that, the compartment rules of the tibial card apply to every fresh tibia and forearm, and a patient who cannot report pain has no warning to preserve but still needs an examinable limb or a pressure monitor.

Oral regimen shape once the gut works: regular paracetamol, an NSAID when cleared, a scheduled opioid with a written weaning plan because the course is weeks long, and an antineuropathic agent for nerve injury or amputation pain rather than by routine. Rebound is moderate and repeated: each staged operation ends with a block wearing off.

Escalation: pain out of proportion in a limb is a compartment syndrome until measured; a rising opioid requirement with fever and a wound is infection; new hypoxia and confusion on day 1-3 is fat embolism syndrome, not opioid toxicity, until the gas and the chest radiograph say otherwise.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The head injury. Hypotension and hypoxia during early fracture surgery are what worsen the brain, not the timing of the surgery itself. A patient with an abnormal head scan needs a mean arterial pressure chosen for cerebral perfusion, no permissive hypotension, and ideally a pressure monitor before a long operation; without one, the short version is the safe version.
  • The chest injury. The strongest predictor of pulmonary complications in the 1,443-patient model, and the injury that makes a reamed nail a risk. Bilateral contusions with a femoral fracture is the textbook borderline patient.
  • The pelvis. The bleeding is venous and from bone in most cases; a binder, a fixator or packing is damage control, and definitive fixation is a day 3-10 operation on the pelvic card.
  • The spine. An unstable thoracolumbar fracture is one of the four injuries the early appropriate care protocol wants fixed within 36 h of adequate resuscitation, because the patient cannot be sat up until it is; see spinal fracture fixation. A prone operation in a patient with a lung contusion is a decision for the gas, not the diary.
  • The elderly patient. Lower-energy mechanisms, anticoagulants, a blunted heart rate and less reserve; the lactate thresholds were derived in a younger population and the margin for a second hit is smaller.
  • Tranexamic acid after 3 h. Not started for the bleeding of the injury; a single dose at the induction of a later planned reconstruction is a different indication and reasonable.
  • Hypothermia and acidosis as surgical decisions. Every exposed limb, every litre of irrigation and every hour on the table lowers temperature. A temperature below 35 C is a reason to stop, not a nursing observation.
  • Too many surgeons. Simultaneous operating by two teams halves the time under anaesthesia and is worth arranging; sequential operating by four teams through a single night is early total care by accident.
  • The stable patient over-treated. A warm, resuscitated patient with an isolated femur and a wrist does not need a fixator and a second anaesthetic; damage control has complications of its own.

Key sources

The framework is well supported for the femur and thin elsewhere. Bone’s trial established that delay harms; EPOFF and Pape’s borderline trial established that early definitive surgery harms a subset; the early appropriate care series supply resuscitation thresholds from one centre’s prospective but non-randomised cohorts. Resuscitation is better evidenced: CRASH-2 with its timing analysis, PATCH in an Australasian system, PROPPR for ratios, and CRYOSTAT-2 as a caution against adding empirical components. The intra-operative stopping rules, the day-count for reconstruction and the staged opening of regional analgesia are the author’s practice built on those, and are labelled as such above.

    178 femoral fractures randomised to early or delayed stabilisation: in the multiply injured, delay brought more pulmonary complications (ARDS, fat embolism, pneumonia), longer intensive care and hospital stay; the trial that founded early total care
  2. Scalea TM, Boswell SA, Scott JD, et al. External fixation as a bridge to intramedullary nailing for patients with multiple injuries and with femur fractures: damage control orthopedics. J Trauma 2000;48:613-621
    43 patients with initial external fixation compared with 284 primary nailings: temporary external fixation was safe in multiply injured patients, the paper that named damage control orthopaedics
  3. Pape HC, Grimme K, Van Griensven M, et al. Impact of intramedullary instrumentation versus damage control for femoral fractures on immunoinflammatory parameters: prospective randomized analysis by the EPOFF Study Group. J Trauma 2003;55:7-13
    35 stable polytrauma patients randomised to primary nailing or external fixation: IL-6 rose over the 24 h after primary nailing and did not rise after external fixation or after the later conversion to a nail; the measured second hit

Spine › Spine

51 Lumbar microdiscectomy and decompression

Microdiscectomy, laminotomy, laminectomy and foraminotomy for radiculopathy and stenosis, open, tubular or endoscopic

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. Paraspinal muscle stripped off the lamina and held under a retractor for an hour, a small bone window, and a nerve root that has been retracted; the pre-operative leg pain is removed by the operation and most of what is left is back and wound pain that fades over a week

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
Surgeon infiltration of the wound edges and paraspinal muscles with long-acting local anaesthetic, with regular paracetamol and an NSAID; bilateral erector spinae plane blocks at the operative level are the regional option when opioid sparing matters
Catheter: no No catheter has a place: the pain is mild, short and incisional, and a single-shot technique or infiltration covers the only night that matters
Alternatives: Bilateral erector spinae plane block (ultrasound, at or one level above the surgical level) for multilevel decompression, the opioid-tolerant patient or the patient who cannot have opioids; Spinal anaesthesia with sedation, prone on a frame, as a whole-anaesthetic alternative in selected single-level cases; Surgeon-applied epidural steroid at closure, which some surgeons use for radicular pain and which is their decision
Position
Prone on a Wilson frame, bolsters or a Jackson-type table with the abdomen free, hips flexed for a microdiscectomy to open the interlaminar window, arms up on boards at less than 90 degrees of abduction, head in a foam support with the eyes free
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
50-150 mL for a single-level microdiscectomy; 200-500 mL for a multilevel laminectomy, almost all of it from epidural veins; transfusion is exceptional
Duration
45-90 min skin to skin for a microdiscectomy; 90-180 min for a two- or three-level decompression; revision through scar adds an hour
Length of stay
Day case or one night for microdiscectomy; one to three nights for multilevel laminectomy in an older patient. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); no implant, single dose
Tranexamic acid
Not needed for a single-level microdiscectomy; TXA 1 g IV before incision is reasonable for a multilevel laminectomy or a revision, where epidural venous bleeding is the whole blood loss
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis and early walking; chemoprophylaxis is withheld in most practice because an epidural haematoma is the complication that matters, and is reserved for the patient's own risk factors after the first day
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; vomiting and straining raise epidural venous pressure in a fresh wound
Tell the patient
The leg pain should be better when you wake up, or within a few days as the nerve settles; what you will feel is a sore back and wound for about a week, and walking is part of the treatment.
The trap
Leg pain that is worse rather than better, new weakness or numbness, or difficulty passing urine after this operation is an epidural haematoma or a retained fragment until the surgeon has looked, and it is a surgical emergency rather than an analgesia problem

What the surgeon is doing and why

A lumbar disc prolapse is nucleus pulposus that has pushed through a tear in the annulus and is sitting on a nerve root in the lateral recess or the foramen. The root is compressed, inflamed and ischaemic, and the patient’s pain is in the leg, in the territory of that root, not in the back. Most prolapses shrink on their own over weeks to months, which is why the operation is offered for pain that has not settled, for progressive weakness, or urgently for cauda equina compression. The surgeon’s aim is narrow: take the fragment off the root and leave everything else alone. The annulus is not repaired, the segment is not fused, and the back pain the patient also has, from the degenerate disc and the facets, is not treated and will still be there afterwards. That sentence is the pain logic of the card and the content of the pre-operative conversation.

Lumbar canal stenosis is the other indication. A degenerate bulging disc, hypertrophied ligamentum flavum and overgrown facet joints have narrowed the canal and the lateral recesses, usually at several levels in an older patient, and the symptom is neurogenic claudication rather than a single root. The operation is a decompression: a laminectomy or bilateral laminotomy with undercutting of the medial facets and removal of the flavum until the dura and the roots are free. It is a bigger bone-and-muscle operation on an older patient, and the version of this card that stays in hospital.

The microdiscectomy has a fixed sequence: localise the level on fluoroscopy; a 2-4 cm midline incision with the paraspinal muscles stripped subperiosteally off the lamina on one side and held with a self-retaining retractor (tubular systems dilate through the muscle instead, endoscopic systems go smaller still); a laminotomy of a few millimetres and excision of the ligamentum flavum, which is the only bone work and it is small; medial retraction of the dura and the traversing root to expose the prolapse; removal of the fragment through the annular defect; haemostasis and closure. Surgeons vary on how much disc they take: a fragmentectomy that removes the loose piece only gives a faster recovery and a higher recurrence; a subtotal discectomy that cleans out the disc space gives more back pain and a lower recurrence.

The far lateral prolapse, which compresses the exiting root outside the foramen, is reached through a paramedian muscle-splitting (Wiltse) approach; no laminotomy is needed, and the step that hurts is the dorsal root ganglion being handled.

The pain follows from what has been done to tissue. The dominant mechanism is muscle: multifidus has been stripped off bone and crushed under a retractor blade, and in a laminectomy across two or three levels that stripping is bilateral and long. Underneath it is a small bone window (the raw cancellous edge of a laminotomy, or the whole posterior arch gone in a laminectomy) and a nerve root that has been retracted for ten or twenty minutes, which produces the transient dysaesthesia and residual leg symptoms that settle over days as the root recovers. Tubular and endoscopic techniques remove most of the muscle mechanism, which is why they are day cases with less analgesia. The pre-operative pain generator, the compressed root, has been removed, so the patient’s dominant symptom is usually gone or much better in recovery. The residual is back and wound pain, worst on day 1, which fades over a week and responds to paracetamol and an NSAID. In the 179-procedure cohort the major spinal operations (fusion and scoliosis) sat at ranks 2, 3 and 6 of all surgery for worst pain on day 1; the discectomy is not among them, and the difference is that between a muscle window and an instrumented, grafted, re-tensioned segment, which has its own card (posterior lumbar fusion).

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative neurology, the scan and the plan for prone

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon operates on the level the MRI shows and the dermatome the patient describes, and will want them to match. A foot drop, a dense sensory loss or any sphincter symptom changes the urgency and the consent.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Document the neurology yourself before anything is given: ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension (L5), plantar flexion (S1), knee extension (L4), the dermatomal sensory loss, and whether the patient has perineal numbness or retention. A deficit that is new in recovery can only be called new if the baseline is written down. Cauda equina compression (bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, retention, loss of anal tone) is an emergency decompression on the next available list, with a catheter in and the retention volume recorded. Ask about the shoulders and neck before you plan the arm position. A patient with severe radicular pain cannot lie flat and needs analgesia before the induction, or an induction in the lateral position.

  2. 2 Induction, airway and the turn

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs the patient prone, flexed at the hips to open the interlaminar space, motionless, and with epidural venous pressure as low as it can be, because the field is a 2 cm window at the bottom of a muscle well and every vein that bleeds obscures it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A reinforced or well-secured tracheal tube is the author’s default for any prone case; a supraglottic airway is used by some for short microdiscectomies in slim patients and is a decision made with the surgeon and the frame in mind rather than a habit. Secure the tube and the eyes before the turn, disconnect for the log roll, and reconnect and check bilateral air entry and capnography before anyone touches the drapes. Then the checks, in order: eyes free of any pressure in the head support and visible through its mirror or cut-out; nose and chin clear; neck neutral; arms on boards with the shoulders below 90 degrees of abduction and the elbows flexed and padded, so the plexus is not stretched over the humeral head and the ulnar nerve is not on an edge; abdomen hanging free, so the inferior vena cava is not compressed and the epidural veins do not fill; breasts and genitals clear of the frame edges; knees padded; feet off the end of the table. Recheck the eyes and the arms after the surgeon has adjusted the flexion of the frame, because that is when the head moves. There is no neuromonitoring in a routine microdiscectomy, so the choice between volatile and total intravenous anaesthesia, and the use of relaxant, are matters of habit.

  3. 3 Localisation and the skin incision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A needle or marker is placed over the intended interlaminar space and a lateral fluoroscopic image confirms the level against the sacrum. Then a short midline incision over that space, or a 1 cm stab for a tube.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin finished before the knife. Lead aprons on for the localisation film. The surgeon may ask for a pause while the image is read; a wrong-level operation is the disaster the pause prevents. Heavy patients and transitional lumbosacral anatomy are the reasons the film takes longer than expected.

  4. 4 Muscle stripping and retraction, or tubular dilatation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The paraspinal muscles are taken off the spinous process and lamina with cautery and a periosteal elevator, one side only for a microdiscectomy, both sides for a laminectomy, and a self-retaining retractor holds them out of the way. Tubular systems pass serial dilators through the muscle to a tube fixed to the table, with the microscope looking down it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the mechanism of the post-operative back pain and the moment at which a light patient moves. Muscle stripping is the most stimulating step before the root is touched; deepen or give opioid in anticipation rather than in response. Bleeding is from muscle and is controlled with cautery; a bilateral multilevel exposure in an anticoagulated patient is where the laminectomy blood loss starts. The retractor crushes the muscle it holds, and the longer it stays the more the back hurts tomorrow; a surgeon who releases it periodically is doing the pain plan’s work.

  5. 5 Laminotomy, flavectomy and the bone window

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A high-speed burr or Kerrison punch takes the inferior edge of the upper lamina and the medial facet, and the ligamentum flavum is lifted off the dura and excised. In stenosis surgery this is the operation: a full laminectomy, or bilateral laminotomies from one side, until the dura pulsates and the roots are free in their recesses.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The bone work is brief and does not bleed much; the first epidural vein bleeds when the flavum comes off. The surgeon now wants a still field with low venous pressure, and the things that raise it are an abdomen on the frame, coughing or straining, high positive end-expiratory pressure, and a head-down tilt. A modest reverse Trendelenburg tilt and a tidal volume that does not drive the abdomen into the bolsters are the levers. Deliberate hypotension buys nothing and adds risk to a prone patient’s eyes and spinal cord.

  6. 6 Root retraction and discectomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The traversing root and the dural sac are retracted medially with a root retractor, which exposes the prolapse and the posterior longitudinal ligament, and the fragment is removed with pituitary rongeurs. Surgeons vary between removing the loose fragment only and clearing the disc space.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The root under retraction is the nerve mechanism. A lightly anaesthetised patient will move a leg when the root is pulled, which in a 2 cm window under a microscope is dangerous. The epidural veins around the root bleed into the field and the surgeon’s requests for lower pressure usually come now; the honest reply is that venous pressure, not arterial, fills the field and the position and ventilation have already been optimised. Pituitary rongeurs placed deep into the disc space can go through the anterior annulus into the retroperitoneum, where the aorta and the iliac vessels lie: sudden unexplained hypotension or tachycardia during the discectomy, with little blood in the wound, is an anterior vascular injury until proven otherwise. It is rare, often unrecognised until the patient collapses in recovery, and the treatment is a supine patient, a vascular surgeon and blood, not a vasopressor.

  7. 7 Dural tear and repair

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The dura is thin, adherent to a prolapse or to scar, and is torn in about 3% of primary microdiscectomies and a fifth of revisions. The surgeon repairs it with a fine suture if it can be reached, adds a sealant, and may ask for a Valsalva to test the repair.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A tear changes the rest of the day. The surgeon will want a still field for a fiddly repair under the microscope, often with a slight head-up tilt to lower the cerebrospinal fluid pressure at the tear; a sustained inflation to 30-40 cmH2O when asked, to show whether the repair leaks; and a smooth emergence with no coughing or bucking, because every strain tests the repair. The post-operative consequences are a positional headache from cerebrospinal fluid loss, which behaves like a post-dural-puncture headache and is treated as one, and a period of flat bed rest that surgeons vary on: the review evidence is that flat rest beyond 24 h after a watertight repair adds medical complications and length of stay without reducing reoperation, but the instruction is the surgeon’s. A tear in a day-case patient means an admission. Document it on the anaesthetic record for the next anaesthetist who considers a spinal or epidural.

  8. 8 Haemostasis, infiltration and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Epidural veins are controlled with bipolar diathermy and a haemostatic agent, the root is checked to be free, and the wound is closed in layers. Many surgeons infiltrate the muscle and skin with long-acting local anaesthetic; some place a steroid on the root, and a few leave a drain after a multilevel decompression.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The infiltration is most of the pain plan and the moment to confirm it has happened. Reverse any relaxant well before the skin closes. A drain after a microdiscectomy tells you the surgeon was worried about bleeding; a laminectomy in an anticoagulated patient is the typical case.

  9. 9 The turn back and emergence

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Nothing surgical remains, but the wound sits over an opened epidural space and a cauterised venous plexus; an epidural haematoma is the complication of the first hours.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Turn supine with the tube secured and the eyes still protected, then inspect the face, the eyes and the arms before the patient wakes: pressure marks on the forehead and cheeks are common and fade, a swollen eye or a complaint of visual change needs an ophthalmological assessment at once. Aim for an emergence without coughing or straining, which raises epidural venous pressure in a fresh field; a dural repair makes this a priority rather than a preference. Extubate when the patient obeys commands and will move both feet to order.

  10. 10 Recovery, the neurological check and the day-case decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the leg pain gone, the neurology at baseline or better, and the patient walking within hours; mobilisation is the treatment for the back pain and the prevention of thrombosis.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Test ankle dorsiflexion, plantar flexion and knee extension against your pre-operative note; a new deficit, or leg pain that is worse than before with a tense wound or increasing back pain, is a haematoma or a retained fragment and the surgeon is called before any opioid is given, because the opioid will mask the progression. Most patients say the leg pain is gone or changed in character; a residual ache or tingling in the same dermatome is the retracted root and settles over days. Retention is common on the first evening after a prone case with opioids and an inflamed root; a bladder scan at four hours prevents the 2 am catheter. Day-case discharge after a single-level microdiscectomy is established practice: the patient walks, passes urine, has pain controlled on oral analgesia, has someone at home and a written note on the red flags (worsening leg pain, new weakness, saddle numbness, inability to pass urine, a leaking wound or a positional headache). A multilevel laminectomy in an older patient stays one to three nights; a drain, an anticoagulant to restart, a dural tear and a bladder are what keep them in.

Pain plan

The mechanism is stripped and retracted muscle over a small bone window, with the pre-operative pain generator removed, so the plan is a short one: regular paracetamol and an NSAID (or a COX-2 inhibitor) from before the infiltration wears off, a surgeon-infiltrated wound, intravenous dexamethasone at induction for its antiemetic and modest analgesic effect, and oral opioid as rescue for day 0 and 1. The defensible default needs no regional block. Most microdiscectomy patients need a few doses of opioid on the evening of surgery and the following day and then nothing stronger than the oral regimen, and the day-case model depends on exactly that.

The erector spinae plane block is the regional technique with evidence in lumbar surgery, and the evidence is mixed in quality. A 2022 meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials in 980 patients, across discectomy, decompression and fusion, found that a bilateral block reduced opioid consumption at 24 h, lowered pain at rest through the first day and roughly halved nausea and vomiting, with heterogeneity wide enough that no milligram figure can be quoted. PROSPECT, writing for complex spine surgery rather than for discectomy, does not recommend the block for lack of procedure-specific evidence. The author’s reconciliation: a bilateral erector spinae plane block at the operative level, placed after induction and before the turn, is worth its ten minutes for a multilevel laminectomy, for a patient who must be opioid-sparing (obstructive sleep apnoea, the frail, the opioid-tolerant) and for the day-case patient whose surgeon does not infiltrate. For a single-level microdiscectomy with a surgeon who infiltrates, it adds little. The catheter question does not arise.

Ketamine, which PROSPECT recommends intra-operatively for complex spine surgery, has no place in a routine microdiscectomy and a sensible one in the opioid-tolerant patient, who is common in this population after months of sciatica on tapentadol or oxycodone and whose plan is in the opioid-tolerant chapter. Gabapentinoids are not recommended by PROSPECT because of their adverse effects; a patient already taking one for radicular pain continues it rather than starting it.

Rebound pain in the usual sense does not happen, because no dense block wears off. What does happen on the first night is back pain and muscle spasm when the infiltration recedes, worse on movement and relieved by walking, and the patient who has been told to expect it does not mistake it for failure. Escalation triggers: pain out of proportion with a tense wound, any new neurology, leg pain that is worse rather than better, or retention are surgical, and the surgeon is called first. A positional headache is a dural leak, declared or not. Pain unchanged from before surgery, in the same leg and distribution, is a root that has not yet recovered or a fragment that was missed: a conversation for the surgeon, not a reason for a stronger opioid.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Microdiscectomy versus laminectomy. The single-level microdiscectomy in a 40-year-old is a 60 minute day case with 100 mL of blood loss. The three-level laminectomy in a 78-year-old on apixaban is a different operation wearing the same name: two hours prone, bilateral stripping, 400 mL from epidural veins, a drain, a night or three in hospital, and a positioning risk that rises with every decade. Plan the second as a fusion without the instrumentation.
  • Tubular and endoscopic techniques. The muscle is dilated rather than stripped, the wound is 1-2 cm, the pain is less and the day case is routine. Endoscopic transforaminal discectomy is often done under local anaesthesia and sedation, with the patient able to report leg pain when the exiting root is touched, which is the surgeon’s neuromonitoring; oversedation removes that safeguard.
  • Spinal anaesthesia. A single-level discectomy or decompression under spinal with sedation, prone on a frame, is a well-described alternative; its limits are the duration of the block, the patient’s tolerance of the position awake, and the surgeon’s willingness to have a patient who can talk.
  • Revision discectomy. Scar between muscle, dura and root; a durotomy rate of nearly one in five; a longer case; more bleeding; more residual leg pain. Not a day case in most hands.
