The response is in the trap line: sit the patient up, call the surgeon, open the skin and platysma at the bedside to let the haematoma out, and only then secure the airway, with a videolaryngoscope and a surgical airway ready, because the larynx will be displaced and oedematous and the intubation may fail. Observation on a ward that can see the neck, with the clip remover at the bedside, is the standard for the first night. Check the arms and legs against the baseline. A hoarse voice is a recurrent laryngeal palsy and a swallow that is painful but safe is retraction; a swallow that is unsafe needs a speech pathologist before the first meal. Day-case discharge of a single-level ACDF or arthroplasty is practised in selected units with a long observation period and a patient who lives near the hospital; it rests on the timing data above, and the first night at home is the one the haematoma series is about.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone work through a muscle-free approach plus retraction oedema, so the plan is short and oral: regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started in recovery, a few doses of oral opioid on the evening of surgery and the first day, and intravenous dexamethasone at induction, which treats the nausea and does something for the throat. No regional block earns its place. PROSPECT’s complex spine guideline was not written for the anterior cervical spine, but its oral backbone (paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, opioid as rescue) transfers without difficulty. Many spine surgeons forbid NSAIDs after a fusion for fear of non-union, and some allow a short course or a COX-2 inhibitor; the question is settled before the day and the alternative, if the answer is no, is paracetamol, a short opioid course and the knowledge that the neck pain is over by day 3 whatever is given. An arthroplasty has no fusion to protect and the NSAID objection does not apply.

The catheter question does not arise. The infiltration of skin and platysma by the surgeon is the only local anaesthetic in the operation, and a superficial cervical plexus block on the side of the approach is an adjunct of small value that is reasonable for a multilevel case and unproven for any. Ketamine belongs to the opioid-tolerant patient, who is less common on this list than on the lumbar cards but exists.

The thing the patient complains about is not the pain. The sore throat, the dysphagia and the hoarse voice are retraction effects, worst on day 1 and 2, present in most patients in the first fortnight and in about one in eight at a year in the umbrella review’s pooled figures; they respond to time, soft food, sitting up and a speech pathologist for the ones who aspirate, and not to opioid. The patient who has been told this beforehand copes; the patient who has not reports the operation as a failure.

Escalation triggers are the neck and the cord before they are the pain. Neck swelling, a voice change, drooling or distress in the first 24 h is the haematoma. New arm or leg weakness is a cord or root injury, a screw or a graft in the wrong place, and the surgeon is called before any opioid is given. Pain that rises after day 2, with fever, a wound that leaks or a swallow that worsens, is an oesophageal injury or an infection until proven otherwise.

Pitfalls and variants

  • ACDF versus arthroplasty. Same approach, same retraction, same first week; the arthroplasty keeps the endplates and needs more fluoroscopy, has no non-union to protect from NSAIDs, and in the randomised trials at four years or more has fewer reoperations at the index level. The anaesthetic does not change.
  • One level versus three, and the corpectomy. Retraction time is the variable: a three-level fusion or a corpectomy means two or three hours of oesophageal retraction, more dysphagia, more bleeding from the epidural veins behind a removed body, a drain, and the highest haematoma and airway risk on the card. Many surgeons keep a multilevel or corpectomy patient intubated overnight or observe them in a high-dependency bed; the decision is made before the drapes come off, not at the first stridor.
  • The myelopathic cord. Neutral neck for intubation, modest extension on the table, a mean pressure kept at the patient’s baseline throughout because a compressed cord has no autoregulatory reserve, and neuromonitoring in many hands. A deficit after the operation in a myelopathic patient is the one that was coming anyway or the one the position caused, and the timing of the baseline examination is what tells them apart.
  • Horner’s syndrome. A retractor on the sympathetic chain; a ptosis and a small pupil in recovery, usually transient, and worth telling the patient about before they find it in a mirror.
  • Oesophageal perforation. Rare, from the retractor, the burr or a screw that backs out years later; presents as fever, neck pain, crepitus and a leaking wound, early or very late. Nothing to eat until the surgeon is happy.
  • Vertebral artery injury. A burr lateral to the uncovertebral joint; torrential bleeding in the depth of the wound, packing, an angiogram, and a stroke risk afterwards.
  • Rheumatoid disease and ankylosing spondylitis. Atlantoaxial instability in the first, a brittle and fixed neck in the second; both change the intubation, the extension and the shoulder tape, and the orthopaedic patient chapter carries the detail.
  • Obstructive sleep apnoea and obesity. A thick neck in which swelling is harder to see and an airway that is harder to secure in a hurry; a longer observation and a lower threshold for the high-dependency bed.
  • Day-case discharge. Reasonable for a single-level case in a slim, fit patient with a short retraction time and a surgeon who places a drain or does not; the haematoma timing data say the first night is the risk, and the discharge decision has to say how that night is covered.

Key sources

There is no procedure-specific pain guideline for the anterior cervical spine, and the card’s oral regimen is PROSPECT’s lumbar backbone transferred. The haematoma data come from a single retrospective series and the literature range it quotes, and the cuff manoeuvre rests on one negative randomised trial and one positive observational study cited in a trial protocol whose own results the author has not seen. The dysphagia figures come from an umbrella review that rates almost all of its component reviews as critically low confidence, and the card presents them as orders of magnitude. The arthroplasty-versus-fusion comparison is cited to establish that the early course is the same operation, not for its long-term claims, several of which did not survive the authors’ own sensitivity analysis.

  1. Song KJ, Choi BW, Lee DH, Lim DJ, Oh SY, Kim SS. Acute airway obstruction due to postoperative retropharyngeal hematoma after anterior cervical fusion: a retrospective analysis. J Orthop Surg Res 2017;12:19
    785 anterior cervical fusions: airway obstruction from haematoma in 1.15%, literature range 0.2-1.9%; two thirds presented within 24 h and the rest at a median of 72 h; four needed evacuation, one a cricothyrotomy after failed intubation for laryngeal oedema; no pre-operative risk factor identified
  2. Muthu S, Viswanathan VK, Subramanian V, et al. How common is dysphagia after anterior cervical spine surgery, what drives it, and can it be prevented? An umbrella review of systematic evidence. Global Spine J 2026
    32 systematic reviews: early dysphagia in up to 71%, persistent at 12 months in 12-14%; female sex, multilevel surgery, C3-4, anterior plating and rhBMP-2 raise the risk; zero-profile implants, cuff pressure control and perioperative steroids linked to less early dysphagia in low-confidence reviews; no preventive strategy recommendable as standard
  3. Arts MP, Rettig TCD, de Vries J, Wolfs JFC, in't Veld BA. Maintaining endotracheal tube cuff pressure at 20 mm Hg to prevent dysphagia after anterior cervical spine surgery; protocol of a double-blind randomised controlled trial. BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2013;14:280
    Protocol only; cites a recurrent laryngeal nerve injury rate of about 2% after ACDF irrespective of side, a randomised trial in which cuff pressure adjustment did not reduce vocal cord immobility, and an observational study in which it did; cuff pressure rises with retractor placement
  4. Zhang Y, Ju J, Wu J. Comparison of cervical disc arthroplasty versus anterior cervical discectomy and fusion for the treatment of single-segment cervical degenerative disc disease with a minimum of 4-year follow-up: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. J Orthop Surg Res 2025;20:758
    17 randomised trials, 3,303 patients: arthroplasty had fewer index-level reoperations (OR 0.39) and less adjacent segment degeneration (OR 0.56, not robust to sensitivity analysis); the approach, the discectomy and the early course are the same operation
  5. Waelkens P, Alsabbagh E, Sauter A, Joshi GP, Beloeil H, on behalf of the PROSPECT Working Group of ESRA. Pain management after complex spine surgery: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2021;38:985-994
    Written for instrumented thoracolumbar surgery, not the anterior cervical spine; cited for the oral backbone (paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, opioid as rescue) that transfers

Spine › Spine

55 Posterior cervical decompression and fusion

Cervical laminectomy, laminoplasty, posterior foraminotomy, and posterior instrumented fusion with lateral mass or pedicle screws, including occipitocervical and atlantoaxial fixation

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. The posterior neck muscles stripped off the spinous processes and laminae on both sides over three to six levels and held under retractors for hours, with laminae removed or hinged, lateral masses drilled and screwed, and facets decorticated; the nuchal muscles then have to hold the head up on day 1

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
No regional block; intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion, regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the surgeon permits it, surgeon infiltration of the wound edges, and oral opioid on days 0-3
Catheter: rarely A surgeon-placed epidural or wound catheter is PROSPECT's lumbar recommendation and has no established place in the cervical spine; the author's default is ketamine and the oral regimen, with a wound catheter only for the opioid-tolerant multilevel patient and only in units that have used one here before
Alternatives: Bilateral cervical erector spinae plane or interfascial plane blocks by the surgeon under direct vision before closure, an adjunct with case series behind it rather than trials; Intravenous lidocaine infusion for the opioid-tolerant where ketamine is contraindicated; Intrathecal morphine is not used here: the surgeon is not in the dura and a lumbar injection for a cervical wound is not the author's practice
Position
Prone with the head fixed in a three-pin skull clamp attached to the table, neck in neutral or slight flexion to open the interlaminar spaces, reverse Trendelenburg to lower venous pressure in the neck, arms tucked at the sides and the shoulders taped down for the lateral image; the face is free of all pressure and the eyes can be inspected
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
200-500 mL for a laminoplasty or a two- or three-level fusion; 500-1000 mL for a long construct, an occipitocervical fusion or a revision, from the muscle and the epidural venous plexus
Duration
120-180 min for a laminoplasty or a short fusion; 180-300 min for a long construct or occipitocervical fixation; a single-level foraminotomy 60-90 min
Length of stay
2-4 nights; a posterior foraminotomy one night or a selected day case. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), repeated at 4 h; a long case with implants in a wound that sits in a sweaty crease and has the highest infection rate of the elective spine
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision, repeated at 3 h or infused, for any fusion; not needed for a foraminotomy
VTE
Mechanical from induction; chemoprophylaxis from day 1 or 2 once the surgeon is content the epidural space is dry, because a haematoma under a cervical laminectomy is quadriplegia
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; vomiting after a cervical fusion loads the construct and the wound
Tell the patient
The back of the neck will be very sore and stiff for the first few days and the muscles will feel too weak to hold your head up; that improves day by day, and the hands and walking improve slowly over months if they improve at all.
The trap
The anaesthetic for this operation is decided by the cord, not the airway: in a myelopathic or unstable neck the intubation, the turn and the pinning are three separate opportunities to extend or move a spine that has no room, and each needs the neck held where the surgeon wants it and a check that the patient can still move their feet before the drapes go on

What the surgeon is doing and why

The posterior approach to the cervical spine is chosen when the compression is behind the cord or at many levels, when the canal is congenitally narrow, when the ligament behind the vertebral bodies has ossified over several segments (OPLL), or when the spine is unstable and needs screws. A laminectomy takes the laminae and the ligamentum flavum off the back of the canal so the cord can drift backwards away from whatever is in front of it; a laminoplasty hinges the laminae open on one side like a door and props them with small plates, which enlarges the canal while keeping a roof on it and some of the muscle attachments. A posterior foraminotomy drills a keyhole through the facet to free one root and is the small operation on this card. An instrumented fusion puts screws into the lateral masses (C3-C6), the pedicles (C7 and the upper thoracic spine) or C2, connects them with rods, decorticates the facets and lays graft, and is added to a laminectomy whenever enough bone has been removed to make the spine unstable, or when it was unstable already. At the top, atlantoaxial and occipitocervical fusions fix C1 to C2 or the skull to the upper cervical spine for rheumatoid instability, odontoid fractures and tumours.

The sequence of a laminectomy and fusion is the card’s spine. A midline incision from the occiput to the upper thoracic spine, bilateral subperiosteal stripping of the posterior neck muscles off the spinous processes, laminae and lateral masses, and self-retaining retractors that stay in for hours. Lateral mass screws placed by landmarks and fluoroscopy, each angled up and out away from the vertebral artery in front and the exiting root below. Laminectomy with a high-speed burr and punches, with the dura directly beneath. Decortication of the facets and the laminar remnants, rods contoured and locked, graft laid down, a drain and a layered closure. The laminoplasty replaces the screws and the laminectomy with a hinge and plates and leaves one side of the muscle more intact. The surgeon’s first and last concern is the cord: a myelopathic cord has no room and no reserve, and every step from the intubation onwards can injure it.

The pain logic. The dominant mechanism is muscle, and in the neck it is worse than in the lumbar spine for a reason the lumbar cards do not have: the stripped muscles are the ones that have to hold the head up when the patient sits on day 1. Bilateral stripping of the semispinalis, splenius and multifidus over four to six levels, hours under a retractor, and then the load of a head on a neck that cannot brace; the ache is deep, position-dependent, worse sitting than lying and relieved by a collar that many surgeons do not want worn. Under it is bone (lateral masses drilled, facets decorticated, laminae burred), nerve (a decompressed cord and roots, and the C5 root that may be tethered as the cord shifts back), and retension where a kyphotic neck has been pulled into lordosis across the construct. The nuchal muscle pain is the reason this card’s trajectory stays above the ACDF’s at every point and why it is a 4 while the anterior operation on the same disease is a 3. In the 179-procedure cohort the spinal fusions occupy three of the top six places for worst pain on day 1; the cervical fusion is not separated out, but its mechanism puts it among them. Compare the ACDF, where no muscle is touched and the complaint is the swallow.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The cord, the airway and the plan for three dangerous moments

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has a myelopathic, stenotic or unstable neck on the imaging and wants it to arrive on the table without having been extended, flexed or rotated beyond what the canal will tolerate; the baseline neurology is written down because any change afterwards will be attributed to the operation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Examine and record the neurology yourself: hand function, gait, reflexes, the dermatomal level, and whether the deltoid (C5) is already weak. Then decide the airway from the imaging rather than from the Mallampati score. A stable neck with mild myelopathy is intubated asleep with a videolaryngoscope and manual in-line stabilisation, which limits extension, and the randomised evidence in collared patients shows videolaryngoscopy beats flexible bronchoscopy on first-attempt success and time with the same complication rate. An unstable neck (atlantoaxial subluxation, a fracture, a rheumatoid pannus) or a cord with no room on the sagittal image is intubated awake with a flexible scope or a videolaryngoscope under topical anaesthesia and sedation, so the neurology can be checked after the tube is in and again after the turn. The evidence that awake intubation protects the cord is physiological and observational, and the decision is a judgement made with the surgeon, who may want the neck in a collar until the pins are on. Ask what traction or reduction the surgeon intends, because a halo or tongs change the airway plan entirely. Rheumatoid patients bring a stiff jaw, a cricoarytenoid joint and an atlantoaxial subluxation to the same airway.

  2. 2 Induction, lines, neuromonitoring and the baseline before the turn

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The monitoring team wants baseline somatosensory and motor evoked potentials with the patient supine and the neck in a neutral position, so that a change after the turn or the pinning can be attributed to position and reversed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A reinforced tube, secured on the side and padded where the face will rest, with a bite block if motor evoked potentials are planned. An arterial line for every fusion, because the cord’s perfusion pressure is the one variable you control and the mean pressure is kept at the patient’s baseline from now until the drapes come off; two cannulae; a urinary catheter. Propofol and remifentanil, no neuromuscular block after the intubating dose, and the baseline signals recorded before anyone moves the patient. In an awake intubation the neurology is checked with the tube in and the patient still awake; induction follows only when the feet still move.

  3. 3 The skull clamp and the turn

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The head is fixed in a three-pin clamp so the surgeon can set the neck’s position exactly and hold it motionless for hours, with the face free; the clamp is attached to the table after the patient is turned.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Pinning is a brief, intense stimulus that produces hypertension and tachycardia, which is bad for a cord with no reserve and a canal full of veins; a bolus of opioid or a deepening before the pins go in, and local anaesthetic at the pin sites, blunt it. The turn is a log roll onto the chest with the head held by the surgeon or the most experienced person in the room, the neck kept in the agreed position, and the tube held by you. Once prone, the surgeon sets flexion or neutral and the clamp is locked; then the checks: eyes free and visible, nose and chin clear, no pressure on the face at all, neck neutral or as agreed, shoulders below 90 degrees if the arms are up (they are usually tucked for a cervical case), elbows padded, abdomen free, breasts and genitals clear, knees padded. Reverse Trendelenburg lowers venous pressure in the neck and is the surgeon’s friend; the head above the heart raises the question of air embolism if a vein is opened, which is a real if rare event in the sitting position and a theoretical one here. The neuromonitoring team repeats the signals once the position is set: a loss after the turn is the position, and the position is changed before anything else.

  4. 4 Exposure: bilateral stripping of the nuchal muscles

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The posterior neck muscles are taken subperiosteally off the spinous processes, laminae and lateral masses from the midline outwards on both sides, over the levels to be decompressed and instrumented, and retractors hold them apart.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Antibiotic and tranexamic acid finished before the knife. This is the pain mechanism and the main bleeding; the muscle bleeds steadily and the surgeon controls it with cautery. The stimulus is sustained, and in an unrelaxed patient the response is a lighter plane rather than movement, which the monitoring team sees as a change in signals before you see it on the pressure. The ketamine infusion is running from now. The C2 spinous process carries the attachment of the semispinalis cervicis, which surgeons try to preserve or reattach because its loss is the axial neck pain that persists for months after a laminectomy that included C2.

  5. 5 Lateral mass or pedicle screw placement

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Screws go into the lateral masses from C3 to C6, into the pedicles at C7 and below, and into the pars or pedicle of C2 or the lateral masses of C1, each trajectory chosen to avoid the vertebral artery in front and the exiting root below and the facet above. Fluoroscopy or navigation confirms them.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The screw that goes wrong goes into the vertebral artery or the root, and the first is a sudden deep arterial bleed that the surgeon controls with the screw itself and packing, followed by an angiogram; the second is a radiculopathy in recovery. A C1-2 construct puts the vertebral artery at risk on both sides and the screws are placed with the artery’s course mapped on the pre-operative CT angiogram. Neuromonitoring is watched during the drilling, and a drop in signals in one arm is a root.

  6. 6 Laminectomy or laminoplasty: the decompression

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The laminae are thinned with a burr and lifted off the dura, or the laminae are cut through on one side and hinged on the other and propped open with plates; the ligamentum flavum is removed; the cord, which has been flattened for months, is seen to pulsate and drift backwards.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The burr is on the dura; this is the moment for a motionless patient and a steady mean pressure, with no rise to drive bleeding and no fall to starve a cord that has just been released. The epidural veins bleed as the flavum comes off and are controlled with haemostatic agents and venous pressure, not arterial. A durotomy here is in the cervical dura with the cord beneath; the repair is fiddly and the Valsalva is requested; a cerebrospinal fluid leak into the wound in the neck is a pseudomeningocele or a fistula. The backward drift of the cord is the mechanism of the C5 palsy: the C5 root, the shortest and most horizontal, is tethered as the cord moves and is stretched, which appears as a deltoid and biceps weakness between two days and six weeks after surgery, in about 5% after laminoplasty, 7% after decompression and fusion and 8% after laminectomy in the pooled data, with permanent weakness in about 1%. Nothing anaesthetic prevents it, and documenting the pre-operative deltoid is the one contribution.

  7. 7 Decortication, rod placement, graft and the correction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The facets and laminar remnants are decorticated to bleeding bone, rods are contoured into lordosis and locked to the screws, and in a kyphotic neck the construct is used to pull the spine into alignment; graft is laid along the construct.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Decortication is the last bone bleeding. A correction across the construct is a change in the shape of a canal with a cord in it; the monitoring team checks the signals after the rods are locked, and a loss here is a call for a higher mean pressure, a haemoglobin, warmth and a surgeon who loosens the rod. An occipitocervical construct fixes the skull to the neck in a position that the patient will live in: a head fixed in flexion cannot see the horizon, and a head fixed in extension cannot swallow, and the surgeon will spend time on the lateral image at this point for exactly that reason.

  8. 8 Closure, drain, the release from the pins and the turn back

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A drain, a layered closure of a thick muscular wound, and the skull clamp released after the dressings are on.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the second antiemetic. The head comes out of the pins with the neck supported, and the turn back is a log roll with the head held; a collar goes on if the surgeon wants one before the patient wakes. Inspect the face and the eyes, and the pin sites, which bleed. Extubation is the fourth dangerous moment: a patient who has been prone for four hours with the head below the heart during any part of it, or who has had a long upper cervical or occipitocervical case, has a swollen tongue, pharynx and larynx, and a tube that comes out of an oedematous airway cannot always go back in. The honest test is a cuff leak and a look at the tongue, and the honest decision for a long upper cervical case is often a night in intensive care with the tube in. Extubate a patient who is awake and moves both feet and both hands to order; one who does not is a surgical conversation before they leave the table.

  9. 9 Recovery and the first night: the cord, the airway and the neck

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the neurology confirmed and rechecked, the drain output watched, the wound dry, and the patient sitting up and walking on day 1 with or without a collar.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Neurology against the baseline in recovery and then at intervals overnight: a haematoma under a cervical laminectomy presents as rising neck pain and then arm and leg weakness over an hour or two, and the window for evacuation before a permanent cord injury is short. The deltoid is tested on both sides daily for the first week because the C5 palsy is a delayed presentation. The regular analgesia starts in recovery and the opioid is charted for the night and before the first sit-up, which is the moment the nuchal muscles are first loaded. A patient who cannot hold their head up on day 1 is not weak from the cord; they are sore from the muscle, and the distinction is the one the physiotherapist needs to hear.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bilateral stripping of the muscles that hold the head up, over a bone-and-nerve operation, so the plan is multimodal and systemic rather than regional, because there is no block that covers the posterior neck reliably without reaching the cord’s own territory. PROSPECT’s complex spine guideline was written for the thoracolumbar spine and its systemic recommendations transfer: paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the surgeon allows it after a fusion (a laminoplasty or a foraminotomy has no fusion to protect), an intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion (grade A, and the one intervention that most changes the first two days in the author’s judgement), opioids as rescue and no gabapentinoids. Its regional recommendation, a surgeon-placed epidural catheter, has no established place in the cervical spine and the author does not use one here. Intrathecal morphine is not part of the plan because the surgeon is not in the dura and a lumbar injection for a cervical wound is an extrapolation the author is not willing to make.

The defensible default is ketamine at induction and by infusion to closure, surgeon infiltration of the wound edges and the pin sites with long-acting local anaesthetic, dexamethasone at induction, the oral regimen from recovery, and an oral opioid charted for the first three days with a dose timed before the first sit-up and before physiotherapy. Bilateral cervical erector spinae or interfascial plane blocks placed by the surgeon under direct vision before closure are an adjunct with case series behind them and are a reasonable addition in a multilevel or opioid-tolerant patient; the evidence does not yet justify calling them standard. A wound catheter is for the opioid-tolerant multilevel patient in a unit that has used one here, and is otherwise not placed.

The opioid-tolerant patient is common on this list, particularly the rheumatoid patient with years of neck pain, and the plan is the one in the opioid-tolerant chapter: the baseline opioid continued, ketamine, and a pain service involved before the second night.

Escalation: rising neck pain with any new arm or leg weakness in the first 24 h is a haematoma and the surgeon is called before any analgesic change. Shoulder abduction weakness appearing between day 2 and week 6 is a C5 palsy and is explained, not treated. Pain that is worst on sitting and relieved by lying is the nuchal muscle and the expected course, and it is treated with the oral regimen, heat and a soft collar if the surgeon permits one. Pain still 6 or more at a week with a dry wound is the rheumatoid or chronic pain patient’s baseline reasserting itself.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Laminoplasty versus laminectomy and fusion. The laminoplasty keeps a roof and one side’s muscle and has no screws and no non-union to protect, so the NSAID objection falls away and the pain is a notch lower; the fusion is for the unstable or kyphotic neck and sits at the top of this card’s range.
  • The posterior foraminotomy. A single-level muscle-splitting or tubular keyhole through the facet for one root: 60-90 min, little blood, one night or a day case in a fit patient, and a pain score of 2. The airway and positioning rules still apply because the patient is still prone in pins.
  • The myelopathic cord and the mean pressure. A compressed cord has lost its autoregulatory reserve; the arterial line is there so the mean pressure can be held at the patient’s own baseline for the whole case, and a vasopressor infusion started early is better than boluses chasing a dip during the stripping.
  • Awake versus asleep intubation. The collar trials say videolaryngoscopy is the faster, more reliable tool in an immobilised neck; the unstable or room-less canal is still intubated awake in most hands so the cord can be examined with the tube in and after the turn, and the decision is made with the surgeon and the imaging.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis. Atlantoaxial and subaxial instability, a pannus behind the dens, cricoarytenoid stiffness, a small mouth, steroid cover, a tendency to bleed, and a long occipitocervical construct; the orthopaedic patient chapter carries the detail.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis. A fixed, brittle neck that fractures through the ankylosed segment with the slightest extension, including during a laryngoscopy; the neck is positioned exactly where it was and no further, and the pins are placed with that in mind.
  • The upper cervical and occipitocervical construct. Longer, bloodier, the vertebral artery at risk on both sides, a head position the patient must live with, airway oedema from the prone time and the proximity to the pharynx, and the strongest case on the card for leaving the tube in overnight.
  • Postoperative visual loss. A long prone case with blood loss and the head in pins carries the described risk profile, and the pins at least keep the face off the pillow; the head above the heart, a normal haemoglobin and no sustained hypotension are the modifiable parts (see spine essentials).
  • Infection. The posterior neck wound has the highest infection rate of the elective spine; the antibiotic is redosed at 4 h and many surgeons add vancomycin powder.
  • The patient who cannot lift their head on day 1. Muscle, not cord, in a patient whose neurology is otherwise unchanged; the physiotherapist needs to hear it from you.

Key sources

No procedure-specific pain guideline exists for the posterior cervical spine, and the card’s plan is PROSPECT’s lumbar backbone with the regional recommendations stripped out and the reasons given. The C5 palsy figures come from a 155-study meta-analysis and a single-centre laminoplasty series that discusses the mechanism; the airway evidence is a randomised comparison in collared volunteers and patients that says nothing about myelopathy, and the awake intubation advice is physiology and judgement, which the card says. The nuchal muscle mechanism and the day 1 head-holding problem are clinical observation rather than measured outcomes.

  1. Stockman IG, Soliman MA, Quiceno E, et al. Incidence of C5 palsy and recovery rate after cervical spine surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Neurosurgery 2025
    155 studies: C5 palsy after laminectomy 8%, posterior decompression and fusion 7.0%, laminoplasty 5.1% and ACDF 2.6%; permanent palsy 1.4%, 1.0%, 0.3% and 1.1% respectively
  2. Chen G, Wang Y, Wang Z, et al. Analysis of C5 palsy in cervical myelopathy with massive anterior compression following laminoplasty. J Orthop Surg Res 2018;13:26
    118 open-door laminoplasties: C5 palsy in 10.2%, 16.4% when the anterior occupying ratio exceeded 50%; onset 2 days to 6 weeks; recovery over 5-12 months and incomplete in some; mechanisms discussed are root tethering from posterior cord shift, reperfusion injury and thermal injury
  3. Guo N, Wen X, Wang X, et al. Comparison of outcomes between video laryngoscopy and flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy for endotracheal intubation in adults with cervical neck immobilization: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. PLoS One 2024;19:e0313280
    Six randomised trials, 694 patients in cervical collars: videolaryngoscopy had higher first-attempt success and faster intubation than flexible bronchoscopy with similar complications; the patients were immobilised to simulate difficulty, not studied for cervical pathology
  4. Waelkens P, Alsabbagh E, Sauter A, Joshi GP, Beloeil H, on behalf of the PROSPECT Working Group of ESRA. Pain management after complex spine surgery: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2021;38:985-994
    Written for instrumented thoracolumbar surgery: paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion (grade A), opioids as rescue, surgeon-placed epidural catheter (grade B); gabapentinoids not recommended; the cervical spine was not studied
  5. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJ, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery at ranks 2, 3 and 6 of 179 procedures for worst pain on day 1, median 7; the posterior cervical fusion sits with them on mechanism

Spine › Spine

56 Adult deformity and scoliosis correction

Long posterior instrumented fusion for adult spinal deformity and adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: pedicle screws over 10-16 levels, posterior column and three-column osteotomies, correction under motor and sensory evoked potential monitoring, with the paediatric points where they differ

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. Paraspinal muscle stripped subperiosteally from both sides of 10-16 vertebrae and held under retractors for 4-10 h; every facet joint in the fusion excised, 20-30 pedicle screws, the posterior elements decorticated to bleeding bone, and then the whole trunk re-tensioned into a new shape so that ribs, discs, hips and unfused segments all sit at a new length. Bone and retension run under the muscle injury, and the first movement loads all three

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Intrathecal morphine (single shot before incision or placed by the surgeon under direct vision) with an intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor once the surgeon and the kidneys permit; opioid patient-controlled analgesia from recovery
Catheter: selective One or two epidural catheters placed by the surgeon under direct vision at closure (PROSPECT grade B for complex spine surgery) for the opioid-tolerant adult and where the unit can run them; the author's default is intrathecal morphine and ketamine without a catheter, since a dilute epidural infusion still clouds the leg examination that everyone wants hourly on the first night
Alternatives: Surgeon-placed epidural catheter (single or double) with low-concentration local anaesthetic and opioid, started after a normal neurological examination; Intra-operative methadone 0.2 mg/kg IV at the start of surgery in place of intrathecal morphine; Bilateral erector spinae plane blocks or catheters at two levels as an adjunct, without procedure-specific evidence
Position
Prone on an open Jackson-type frame with the abdomen hanging free, hips extended to keep lordosis, arms abducted below 90 degrees, head in a foam or pin holder at or above heart level with the eyes free and checked on a schedule; halo-femoral traction on the table for severe rigid curves
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Sometimes. Cement-augmented fenestrated screws or prophylactic vertebroplasty at the top of the construct in osteoporotic adult deformity; small volumes under fluoroscopy, with venous leak and pulmonary cement embolism as the risk
Blood loss
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis 800-1,000 mL with tranexamic acid (about 80 mL per level fused); adult deformity 1.4-1.8 L, and 2-4 L or more with a three-column osteotomy, a revision or neuromuscular scoliosis; loss continues into the drains at several hundred millilitres over the first day
Duration
4-6 h for an adolescent idiopathic curve; 6-10 h for adult deformity to the pelvis; longer or staged over two days with three-column osteotomy or combined anterior and posterior surgery
Length of stay
4-6 nights for an adolescent; 7-10 nights for an adult, the first one or two in intensive care or a high dependency unit. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg; 30 mg/kg in children), repeated every 4 h and after each 1.5 L of blood loss; many surgeons add vancomycin powder to the wound; neuromuscular patients often have Gram-negative cover added
Tranexamic acid
High-dose tranexamic acid: the adolescent trial regimen was 50 mg/kg IV loading then 10 mg/kg/h; adult deformity regimens range from 10 mg/kg then 1 mg/kg/h to 30-50 mg/kg then 5-10 mg/kg/h, with less bleeding at the higher doses and a retrospective signal for atrial fibrillation and myocardial infarction in older adults
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis from induction; chemoprophylaxis delayed to day 1-3 at the surgeon's instruction because an epidural haematoma under a long laminectomy is paralysis; early mobilisation is the main measure in adolescents
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV (0.15 mg/kg in children) and ondansetron 4 mg IV, with a second-line agent charted because intrathecal morphine and a long propofol-remifentanil anaesthetic both add nausea
Tell the patient
This is one of the biggest operations in orthopaedics: you will wake with a straighter, stiffer back that is very sore for the first three days, you will be helped out of bed on the first day, and it takes six to twelve weeks before the pain is no longer part of every day.
The trap
The cord is at risk at the moment of correction, and three of the things that make the signals disappear are yours: a mean arterial pressure that was lowered for the exposure and never raised for the correction, a haemoglobin nobody has checked for an hour, and a volatile or relaxant that crept in. Raise the pressure before the rods go in, not after the alert

What the surgeon is doing and why

A deformed spine is a column that has lost its balance. In the adolescent with idiopathic scoliosis the vertebrae have grown into a rotated, laterally curved stack; the child is healthy, the curve is flexible, and surgery is offered when the Cobb angle passes about 45-50 degrees because curves of that size continue to progress in adult life. In the adult the problem is different and worse. Discs and facets have degenerated asymmetrically, the lumbar lordosis has flattened, and the head now sits in front of the pelvis instead of over it; the patient has to hold themselves upright with their hip extensors and paraspinals all day, and it is that, with the stenosis that accompanies it, which produces the pain and disability. The adult curve is stiff, the bone is often osteoporotic, and the patient is 55-75 years old with the comorbidities of that age.

The operation is the same in outline for both. The surgeon exposes the back of the spine over the whole length to be fused, puts a pedicle screw into most or all of the vertebrae on both sides, loosens the spine enough to move, moves it into the planned shape with two rods, and then makes the corrected segment fuse by decorticating the posterior elements and packing bone graft. Four things decide how big the operation is.

The length. An adolescent thoracic curve is fused over 8-12 levels and stops above the lower lumbar spine to preserve motion. Adult deformity is commonly fused from the upper thoracic spine to the pelvis, 14-16 levels with iliac or sacral-alar-iliac screws, because a long fusion that stops at L5 fails at the level below.

The release. A flexible curve needs only the facet joints excised. A stiffer one needs posterior column (Ponte or Smith-Petersen) osteotomies, in which the facets, the ligamentum flavum and the spinous process are removed at several levels so the back of the spine can close; each gives about 10 degrees and opens the epidural veins. A fixed deformity needs a three-column osteotomy: a pedicle subtraction osteotomy, a wedge taken through the vertebral body so the spine hinges on its anterior cortex for 30 degrees or more of lordosis, or a vertebral column resection, in which a whole vertebra is removed and the spine is held only by temporary rods with the cord draped across the gap. These are the steps with litres of blood loss and the highest cord risk.

The correction. Rods are contoured to the intended shape and the spine is brought to them by rotation, translation, compression and distraction. Every manoeuvre changes the length and the blood supply of the cord. Distraction on the concave side stretches it; closing an osteotomy can buckle the dura or trap a root; a screw can sit medial in the canal.

The bone. In the adult the screws must hold in osteoporotic vertebrae, so the surgeon adds cement, more fixation points, interbody cages at the bottom of the construct, and sometimes tethers or cement at the top to prevent the junction above from failing.

What this costs the patient is recorded plainly in the deformity literature. In a prospective multicentre series of 291 adults, 52% had a perioperative complication, 70% had one by two years, and 28% needed a revision. In the 272-patient Scoli-RISK-1 study of complex adult deformity, leg motor scores had fallen in 22% at discharge and were still down in 11% at six months. Adolescent idiopathic surgery is a different order of risk: in 1,121 consecutive operations, 0.8% woke with a deficit and all recovered.

The pain logic. The dominant mechanism is muscle: the erector spinae stripped off the laminae and transverse processes on both sides over a 30-45 cm wound, denervated and ischaemic under self-retaining retractors for hours. Beneath it is bone (dozens of facetectomies, screw tracks and a decorticated bed the length of the spine) and retension, because the trunk has been made a different shape and every rib, costovertebral joint, hip flexor and hamstring is at a new length. In the 179-procedure cohort, spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery took ranks 2, 3 and 6 for worst pain on day 1, with medians of 7. It earns a 5 on this book’s scale for the peak and for the tail: severe for three to four days, movement-evoked for weeks, and in the adult usually superimposed on years of opioid use.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Before the day: the plan, the lungs and the briefing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has planned the levels, the osteotomies and whether the operation is staged, and that plan sets the blood loss and the duration more than anything you do.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Ask for four facts: levels, number and type of osteotomies, whether the pelvis is included, and one stage or two. For an adult, treat the work-up as for major vascular surgery: cardiac function, haemoglobin optimised (iron given weeks ahead), anticoagulants planned, opioid dose known. For a neuromuscular or severe thoracic curve the vital capacity predicts whether the patient will come off the ventilator; a forced vital capacity under about 30-40% of predicted means planned postoperative ventilation or non-invasive support. Tell every patient about the wake-up test in plain words (they may be asked to move their feet during the operation, they will not be in pain and may not remember), because a briefed patient performs it and an unbriefed one thrashes.

  2. 2 Induction, lines and an anaesthetic the monitoring can read through

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The neurophysiologist needs motor evoked potentials (transcranial stimulation, recorded from leg and hand muscles) and somatosensory evoked potentials throughout, and free-run and triggered electromyography for the screws.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Total intravenous anaesthesia with propofol and remifentanil, a single intubating dose of relaxant and none afterwards, and no volatile or at most a low fixed fraction; ketamine supports the signals and is the analgesic the guideline grades A, so start 0.5 mg/kg IV then 0.1-0.25 mg/kg/h. Soft bite blocks between the molars on both sides, because transcranial stimulation contracts the masseters hard enough to lacerate the tongue or bite through a tube. Arterial line, two large cannulae and, for adult deformity, central access; urinary catheter; temperature probe. Cell salvage set up from the incision. Tranexamic acid loaded now. Intrathecal morphine, if it is to be yours rather than the surgeon’s, goes in before turning: the trial doses in children were 2 and 5 microg/kg, with no analgesic advantage to the higher one.

  3. 3 Turning prone and the baseline

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A free abdomen lowers the pressure in the epidural veins, which is the difference between a dry field and a wet one; hip extension preserves the lordosis the surgeon is about to fuse into place.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Turn with the lines disconnected to the minimum and reconnect in a fixed order. Check the abdomen is hanging free, the head is neutral and at or above the heart, the eyes and nose are clear of the support, the arms are below 90 degrees with the ulnar nerves padded, and the breasts and genitalia are free. Then have baseline potentials recorded before the incision, in the final position at the working blood pressure: a signal that was never present cannot be lost, and an arm signal that fades in the first hour is a brachial plexus under stretch that repositioning cures. Note the time for the eye checks, which continue every 30 min by direct look or a mirror.

  4. 4 Exposure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The paraspinal muscles are stripped subperiosteally from the spinous processes out to the tips of the transverse processes over the whole fusion length, because the screws start at the junction of the transverse process and the facet and the graft has to lie on bone.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A 40 cm wound bleeds from muscle and bone along its entire length, and the first 500 mL in an adult are lost here. This is the phase in which a lower mean arterial pressure helps: in the adolescent antifibrinolytic trial the benefit depended on a mean below 75 mmHg during exposure. That figure belongs to healthy teenagers before the cord is under threat; for an adult with vascular disease, stay near the patient’s own baseline throughout. Start counting: swabs, suction, salvage reservoir, and a blood gas with haemoglobin every hour from now on.

  5. 5 Facetectomies and pedicle screws

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Removing the facet joints mobilises each segment and provides fusion surface. Screws are placed through the pedicle into the vertebral body at each level by anatomical landmarks, fluoroscopy, navigation or a robot, 20-30 in a long construct, and checked by imaging and by stimulating the screw to see whether the current reaches a nerve root.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Triggered electromyography is meaningless under relaxant, which is the practical reason none is given. Screw placement is steady bleeding from cancellous bone at each hole, usually an hour or more. An intra-operative CT spin means everyone leaves the room and you watch from the door: before it, check depth, the infusion volumes and the tube. A sudden burst on free-run electromyography or a motor signal lost in one leg just after a screw is that screw until it is removed.

  6. 6 Osteotomies

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Posterior column osteotomies at the stiff levels let the back of the spine shorten. A pedicle subtraction osteotomy or vertebral column resection is done for fixed sagittal or sharp angular deformity: the canal is opened widely, the pedicles and a wedge of body are removed around the dura with temporary rods holding the spine, and the gap is closed by compressing the rods or extending the table.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the blood loss step. Epidural veins and cancellous body bleed fast and cannot be clamped: 1-2 L in 30-60 min is ordinary for a three-column osteotomy. Be ahead of it, with blood in the room and checked, the salvage running, a second gas sent as the surgeon starts on the pedicle, and fibrinogen and platelets requested on trend rather than at 2 L. Calcium with the red cells. It is also the highest-risk step for the cord: the pressure target moves up before closure of the osteotomy, not after, and the neurophysiologist runs motor potentials repeatedly as it closes.

  7. 7 Rods and the correction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The contoured rods are seated and the spine is rotated, translated, compressed and distracted to them. In an adolescent the vertebrae are derotated to bring down the rib hump; in an adult the main gain is lordosis.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The cord is being lengthened and its radicular supply stretched. Before the first rod is reduced, have the mean arterial pressure at 80-85 mmHg or the patient’s awake baseline, whichever is higher, the haemoglobin known and above about 80-90 g/L, the temperature and carbon dioxide normal, and the anaesthetic unchanged for the past 15 min so that any signal change is surgical. Tell the surgeon and the neurophysiologist that this is so. In the 1,121-patient series nine of the 38 alerts were caused by hypotension alone and reversed with pressure, and sensory potentials lagged the motor ones by about five minutes and missed four of seven motor deficits, which is why motor potentials are run after every corrective manoeuvre.

  8. 8 The alert

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A fall of 65% or more in motor amplitude, or 50% in sensory amplitude, is treated as a cord at risk until proven otherwise. The consensus checklist divides the response among surgeon, anaesthetist and neurophysiologist so that all of it happens at once.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Your list, done aloud. Raise the mean arterial pressure above 85-90 mmHg with a vasopressor now. Send a gas: haemoglobin, oxygenation, carbon dioxide, glucose. Check temperature. Confirm no bolus, no relaxant, no volatile change, and that the infusions are running into the patient. Check the limbs for a positional cause if the change is in one arm. The surgeon releases the last manoeuvre, removes or checks the last screw, and looks for compression; the neurophysiologist checks the leads and repeats. If the signals do not return, the correction is reduced or the rods removed, and a wake-up test is the arbiter: stop the propofol and remifentanil, keep the patient supported by two people at the head and legs, and when the patient obeys a command to squeeze a hand, ask for both feet to move. Expect 10-20 min after a long infusion. The dangers are a patient who coughs or rears on the frame, a tube lost prone, air entrained through open bone on a deep breath, and recall, which the pre-operative briefing turns from a complaint into a memory of being asked to wiggle toes.

  9. 9 Decortication, graft and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The posterior elements are burred to bleeding bone and covered with local bone, allograft or other graft material; this is what makes the fusion. The fascia is closed watertight in layers over drains.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Decortication reopens the whole field and adds several hundred millilitres after the difficult part appears to be over; closure of a 40 cm wound takes 45-60 min. Use the time: a coagulation screen or viscoelastic test, a final haemoglobin, warming, and the analgesic load (paracetamol, the ketamine continued, the first long-acting opioid). If the surgeon is placing the intrathecal morphine or epidural catheters, it happens now under direct vision. The eye check continues to the end.

  10. 10 Turning supine, the face and the first examination

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a neurological examination as soon as the patient can cooperate, because a deficit found in the first hour can be taken back to theatre.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    After 6-10 h prone with litres of fluid the face, tongue and airway are swollen. Extubate the adolescent with idiopathic scoliosis on the table or in recovery; for the adult after a long case with large-volume resuscitation, look at the face, do a cuff leak test, and keep the tube overnight if in doubt. Plan the emergence so that the patient moves both feet to command before leaving theatre and write the time. Ask about vision as soon as the patient is lucid: the multicentre case-control study tied ischaemic optic neuropathy to male sex, obesity, the Wilson frame, each extra hour of anaesthesia (OR 1.39) and each extra litre of blood loss (OR 1.34), with colloid protective, and every deformity operation has two of those by design.

  11. 11 The first three days

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The construct is stable from the moment the rods are locked, and the surgeon wants the patient standing on day 1 to protect the lungs, the gut and the veins.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The intrathecal morphine carries the first 18-24 h and then stops, and the day 1 afternoon peak is the rebound of this operation; the patient-controlled opioid, the ketamine infusion and the regular oral drugs have to be running before it. Drains lose another 500 mL or more in the first day and the haemoglobin falls again on day 2. Ileus is usual for two to three days after a long thoracolumbar fusion with opioids. Hyponatraemia from antidiuretic hormone excess is common in adolescents on day 1-2; avoid hypotonic maintenance fluid. In the thin teenager whose spine has been lengthened, bilious vomiting at the end of the first week is superior mesenteric artery syndrome, not opioid nausea.

Pain plan

The mechanism is 30-45 cm of stripped muscle over a decorticated, instrumented and re-shaped spine, so no single technique covers it and the plan is layered. PROSPECT’s complex spine guideline, which includes scoliosis surgery, recommends paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor (grade A), an intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion (grade A), opioid as rescue, and a surgeon-placed epidural catheter with dilute local anaesthetic at the end of surgery (grade B). It declines to recommend intrathecal opioid, plane blocks, lidocaine or dexmedetomidine for want of procedure-specific trials, and recommends against gabapentinoids and methadone on adverse effects.

The author’s plan departs from the guideline in one place and says so. Intrathecal morphine is used: the paediatric scoliosis trial found that 2 or 5 microg/kg cut 24 h patient-controlled morphine from 49 mg to 19 and 12 mg with better pain at rest and no more side effects, and the adult fusion data on the posterior lumbar fusion card point the same way. It needs respiratory monitoring for 24 h, which these patients have anyway. Ketamine runs from induction and continues at 0.1-0.2 mg/kg/h for 24-48 h in the opioid-tolerant adult. The NSAID is the contested drug: the guideline grades it A, many deformity surgeons withhold it for fear of non-union in a long fusion, and after a 2 L blood loss the kidneys decide the first 24 h anyway; a short course from day 1 in a patient with normal renal function is the defensible middle, with the surgeon’s agreement.

Catheter decision: selective. A surgeon-placed epidural (or two, for a long construct) works and has guideline support, but it competes with the hourly leg examination, it is displaced easily under a long wound, and many units cannot run it. It is the right choice for the adult on long-term opioids in whom the systemic plan is predicted to fail, started after a normal examination. Methadone 0.2 mg/kg IV at the start of surgery is the alternative with the best single trial (day 1 hydromorphone 4.6 against 9.9 mg, with lower pain to day 3) and is reasonable where intrathecal morphine is not used; the two are not combined.

Oral regimen shape: regular paracetamol; NSAID as agreed; a regular modified-release or scheduled opioid from day 1-2 with a weaning plan written before discharge, since deformity surgery is a common route into persistent opioid use; a muscle relaxant such as diazepam for spasm in adolescents is widespread practice without good trials; a laxative from day 0. The adult already on opioids continues the baseline dose from the morning of surgery, with everything else added on top.

Rebound is high and scheduled: the afternoon of day 1. Escalation: pain is expected, so the signals that matter are neurological rather than analgesic. New leg weakness, numbness or sphincter change with rising back pain in the first 48 h is an epidural haematoma until an MRI says otherwise. Chest pain and breathlessness may be a pneumothorax or haemothorax from a thoracic screw or thoracoplasty. Calf or shoulder-tip pain in a patient who cannot yet have anticoagulants has the usual meaning.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Healthy patients, flexible curves, 4-6 h, about 800-1,000 mL with tranexamic acid, transfusion uncommon with cell salvage, extubated at the end, and home within a week on enhanced recovery pathways. Weight-based dosing throughout. The family is part of the pre-operative conversation, including the wake-up test.
  • Neuromuscular scoliosis. Cerebral palsy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy, myelomeningocele: fusion to the pelvis, far more bleeding per level, poor respiratory reserve, a cardiomyopathy to look for in Duchenne, no suxamethonium and no volatile in the dystrophies, latex precautions in myelomeningocele, unreliable baseline potentials, seizures and baclofen pumps. Planned intensive care.
  • Three-column osteotomy and vertebral column resection. The largest blood loss and the highest neurological risk in elective orthopaedics; a second anaesthetist is reasonable, and staging over two days is a legitimate decision for you to raise.
  • Staged and combined surgery. Anterior or lateral interbody fusion first, posterior instrumentation the same day or days later (anterior and lateral lumbar fusion). The second stage meets a patient who is anaemic and has an ileus.
  • The request for hypotension. Sensible during exposure in a healthy adolescent, wrong during correction in anyone and wrong throughout in an adult with vascular disease; it is also on the causal path to optic neuropathy.
  • High-dose tranexamic acid in older adults. Less bleeding and fewer units in the retrospective adult comparison, with atrial fibrillation in 5% and myocardial infarction in 1.7% of the high-dose group against none; with renal impairment the drug accumulates and seizures are the described toxicity. A moderate regimen for the 70-year-old with coronary disease is the author’s judgement.
  • Signals absent from the start. Pre-existing myelopathy, neuromuscular disease, a small child or a volatile-based anaesthetic. Decide before the incision whether the case proceeds on sensory potentials alone, with a planned wake-up test after the correction.
  • Vision loss. Head neutral and at or above the heart, no pressure on the globes, avoid the Wilson frame, use some colloid, limit the hours by staging, and avoid prolonged hypotension and anaemia. Any visual complaint in recovery needs an ophthalmologist the same day.
  • Venous air embolism. A large area of open bone above the heart in a prone patient; a sudden fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide with hypotension during decortication or osteotomy is the presentation.
  • Massive transfusion coagulopathy. After one blood volume the bleeding is partly yours; viscoelastic testing and fibrinogen early. The principles are in the blood management chapter and the prone and monitoring detail in spine essentials.
  • Proximal junctional failure and revision. Adult patients come back; a revision through scar bleeds more and takes longer than the index operation.

Key sources

Blood conservation in adolescent surgery rests on two randomised trials; the adult high-dose data are retrospective and carry a cardiac signal that has not been tested prospectively. Neuromonitoring practice rests on a large multicentre case series and a consensus checklist, not on trials, and will stay that way. The visual loss evidence is one case-control study and an advisory. For analgesia, PROSPECT covers the operation but found too little procedure-specific evidence to back intrathecal morphine, which this card recommends on the strength of a 30-patient paediatric trial and the adult lumbar fusion literature; the methadone trial is single-centre and adult. The adult complication figures come from prospective multicentre registries and are the numbers to quote when a patient asks how big the operation is.

    50,523 patients: spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery occupied ranks 2, 3 and 6 of 179 procedures for worst pain on the first day, with median scores of 7

Spine › Spine

57 Thoracolumbar and cervical fracture fixation

Percutaneous and open pedicle screw fixation of thoracolumbar burst and flexion-distraction fractures, anterior and posterior cervical fixation, halo application, and the patient with an acute spinal cord injury

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. Open posterior fixation strips the paraspinal muscles from four to six vertebrae around a fractured, bleeding segment and adds a laminectomy when the canal is decompressed; the fracture pain itself (bone) falls once the segment is rigid. Percutaneous fixation swaps the stripping for eight to twelve stab incisions through muscle and behaves as a 3. Below a complete cord injury the wound is silent and the pain is at-level neuropathic and in the shoulders and neck

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
No neuraxial technique in an injured canal: general anaesthesia with opioid, low-dose ketamine infusion and paracetamol, surgeon's infiltration of the wound or of every percutaneous stab incision with long-acting local anaesthetic, and an NSAID once bleeding and renal function allow
Catheter: rarely No catheter by default: an epidural in a fractured canal with a possible dural tear and an evolving neurological examination is the wrong device; erector spinae plane catheters above and below the construct are an option for the opioid-tolerant patient or the patient with rib fractures as well, without procedure-specific evidence
Alternatives: Bilateral erector spinae plane blocks one level above the fixation, placed after positioning or by the surgeon under vision, as an adjunct; Superficial cervical plexus block for an anterior cervical approach; Opioid patient-controlled analgesia with ketamine infusion and no regional component
Position
Prone on an open radiolucent frame after a log roll or a table-to-table turn that keeps the spine in line, the head in a foam support, a three-point clamp or traction tongs for cervical work; supine with the head in neutral or gentle traction for anterior cervical fixation; sitting or supine for a halo
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Sometimes. Cement-augmented screws or a kyphoplasty of the fractured body in osteoporotic bone; small volumes under fluoroscopy, with venous and canal leak as the risk
Blood loss
Percutaneous thoracolumbar fixation 50-200 mL; open posterior fixation 400-1,000 mL and more with a laminectomy, a fracture-dislocation or an ankylosed spine, whose fractures bleed like long bones; anterior cervical fixation under 200 mL; posterior cervical 200-500 mL
Duration
Percutaneous fixation 60-120 min; open posterior thoracolumbar fixation with decompression 150-240 min; anterior cervical discectomy or corpectomy and plate 90-150 min; posterior cervical fixation 120-240 min; halo application 30-45 min
Length of stay
3-5 nights for an isolated fracture without neurological injury; weeks, starting in intensive care and ending in a spinal injuries unit, for a cord injury. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), repeated at 4 h
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision for open posterior fixation; within 3 h of injury on the trauma indication for the bleeding polytrauma patient
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis from admission; low molecular weight heparin as soon as surgical haemostasis allows, usually within 24-72 h, because acute cord injury carries one of the highest thrombosis risks in the hospital; the timing after decompression is the surgeon's and is written down
Antiemetic
Ondansetron 4 mg IV; dexamethasone 8 mg IV is reasonable where high-dose methylprednisolone is not being given
Tell the patient
The screws and rods hold the broken part of the spine still so it can heal and so you can sit and stand without a brace doing all the work; the back is sore for a few days where the muscles were moved, and most people are up with the physiotherapist the day after.
The trap
In a cord injury the blood pressure is the only neuroprotective treatment you have, and the patient cannot defend it: no sympathetic response to induction, to blood loss or to the turn prone, an unopposed vagus at laryngoscopy, and a guideline floor of 75-80 mmHg mean that starts at the first set of observations, not in intensive care

What the surgeon is doing and why

The spine does two jobs: it carries load and it protects the cord and roots. A fracture can fail either. The surgeon reads the scan for three things: whether the column can still bear load without deforming (a burst fracture has lost its anterior and middle support and will fold into kyphosis; a flexion-distraction injury has torn the posterior ligaments and will hinge open), whether bone or disc is sitting in the canal, and what the neurology is. The answers sort patients into those who can be braced, those who need the spine held, and those who need the canal emptied as well as the spine held.

Holding the spine means pedicle screws and rods. For the thoracolumbar junction, where most burst fractures occur, screws go into the vertebrae above and below the fracture (often two above and two below, sometimes into the fractured body as well) and the rods act as an internal splint. This can be done two ways. Percutaneous fixation places each screw through its own 2 cm stab incision over a guidewire under fluoroscopy or navigation and tunnels the rods beneath the fascia; distraction on the screws pulls the posterior longitudinal ligament taut and can push retropulsed bone forward out of the canal (ligamentotaxis). No muscle is stripped and nothing is fused, so the screws may be removed in a year. Open fixation is the midline subperiosteal exposure of the fusion card, chosen when the canal has to be decompressed directly by laminectomy, a dural tear repaired, a dislocation reduced under vision, or a fusion laid down. In the pooled comparative studies percutaneous fixation was 19 min shorter, bled less, infected less often (relative risk 0.36), hurt less and shortened the stay by 5.7 days, with the same screw accuracy and the same correction.

The cervical spine is fixed from the front, the back, or both. Anteriorly, through the approach on the ACDF card, a disc or a burst vertebral body is removed, the cord decompressed, and a graft or cage and plate inserted. Posteriorly, lateral mass or pedicle screws and rods span the injury, as on the posterior cervical card. A facet dislocation is reduced first, awake in traction or open. The halo, four pins into the outer table of the skull joined to a vest, is an external fixator for the neck: definitive for some upper cervical fractures, temporary for others.

Timing has moved earlier. For the cord, the prospective STASCIS cohort of 313 cervical injuries found a two-grade neurological improvement in 19.8% of those decompressed within 24 h against 8.8% later, and the pooled individual data of 1,548 patients showed recovery falling steeply with every hour of delay across the first 24-36 h. Neither is randomised. For the column, stabilising a thoracic fracture within 72 h shortened ventilation and intensive care stay in a systematic review, because a patient with an unstable spine is nursed flat and gets pneumonia; in the polytrauma patient the spine is one of the four fractures the early appropriate care protocol wants fixed as soon as resuscitation is complete (see the polytrauma card).

The cord injury is the other half of this card. Above T6 the injury cuts the sympathetic outflow to the heart and the splanchnic bed, leaving vasodilatation and an unopposed vagus: neurogenic shock, a warm, hypotensive, bradycardic patient. It is less common at presentation than taught (19% of isolated cervical cord injuries on arrival in a 490-patient registry, 7% of thoracic) and may develop over the following hours. The injured cord has lost autoregulation, so its perfusion follows the mean arterial pressure, and pressure support is the one intervention believed to limit secondary injury; the 2024 guideline suggests a floor of 75-80 mmHg and no active augmentation beyond 90-95 mmHg for three to seven days, on evidence it grades as very low.

The pain logic. For open fixation the mechanism is muscle, as for any posterior instrumented operation, with a shorter construct and a patient who was in severe fracture pain beforehand and is partly relieved by a rigid segment: a 4. Percutaneous fixation is a 3. The cord-injured patient is a special case: nothing is felt below a complete lesion, but pain at the level of injury, in the neck and shoulders, and neuropathic pain in the zone of partial preservation are common and early.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Reading the injury before meeting the patient

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has classified the fracture, graded the neurology on the ASIA scale, and chosen the approach and the urgency: within 24 h for a cord injury with compression, within 72 h for an unstable thoracic fracture, the next list for a neurologically intact burst fracture.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Establish the level and completeness of any cord injury, because it predicts everything: above C5 the diaphragm is threatened, above T1 the cardiac accelerator fibres are lost, above T6 the splanchnic bed. Record vital capacity and whether the patient can cough. Ask what else is injured: a thoracolumbar fracture from a fall keeps company with calcaneal fractures, a second spinal fracture at another level, and abdominal injuries; a flexion-distraction (seat belt) fracture carries a bowel or mesenteric injury until the scan says otherwise. Note the time of injury for the suxamethonium rule in step 3.

  2. 2 Hypotension: bleeding until proven otherwise, then the pressure target

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a perfused cord before, during and after the decompression, and needs to know the patient is not bleeding from somewhere else.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A hypotensive trauma patient with a cord injury is bleeding until the chest, abdomen, pelvis and long bones are cleared; the cord injury removes the tachycardia and the abdominal signs that would have told you. Only then is the hypotension neurogenic. Treat it with volume to normovolaemia and then a vasopressor with some chronotropy (noradrenaline is the usual choice; the guideline declines to name one), an arterial line placed before induction, and a mean pressure held within the guideline range of 75-80 mmHg as the floor and 90-95 mmHg as the point beyond which you do not push. In 100 monitored patients it was the time spent below 85 mmHg in the first two to three days, more than the average, that tracked with worse recovery. Bradycardia responds to atropine or glycopyrrolate; a patient with a high cervical injury who becomes asystolic on tracheal suction has an unopposed vagus, not a cardiac problem.

  3. 3 Airway and induction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the spine no worse after intubation than before it, and for a cervical injury often wants a neurological examination after positioning.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For the unstable cervical spine the 2024 multi-society guideline is the reference and its evidence is modest: videolaryngoscopy with manual in-line stabilisation, the front of the collar removed, and no single technique shown to be safer. The older review makes the uncomfortable point that secondary deterioration occurs in 2-10% of cervical injuries regardless of how the airway is managed. Awake intubation earns its place when the surgeon wants the patient to position themselves or be examined after the turn, in the fixed deformity of ankylosing spondylitis, or with a halo already on. Induction in a cord-injured patient needs the vasopressor running first: there is no sympathetic reserve to buffer propofol or positive pressure ventilation. Suxamethonium is safe in the first 48 h; the potassium-releasing state begins about 5-15 days after denervation and lasts for months, so the rule is none from 48-72 h after injury (day 3) for at least six to nine months, and some texts extend that for as long as the paralysis persists, and rocuronium with sugammadex makes the question academic. If motor potentials are to be monitored, one intubating dose and no more.

  4. 4 Monitoring the cord, or not

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With an intact or incomplete cord and a reduction or decompression planned, the surgeon may ask for motor and somatosensory evoked potentials. With a complete injury there is nothing below the level to monitor.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Monitoring means total intravenous anaesthesia, no relaxant after intubation and bite blocks, as on the deformity card. Obtain baselines before the turn where possible and again after it: a signal lost on turning is a malreduced spine and a reason to turn back. Temperature matters more than usual, because a patient with a high cord injury cannot vasoconstrict or shiver below the lesion and cools to the temperature of the theatre.

  5. 5 The turn

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The spine is unstable until the screws are in, and the turn prone is the largest movement it will undergo. Surgeons use a log roll with enough people, or a rotating table that sandwiches the patient between two frames. Lying an injured thoracolumbar spine prone on chest and pelvic supports often partly reduces a kyphotic burst fracture, which is intended.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    You hold the head and call the turn. Keep the collar on, or the tongs or head clamp attached, and the neck in line with the trunk. In a cord-injured patient the turn is a haemodynamic event: venous pooling with no reflex response, so give the vasopressor before rather than after, and transduce the arterial line through the turn. Check the abdomen is free, the eyes are clear and the arms are not forced above 90 degrees. The insensate skin below the lesion gets the same padding as any other, with more reason.

  6. 6 Percutaneous screws and rods

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Each pedicle is entered with a needle under two-plane fluoroscopy or navigation, a guidewire passed, the track tapped and a cannulated screw placed over the wire; rods are slid through the screw heads beneath the fascia and locked after distraction or lordosis is applied.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A quiet step with almost no blood loss. The demands are stillness (a cough with a guidewire through the anterior cortex of a vertebral body puts it in the aorta or the bowel), radiation, and a table that the C-arm can swing around. Distraction for ligamentotaxis is the manoeuvre at which signals are checked if monitored. Ask for every stab incision to be infiltrated down to the facet with long-acting local anaesthetic before the screws go in; with 8-12 punctures it is most of the analgesia.

  7. 7 Open fixation, decompression and the dura

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through a midline incision the muscles are stripped to the facets, screws placed by landmark, and, where bone in the canal is compressing neural tissue, a laminectomy is done and fragments tamped forward or removed. Lamina fractures in a burst injury may trap roots and tear the dura, which is repaired.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Blood loss is from muscle, cancellous bone, fracture haematoma and epidural veins at the laminectomy, typically 400-1,000 mL; tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision, a blood gas hourly, and cell salvage for a fracture-dislocation. Do not buy a dry field with the cord’s blood pressure: the floor from step 2 applies throughout, and this is the reverse of the deliberate hypotension that an elective spine exposure tolerates. A dural tear means cerebrospinal fluid loss, a patient kept flat for a day or two afterwards, and no neuraxial drug.

  8. 8 Cervical fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why
